title: ‘Newsnight’s kindest critic’: Bonnie Greer was always effortlessly in command | Bonnie Greer | The Guardian
description: Playwright was an unusual mix of originality and authority and in high demand as a cultural critic
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: Playwright was an unusual mix of originality and authority and in high demand as a cultural critic
Content: Bonnie Greer grew up in Chicago but lived in the UK for 40 years.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBonnie Greer grew up in Chicago but lived in the UK for 40 years.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianBonnie Greer‘Newsnight’s kindest critic’: Bonnie Greer was always effortlessly in commandPlaywright was an unusual mix of originality and authority and in high demand as a cultural criticZoe WilliamsWed 16 Sep 2026 14.54 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 17.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBonnie Greer, who has died at the age of 77, moved to the UK from New York in 1986. She grew up in Chicago with six younger siblings. Her father worked in a factory and her mother “kept house”, she said once – in a tone so elegantly ominous, she conjured an image of a woman holding up a full dwelling with seven children in it, with her bare hands. Greer was ambitious and, academically, a high flyer, but abandoned her law degree, facing baked-in sexism from professors. Yet, given she started writing plays aged nine, arguably she was only hastening a creative career that was inevitable.The Actors Studio was what drew her to the West Village in Manhattan in the late 70s, and she was there at the height of the Aids crisis, a brutal time of mass bereavements and poisonous prejudice. She lost about 35 of her friends, and later told the Sunday Times: “I owe those people my life. If I hadn’t met my gay friends I would be a suburban SUV-driving granny. They taught me the value of insurrection and fun. Nearly 30 years on, I’m still that 25-year-old, on top of some bar, in one of those vintage dresses, dancing with those guys.” But when she arrived, touring, at the Edinburgh festival, it felt like a release, from the “shadow of death”, and a New York theatre scene bereft of its heart. She stayed in the UK permanently.Greer was a remarkable talent as a playwright: witty, dry, serious, unflinching. She was playwright in residence at the Soho theatre in the late 80s and was writing plays for Radio 3 and 4 by the early 90s. Marilyn and Ella Backstage at the Mocambo, in 2005, is perhaps the most famous, and was later adapted as a stage musical. It dramatises the solidarity between the actor and the singer – Monroe persuaded the club to book Fitzgerald, with the promise that she (mid-1950s, the height of her fame) would sit in the front row every night. Fitzgerald later said she never had to play a small jazz club again thanks to this intervention, and it redrew the boundaries of what was acceptable, in racism, in jazz, in Hollywood. In Greer’s telling, there is no white saviour narrative, only a dynamic creative symbiosis between two geniuses.View image in fullscreenBonnie Greer in 1999.Photograph: Roger Tooth/The GuardianBonnie Greer was a joiner. She was on the board of everything, from the Women’s prize for fiction to the British Museum, she was president of the Brontë society – she got stuck in. An unusual mix of originality and authority, she was in high demand as a cultural critic, particularly in broadcasting. She was a regular contributor to Newsnight Review on BBC Two, as well as a critic for Time Out and a political commentator for newspapers, including this one.Out of all that came her appearance in 2009 on Question Time with Nick Griffin, then leader of the BNP. It was a frankly bizarre, though not uncharacteristic, bit of political curation from the BBC, since Griffin was a holocaust denier and racist, tried three times and once convicted (in the late 90s) for inciting racial, Islamophobic or antisemitic hatred. Many wondered why the BBC felt such a duty to platform so toxic a figure, and Sayeeda Warsi, also on the panel, asked Greer before whether she was OK to sit next to him (Greer replied: “I’m from Chicago, I’m not scared of this guy”). She said later to the Evening Standard that it was “probably the weirdest and most creepy experience of my life”, but onscreen she was unruffled and effortlessly in command, and she later turned that weird creepiness into an opera for the Royal Opera House, on whose board she also served, along with the London Film School’s.She was very generous on a panel, receptive and softly spoken while absolutely trenchant, and vividly engaged; she was never without a view. She wrote two novels, Hanging by Her Teeth in 1994 and Entropy in 2009, but her more natural metier was in the discursive, collaborative arts and broader culture. She was once called “Newsnight’s kindest critic”, and said of her stage writing: “I was taught that theatre is supposed to slow the world down so it can be looked at, and the person who looks is not supposed to be the same when they walk out. Otherwise, there’s no fucking point. Art is not a leisure activity. It’s about engagement.”Explore more on these topicsBonnie GreerfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ed Sheeran wants to stay out of politics. By quitting his tour, his support acts have exposed the hollowness of neutrality | Music | The Guardian
description: By standing behind support act Macklemore, who was removed from the tour for his vocal support of Palestine, these artists are demonstrating the self-sacrifice necessary to stand against those crushing free speech
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: By standing behind support act Macklemore, who was removed from the tour for his vocal support of Palestine, these artists are demonstrating the self-sacrifice necessary to stand against those crushing free speech
Content: ‘Creating inconvenience is precisely what it takes to show backbone’ … Ed Sheeran (left) and Macklemore.Photograph: Kevin Winter/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Creating inconvenience is precisely what it takes to show backbone’ … Ed Sheeran (left) and Macklemore.Photograph: Kevin Winter/Getty ImagesOpinionMusicEd Sheeran wants to stay out of politics. By quitting his tour, his support acts have exposed the hollowness of neutralityLaura SnapesBy standing behind support act Macklemore, who was removed from the tour for his vocal support of Palestine, these artists are demonstrating the self-sacrifice necessary to stand against those crushing free speechWed 16 Sep 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 13.26 EDTShareIn a statement aboutMacklemorebeing dropped from his US stadium tour for making pro-Palestinian comments, Ed Sheeran defended his own publicly apolitical stance: “If we only ever focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change.”Every other musician involved with the tour – support acts Finneas (Billie Eilish’s brother), Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish songwriter Aaron Rowe, plus Sheeran’s Irish backing band, Beoga – has made their approach to advocating for change clear, pulling out of the remaining dates to protest against the censorship of Macklemore and to express support for the Palestinian people.In a statement released yesterday, Sheeran stressed that it wasn’t his decision to remove Macklemore, who called for a free Palestine on stage at the MetLife stadium in New Jersey last week. “I am not complicit,” Sheeran wrote. Macklemore (who in 2014 had to apologise after being accused of perpetuating antisemitic stereotypeswith an onstage costume) wrote that his removal from the tour was organised by New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium outside Boston, where Sheeran’s Loop tour is due to play in late September.Kraft confirmed he barred Macklemore from opening for Sheeran at the Gillette Stadium, but did not respond to claims he organised the boycott by the other venues. (In a statement he said his decision was “not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf” but that such advocacy “should not obscure the responsibility of Hamas”.)Sheeran explained that he doesn’t use his platform for politics in order to be “a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open”. Though this isn’t accurate: he performed at the Concert for Ukraine in 2022, signed an open letter to Theresa May about Brexit, endorsed Jeremy Corbyn and supported the equality act in the US.Either way, the consequences of his apolitical stance have proven beyond doubt that there is no such thing as a neutral position, especially when you’re operating in a political culture that rarely obstructs corporate overreach. Kraft is friends with Trump and is a major donor to Israel: Netanyahu said at a 2019 awards ceremony honouring Kraft that “Israel does not have a more loyal friend”.10:05Ed Sheeran support acts quit after Macklemore ‘Free Palestine’ row - The LatestThe decisive actions of every other musician on the tour have made a mockery of Sheeran claiming to be powerless in this situation. In his statement, Sheeran wrote that he would never “let down the fans who had made plans” by cancelling shows, “nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living”. What might initially appear as a sign of solidarity – not inconveniencing fans, not leaving other artists and crew out of pocket – has been upended by a group of artists who understand that losing financial and professional opportunities and creating inconvenience is precisely what it takes to show backbone and stand against genocide and billionaires crushing free speech.Macklemore’s speech in New Jersey introduced his 2024 song Hind’s Hall, which castigates censorship of protest against Israel’s genocide in Palestine, particularly the student encampment at Columbia University in New York,and is named after Hind Rajab, a five-year-old Palestinian girl killed by Israeli forces. “What you willin’ to risk?” he asked in the song. “What you willin’ to give?” Many musicians and actors who have spoken out against Israel’s actions in Gaza have talked about losing work as a result: Susan Sarandon said last week at the Venice film festival that she has had acting gigs taken away; Irish pop star CMAT said alucrative beauty contract was withdrawn; Swedish star Zara Larsson said she was dropped from brand deals and awards shows.That hasn’t stopped them and other figures from continuing to speak out, putting moral imperative above personal gain, and recognising that any such “loss” bears no relation to what is happening to human life and habitat inGaza, where Israel’s military offensive is estimated to have led to a death toll of 70,000. Dublin songwriter Aaron Rowe, by far the smallest support act on Sheeran’s tour and thus the one with the most to lose, thanked him for the life-changing opportunity. “But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation,” his statement continued. “I need to be true to myself and my ancestors who resisted colonisation, and fought for a freedom that I enjoy today in Ireland.”Sheeran and countless others take the line that pop culture should be somewhere fans can go to escape politics. “I do understand that for a lot of people, they just want to leave politics aside for a bit and be able to enjoy the music,” culture secretary Lisa Nandy said of the Sheeran situation on LBC this morning. But the fact that most right-wing politicians also take that view indicates the fact that they see pop cultural figures, with their largely left-leaning views and huge reach among young people, as a genuine threat best silenced.As Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said yesterday, this isn’t just about the musicians on Sheeran’s tour, but “how just a handful of stadium owners can prevent [discussion of] an entire massive issue, in this case, the genocide in Gaza”. Prominent figures who go along with that view and deny the power of their voice allow these billion-dollar corporations to rob us of our rights step by step until one day there is nothing left. “We need to be very clear about how dangerous a precedent this is,” said Ocasio-Cortez.At worst, Sheeran – who has always been open about his commercially minded approach to pop – looks like a corporate shill; at best, wilfully naive. Sheeran loves to dabble in the music of other cultures to present a toothless pan-global vision of togetherness lifted from the latter-day Coldplay playbook. But you can’t play with the aesthetics of global music without also being willing to engage in the lived reality of those cultures.“Those who have been to one of my shows will know that they are about unity, joy, escapism, love and a place for everyone to feel welcome,” Sheeran wrote in his statement. Just as long as they shut up and sing: Sheeran’s inaction and humiliation at the hands of his principled supporting musicians have irrevocably compromised a position that’s no longer fit for purpose, if it ever was.Explore more on these topicsMusicOpinionEd SheeranMacklemorePop and rockGazaIsrael-Gaza warMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Africa is bigger than we’ve been led to believe – what next? | United Nations | The Guardian
description: A new map of the world rescales the size of Africa and calls into question our perception of land, power and influence
Author: Nesrine Malik
Headline: A new map of the world rescales the size of Africa and calls into question our perception of land, power and influence
Content: The UN passed a resolution, brought by Togo, to replace the current map with one that shows the true scale of territories.Illustration: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Alamy/GettyView image in fullscreenThe UN passed a resolution, brought by Togo, to replace the current map with one that shows the true scale of territories.Illustration: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Alamy/GettyThe Long WaveUnited NationsAfrica is bigger than we’ve been led to believe – what next?A new map of the world rescales the size of Africa and calls into question our perception of land, power and influenceNesrine MalikWed 16 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis month, the UN passed a resolution, brought to the assembly by Togo, to phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe and replace it with another that shows the real scale of territories. That’s right – when it comes to size, the map of the world we have all grown up with is not accurate. The main loser of land on the Mercator map is Africa, and the new “Equal Earth” map reflects its true proportions. I spoke to our west Africa correspondent Eromo Egbejule abouthis extensive reportingon the map changes, and why people feel so strongly about it.Seeing the new map transposed over the old might make you feel oddly disoriented. Logically, there is absolutely no immediate tangible impact on one’s life that comes out of knowing that the entire top part of the northern hemisphere is so much smaller than you were led to believe. And yet, there is still something agitating about it, like you’ve been the subject of a lifelong trick, or at least a breach of trust.The vast geographical inaccuracies of the old map include the shortening of Africa, and the relative expansion of North America and Eurasia. The new projection shows Africa as taking up almostdouble the ratioof total land area shown on the map. It all feeds into a sense that there is something domineering about it, portraying some countries as not just political and economic powers, but geographical ones as well, and therefore natural hegemons. It is an emotional response more than anything, but a testament to how much our perceptions of the physical world are linked to our estimations of stature.View image in fullscreenThe geographical inaccuracies of the old world map include the shortening of Africa, and the relative expansion of North America and Eurasia.Illustration: FlexagoonNo, the world map has not gone ‘woke’The Guardian’s westAfricacorrespondent Eromo Egbejule is struck by how, despite its disproportionality, there was still opposition to retiring the 16th-century map. The US was the only country that vetoed the UN resolution, and six other nations abstained. The US dismissed the effort as “superfluous”, but Eromo sees this as a euphemism for “ideological” or “woke”. “I don’t see why it feels so strongly,” he told me. “This is a scientific discussion. It’s not an imposition.”There is nothing binding about the resolution, and yet, there is something revealing about the world’s superpower opposing it. It suggests that the US would like to preserve that connection between size and status, even when appearances are deceiving. US president Donald Trump’s interest in Greenland wasreportedly influencedby its inflated size on the old map, an acquisition that would swell US territory in the political imagination. Greenland is “massive” said Trump – but in actuality, it’s afractionof its size as shown in the Mercator projection. The old map depicts it as roughly the same size as Africa, despite it being 14 times smaller. Could huge geopolitical tensions, and confrontation with Europe, could have possibly been avoided by simply showing Trump an accurate map?Do maps really matter?View image in fullscreen‘It’s grains of rice that fill up a pot’ … one small change could pave the way for a ‘multipolar world order’.Photograph: Klaus Vedfelt/Getty Images“It does matter. Make no mistake,” said Eromo. In his view, the significance is in the momentum such a resolution triggers. “There’s two proverbs we have in pidgin,” Eromo said: “every dance begins with a clap” and “it’s grains of rice that fill up a pot”. In other words, this might feel like a small change, but the boost of one successful campaign could pave the way to what Eromo describes as a “multipolar world order”. He points out that this resolution comes on the heels of a separate landmark one – the UN vote torecognise the transatlantic slave trade as a crimeand call for reparations, an effortalso led by an African country.There is a growing traction around a particular kind of advocacy: one that uses the procedures of high-profile international institutions to challenge dominant western understandings of history and reality. These interventions in how we make sense of the world may be symbolic – but they are meaningful, and they are gaining ground.Moving towards a shared reality?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenCountries were stolen from in terms of landmass on a map, and also the subordinating cultural and political associations that followed.Composite: Equal-earth.com/ Getty ImagesIt is staggering that the Mercator map has pretty much remained the unchanged standard for over four centuries. In questioning what was once assumed to be fact, the resolution has not only addressed issues of accuracy. It has also, somehow, punctured the vast and abstract unrealities established throughout history by the west. The theft of resources and people is only one part of what was stolen from many regions of the world during colonisation. Countries were then stolen from, again, in terms of landmass on maps, and also the subordinating cultural and political associations that followed. There is something intangible and deeply political about the map’s significance – which is symbolic and threatening.Eromo said that this sort of change makes people nervous because it ties in to all the ways in which legacies of literally carving out the continent and enslaving its populations still resonate. Hanging over the resolution are questions of precedent, of the floodgates being opened – the sort of building pressure that has resulted incalls to decolonise curriculums, for example. If the map that hangs in classrooms all around the world is changed, people may ask: “What else are my children going to be taught now?” Eromo said that there is something diminishing about learning that behemoths such as the US, China and Russia “can all fit into Africa with some space to spare.”There are broader anxieties at stake – about what constitutes our shared reality, one that is increasingly fractured by social media and AI. These make tussles about maps a matter of holding on to the little that we can establish as concrete and true, in the face of vast political and digital forces that are warping our perceptions of the world. Eromo cites a statement that stood out for him, issued byAfrica No Filter, an advocacy group that has been a part of the map justice campaign: “If we got something as basic as Africa’s size wrong for this long, what else about Africa have we simply accepted without questioning?”Tap inIf you could bring a resolution to the UN related to the Black diaspora, what would it be? Send us your thoughts by emailing us atthelongwave@theguardian.comor replying to this email and we may include your response in a future issue.To receive the complete version of The Long Wave in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsUnited NationsThe Long WaveTogoGeographyAfricaMapsnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: I have faced abuse, assaults and death threats because I’m an MP. It’s making politics a no-go zone | Dawn Butler | The Guardian
description: A new report highlights the dangers experienced by those who seek to serve the public. People are being deterred and your democracy is suffering, says Labour MP Dawn Butler
Author: Dawn Butler
Headline: A new report highlights the dangers experienced by those who seek to serve the public. People are being deterred and your democracy is suffering, says Labour MP Dawn Butler
Content: ‘We know Diane Abbott has received extraordinary levels of abuse, while I often feel specifically targeted because I am a Black woman.’Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAView image in fullscreen‘We know Diane Abbott has received extraordinary levels of abuse, while I often feel specifically targeted because I am a Black woman.’Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAOpinionOnline abuseI have faced abuse, assaults and death threats because I’m an MP. It’s making politics a no-go zoneDawn ButlerA new report highlights the dangers experienced by those who seek to serve the public. People are being deterred and your democracy is sufferingWed 16 Sep 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 12.28 EDTShareThere is a rising tide of abuse in our politics and I feel it every day. This week, the Electoral Commissionwarnedthat harassment and intimidation arechanging how candidates campaign, what they feel able to do and whether they stand again. This is a threat to our democracy – and we cannot ignore it.The figures are stark. Commission research into the May 2026 local and mayoral elections in England found that 55% of candidates said harassment or intimidation was a problem, up from 47% in 2025. Women, ethnic minority candidates and those with disabilities were most likely to encounter abuse. The experience was so unpleasant that a third considered not standing again.But none of it is a surprise. I have seen first-hand how abuse, threats and violence have increased in our politics over the years. Since I was elected as an MP in 2015, numerous people have been convicted for attacks, threats and abuse against me. Someone was sent to prison for saying a “bullet” to the back of my head was justified, while another person was convicted for telling me “come the revolution, you will be one of the first”.Followers of my social media know how bad it can be. I have a regular “block of the month” feature to raise awareness of the disgusting racist abuse sent to me every day – the N-word, “monkey” and “ape” are common insults. The deluge of abuse has a detrimental impact on my mental health, and on those around me.The abuse is not limited to the internet. I have been physically assaulted going home from work, and followed and verbally abused right outside parliament. During the last general election and again in this year’s local elections, I was accosted on the street by a local man who made me fear for my safety. I was told I wasn’t welcome in the area, despite being the MP for Brent East, and that next time “I should come prepared”. I reported the incidents to the police.This is the hatred I face every day. And inevitably, it changes how MPs operate, how representatives serve the people who elected them.Several years ago, I had toclose my physical constituency officepartly due to threats. We had a brick thrown through the window, and on one occasion my staff physically removed someone who turned up with a golf club. While I was once able to host walk-in constituency surgeries, the increased security threat has meant they are now roving, with the constituents pre-vetted. I also have to be accompanied to every event and notify the police of potential dangers. The constant fear risks making our politics less accessible.Some findings from the Electoral Commission report reflect what I hear from young candidates, especially from minority backgrounds. They worry about canvassing and are also targeted online. Our representatives should reflect the diversity of the population, but this rising abuse will put talented people off entering the political system altogether.It is important to acknowledge that improvements have been made. The policelaunched initiativesto strengthen security and support for councillors, elected mayors, candidates and others. In my experience, this has helped. But there is still far more to do. I want stronger and quicker action to clamp down on online abuse, with social media companies tackling it at source, as we know the threat can become physical when culprits feel emboldened. If social media companies fail to remove this content, they should face substantial fines.I report countless instances of vile racism every month, but very few are pursued. So the police must do more to identify those responsible – and the justice system must show zero tolerance with sentences. I also support restorative justice, so we can work towards repairing the harm caused.It’s also important that more help is directed to those who are disproportionately targeted. We know that Diane Abbott, for example, has receivedextraordinary levels of abuse, while I often feel specifically targeted because I am a Black woman.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd we all have a responsibility to lower the temperature of our politics. I recently wrote to Reform UK to call out theoffensive and divisive remarksof the party’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, regarding the birthplace of Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee from Somalia who isrunning as the Labour candidatein the Holborn and St Pancras byelection next month. This kind of politics inflames divisions. Yusuf is fuelling hate to boost Reform’s popularity, without caring about the consequences. For him it is a political strategy, but for society it has lasting damage.We must act now to protect those who put themselves forward to serve, from all parties, and hold perpetrators to account in order to ensure no one is driven out of our democracy by fear and intimidation. If we allow abusers to decide who feels able to participate in our democracy and who is muted, those seeking to silence us will have won. That simply cannot happen.Dawn Butler is Labour MP for Brent EastDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The secret of Mozart’s genius unlocked – has a teenager succeeded where generations of musicologists have failed? | Classical music | The Guardian
description: US student Linus Chen-Plotkin has analysed music by four canonical composers looking for patterns. Turns out Mozart’s music moves in the least predictable way
Author: Tom Service
Headline: US student Linus Chen-Plotkin has analysed music by four canonical composers looking for patterns. Turns out Mozart’s music moves in the least predictable way
Content: Sensual and surprising … the Sacconi Quartet perform Mozart at the Wigmore Hall in London.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverView image in fullscreenSensual and surprising … the Sacconi Quartet perform Mozart at the Wigmore Hall in London.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverTom Service on musicClassical musicThe secret of Mozart’s genius unlocked – has a teenager succeeded where generations of musicologists have failed?Tom ServiceUS student Linus Chen-Plotkin has analysed music by four canonical composers looking for patterns. Turns out Mozart’s music moves in the least predictable wayWed 16 Sep 2026 11.06 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 19.48 EDTShareIt’s a question that has taxed musical thinkers for centuries: just what is it about one composer’s music that makes it more distinctive than anyone else’s? Entire disciplines of academic thought, of music analysis and historical musicology, as well as the formation of classical music’s canon of “great” composers, have been given over to this single idea: can it be proved that Mozart, say, was measurably “better” than other composers?Our instinctive feeling about the sensual magic of Mozart’s music is part of the equation, but accounting for preciselyhowhis pieces can sustain a lifetime of listening,whytheir pleasures never seem to pall and are still capable of seeming to surprise us even when we know them inside out: that’s the million-dollar musicological question.double quotation markMozart sets up patterns of expectation in his melodies that he confounds rather than confirmsWhat generations of music analysts have tried and largely failed to do through imperfect means of variously subjective techniques, an 18-year-old US student has managed to prove through a combination of data and interpretative ingenuity.A recent study by Philadelphia studentLinus Chen-Plotkindemonstrates that Mozart’s melodies are more surprising in the way they unfold, moment-by-moment and note-by-note, than those of his contemporaries and successors, Haydn, Beethoven and Schubert.View image in fullscreen‘Better’ than other composers: Will Sharpe as Mozart in Sky TV’s Amadeus.Photograph: Adrienn Szabo/Sky UKChen-Plotkin put 600 movements of these four composers’ piano sonatas and string quartets through his bespoke software to analyse their tunes, based onMarkov chainsand other statistical and mathematical tools (he explains his work here). The data revealed that Mozart’s tunes have a shorter “memory” than other composers. That means the way they move is less predictable: that Mozart sets up patterns of expectation in his melodies and ideas that he confounds rather than confirms.You can instinctively hear that at work in so many moments of his string quartets:the opening idea of the E flat major quartet, K428, which is already slipping out of the realms of the expected as early as its third note; or the opening ofthe Dissonance Quartet, K465, whose entire introduction is a chain of ever-more surprising moves of melody and harmony.View image in fullscreenAnalysis … Linus Chen-PlotkinPhotograph: Chris Ayers/Society for ScienceChen-Plotkin is circumspectabout the consequences of his work, recognising its limits as well as its possibilities. In fact, his statistical analyses shore up the conclusions that musicologists have often made about Mozart’s music: that it’s dizzyingly rich and strange in how it moves from note to note and phrase to phrase, but that Mozart was less interested in finding new or unpredictable structures across entire movements. In fact, if Chen-Plotkin were looking at unpredictability across whole pieces and not at the smaller scale of individual tunes and melodies, he would probably have come up with very different results: my hunch at least would be that Beethoven and Haydn would win those contests.Mind you, Chen-Plotkin isn’t suggesting that maths replaces musicology. As well as being against the use of generative AI in art-making, his ambition is simply to show how statistical analysis can help reveal the underlying patterns behind human creativity. And his work has just begun: he enrols at university this autumn, and has already embarked on a computational analysis of the works and words of Chaucer.Anyway: I’m back to put more Mozart through the random note generator of my fingers as I try – and fail, yet again – to play even one movement of his piano sonatas without making a mistake that not even Chen-Plotkin’s software or Markov’s chains could predict.The Royal Philharmonic Orchestra is 80 this week, and, as you can see on their anniversarytimeline, there’s a lot to celebrate. Which other orchestra can claim a legacy that encompasses some of the most exciting performances of Sibelius ever recorded in the 1950s and 60s? Listen to their founder Thomas Beecham’sperformance of Tapiolato hear the edge of orchestral possibility, just as Sibelius pushes his music to new limits of wildness and experimentalism. Then, in the orchestra’s years with Rudolf Kempe in the 60s and early 70s, it transformed London’s musical life, and made pioneering recordings such asJanáček’s Glagolitic Mass.But this is also the orchestra that Beecham insisted was men-only for as long as he conducted them (until his death in 1961), and which only had its first female musician over a decade later –clarinettist Prudence Whittaker.View image in fullscreenHappy 80th RPO: Vasily Petrenko conducts the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra at the Royal Festival Hall in April 2025’s Multitudes festival.Photograph: Mark AllanIt’s also the same ensemble who would find new dimensions of orchestral kitsch with Hooked on Classics in the 1980s, who recorded the Champions League theme in the 90s, and played at King Charles’s coronation in the 2020s; and it’s the orchestra that played this summer withMandle Cheung, who paid an undisclosed amount to conduct Mahler’s Resurrection Symphony.The RPO have soundtracked the decades from the sublime to the ridiculous; and they’ve surfed financial crisis after crisis over the years. Under Vasily Petrenko’s music directorship since 2021, here’s hoping the sublime continues to win out.This week, Tom has been listening to:Riccardo Minasi’s recording ofMozart’s last three symphonies with Ensemble Resonanz. I’ve been blown away by their ferocious imagination. The rhetorical volatility of these performances, their mix of styles, genres and ideas, isn’t an outlier in how this music should be performed – it’s in the fabric of how these symphonies are composed, and what they mean. Mozart reallyisunpredictable! Listen onSpotify| Apple ClassicalExplore more on these topicsClassical musicTom Service on musicWolfgang Amadeus MozartcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Very authoritarian, very brutal’: three decades after the UK’s anti-rave crackdown, why is France doing the same? | Dance music | The Guardian
description: With tear gas, grenades and a new law, French authorities are targeting unlicensed music gatherings. Those in the rave scene explore the parallels with the UK in the 90s
Author: Whitney Wei
Headline: With tear gas, grenades and a new law, French authorities are targeting unlicensed music gatherings. Those in the rave scene explore the parallels with the UK in the 90s
Content: ‘Franch ravers completely understood the concept’ … Spiral Tribe rave in Paris, 1993.Photograph: Spiral Tribe Exhibition ArchiveView image in fullscreen‘Franch ravers completely understood the concept’ … Spiral Tribe rave in Paris, 1993.Photograph: Spiral Tribe Exhibition ArchiveDance music‘Very authoritarian, very brutal’: three decades after the UK’s anti-rave crackdown, why is France doing the same?With tear gas, grenades and a new law, French authorities are targeting unlicensed music gatherings. Those in the rave scene explore the parallels with the UK in the 90sWhitney WeiWed 16 Sep 2026 10.29 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Spiral Tribe fled England in 1992, they left behind an indelible mark on rave history. The itinerant sound system collective are best known for their involvement with Castlemorton Common festival, an unlicensed free party drawing more than 30,000 people and lasting nearly a week. After a drawn-out and notoriously expensive trial for public order offences, Spiral Tribe were acquitted of all charges. They decided to drive their repurposed military caravans out of the UK and never look back.Their documented history often stops there. But little known is the fact that they then kicked off “the biggest illegal underground movement thatEuropehad ever seen”, says Spiral Tribe associate Sebastian Vaughan, AKA electronic musician 69db.Many Spiral members, including Vaughan, settled throughoutFranceafter a warm response to the Spiral sound – a 160bpm sped-up version of hip-house with delayed kick drums, known as hardtek or tribe – and to the collective’s punk-rave aesthetic. Over the last three decades, their underground Teknival parties in France grew from about 1,000 attendees in 1993 to tens of thousands in 1995 and up to 100,000 people by the early 2000s, far exceeding the turnout at Castlemorton. French ravers, Vaughan says, “completely understood what the concept was, and they weren’t just following it, they were creating it themselves”. He attributes Spiral’s underground appeal to the country’s likeminded appetite for resistance.But equally, “the French have always been very authoritarian and very brutal in their response to free parties”, says Mark Harrison, another Spiral Tribe founding member. He says he has witnessed the French riot police, known as Compagnies Républicaines de Sécurité (CRS), descend on dancefloors armed with stun grenades and rubber bullets in events from the mid-90s onwards.In 2019, a police raid caused revellers at a Fête de la Musique concert in Nantes to fall into the Loire river, and 24-year-oldSteve Maia Caniçowas found drowned. Two years later, the CRS raideda Teknival rave in Rendonheld in Caniço’s memory armed with tear gas and sting ball GM2L grenades. There were no attempts beforehand at dialogue or de-escalation. The violence resulted in a 22-year-old partygoer losing his hand. Another woman had her cheek pierced and teeth broken by a grenade fragment. Amnesty International France reported on the unnecessary use of force at the Rendon event asa human rights violation.Now, the French parliament has formally enacted theRipostpublic disorder law, targeting unlicensed music gatherings of more than 250 people. Free party organisers could face two years’ imprisonment, confiscation of their vehicles and sound equipment, and a fine of up to €30,000. Even attendees could face up to six months in jail and a €7,500 fine.View image in fullscreenA Teknival event in Italy, 1993.Photograph: Spiral Tribe Exhibition ArchiveIt feels similar to the crackdown Spiral Tribe faced in the wake of Castlemorton: two years later, theUK’s Criminal Justice and Public Order Actcriminalised gatherings of more than 20 people where “the emission of a succession of repetitive beats” was deemed to “cause serious distress to the inhabitants of the locality”.The newly enacted French law aims to protect rural communities whose land has been misused by ravers, such as a May 2024 party thrown in heritage vineyards in the Loire Regional National Park or one inSeptember 2025 in Audeshortly after the region was devastated by wildfires. In May, interior minister Laurent Nuñez, who publicly championed the bill, visited a protest against the policy in his home town of Bourges. The demonstration,he told the press, only served to “strengthen the government’s determination to crack down more harshly on this kind of wild event, which our fellow citizens do not understand”.But critics argue that the law disproportionately affects young, working-class citizens, and free party proponents claim that the gatherings that have gone awry are only a few out of the thousands held every year.Mouillette, a volunteer with the Fonds de Soutien Juridique des Sons, a group of French lawyers supporting free party sound systems, distributes literature on how to properly prepare a party, choose a location and secure and manage the event within legal grounds while also making sure that the rave is a good experience for everyone involved. “Many organisers are very young and need to learn,” she says, “but with the government against us, we cannot educate them.”She says that the prison sentence for partygoers is an illogical move for legislators. The French prison system is already facing adangerous overcrowding crisis– considered the second worst in Europe in a 2025annual penal statistics report– with records earlier this year revealing 86,229 inmates in spaces only suitedfor 62,000.“We will be locked up alongside murderers,” Mouillette claims.When Spiral Tribe and other free party sound systems were created more than 30 years ago, they were a reaction against capitalism and state powers enforcing “a path of normativity that [was] very obedient and subservient”, says Harrison. He thinks that the underground rave movement remains an important laboratory for alternative forms of society. However, “the narrowing of imagination, the narrowing of opportunities created by this authoritarian direction that we’re all being pushed [into] is very disturbing”, he says, calling it “anti-culture”.“For us, Ripost is part of the ongoing trend towards the gradual erosion of individual freedoms and the right’s state surveillance of the population that we are facing since the Covid pandemic,” says Kamille, a pseudonymous spokesperson ofTekno Anti-repression. This collective of French free party advocates assembled in 2022 to change the mainstream narrative around the underground movement after 30 years of virtually no organising power. “There is more and more repression of social movements and protests,” Kamille says. “We consider [this] a global shift towards the right and their desire for mass control of people who are against the system.”‘I fell in a deep puddle running from police’: photographing London’s underground ravesRead moreHow strictly the French government will enforce the Ripost law remains to be seen. But Spiral Tribe members believe that more and more young people are waking up to the hypocrisy and corruption around them.“You would have to be living under a rock to not see the double standards imposed on the population by the establishment,” says Vaughan, citing the abuses exposed in the Epstein files. “The world we live in is a nightmare.” He urges ravers to vote for the far-left La France Insoumise, the only party supportive of the free movement.“We have to remain optimistic,” Harrison adds. “I think this is one of the reasons why power attacks free parties. They want to kill that spirit because they know that one of the most powerful things about a good party is that you feel connected. You feel that unity.”Unmasked presents: Spiral Tribe Exhibition is atReinstate, London, 16-19 September. An accompanying rave, SP23, is at Distillery, London, on 19 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsDance musicFranceEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Body found in search for three-year-old Noah Woods | Suffolk | The Guardian
description: Body found in pond in Suffolk village of Brantham, where Noah was last seen on Tuesday afternoon
Author: Jamie Grierson
Headline: Body found in pond in Suffolk village of Brantham, where Noah was last seen on Tuesday afternoon
Content: Noah Woods, 3, went missing after a visit to a play area where he became separated from a relativePhotograph: Suffolk PoliceView image in fullscreenNoah Woods, 3, went missing after a visit to a play area where he became separated from a relativePhotograph: Suffolk PoliceSuffolkBody found in search for three-year-old Noah WoodsBody found in pond in Suffolk village of Brantham, where Noah was last seen on Tuesday afternoonJamie GriersonWed 16 Sep 2026 13.51 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 12.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice searching for a three-year-old boy who went missing from a playground on the Suffolk-Essex border have found a body.Noah Woods was last seen at 3pm on Tuesday in Merriam Close, Brantham, near Manningtree, before becoming separated from a relative.The body was found in Decoy Pond in the village.In a statement, Supt Tom Pearse, from Suffolk constabulary, said: “Police and fire teams this afternoon sadly recovered the body of a child from Decoy Pond in Brantham.“Formal identification has yet to take place, but the family of Noah Woods have been informed of this development. The discovery of the body is currently being treated as not suspicious, but unexplained.“The coroner will be informed of this development. Since Noah was reported as missing, officers have carried out multiple inquiries, including the deployment of special search officers and dog units, and received support from various agencies, including helicopters from the National Police Air Service and HM Coastguard.View image in fullscreenSupt Tom Pearse said the search teams ‘have been overwhelmed by the outpouring of public support’.Photograph: Will Colebourne/PA“Additional assistance on the ground has been provided by HM Coastguard, Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service, Suffolk Lowland Search and Rescue and over 1,300 members of the public supporting the search.“First and foremost, our thoughts are with Noah’s family and all those who know them. Since Noah was reported missing, vast numbers of our officers and staff have been deployed in numerous functions in the search for Noah, and the support for his family.“We have been overwhelmed by the outpouring of public support and people putting on their boots to help us with the search.“As a parent myself, I completely understand why people would want to help, and such a response is one that typifies the strong sense of community and the heartwarming nature of Suffolk people that make the county such a special place.“I’m sure you appreciate that the family now need time, space and privacy, and I thank you for your understanding of this.”View image in fullscreenMembers of HM Coastguard Search and Rescue searched for Noah.Photograph: Will Colebourne/PAEarlier in the search, officers from Suffolk constabulary said Noah, who was autistic and non-verbal with partial hearing loss, was reported to have run down an alley near a playground towards a housing estate.Searches of Decoy Pond started earlier on Wednesday after it was cordoned off by police tape.A massive search operation had been under way in and around the village since Noah’s disappearance, supported by hundreds of volunteers.Volunteers wept in a garden area at Brantham Leisure Centre as Pearse updated them. “You will have heard the news,” he said. “First and foremost our thoughts are with Noah’s family and all those who knew him.”He said that the agencies involved in the search, and Noah’s family, “have been overwhelmed by the outpouring of public support, people putting on their boots and helping us with the search and that, ladies and gentlemen, is yourselves”.The officer’s voice cracked with emotion at times as he addressed the crowd of volunteers.View image in fullscreenVolunteers gathered at Brantham leisure centre.Photograph: Will Colebourne/PANoah went missing after a visit to a play area where he became separated from a relative. Police had said Noah would not respond to his name if called.Earlier on Wednesday, Pearse said there was no indication anything sinister had happened.Volunteers could be seen in hi-vis jackets helping to search the area, with efforts being coordinated from the village hall and a leisure centre.Police, fire, coastguard and search and rescue teams, with sniffer dogs and a helicopter, were all deployed.As well as the ground search, officers scoured CCTV and other available video footage, going door to door and carrying out aerial and thermal imaging searches.Earlier, Noah’s father posted on social media asking volunteers to widen their search beyond the village where possible.He wrote: “I cannot go another night knowing he’s out there alone, please don’t give up on him guys. He is out there somewhere and I appreciate every single one of you.”Explore more on these topicsSuffolkEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Climate crisis likely behind devastating Nepal-Tibet floods that killed more than 1,300, first study finds | Climate science | The Guardian
description: Scientists say global heating was a destabilising factor in collapse of 200,000 sq metre glacier in August
Author: Damien Gayle
Headline: Scientists say global heating was a destabilising factor in collapse of 200,000 sq metre glacier in August
Content: Devighat Bazaar, a Nepalese town devastated by last month’s flash flooding.Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAPView image in fullscreenDevighat Bazaar, a Nepalese town devastated by last month’s flash flooding.Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAPClimate scienceClimate crisis likely behind devastating Nepal-Tibet floods that killed more than 1,300, first study findsScientists say global heating was a destabilising factor in collapse of 200,000 sq metre glacier in AugustDamien GayleWed 16 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClimate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing hundreds of people in Nepal andTibetlast month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found.Researchers identified unusually warm conditions beforethe glacier’s collapse, which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3,885 cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale,hitting communities downstreamwithout warning.How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guideRead more“Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,” said Dr Friederike Otto, a climate science professor atImperial College London, which carried out the study.“When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction. Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come.”View image in fullscreenA impromptu memorial in Kathmandu commemorates some of the people killed in the flooding.Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPAMore than 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing after a massive section of overhanging glacier and rock measuring roughly 200,000 sq metres (2,153,000 sq ft) fell from Langtang Lirung mountain on 26 August.It dropped about 1,400 metres (4,660ft), slamming into the valley floor with such intensity that it registered as an earthquake, liquidising ice and sparking a freezing flood that careened downriver at speeds exceeding 110 mph.The devastating flood of water, ice, rock and sediment swept away families, homes, settlements, roads, bridges and other infrastructure, leaving survivors stranded and cut off.“Rock avalanches of this size are rare, with annual frequency estimates of approximately one event this size every 1,000–10,000 years,” the study said. “This event shows that limits to adaptation are already being reached.”The research was unlike previous studies by Otto and her team at World Weather Attribution (WWA) – a collaborative project between Imperial and other climate specialists worldwide – in that the role of climate breakdown could not be ascribed to one particular weather event.Instead, the researchers found the disaster was the result of a compound crisis, with a number of factors made worse by decades of atmospheric heating as a result of greenhouse gas pollution.Dr Ben Clarke, who researches extreme weather and climate change at Imperial, said the “fingerprints of climate change” were clear in the long-term changes that happened around the glacier before its catastrophic collapse.View image in fullscreen‘Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,’ said Dr Friederike Otto.Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAPAmong the study’s key findings were:skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the region where the collapse happened, climate breakdown has caused about 2C of warming since pre-industrial times, and about 1.5C of warming in July and August specifically;July and August 2026 were the warmest on record locally, reaching 5C above the 30-year average in the days before the collapse;The freezing threshold in the Himalayas has risen by about 100 metres per decade since the 1980s, with higher and longer thaw temperatures weakening mountain slopes shaped by permafrost;The warming temperature had already driven substantial glacier recession, removing stabilising ice from around the site where the collapse occurred and contributing meltwater;A 7.8 magnitude earthquake in 2015further contributed to slope failure, though its specific contribution to the disaster in August could not be confirmed.Otto, Clarke and the WWA team said their study did not directly ascribe climate breakdown as the fundamental cause of the catastrophe. Instead, it was best understood as a destabilising factor on the existing geology.Clarke said: “We found that climate change is transforming the high mountain environment, influencing many of the possible drivers of this collapse.”View image in fullscreenA major earthquake in Nepal in 2015 may also have contributed to the glacier’s collapse.Photograph: Ishwar Rauniyar/The GuardianNepal has filed a formal request with the UN loss and damage fund for financial support to address the destruction caused by the flood, a process that requires proof of a link to the climate crisis. The country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, has also demanded that top emitting nations such as China and India“wake up” and accept shared responsibilityfor the disaster.Madhab Uprety, senior technical advisor for the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, which is part of WWA, said only aggressive cuts to global emissions could begin to address the “losses and damages faced by vulnerable frontline communities”.He added: “In addition to the human tragedy on an unimaginable scale, the cost of recovery for this disaster is substantial. For a nation that’s done virtually nothing to contribute to this problem, it underlines the need to find fairness in helping climate vulnerable nations cope with the problems they have not unleashed.”Explore more on these topicsClimate scienceNepal-Tibet flood disasterClimate crisisFloodingNepalTibetExtreme weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Made in Europe’ law threatens UK plans for reset with EU | European Union | The Guardian
description: Government sources say legislation aimed at China poses a risk to British businesses and must be addressed
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Government sources say legislation aimed at China poses a risk to British businesses and must be addressed
Content: A UK government source said ‘Made in Europe should be on the table’ in reset negotiations with the EU.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenA UK government source said ‘Made in Europe should be on the table’ in reset negotiations with the EU.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAEuropean Union‘Made in Europe’ law threatens UK plans for reset with EUGovernment sources say legislation aimed at China poses a risk to British businesses and must be addressedLisa O’CarrollandJessica ElgotWed 16 Sep 2026 15.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK government’s EU reset summit will be delayed again unless the bloc agrees to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry, government sources have said.The“Made in Europe” legislation– formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act – is designed to curb China’s increasing presence in European industry, but was not onthe reset plan agreed by the former prime minister Keir Starmerand the European Commission chief, Ursula von der Leyen, in London in May 2025.A follow-up summit was due to be held in July this year, but wascancelled after Starmer’s resignation. The government is now looking to change the roadmap, with one source saying that “Made in Europe should be on the agenda”.It is understood that Hamish Falconer, the new cabinet minister with responsibility for the reset, told the EU’s trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, this was the UK’s new priority when the pair met last week.The trade minister, Anas Sarwar, told a gathering of UK business leaders on Tuesday they needed to let their EU partners know the risks posed by Made inEurope, which will prioritise EU suppliers in key industries including car manufacturing and defence.Ministers have privately expressed fears that the reset has lost significant momentum since Andy Burnham became prime minister, with his focus on the domestic agenda. Agreements have yet to be reached on several key issues, includingwhat tuition fees will be paid by EU students coming to the UKon a mooted “youth experience” programme.View image in fullscreenKeir Starmer and Ursula von der Leyen set out plans for a UK-EU reset in London in May 2025.Photograph: Carl Court/PAUK sources say that whilea food and drink dealand a youth mobility scheme are still on the agenda, the government will not agree to a new summit date until the bigger issues of the Industrial Accelerator Act are included in discussions.There was talk in London and Brussels that a meeting could be convened on 6 November, but it is understood this could now be pushed backuntil the end of November or beyond.One government source said: “Weare willing to negotiate on the things that matter to them, but they have to be able to negotiate the thing that matters to us. Made in Europe should be on the table, definitely.”The UK fears the Made in Europe laws could jeopardise billions of pounds worth of trade if British goods are not categorised as European, locking it out of key contracts on the continent.France, which conceived the Made in Europe laws, is pushing to have the legislation passed by the end of the year, deepening fears that British manufacturing could be left behind.It is thought that France is sympathetic to the UK’s position, but believes increasing competition from China makes it more important to get the legislation on the books now, and make allowances for third countries later, a process that could take years.View image in fullscreenA Chinese-made electric bus on the streets of Copenhagen, Denmark.Photograph: Francis Joseph Dean/Dean Pictures/AlamyOne EU diplomat said that there was substantial backing among key member states for the UK to be included in Made in Europe, though not all agreed. “The problem is the benefits are seen as asymmetrical,” the diplomat said. “The UK gets more out of it than the EU.”It is understood the Netherlands, Germany, Poland and Italy are all in favour of the UK’s inclusion, but France remains unconvinced.The government’s newly assertive approach could give the UK some leverage in negotiations over concessions on youth mobility, something that is a political priority for many EU capitals.Another UK source said a deal on Made in Europe would be “a good faith demonstration that we can find answers and almost everything else”.A government spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and trusted European partner, committed to our shared security and economic cooperation.“We will continue to engage with the EU on Made in Europe and work together, as like-minded partners, to boost growth and open up trade.”The UK’s desire for a deal on manufacturing rules comes at time when the EU is under pressure from industry across the bloc to loosen China’s growing presence in supply chains.Last week, manufacturing bosses warned of apotential loss of 300,000 jobs this yearunless incentives were put in place to make European products more attractive than cheaper parts from China.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe EU’s deficit with China is now running at €1bn a day, with fears thatEuropean companies are being cannibalised from within.Fears of new China shock as EU industry’s reliance on imports growsRead moreIn her state of the union address to the European parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen said the EU needed to grow non-Chinese supplies of rare earths and critical minerals vital to manufacturing.Hersurprise offer of an associate membership deal with Canadademonstrated how far Brussels can go to court third-country partners.Speaking in the presence of the Canadian prime minister,Mark Carney, the EU chief said: “We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. We must urgently reimagine our partnerships.”The EU andCanadaare to hold a summit in late October to develop their future relationship. The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, though it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, enabling deep economic integration with these countries, which follow many EU rules including free movement – a red line for the UK.Carney, who is to address the European parliament on Thursday, has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU, as his country seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade.View image in fullscreenMark Carney and Andy Burnham in Liverpool on Wednesday night.Photograph: John Clifton/Action Images/ReutersBurnham met Carney at a football match in Liverpool on Wednesday night, where the two Everton fans watched their team in theEFL Cup. Burnham is also due to meet the US president, Donald Trump, for the first time at the UN general assembly in New York next week.The potential new alliance between the EU and Canada will worry UK ministers that the bloc’s priorities are shifting. Should Burnham fail to complete a food and drink deal that was already on Starmer’s reset agenda, it could have implications for October’s budget, as the economic effects of easing trade with the EU is priced in as part of growth calculations.The Conservatives criticised the UK-EU reset on Wednesday, saying a future Tory government would build a wholly independent regulatory system.Alex Burghart, the party’s deputy leader, and Victoria Atkins, the shadow environment secretary, warned the plans would make Britain less competitive.Speaking at the Policy Exchange thinktank, Burghart said: “Labour’s EU reset is the worst of both worlds and will leave Britain unable to take advantage of our country’s future growth potential.“The next Conservative government would not be bound by this arrangement and will begin work now on a genuinely independent regulatory system.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionBrexitAndy BurnhamUrsula von der LeyenForeign policyMark CarneyCanadanewsShareReuse this content

title: Prisoners to ‘double up’ in one-person prefab cells, leaked documents show | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Ten category C prisons in England and Wales asked to add second beds, in breach of safe occupancy limits
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Exclusive: Ten category C prisons in England and Wales asked to add second beds, in breach of safe occupancy limits
Content: An example of an existing category C prison cell.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenAn example of an existing category C prison cell.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyPrisons and probationPrisoners to ‘double up’ in one-person prefab cells, leaked documents showExclusive: Ten category C prisons in England and Wales asked to add second beds, in breach of safe occupancy limitsRajeev SyalHome affairs editorWed 16 Sep 2026 14.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Prison Service has drawn up plans to “double up” hundreds of prisoners in temporary prefabricated cells built for one person, at the request of the Ministry of Justice, leaked documents show.Amid an ongoing overcrowding crisis inEnglandand Wales, governors of 10 category C prisons have been asked to sign off the installation of second beds in “rapid deployment cells [RDCs]”.The units, some of which measure 2.9 metres by 3.4 metres and include a bed, toilet and shower, were placed in the grounds of more than 15 prisons as a temporary solution to past overcrowding problems.Estimated to have a 15-year lifespan, the steel-framed “pods” can be stacked to be two storeys and are usually occupied by low-risk prisoners, some of whom have been allowed to move into them as a reward for good behaviour.According to leaked emails, the planned doubling-up suggested by Ministry of Justice officials would increase the overall capacity of the prison estate by 476.Responding to the leaked documents, governors and prison officers said the numbers being proposed by Whitehall could breach health and safety laws and make jails unsafe for prisoners, staff and the public.Map of prisons where ‘doubling up’ has been proposedThe plans were disclosed in an email sent on 27 August by a senior Prison Service executive to governors.“As you are aware, maximising available prison capacity is of high ministerial interest, and HMPPS [His Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service] have been asked to explore the viability of crowding Rapid Deployment Cell accommodation,” the executive wrote.“The physical viability of installing a second bed in these units has been worked through at pace, and the assessment … is that ground floor units only are suitable to install a second bed.“Given continued high population growth, and less supply coming online than anticipated, it is important that all potential capacity is identified quickly, and as such the panels need to take place over the next few days.”The email was sent three days before Andy Burnham announced a substantialnarrowing of prisoners’ eligibility for the government’s early release scheme, blocking hundreds of violent criminals from being freed.What is Burnham doing to the early prison release scheme and why?Read moreAccording to a second leaked document, the doubling up plans would include beds being added to temporary cells in the following prisons: Wayland, in Norfolk (43 beds); Littlehey, in Cambridgeshire (60); Erlestoke, in Wiltshire (66); and Rochester, in Kent (60).Other prisons asked to find extra capacity in temporary cells include The Verne, in Dorset; Wymott, in Lancashire; Channings Wood, in Devon; Whatton, in Nottingham, which is a prison for people convicted of sexual offences; The Mount, in Hertfordshire; and Huntercombe, in Oxfordshire.The second document also shows that the doubling up proposals would breach “operational capacity”, putting the number of prisoners above safe occupancy levels.Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the Prison Officers Association, said capacity breaches could prompt industrial action by his members. “By law our members cannot strike, but I know they would walk out on health and safety grounds if asked to oversee prisons which cannot cope with the numbers being proposed,” he said.“Creating more space increases the pressure on an already overcrowded prison estate and risks the stability of prisons. If the government are convinced that early release schemes are sufficient, you have to ask why they are now insisting prisons source every available bit of spare capacity.”Tom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors Association, said a full risk assessment would have to be carried out on each prison to ensure the public and staff remained safe if doubling up occurred.“RDCs are amongst the least secure accommodation in the prison estate and prisoners located in them will have to be risk assessed. If you don’t do this, the prison won’t be sufficiently safe or secure,” he said.“Increasing the operational capacity of a prison isn’t as simple as putting bunk beds in cells. There needs to be staff available to supervise the additional prisoners and there needs to be additional regime activities.”Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League for Penal Reform, said the proposal was an act of desperation.“Rapid deployment cells were themselves meant to be a short-term response but, ironically, they have come to be seen as being among the more positive parts of the prison estate, with fewer issues related to violence, debt and drug misuse. The risk now is that all this will be undermined as more and more people get crammed in,” she said.There are 87,111 people in prison in England andWales. Under the Ministry of Justice’s own definition of safety and decency, the prison estate should not hold more than 81,616 people.Reacting to the leaked documents, a ministry spokesperson said the department was investing up to £4.7bn creating 14,000 new prison places.“As the public would expect, we’re pulling every lever available to ensure there is always space to lock up dangerous offenders,” the spokesperson said.“Cells are only doubled up where it is safe to do so, and no final decision has been taken on these units.”Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationEnglandWalesUK criminal justicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Netanyahu seeks to strip citizenship from Israelis as threats to NAZA film directors intensify | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Israeli prime minister to pursue new laws as directors of Guardian-produced film face threats from far-right officials and activists
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: Israeli prime minister to pursue new laws as directors of Guardian-produced film face threats from far-right officials and activists
Content: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor with the trophy of the special jury award at the Venice international film festival.Photograph: Kristina Afanasyeva/Capital Pictures/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenYuval Abraham and Rachel Szor with the trophy of the special jury award at the Venice international film festival.Photograph: Kristina Afanasyeva/Capital Pictures/Alamy Live News.GazaNetanyahu seeks to strip citizenship from Israelis as threats to NAZA film directors intensifyIsraeli prime minister to pursue new laws as directors of Guardian-produced film face threats from far-right officials and activists‘They know the house they are bombing is full of children’: NAZA’s directors on their devastating film about Israeli intelligenceLorenzo Tondoin JerusalemWed 16 Sep 2026 16.54 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 09.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBenjamin Netanyahu said on Wednesday that he would seek new laws allowingIsraelto strip citizenship from people who “smear” Israeli soldiers, escalating the campaign against the Oscar-winning film-makers behind the Gaza documentary NAZA, who have faced threats from senior government and military officials and groups of far-right Israelis gathering outside their families’ homes.NAZA, which was produced by the Guardian, concerns the country’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza and is named for an acronym used euphemistically by Israel’s intelligence service to indicatehow many civilians it expects to die in an airstrike. The film builds on revelations first published by the Israeli-Palestinian publication +972 Magazine, the Hebrew-language outlet Local Call and the Guardian from 2023 to 2025.The 80-minute documentarywon the special jury prizeat this year’s Venice film festival on Saturday, after receivinga 25-minute standing ovation– a festival record.Soon afterwards, however, the film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, came under attack from members of Israel’s government, with the culture minister, Miki Zohar, calling for their citizenship to be revoked, and accusing them of “treason against the state”.Zohar on Wednesday thanked the Israeli prime minister for his announcement to change the law in order to revoke their citizenship, saying it was “time to put an end to this disgrace”.“We will revoke citizenship for anyone who defames IDF soldiers around the world – he will be deeply hurt in his pocket,’’ said Netanyahu, who intends to promote two government bills concerning defamation of IDF soldiers and the state of Israel.According to media reports, the first bill, which will be submitted through the justice ministry, will double the amount of a defamation claim to 1 million shekels without proof of damage. The second bill, which will be submitted through the interior ministry, will stipulate the revocation of citizenship for anyone who defames IDF soldiers and the state of Israel around the world.On Wednesday evening,dozens of rightwing activists gathered outside the home of the parents of Rachel Szor, one of the directors of NAZA. Among the organisers were activists and campaign staff linked to the far-right Otzma Yehudit party of Itamar Ben-Gvir, the national security minister. Messages circulated in activist groups earlier on Wednesday urged supporters to gather outside her house. Some of the messages included explicit calls for violence.Police and border police officers were deployed at the scene.One protester called for the “death penalty for traitors” and demanded that the homes of the film-makers’ families be demolished.The latest attacks followed a series of threats and incidents targeting the directors.Ben-Gvir had called the directors “a disgrace” whileNetanyahu condemned the film as “intolerable”, saying it portrayed the Israel Defense Forces as war criminals.On Tuesday, the IDF’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, said the military would “not allow IDF soldiers to be made targets through lies and blood libels” and would use “every tool at our disposal” against the film. The Israeli television channeli24 later reportedthat the military had opened a leak investigation and was seeking assistance from Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security and counterintelligence agency. The agency would respond only after receiving a formal request from the military prosecutor, who would probably first consult the attorney general, the channel reported.Netanyahu posted a videowhich included an old clip of Abraham confronting a soldier in the occupied West Bank’s South Hebron Hills, an area where Israeli forces have repeatedly been accused of supporting settlers during attacks on Palestinians. In the video, the Israeli PM says: “The same director who produced that terrible film that slanders IDF soldiers.”On Wednesday,far-right Israeli journalists, influencers and activists escalated their threats against the two film-makers. Rightwing activists were organising protests outside addresses linked to the directors and their colleagues.This comes after the Channel 14 journalistYehuda Schlesingersaid the directors should be “pursued” or “hunted” wherever they went, and prevented from returning to Israel. He urged Jews in Israel and abroad to make clear that what he described as “25 minutes of antisemitic applause” in Venice would come at a “heavy price”.A rightwing activist with tens of thousands of followers separately called for protesters to target Abraham’s family and associates, saying: “We’ll show him ‘collateral damage’.” He shared a photograph of Abraham’s mother and sought information about the director’s return flight so supporters could “welcome” him at the airport.A mural appeared in Ashdod depicting Abraham and Szor with crosshairs, horns, swastikas and the word “traitors” emblazoned over the top. A video showing its creation was shared by the far-right rapper Yoav Eliasi, who has more than 750,000 followers on Facebook.In aninterview with Israel’s Channel 13, Abraham commented on the campaign of vilification, saying: “Of course it’s hard … [Israel] is my home, it’s the only place I want to live, a place that is important to me. So of course I’m afraid I won’t be able to return.”View image in fullscreenA man rides a scooter past graffiti depicting Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, with the word ‘traitors’ in Hebrew, on a wall in Ashdod, southern Israel.Photograph: Amir Cohen/ReutersAs the threats against the directors intensified, film-makers and human rights groups voiced support for the pair.In a joint statement, 43 local human rights organisations urged Israeli authorities to stop what they described as incitement and threats against the film-makers, and not to prosecute either them or their sources.“The institutional response to the film and the threats against its creators are characteristic of dictatorial regimes,” said the statement, signed by groups including Peace Now, Adalah, B’Tselem, Physicians for Human Rights Israel and Breaking the Silence.More than 1,500 Israeli film-makershave also signed a petition defending “freedom of expression and creation” and expressing solidarity with Szor and Abraham.“In recent days, we have witnessed an unprecedented smear and incitement campaign against the film-makers, with the line between this rhetoric and physical violence or threats to their lives narrowing rapidly,” the petition said.The signatories said the role of art and journalism was to reflect society and encourage debate, “even when facing a harsh reality”, and called for the film to be released in Israel so audiences could judge it for themselves.Szor and Abraham won an Oscar for their previous documentary, 2024’sNo Other Land(co-directed with Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal), which spotlighted Palestinian resistance in the occupied West Bank.The NGOs called for a “thorough” investigation into the high number of casualties inGaza, particularly among civilians, and for journalists to be granted unimpeded access to the territory, from which Israel has largely barred foreign reporters since October 2023.Prominent figures in international cinema have also expressed solidarity with Abraham and Szor. Laura Poitras, who directed the 2015 Oscar-winning documentary Citizenfour, about the whistleblower Edward Snowden, called the threats by Israeli government officials “a threat to journalists worldwide”.Diplomatic and foreign ministry sourcestold Haaretzthat threats to punish the directors may have actually have boosted international media attention on the documentary.“It would have made headlines anyway, but they really helped amplify it,” a source at the Israeli foreign ministry told the newspaper. “The very fact that the government responded drew attention and headlines.”Late on Wednesday, +972 Magazine posted a video showing a manpainting overthe mural of the NAZA directors, replacing the word “traitors” with “heroes”.In a statement, the Guardian said said was “disturbed to see the authoritarian response toNAZAin Israel.“Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor are brave journalists and filmmakers. The attacks against them come from people who have not yet seen the film.“NAZA is based on more than three years of investigative journalism.
