The testimonies it contains are true and we believe they deserve to be heard. The interviews were given by confidential journalistic sources.“We will robustly defend NAZA – and the team behind it – from any attacks or attempts at censorship.”Explore more on these topicsGazaNAZAIsraelPalestineIsrael-Gaza warnewsShareReuse this content

title: Earl Spencer’s memoir claims Prince Charles said of Diana: ‘We’ll forget her soon enough’ | Books | The Guardian
description: Charles Spencer’s book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister alleges comments were made during argument over Princess of Wales’ funeral arrangements
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Charles Spencer’s book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister alleges comments were made during argument over Princess of Wales’ funeral arrangements
Content: In his memoir, Earl Spencer writes Prince Charles’ comments reflected ‘his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death’Photograph: Neil Spence/AlamyView image in fullscreenIn his memoir, Earl Spencer writes Prince Charles’ comments reflected ‘his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death’Photograph: Neil Spence/AlamyBooksEarl Spencer’s memoir claims Prince Charles said of Diana: ‘We’ll forget her soon enough’Charles Spencer’s book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister alleges comments were made during argument over Princess of Wales’ funeral arrangementsCaroline DaviesWed 16 Sep 2026 16.19 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePrince Charles told Earl Spencer days after the death of his sisterDiana, Princess of Wales, that “rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough”, it is alleged in a memoir to be published this month.Charles Spencer’s book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, contains the claim that the comments were made by the now king during a heated argument over funeral arrangements.TheDaily Mail, which is serialising the book, said Spencer insisted to the then Prince of Wales that Diana would not have wanted her sons, William, then 15, and Harry, then 12, to walk in their mother’s funeral procession.Spencer writes that the comments “unleashed” by Charles almost 30 years agoreflected “his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death”the Daily Mail reported.Diana’s ‘revenge dress’, worn when Charles revealed infidelity, up for auctionRead moreIn his book, Spencer writes that when one of Queen Elizabeth’s most senior aides told him in the days before the funeral that William and Harry would take part in the procession, he responded: “That’s not going to happen,” the paper said.But minutes later he received a phone call from Charles, who insisted it should. It was during the ensuing argument between the two men that Charles allegedly made the comment, with Spencer reportedly writing: “Rest assured,” he hissed, “we’ll forget her soon enough!’”Spencer wrote that he was stunned by the alleged remark and took a few seconds to reply, writing: “‘I can’t believe you just said that,’ I said flatly, before hanging up.”Swan Song is due to be published worldwide next Tuesday – in the UK by Penguin Michael Joseph, a division of Penguin Random House.Four copies of the Dutch language edition were reportedly taken from a truck while it was en route from the Dutch publisher’s printers to their warehouse in the Netherlands.Diana, who died aged 36 after a car crash in Paris in 1997, would have turned 65 on 1 July this year.Spencer said that he had been inundated with interview requests in advance of the 30th anniversary of her death next year, and wanted to write down his own thoughts and memories rather than “having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others”.“The aim of this book is to tell the truth about Diana from her brother’s perspective, just as I attempted to do when speaking at her funeral,” he added, referring to the eulogy he gave in Westminster Abbey.ABuckingham Palacespokesperson said: “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss.”Explore more on these topicsBooksDiana, Princess of WalesMonarchyKing Charles IIIBuckingham PalaceQueen Elizabeth IIDaily MailShareReuse this content

title: Women with same health conditions as men ‘less likely to be offered active treatment’ | Medical research | The Guardian
description: Men with heart, kidney or liver conditions more likely to be offered intervention compared with women, global analysis finds
Author: Anna Bawden
Headline: Men with heart, kidney or liver conditions more likely to be offered intervention compared with women, global analysis finds
Content: The study concluded the discrepancy was not a result of the need for different clinical approaches to women’s health.Photograph: Mike Ford/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe study concluded the discrepancy was not a result of the need for different clinical approaches to women’s health.Photograph: Mike Ford/AlamyMedical researchWomen with same health conditions as men ‘less likely to be offered active treatment’Men with heart, kidney or liver conditions more likely to be offered intervention compared with women, global analysis findsAnna BawdenHealth and social affairs correspondentWed 16 Sep 2026 14.06 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 15.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWomen with the same medical condition as men are less likely to be offered treatment such as surgery, a stent or a strong painkiller, research has found.A review of global research found that for several health problems, including cardiovascular conditions, kidney disease and Parkinson’s, women were less likely to receive the same treatment as men, revealing the extent to which women have significantly unequal care.Researchers at the University of St Andrews analysed 38 studies and found that in 33 of them women were less likely to be offered active treatment. Women with myocardial infarction, heart failure or an irregular heart beat were more likely to be given medication, whereas men were more likely to receive a coronary bypass, stent or other surgical treatment. Women were also less likely to be prescribed statins, according to the analysis, which was published in the journal Plos One.Men with Parkinson’s were more likely to be referred for deep brain stimulation, while those with liver failure were more likely to receive a transplant than women. Female kidney patients requiring dialysis were less likely to be given permanent access and had to spend longer using a catheter. And women were also less likely to be given opioids for pain management.For stroke and diabetes, however, there was no significant difference between the sexes in treatment. And women were more likely to be treated for dementia.The findings come amid growing concern about the gender health gap. In March, the then health secretary, Wes Streeting, said women were being let down by “medical misogyny”. The previous Conservative government appointed Lesley Regan as England’sfirst women’s health ambassador, to help tackle the gender gap.The analysis concluded the discrepancy was not a result of the need for different clinical approaches to women’s health. It found that none of the studies identified any guideline recommending different treatment by sex, raising the question of whether unequal care was a factor.Dr Andrew O’Malley, who co-led the study, said: “For clinicians, the findings are a prompt to check whether treatment is being offered on clinical grounds rather than assumption.”He said studies showed doctors more often attributed women’s symptoms to anxiety and made more diagnostic errors with female patients, even when test results were positive.Dr Miriam Veenhuizen, an honorary lecturer in the School of Medicine at St Andrews, said: “While the direction of the findings was not a surprise, the consistency was. The same pattern appeared in cardiology, surgery, transplant medicine and emergency care, and it survived statistical adjustment in most studies.”Explore more on these topicsMedical researchHealthWomen's healthMen's healthHeart diseaseParkinson's diseasenewsShareReuse this content

title: Macklemore pledges his $1m Ed Sheeran tour salary to Palestine | Macklemore | The Guardian
description: Ed Sheeran and Robert Kraft will also reportedly donate $2m each after Kraft was challenged by the rapper, who was dismissed from the tour after speaking in support of Palestine
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Ed Sheeran and Robert Kraft will also reportedly donate $2m each after Kraft was challenged by the rapper, who was dismissed from the tour after speaking in support of Palestine
Content: Rapper Macklemore, who was dismissed as opening act of Ed Sheeran’s tour after speaking on-stage in support of Palestine. Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and prominent Israel donor, refused to let Macklemore play at his Gillette Stadium outside Boston.Photograph: Arnaud Finistre/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRapper Macklemore, who was dismissed as opening act of Ed Sheeran’s tour after speaking on-stage in support of Palestine. Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and prominent Israel donor, refused to let Macklemore play at his Gillette Stadium outside Boston.Photograph: Arnaud Finistre/AFP/Getty ImagesMacklemoreMacklemore pledges his $1m Ed Sheeran tour salary to PalestineEd Sheeran and Robert Kraft will also reportedly donate $2m each after Kraft was challenged by the rapper, who was dismissed from the tour after speaking in support of PalestineAdrian HortonandSian CainWed 16 Sep 2026 17.26 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMacklemorehas announced he will donate the $1m salary he was paid as an opening act forEd Sheeran’s Loop tour to organizations working with Palestinian people and relief in Gaza, after beingdroppedfrom the tour following backlash to his onstage comments in support ofPalestine.The rapper also challenged Robert Kraft, the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots and prominent Israel donor who refused to letMacklemoreplay at his Gillette Stadium outside Boston, to match his donation.“With everything that has happened over the last 48 hours, I want to bring the conversation back to where it belongs: to the Palestinian people who are still being killed, still living under military occupation, and still fighting for their freedom,” the Grammy-winning artistwroteon Instagram.“I will be donating the entire $1 million of my net earnings from Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour to six organizations working directly to support the Palestinian people. And I invite Robert Kraft to match my donation. Whatever we disagree about, perhaps we can agree on this: Palestinian lives are worth protecting. A Palestinian life is no less valuable than any other life on this earth.”In response, Kraft issued a statement announcing that he and Sheeran would donate $2m each “to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis”, without specifying which organisations or charities would receive the money.“I have dedicated much of my life to building bridges between all people. I believe deeply that all lives are worth protecting,” Kraft said. “Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis. Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges.”Ed Sheeran wants to stay out of politics. By quitting his tour, his support acts have exposed the hollowness of neutralityRead moreIn a two-minute speech during his set at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey earlier this month, Macklemore expressed his desire to see a “free Palestine. I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them.” His remarks prompted apetitionfrom the Israeli-American Council demanding his removal from the tour.Speaking again on stage the following day, he reiterated his support forPalestineand addressed Jewish members of the audience: “Criticism of Israel, criticism of apartheid, being against genocide in no way is a criticism of you. My message is for peace, love; for all human beings to be treated with dignity, respect and equality.”According to Sheeran, who posted hisown explanationon Tuesday morning outlining his desire to remain publicly neutral on political causes, Kraft, along with several other venue owners, informed the English singer that his tour could not play at their stadiums if Macklemore continued as an opener, prompting his removal. A day later, all four of Sheeran’s opening acts for the remainder of the Loop tour – Finneas, Aaron Rowe, Boega and Lukas Graham –withdrew from the tourin solidarity with Macklemore and Palestine.In his post, Macklemore said he hoped to “center the parents carrying their children into hospitals without the basic resources to treat them, and the physicians, paramedics, journalists and aid workers who keep going back in. I want to center the organizers and activists who have paid real costs for standing with Palestine. Their risk is of a far different order than mine.”He added: “Palestinians have lived for decades without basic rights and should not have to wait another day to be free. That is where my focus will remain. I will continue to stand with the Palestinian people and their fight for liberation. When the news cycle moves on, which it will, don’t move with it. Free Palestine.”Earlier Wednesday, Colin Kaepernick,whose NFL career was effectively endedby the NFL’s resistance to his protests against US police violence,joinedthe chorus of prominent figures criticizing Macklemore’s removal at the behest of NFL stadium owners. “The part that I hope people appreciate and take away in this moment is what [New England Patriots owner] Robert Kraft and what they’re saying by denying Macklemore the opportunity to go out and perform with Ed Sheeran is they are willing to collude,” the former quarterback said on theMeidasTouch podcast. “The [NFL owners] are openly colluding.”Kaepernick added that he thought NFL owners tried to hound outMacklemorein a similar way to him. “When we filed the grievance, it was like, well, the owners wouldn’t do that,” Kaepernick said. “Everybody just wants to win within theNFL. And the realization is, no. They want to protect their interests. They want to protect their power. They want to protect their money.”In his own Monday statement, Kraft said his decision to ban Macklemore from the Patriots’ stadium was due to his “recent actions” and “a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”.Explore more on these topicsMacklemoreIsrael-Gaza warPalestineEd SheerannewsShareReuse this content

title: Fresh evidence of C of E’s role in enslavement uncovered as church wrestles with reparations debate | Anglicanism | The Guardian
description: Register of British Slave Traders shows clergymen financed company that trafficked enslaved Africans on hundreds of voyages
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: Register of British Slave Traders shows clergymen financed company that trafficked enslaved Africans on hundreds of voyages
Content: Fresh questions are being raised about whether the Church of England is doing enough to atone for its role in enslavement, experts say.Composite: Guardian/Getty/Wayne CrichlowView image in fullscreenFresh questions are being raised about whether the Church of England is doing enough to atone for its role in enslavement, experts say.Composite: Guardian/Getty/Wayne CrichlowEnslaving nationAnglicanismFresh evidence of C of E’s role in enslavement uncovered as church wrestles with reparations debateRegister of British Slave Traders shows clergymen financed company that trafficked enslaved Africans on hundreds of voyagesChris OsuhCommunity affairs correspondent. Photography by Wayne CrichlowWed 16 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNearly 250 years after the abolitionist Ottobah Cugoano made the Christian case for reparative justice, the archbishop of Canterbury, Sarah Mullally, visited the Ghanaian shore where he was enslaved as a boy.After witnessing the dungeons beneath the chapel at Cape Coast Castle, once run by the Royal African Company (RAC), Mullally recommitted the Church of England to its “journey of repentance” for its role in slavery.View image in fullscreenRight: Archbishop Sarah Mullally visits Cape Coast Castle in Ghana, where the abolitionist Ottobah Cugoano, pictured left, was enslaved as a boy.Back in Britain, historians working on the newly digitisedRegister of British Slave Traderswere uncovering evidence that C of E clergy financed the RAC, which trafficked more African men, women and children than any other single organisation in the history of the slave trade.The register, which documents investors in Britain’s nearly 250-year transatlantic slave trade, includes 45 C of E clergymen, whose investments helped fund hundreds of slaving voyages and a 1720 relaunch of the RAC. Among them was Henry Brydges, later a canon at St Paul’s Cathedral, who bought half of his £10,000 shareholding on the day he became the Archdeacon of Rochester.Prof William Pettigrew, who led the project, said the register showed a “truly national picture”. Profits from enslavement filtered down to communities “from Cumbria to the Cotswolds” through bequests to parishes – evidence of a history of the C of E “giving slavery its blessing” and raising fresh questions about whether the church is doing enough to atone.In 2023, church commissioners – the C of E’s asset managers – launchedProject Spire,a £100m impact investment fund for communities affected by slavery’s legacies, which has caused division within the church. It is not a reparations fund, but is central to the church’s determination to be a force for justice and healing in the world. It was launched nearly 20 years after Rowan Williams, the former archbishop of Canterbury,rejected the idea that today’s church bears no responsibility for the past.View image in fullscreenThe register includes 45 C of E clergymen, whose investments co-funded hundreds of slaving voyages. Among them was Henry Brydges, later canon of St Paul’s Cathedral, pictured.However, Spire mainly responds to historic investments in the South Sea Company, which trafficked close to 45,000 enslaved Africans. That represents a “sliver of church complicity”, said Prof Alan Lester, a historical geographer at the University of Sussex.That complicity helped shape modern Britain, Lester said. Plantation profits helped fuel the Industrial Revolution, railways, public health, welfare, universities, schools, church building and the public finances. “Look at Anglican parishes in Jamaica, their ability to withstand climate change, and compare that with the wealth generated in Britain by the plantation complex,” he said.For the Rev Natasha Beckles, the dean of racial justice for Willesden, reckoning with this past goes to the heart of Christian faith.“What was the purpose of the cross if we’re not able to talk about this?” she said. “Slavery made the image of God transactional. There has to be an understanding of the impact on the world.”View image in fullscreen‘The public and people within the church don’t even know what the extent of the church’s involvement was,’ Dr Leona Vaughn says.Dr Leona Vaughn of the University of Liverpool, a co-organiser of a 2025 Anglican “truth-telling” event, said: “The public and people within the church don’t even know the extent of the church’s involvement.“We’ve not even started to come to terms with the ‘Slave Bible’,” she said, a C of E-sanctioned, heavily edited Bible, stripped of liberation narratives, that planters used as a tool of social control from 1807.The history of the United Society Partners in the Gospel (USPG), the C of E’s 325-year-old missionary partner, shows how powerful Anglicans practised and perpetuated transatlantic chattel slavery – a uniquely racialised, violent system of human commodification and forced mass migration. Today, members of USPG – of which Mullally is president – have committed to “the gospel’s call to break every chain of injustice”.View image in fullscreenThe ‘Slave Bible’, a C of E-sanctioned, heavily edited Bible that planters used as a tool of social control from 1807. Right, the Codrington estate in Barbados, where the SPG enslaved people.USPG’s forerunner, the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts (SPG), supplied chaplains to the RAC at Cape Coast Castle. For more than 120 years, with the involvement of C of E leaders, SPG enslaved people on the Codrington estate in Barbados, which generated the equivalent of £5m a year in today’s money.At Codrington, enslaved Africans were branded with the word “Society”, tortured with the lash, straitjacket and iron collar, and worked to death.In seven months in 1746, 19 enslaved people died– including Daniel, who was “shot by accident” – with three deaths in a single day.Pettigrew said the “clear signal” sent by the C of E’s relationship with Codrington was “if the church is doing it, why shouldn’t I?”After abolition, SPG and at least 96 clergy who enslaved people received millions in compensation for “loss of property”. In 2023,USPG launched its own £7m reparative justice programme.Christian collusion can be traced back to a 1452 papal bull authorising the enslavement of non-Christians, the author Malik Al Nasir said. He wants the C of E to digitise its records in the UK and the Caribbean.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toCotton CapitalStarting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the 17th century, John Cotton, a former Lincolnshire vicar, co-drafted a charter legalising slavery in New England.By the 1750s, high churchmen were codifying pro-slavery ideology: Thomas Newton, later the dean of St Paul’s Cathedral, argued Africans were destined to be “servants of servants”, while Thomas Francklin, later the chaplain to George III, said: “We use [African] bodies for our support and happiness.”View image in fullscreenThe London skyline from St Paul’s Cathedral, with the City in the distance. Experts say the C of E’s complicity in enslavement helped shape modern Britain.Some Anglican voices did oppose slavery. Condemning it in 1685, the preacher Morgan Godwyn said: “We have … conspired with Satan.”Project Spire’s critics have instead focused on the legacy of Anglican abolitionist MPs, such as William Wilberforce. Wilberforce’s 1823 anti-slavery petition was followed by his colleague Sir Thomas Fowell Buxton acknowledging that “we owe a large and liberal atonement”.In his 1787 book,Cugoano – who won his freedom in England– wrote that the injustice done to Africans “cries aloud for universal reformation and national repentance”. He drew on biblical scriptures such as Numbers, Leviticus, Exodus and Deuteronomy that included reparative principles.Class shaped church complicity, Beckles said. “The oldest child got the land, the second child they put in the church, the third was sent to the Caribbean.” That meant, Al Nasir said, that “one sibling could profit from slavery while another absolved it – the right hand washing the left”.Enslaved African Christian leaders helped force the issue of abolition – includingSamuel Sharpe, the deacon executed for leading Jamaica’s 1831-32 Baptist war.The posthumously published Demerara diaries of the English Methodist theRev John Smithalso educated the British public about the relentless beatings, toil and meagre diet – raw yellow plantains – endured by enslaved Africans. Smith’s preaching was blamed by Anglican planters for Guyana’s 1823 Demerara rebellion. He died awaiting execution.View image in fullscreenThomas Newton, who became the dean of St Paul’s Cathedral, said in the 18th century that Africans were destined to be ‘servants of servants’.The moral conviction of English non-conformists – such as Smith andQuaker abolitionists– contrasts with the 45 C of E clergymen in the register.The C of E already has an impact investment fund, so insiders have expressed surprise at the backlash against Spire, which is facing alegal challenge. In the House of Commons in September, the MP Marsha de Cordova, the second church estates commissioner, rebutted claims from rightwing critics that Spire diverts money from English churches.She said the church regarded historic links to slavery with profound regret, that Spire is funded from the commissioners’ own income rather than parish collections, and that the English ministry would receive £1.6bn over three years.A 2023 reportestimated Britain’s slavery debt at £18.6tn. For Beckles, no sum could be enough. “What do you say to a mother who has had her child taken from her? To talk about a figure is grotesque,” she said. “For that level of human suffering, you’d be writing a blank cheque.”In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing that the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a 10-year restorative justice initiative.Explore more on these topicsAnglicanismEnslaving nationChristianityReligionSlaveryReparations and reparative justiceColonialismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds | Slavery | The Guardian
description: Dozens of Bank of England directors and founding subscribers invested in trafficking of enslaved Africans
Author: David Conn
Headline: Dozens of Bank of England directors and founding subscribers invested in trafficking of enslaved Africans
Content: The scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged.Composite: Guardian/Diana EjaitaView image in fullscreenThe scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged.Composite: Guardian/Diana EjaitaEnslaving nationSlaverySlave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research findsDozens of Bank of England directors and founding subscribers invested in trafficking of enslaved AfricansDavid ConnInvestigations correspondentWed 16 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTShareTheBank of Englandand the British financial system were for centuries deeply involved in the enslavement and transatlantic trafficking of millions of African people, according to new research on Britain’s slavery history.Research by historians compiling theRegister of British Slave Tradershas found that the scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged. The Bank of England, the central bank owned by the government since nationalisation by Clement Attlee’s Labour administration in 1946, had dozens of financiers involved in its foundation who were also significant investors in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.Dr Michael Bennett of the University of Sheffield, who has conducted extensive research on the Bank’s historical involvement in enslavement, has found that 24 directors were investors in the trafficking of enslaved African people. Four were among the London elites who were founding directors of the Bank in 1694. The other 20 were in office at Threadneedle Street over the next century.The last, Christopher Puller, was a shipper of weapons for the slave trade and co-owner of a 1786 voyage that trafficked enslaved people from the Gambia to Jamaica, according to the register. Puller was a director for 11 years before he died in 1789. Nine of the 24 were also governors of the Bank.View image in fullscreenWealth generated from the slave trade formed part of the Bank of England’s initial capital, according to Dr Michael Bennett.Photograph: Alexander Spatari/Getty ImagesBennett also researched the founding subscribers to the Bank of England, finding that at least 30 invested in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. At their head were the king and queen of the day, William III and Mary II, who held shares in the Royal African Company. It is clear, Bennett said, that wealth generated from the slave trade formed part of the Bank’s initial capital.“Slave traders and their wealth were firmly embedded within Britain’s, especially London’s, private banks and financial corporations during the 17th and 18th centuries. They shaped the development of the financial system,” he said. “Banks and other institutions, like insurers, provided the financial services that supported, and made great wealth from, the transatlantic slave economy.“The Bank of England supported this system throughout, and directly provided financial services to the slave trade. Its clients included the Royal African Company and the South Sea Company.”An archetypal example of a Bank of England director in the register is John Rudge,the MP for Evesham. He was a director of the Bank between 1699 and 1740, and governor in 1713-15. Rudge was also a shareholder and assistant (director) in the RAC and deputy governor of the South Sea Company.The findings of the register add to the research carried out by historians behind theLegacies of British Slavery(LBS) archive at University College London, which documents owners of enslaved people on plantations. That research found that 16 past governors of the Bank of England and 26 directors had a financial interest in the ownership of enslaved people and plantations in the period before abolition in 1833. The Bank itself, and the Treasury, were centrally involved in paying out £20m, the equivalent of £23bn today according to one method of calculation, in “compensation” to enslavers under the abolition legislation. Nothing was paid to the people who had been enslaved and trafficked.View image in fullscreenThe Black Lives Matter protests in 2020 prompted several high street banks and financial institutions to acknowledge their historical involvement in slavery.Photograph: pawopa3336/Getty Images/iStockphotoThe Black Lives Matter protests of 2020 prompted several high street banks and financial institutions toacknowledge their historical involvement in slavery. Dr Nicholas Draper, who led the LBS research, was also a lead investigator for the register and he discovered many more historic slave traders who were founders of private banks and other financial organisations.Research by Bennett after the BLM protests found that the Bank of England hadowned 599 enslaved peopleon two plantations.An exhibition at the Bank in 2022 included the names of the enslaved people. Most of the men, women and children listed had European names such as Pierre, Catherine and Alexandre, with no information about the country from which they were taken.The Bank also acknowledged andapologised forpast governors and directors having been involved in the slave trade.Humphry Morice, a longtime director and governor from 1727-29,was also an MPand defrauded the Bank to fund his trafficking operations.Morice was described by Prof Matthew David Mitchell, in an articlepublished on the Bank’s website, as “the biggest London-based trafficker of enslaved human beings from Africa to the British colonies in America.” Morice was responsible for equipping about 110 ship voyages between 1704 and 1732, transporting more than 30,000 enslaved men women and children to Jamaica, Barbados, Virginia and elsewhere in America, Mitchell wrote. “This was his principal commercial activity, and it is for this that he must chiefly be remembered.”While the Bank has acknowledged this history and apologised, the Treasury has not publicly done so. This is in line with the government’s position of resisting the discussion of reparations and not acknowledging culpability for the centuries of trafficking and enslaving.Bennett’s further findings will increase the pressure on the government to do so, which is buildingfrom Caribbean and African countries.A Bank of England spokesperson said it had explored its connections to enslavement in depth in its 2022 exhibition, adding: “We are grateful for Dr Bennett’s collaboration on that work.”In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing that the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a 10-year restorative justice initiative.
