title: Is EU’s offer to Canada a blueprint for Britain – or a reminder it is out in the cold? | European Union | The Guardian
description: Ursula von der Leyen has opened door for Canada to become associate member to deepen links in ‘openly hostile world’
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Ursula von der Leyen has opened door for Canada to become associate member to deepen links in ‘openly hostile world’
Content: Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, and Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, in Strasbourg, France.Photograph: Justin Tang/The Canadian Press/APView image in fullscreenCanada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, and Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, in Strasbourg, France.Photograph: Justin Tang/The Canadian Press/APEuropean UnionAnalysisIs EU’s offer to Canada a blueprint for Britain – or a reminder it is out in the cold?Lisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentUrsula von der Leyen has opened door for Canada to become associate member to deepen links in ‘openly hostile world’Wed 16 Sep 2026 14.57 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareCanada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has been advocating closer alignment with “middle powers” since January in the face of recklessness in Washington.But what should worry another middle power, the UK, is that it was Brussels that came up with Wednesday’s big reveal in Strasbourg.To a standing ovation at her State of the Union address, Ursula von der Leyen said she wanted toopen the door to Canada becoming the EU’s first “associate member”in a push to forge new ⁠links among allies in “an openly hostile world”.The European Commission president’s deal could be seen as an “earthquake” offersaid Joël Reland, of UK in a Changing Europe,though it remains “deliciously vague”.But it also sets Canada apart from the UK, which could, once upon a time, have had some sort of associate membership with the EU were it not for the drive for a clean-break Brexit.The last time associate membership of the EU was mooted was in relation to Ukraine as an off-the-books novel way of bringing Kyiv closer to the bloc without become a fully fledged member state.New partnerships, von der Leyen said, were needed “in the cold fragility of today’s world” and in the face of an increasingly assertive China.Just moments earlier she spoke about the need for the EU to diversify urgently its supply of critical raw materials (CRM) and rare earths currently dominated by China, allowing it to follow Japan and stockpile said minerals needed for everything from the car to the defence industries.It is not a new subject – after all the EU has been grappling with China’s export surplus since 2023 and it introduced the Critical Raw Materials Act as far back as 2024.The prospect of an enhanced relationship with Ottawa is one that Keir Starmer might have dreamed of.Canada has something the EU desperately needs – rich supplies of CRM and rare earths – and the EU has something Canada urgently wants: new markets for products it can no longer sell into the EU in the face of a trade war with Donald Trump.Speaking before von der Leyen’s speech, Tobias Cremer, a German social democrat MEP, said a new deeper relationship between the EU and Canada could be a blueprint for other countries, including the UK.Bernd Lange, the influential chair of the European parliament’s international trade committee, said associate membership could “become a model for close transcontinental partnerships with democratic countries against the new model of the law of the strongest”.After Iceland’s rejection of membership of the EU, Fabian Zuleeg, the chief executive and chief economist of the European Policy Centre, suggestedit was time that the EU developed new models, beyond the European Economic Area, that might offer “partial, gradual or associated membership options”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReland said the vagueness of the offer extended to Canada could be promising for the UK’s hopes for a similar offer.“Any deep Canadian integration into the EU market would take some very heavy work to negotiate a defined set of treaty-bound rights and obligations, and so it seems more likely that – at least in the short term – cooperation will focus on more vaguely constructed alliances for ‘prosperity’ and ‘security’,” which aligns with the UK government’s desires, Relandwrote on Wednesday.In the current political climate in the UK, it is difficult to envisage a world in which Andy Burnham would encourage any associate membership of the EU. He has a steely focus on domestic issues and is keen to avoid going down any Brexit wormholes.The UK is seeking a reset with the EU, but the goals in the first year were modest and have yet to be achieved.The offer to Canada suggests the bigger ambitions for relations with the EU the better.Additional reporting: Jennifer RankinExplore more on these topicsEuropean UnionEuropeCanadaUrsula von der LeyenCritical mineralsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: England ’Til I Die review – a chilling portrait of a town turning on its neighbours  | Television | The Guardian
description: Film-maker Jamie Roberts follows a Sussex man’s journey into the far right. If it wasn’t so horrific, parts could feel like they’d been written by Chris Morris
Author: Hannah J Davies
Headline: Film-maker Jamie Roberts follows a Sussex man’s journey into the far right. If it wasn’t so horrific, parts could feel like they’d been written by Chris Morris
Content: Liam Tomsett in England ’Til I Die.Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreenLiam Tomsett in England ’Til I Die.Photograph: Channel 4TV reviewTelevisionReviewEngland ’Til I Die review – a chilling portrait of a town turning on its neighboursFilm-maker Jamie Roberts follows a Sussex man’s journey into the far right. If it wasn’t so horrific, parts could feel like they’d been written by Chris MorrisHannah J DaviesWed 16 Sep 2026 18.05 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 18.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStanding in the street shouting virulent slogans or chanting loaded refrains about Islam was the mainstay of British far-right groups such as the EDL in the early 2010s. Now, that behaviour feels almost quaint. Recent weeks have seen major anti-immigration blockades in Dover led by balaclava-wearing men, and direct action against asylum seekers arriving on a small boat in Portsmouth.Clearly, in 2026, the blame for much of the societal rot that has set in has been placed frequently at the feet of migrants, and vigilante tactics are on the rise. Channel 4’s one-off documentary arrives with depressing timeliness, then, telling a story that serves as a synecdoche for events playing out across the UK, at large. It is, says its maker, “the story of a community on the frontline of Britain’s broken asylum system, and one man’s journey into the heart of the far-right movement”.Film-maker Jamie Roberts – whose previous documentaries includeAngry, White and ProudandUkraine: Enemy in the Woods– has form in finding people whose personal stories speak to a wider malaise, and letting them recount those stories in their own words. We aren’t told whether or not utilities manager turned anti-immigration activist Liam Tomsett is in the wrong for the way he behaves in his Sussex town of Crowborough, where he blocks contractors from making deliveries to an asylum centre. But it would be a stretch to say that Tomsett comes out of the programme looking overly reasonable – not least when he finds himself in an altercation with some of the contractors at the site, and is arrested and charged with common assault and possession of an offensive weapon. (For Tomsett, it is about “keeping your community safe”, while he says the hammer found in his car was for DIY.) The charges are later dropped.In Crowborough – once a sleepy market town known for its associations with Arthur Conan Doyle and Winnie-the-Pooh – we learn how an asylum accommodation centre at a disused army camp has become the centre of local tensions. Green councillor (and the party’s deputy leader) Rachel Millward is abused and heckled by her constituents at a council meeting, where one woman asks: “I’d like to know how she’d feel if it was her being raped – would she be OK with them coming here then?” Tomsett is among those who shout down Millward. He then follows her as she walks to her car, calling her “a disgrace” and taunting her as she cries. Elsewhere, he asks local counter-protesters how they feel about having asylum seekers they don’t know living so close by, prompting a 10/10 response from one of the women: “We don’t know you, apart from the fact that you’re out on bail …”View image in fullscreenHighly upsetting … a protest in England ’Til I Die.Photograph: Channel 4If it wasn’t so horrific, parts of England ’Til I Die could almost feel like something written by Chris Morris. One woman launches into an extended rant about burqas, halal meat and dogs, while three men from the asylum centre whom Tomsett and a group of other men follow down the road turn out to be Iranian Christians on their way to church. Tomsett and his Crowborough Says No collaborator Gary believe that their actions are “a fuck-you to the government”. But it seems the people they’re truly hurting are their own neighbours; as one anonymous contributor says, it’s a “really horrible feeling” knowing that people in the town are protesting against others that look like her. Unsettling aerial camera work only emphasises the sense that Crowborough is becoming something of a strange and unknowable place, just not in the way that Tomsett claims.While much of this programme is highly upsetting to watch, Roberts leaves room for nuance – be it about the father Tomsett is yet to grieve, the adult children whose lives he has been absent from, or the online radicalisation he has ostensibly undergone (“mainstream won’t touch it”, he says, scrolling through rightwing content online). Roberts also knows just when to chime in with a killer question: when Tomsett threatens a local business, he asks, “Do you not stop for a moment [and think] that maybe they see you as the dangerous one …?” It’s an incredibly tough topic, but one that Roberts handles with care. It feels particularly crucial, following his last project, Gaza: How to Survive a Warzone, which was mired in controversy around its child narrator’s family, and led toan internal BBC review(in a recent Guardian interview, Roberts said that his company, Hoyo Films, had tightened its editorial procedures).Five months after the council meeting, Millward reflects on the “slightly out-of-body experience” of being shouted down by her constituents. She doesn’t think the asylum centre plan was a good one, nor does she agree with the furtive way it seems to have been organised by central government. But she appears to have been shaken by the reaction in Crowborough, and the division “that feels like it gets deeper and deeper all the time”. Clearly, there are some serious problems to contend with in Britain today, and a working class that has been sorely let down by austerity politics. But it’s hard to come away from England ’Til I Die without the feeling that people like Tomsett are making things so much worse.England ’Til I Die is on Channel 4 nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDocumentaryFactual TVPolitics TVImmigration and asylumreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Charli xcx Music, Fashion, Film tour review – an electrifying and deafening pop evolution  | Charli xcx | The Guardian
description: The tireless star brings her latest, somewhat over-explained album to the stage for a dazzling and euphoric show
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: The tireless star brings her latest, somewhat over-explained album to the stage for a dazzling and euphoric show
Content: Charli xcx performing in New York.Photograph: Henry RedcliffeView image in fullscreenCharli xcx performing in New York.Photograph: Henry RedcliffeCharli xcxReviewCharli xcx Music, Fashion, Film tour review – an electrifying and deafening pop evolutionBarclays Center, BrooklynThe tireless star brings her latest, somewhat over-explained album to the stage for a dazzling and euphoric showAdrian HortonWed 16 Sep 2026 14.55 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 16.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor more than a year now, I have often returned, when seeking a bar for which to measure true pop transcendence, to the memory of Charli xcx taking the Other Stage at Glastonbury: the unofficial headliner, a year out from her culture-shifting opus Brat, commanded a dizzying 60,000 people with an imperious “don’t fucking play with me” and the stunning brute force of a performer at peak power. It was surreal, as a longtime fan, to witness an artist who was as recently as 2022 playing to cult followings in 2,000-cap venues convert thousands more in real time, to see years of hard-earned pop instincts and artistry collide with the zeitgeist in acareer-defining, you-had-to-be-there achievement.Charli xcx: Music, Fashion, Film review – slippery search into selfhood that hits just as hard as BratRead moreBut life goes on, of course, and Charli, like the rest of us who surfed the high of Brat summer 2024, found herself on an inevitable comedown. A lesser artist may have confronted the question of what comes next with blunt commercial logic – more, again – but Charli, a self-professed workaholic and tireless interrogator of one’s own image, proved to be creatively restless, if scattered. A cinephile rebrand, three films at Sundance, an Instagram-dominating celebrity wedding, adefanged satireof her own sudden ubiquity, a windswept soundtrack that more or less saved the otherwisedreadful Wuthering Heights– all suggested a self-aware ambivalence with mainstream success that threatened to corrode all that came after. With the release this July ofMusic, Fashion, Film, her eighth studio album, I worried that she had succumbed to a seemingly manic drive to stay visible. The album, a deceptively vulnerable and winking pivot to rock that was either self-aggrandizing pastiche or genius, depending on what angle/substance/context you beheld it, did not seem to stand up the scrutiny and over-explanation of relentless celebrity promotion.But on Tuesday night at the Barclays Center, for the third night of the album’s tour, Charli proved doubters wrong with the most satisfying answer yet to what comes next: a full-volume tribute to pop’s euphoric potential for obliteration that substantiated the album’s most potent themes (the fragility of self, egoism, mortality), a thesis statement of artistic evolution that seamlessly integrated her past and present. After essentially conquering the art of abrasive minimalism with her solo stunting for Brat, Charli has embraced just enough maximalism to freshen up an arena tour – pyrotechnics, backup dancers (in club-ready bras, of course) and most evocatively, a pyramid set composed almost entirely of layered speakers, befitting a pop artist refreshingly in touch with her death drive. Forget toothless escapism – more than any other main pop girl, Charli has embraced the notion that, as David Cronenberg advises in a spoken-word outro blared from the screen, oblivion is freedom. Fitting, then, to strut and writhe and scream at the altar of a giant, smoking amplifier.View image in fullscreenCharli xcx performing in New York.Photograph: Henry RedcliffeLoudness can, in fact, count for a lot. After several festival headline slots this summer proving the new material’s live mettle, the blown-up Music, Fashion, Film tour confirms the album’s caustic yet restorative vision, or at least that the contested MFF opening salvo Rock Music has its time and place. The new songs suddenly make sense when delivered on high by Charli and her band of underfed musicians that would be seen on stages in 2007 (not coincidentally, also the name of the album’s catchiest track), amped up to the max and crackling with live guitars – deliriously searching, itchy and jagged, even if the crowd’s head-banging in response was at best polite.The bristling arrangements cast the album in a flattering grayscale light, less a pop departure and more an extension of Charli’s longstanding search of catharsis and embrace of contradictions, brash fiendishness by a different name. The transitions from Wuthering Heights track House – a show highlight dripping in strobe-lit distortion – to “surprise” fan-favorite throwback Next Level Charli to new track Dying for You to a relentless five-song Brat mini-show were near seamless, if appropriately deafening from all sides. You can’t really accuse her of riding the contrails of Brat when the tracks – Von Dutch, 365 remix, 360, Sympathy is a Knife among them – still have the propulsion of a jet engine; I may forever hear the echo of gay men, women and apparently children screaming “bumpin’ that” off the Barclays ceiling.But Charli is far, far savvier than to resort to sandblasting fans into ear-ringing submission; the show keeps just enough of her minimalist bent to suggest a morphing of her club-rat persona, embodying the mesmerizing highs and crushing lows of ego. No CGI visuals, no guests, no stage banter, just a singular vision of persona: one minute she’s strutting down the runway under fashion lights flanked by an army of imitators to the dead-eyed shopaholic requiem Card Declined, the next she’s alone on the floor, then merely a solo silhouette disappearing into fog.Nothing lasts forever, Cronenberg reminds us in the Music, Fashion, Film song of a similar name – No One Lasts Forever – that serves as both the album and show’s sticky finale. Flanked by dancers, Charli struck and held a pose meant to be captured for posterity, backed by the looping certainty of impermanence – “they are dead, they are gone, nothing lasts forever,” no more explanation needed. There are now, conservatively, 10,000 photos of that final tableau, and 10,000 more from the night before that will live in the iClouds of hardcore and bandwagon fans alike probably forever. But the moment is inevitably, sadly, thrillingly gone.Explore more on these topicsCharli xcxPop and rockNew YorkreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ferritin face: the new health scare taking social media by storm | Health & wellbeing | The Guardian
description: Seeing a pallid, washed-out face in the mirror? Prepare to be diagnosed …
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Seeing a pallid, washed-out face in the mirror? Prepare to be diagnosed …
Content: Is your pallor the sign of something serious?Photograph: Posed by model; Ekaterina Demidova/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIs your pallor the sign of something serious?Photograph: Posed by model; Ekaterina Demidova/Getty ImagesPass notesHealth & wellbeingFerritin face: the new health scare taking social media by stormSeeing a pallid, washed-out face in the mirror? Prepare to be diagnosed …Wed 16 Sep 2026 12.40 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Ferritin face.Age:The name is new, but the symptoms are old.Symptoms:Pallor, dull skin, dark circles under your eyes. Looking washed out, basically.What are you, a mirror?Oh no, does this describe you? Do you also have ferritin face?Aren’t those just symptoms for “looking tired”?Is thisone of those social media health scareswith little to no scientific basis?No! I mean, yes, the term has recently become very popular on social media, as reported inthe Washington Post. Ferritin face is not a real medical term (nor are there consistent criteria that define it) – butferritinat least is definitely a thing.Tell me about ferritin, then.It’s a complex globular protein that stores iron in the body in its inactive form. If you have low ferritin levels, it could indicate an iron deficiency.And what happens if I have an iron deficiency?If it is severe and goes untreated for long enough, it could lead to tachycardia, breathlessness, chest pain and heart complications.This is terrible! How can I cure myself?Well, earlier this summer, Allure magazine wrote a long piece entitledWhat It Means to Have “Ferritin Face”, calling iron deficiency an epidemic that women are prone to. It had plenty of advice.Like what? Tell me now, before my dark circles kill me!It can often be overcome with a change of diet, as meat and green leafy vegetables are a good source. But you can also just go and have an intravenous iron infusion.An IV it is!Be warned that, according to a leading iron infusion clinic, it could cost you in the region of £800.Cabbage! Someone get me a cabbage!Alternatively, you could stop crapping your pants at every social media health scare. You should never diagnose and treat yourself via TikTok clips.OK, fine.Think it about it sensibly. There is a vast difference between ferritin face and actual anaemia. Anaemia doesn’t just make you pale and tired-looking; it can leave you fatigued and breathless, with headaches, dizziness, palpitations and a loss of concentration being common symptoms.Oh, I don’t have any of those.Good. But if you do,the NHS recommendsthat you see a GP, who will try to discover the underlying reason for your iron deficiency – which could be anything from heavy periods to cancer – and put you on a course of iron tablets.So I don’t need to worry about ferritin.Probably not, no. But get an early night tonight. You look dreadful.Do say:“You do not have ferritin face.”Don’t say:“But youdohave ferreting face, which is far worse.”Explore more on these topicsHealth & wellbeingPass notesHealthSocial mediaDigital mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Are you cleaning your cat litter box correctly? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: How often should you clean your cat’s litter box? Plus three other tips for peak cat cleanliness
Author: Madeleine Aggeler
Headline: How often should you clean your cat’s litter box? Plus three other tips for peak cat cleanliness
Content: A good litter box setup is important to a cat’s health and happiness – and it’s not that difficult to achieve.Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA good litter box setup is important to a cat’s health and happiness – and it’s not that difficult to achieve.Photograph: Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesWell actuallyAre you cleaning your cat litter box correctly?How often should you clean your cat’s litter box? Plus three other tips for peak cat cleanlinessMadeleine AggelerWed 16 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 16.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThroughout history, people have reveredcats. Ancient Egyptians worshipped feline deities. In Norse mythology, the Viking goddess Freya rode around in a sled pulled by two cats. And my father regularly takes his cat on walks around town in a little bubble backpack so she can see the sights.As anyone who has lived with a cat knows, we serve them and not the other way around. This includes the messy and malodorous task of tending their litter box.According to experts, there is often room for improvement. “The most common mistake people make when it comes to their cat’s litter is creating a setup that works for them instead of for the cat,” says Samantha Bell, cat expert and content strategist for the non-profit rescue Best Friends Animal Society. “But we bring our cats into our homes, so we need to do our best to ensure they are as comfortable as possible, and a litter box is a huge part of their comfort.”Below, what you need to know to ensure your feline overlord’s bathroom satisfaction.How many litter boxes should you have?On TikTok, I once saw someone claim cat owners should have a litter box in every room. I imagined my small apartment crammed with litter boxes and despaired. “Is that what you want?” I desperately asked my cat, who doesn’t speak English and doesn’t respect me enough to answer me even if she did.Unfortunately, I’m allergic to my adorable kitten – here’s what doctors advisedRead moreFortunately, like much TikTok content, this wasn’t true. But more than one litter box is often a good idea, especially if you have multiple cats.“It is recommended that there be one litter box for each cat in the household, plus an extra,” says Dr Lori Bierbrier, Ssenior medical director of community medicine, east coast, for the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty toAnimals(ASPCA). For instance, if you have two cats, three is the ideal number. If you live in a multilevel home, “there should be one litter box on each floor,” she adds; this ensures cats don’t need to travel too far when the need strikes.Cats can share litter boxes, says Dr Marci Koski, certified feline behavior and training consultant and owner of Feline Behavior Solutions. “It can be a good way for them to get to know each other,” she says.But some cats don’t like to share, “especially if there’s a contentious relationship between cats”, Koski says. “That’s all the more reason to have more litter box locations than cats.”What is the ideal litter box setup?“There are quite a few elements that go into creating a good litter box setup for one cat, but it doesn’t need to be complicated or difficult,” says Koski.Graphic with three lines of text that say, in bold, ‘Well Actually’, then ‘Read more on living a good life in a complex world,’ then a pinkish-lavender pill-shaped button with white letters that say ‘More from this section’Make sure the box is big enough. “Most boxes that you find in the pet store are too small,” says Bell. According to experts, a litter box should be 1.5 times the length of your cat, measuring from their nose to the base of their tail. “That should give them enough room to dig, bury and turn around without touching the walls,” says Koski.Use an open box.Though humans may prefer closed boxes that hide the waste, most cats prefer open boxes “because that gives them a wider field of view and helps them feel safe”, says Koski. “Plus, it doesn’t trap unpleasant scents all in one place.” The entrance should also be “low enough for them to get in easily”, says Bell.Choose the right location.“Cats prefer that their litter boxes be located in a quiet but not ‘cornered’ location,” says Bierbrier. This means that they want to be able to see other people and animals approaching, and have multiple escape routes in case they want to leave their boxes quickly. Keep boxes away from “busy, loud or intimidating places”, like next to the washer and dryer, or areas with a lot of foot traffic, says Bierbrier. Additionally, keep the box away from the cat’s food and water, suggests Bell, explaining that cats are extremely clean and don’t want their food too close to their toilet.Use the right litter.Our house cats’ ancestors were wild desert cats, says Bell, and some of those instincts remain. “So when you’re thinking about what kind of litter to use, think about the closest thing to sand,” she says. Most cats prefer unscented, clumping litter with a medium to fine texture, says Bierbrier. As for how much to use, Bell says the litter depth should be “deep enough to be able to cover their waste comfortably” – usually between 2-3in.How often should you clean the litter box?Experts agree that litter should be scooped at least once per day, and maybe more depending on how heavily the litter box is used (if it is used by multiple cats, for example) or if your cat is particularly picky.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe litter also needs to be fully replaced from time to time. Depending on the type of litter you use, Koski says, this could be as frequently as every 2-3 days for some pine or paper litters, or once every month for clumping clay litters.The litter box itself should also be replaced every year or two, says Bell – “especially if you see scratches in it”, because these scratches can harbor bacteria and odor.What are signs a cat is not happy with its litter box?Should you get a cat? Five expert tips for making life-changing decisionsRead moreBierbrier says signs that the cat’s litter box is not being cleaned correctly include:Foul odorscoming from the box.The cat exhibitsstrange behaviorsaround the box, like excessive meowing or crying.The catperches on the edges of the box“to avoid touching dirty litter with their paws”.The catrushes in and out of the boxas quickly as possible, and does little digging.The catscratches at areas around the box, like walls or floors, instead of digging in the litter.One of the biggest red flags is if the cat starts avoiding the litter box altogether. This may be a sign of poor litter hygiene, but it could also be a sign of something more serious.“There are many reasons a cat may eliminate outside of a litter box, and none of them are because they are bad, spiteful, jealous or just ‘being a jerk’,” says Ball. When a cat eliminates outside their box, it is because they are trying to communicate that something is wrong. “They don’t want to do it,” she explains. “They’re clean creatures.”If your cat has accidents outside the litter box, don’t punish it, Ball says. Instead, make an appointment with the vet as soon as possible. Ball’s own cat peed on her one night. The next day, she took him to the vet and discovered that he had diabetes, which causes him to drink more water. “Since he is a senior, he may not have been able to control it while he was asleep.”Not cleaning a litter box properly can also lead to health problems for a cat, says Koski. “Cats can get urinary tract infections from unclean litter boxes, and those can be immensely painful,” she says.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyCatsPetsAnimalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cassandra Wilson obituary | Jazz | The Guardian
description: American jazz singer and songwriter who was inspired by the Delta blues and gospel sounds of her Mississippi childhood
Author: John Fordham
Headline: American jazz singer and songwriter who was inspired by the Delta blues and gospel sounds of her Mississippi childhood
Content: Cassandra Wilson was blessed with a remarkable voice of note-bending elasticity, lustrous textures and a vaulting range.Photograph: Fernand Fourcade/SIPA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenCassandra Wilson was blessed with a remarkable voice of note-bending elasticity, lustrous textures and a vaulting range.Photograph: Fernand Fourcade/SIPA/ShutterstockJazzObituaryCassandra Wilson obituaryAmerican jazz singer and songwriter who was inspired by the Delta blues and gospel sounds of her Mississippi childhoodJohn FordhamWed 16 Sep 2026 12.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 12.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCassandra Wilson, the double Grammy-winning jazz vocalist and songwriter who has died aged 70, was described in 2001 by Time magazine as “America’s best singer”. Superlatives accompanied Wilson throughout her career; her vocal skills supported them.Wilson’s ancestry was West African and European, and the Delta blues and gospel sounds she heard in herMississippichildhood affected her deeply – but so did the guitar harmonies her father taught her, and the early instruction in classical piano she received from her music-teacher mother. Both her parents were Miles Davis and Motown admirers, too.I first heard Wilson live at a small arts festival at London’s Half Moon theatre in 1989. Some of the music press was touting the then 33-year-old as a “jazz singer for the 90s”. But Wilson had been audible on the jazz cognoscenti’s radar for at least four years before that – on her assured contributions to the progressive postbop albums by the US saxophonistSteve Coleman, which spawned the edgy, genre-fluid, new-jazz movement dubbed M-Base. Also there was her own sharply contrasting collection of American songbook classics (including Polka Dots and Moonbeams, and Shall We Dance?) on the acclaimed 1988 release Blue Skies.Wilson offered glimpses of much of what was to come in her work at that Half Moon gig – deftly interweaving horn-like swerves of pitch and fast bebop scat phrasing from the lineage of Ella Fitzgerald and Betty Carter with the spinechilling contralto soulfulness ofNina Simone, alongside abstract sounds more suggestive of free-jazz.She won Grammy awards for the eclectic New Moon Daughter (1996) with its Robert Johnson, Billie Holiday and Monkees covers, and for the highly personal standards-based Loverly (2009). She had also played, to great acclaim, one of the two central roles as enslaved people in Wynton Marsalis’s Pulitzer-winning jazz oratorio, Blood on the Fields (1997).Born in Jackson, Mississippi, Cassandra was the youngest of the three children of Mary (nee McDaniel) and Herman Fowlkes Jr, who were both teachers. Herman was also a bass guitarist in local bands and taught his daughter basic guitar chords after she had had piano lessons from her mother; by the time she entered high school she played the guitar and clarinet, and was beginning to write her own songs.Cassandra had also heard plenty of Delta blues music and the grittily dramatic autobiographical revelations of such African-American blues pioneers as Muddy Waters and Johnson had already enthralled her. But in secondary school, at Millsaps college, her cultural and social connections widened. She played Dorothy in a school production of The Wizard of Oz at 16, discovered Bob Dylan and Joni Mitchell and formed a folk trio with two white fellow-students – a liaison facilitated by Mississippi’s long-delayed desegregation of its schools in 1970, and which she would acknowledge as a musical turning point for her.Wilson attended Jackson State University, graduating in 1980 with a degree in communication techniques and mass-media methods. It was an education that pointed her towards work in television and radio, but she was already performing in coffee-houses and clubs as a jazz/folk singer.In 1981 she moved to New Orleans with Anthony Wilson, her first husband and a radio host. The marriage later ended in divorce. The crescent city’s musical opportunities were plentiful, and Wilson sang the vocal lead on anAllen Toussaint-produced Latin-jazz album called Tropical Breeze, with Jasmine, a local band. She also sat in withEllis Marsalis, and Earl Turbinton Jr, a soul/R&B saxophonist, gave her music lessons.In 1982, Wilson moved to New York, joined jam sessions, studied ear training with the trombonistGrachan Moncur III, and encountered Coleman’s adventurous expansions of bebop into funk, hip-hop, 12-tone modern-classical ideas, and the spontaneous harmony ensemble methods of his namesakeOrnette Coleman.Wilson contributed expressive vocals to Steve Coleman’s albums Motherland Pulse and On the Edge of Tomorrow (1985, 1986), experiences that stretched her talents for impromptu wordless vocals, and the note-bending elasticity, lustrous textures, and vaulting range of her remarkable voice.She began releasing her own albums for the German producer Stefan Winter on his new JMT label, releases that evolved from M-Base’s structural radicalism to more song-based originals and covers drawing on a lyrical soulfulness deep within her Delta background. It was her third album for JMT, the standards-based Blue Skies (1988), that alerted mainstream fans and the music business to Wilson’s wider appeal.In 1989, Wilson was invited to open for Davis, a personal idol, at the Chicago JVCJazzfestival, and by 1993 she was signed to the renowned Blue Note label. With the albums Blue Light ’Til Dawn and New Moon Daughter (her first Grammy-winner), Wilson revealed how powerfully she could re-imagine a famous song such as Strange Fruit, as well as classics by Mitchell, Johnson, Van Morrison – and the Monkees’ Last Train to Clarksville, chosen by Wilson for its Vietnam-bound US soldier’s message. She tended to undersell her fine original compositions such as Until and Memphis, and her sensitive delivery of them deserved more attention than they received in her most cover-devoted years.Travelling Miles, Wilson’s 1999 tribute, featured some of her most expressive singing – especially on the evocative Time After Time – although her lyrics overlaid on what had been spontaneous Davis instrumentals occasionally detracted from the original pieces’ implacably hypnotic drive. Belly of the Sun (2002) was a personal homage to blues of all kinds (recorded in an abandoned Mississippi railway station) that included Wichita Lineman, and Dylan’s Shelter from the Storm; and Loverly (2008) was an affectionate return to standard songs after a long gap, enhanced by the presence of the pianistJason Moranin the lineup.Wilson released her final solo album, the respectful homage to Holiday, Coming Forth By Day, in 2015. The same year, she returned to live in Jackson, founding a jazz club and a record label with an old friend, the singer Rhonda Richmond, to promote the arts in Mississippi.Boston’s Berklee College of Music awarded Wilson an honorary doctorate in music in 2020, and in 2022 the US government presented her with its highest jazz award, a National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Master fellowship. Her final live performance came in June this year, at the Toronto jazz festival.Her further marriages to Bruce Lincoln and Isaach de Bankolé ended in divorce. She is survived by her son Jeris, from her first marriage.Cassandra Marie Fowlkes Wilson, singer, born 4 December 1955; died 1 September 2026Explore more on these topicsJazzMiles DavisMotown recordsElla FitzgeraldMississippiobituariesShareReuse this content

title: No matter how deranged and delusional your podcast is, Liz Truss can go further | John Crace | The Guardian
description: In the Trusster’s latest appearance, she says Blair and Brown had a plot to dismantle civilisation and the Tories were part of the woke establishment
Author: John Crace
Headline: In the Trusster’s latest appearance, she says Blair and Brown had a plot to dismantle civilisation and the Tories were part of the woke establishment
Content: Liz Truss is every rightwinger’s favourite guest. She makes everyone else seem almost normal.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLiz Truss is every rightwinger’s favourite guest. She makes everyone else seem almost normal.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianThe politics sketchPoliticsNo matter how deranged and delusional your podcast is, Liz Truss can go furtherJohn CraceIn the Trusster’s latest appearance, she says Blair and Brown had a plot to dismantle civilisation and the Tories were part of the woke establishmentWed 16 Sep 2026 13.15 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareSome things you can set your watch by. Like every time small boats are in the news, the shadow home secretary, Chris Philp, will manoeuvre himself in front of a camera to suggest that all male migrants are either murderers or rapists. Probably both.But some things feel older than time itself. LikeLiz Trusstrying to persuade the world she was right all along. Most former prime ministers leave Downing Street relatively quietly. Lord Big Dave, the Maybot and even Boris nurse their grudges in private. Rishi lives in semi-retirement – almost a recluse – and only attends parliament when it suits him. Keir has been almost totally airbrushed out of history in a couple of months.Liz, though, is the outlier. She refuses to give up. The last cockroach alive after a nuclear apocalypse. Even now, she probably has a platoon of nuns locked up in her basement in south-east London where they are being forced to embroider a 70-metre tapestry dedicated to a revisionist history of her 49 days in office. One in which an old monarch dies and a new king ascends the throne. As one Elizabethan era ends so another Elizabethan era begins and a grateful nation bows down to her genius.You have to wonder if this obsession is healthy. Most normal people might be slightly embarrassed to be remembered as the UK’s shortest serving prime minister. And by far and away the dimmest in living memory. But Truss seems devoid of affect. No sense of shame. If anything she seems proud of her 49 days. That long! In Liz’s mind, she was simply too good for us. We weren’t ready for her. Give it a thousand years and her tapestry will be on show in the British Museum.One thing you can guarantee: offer Liz a platform to speak and she will bite your hand off. No matter how deranged and delusional it may be, Liz is confident she can be yet more deranged and delusional. She is every rightwinger’s favourite guest. Not only is she guaranteed to say yes, she will also make everyone else seem almost normal. Win-win. She’s done all sorts of weird stuff in the US, and in the UK she has her own podcast where she pretends to be interested in someone other than herself on Mike Graham’s YouTube channel. Graham, you might remember, isthe man who thinks you can grow concrete. And Liz is sure he’s right.The new kid on the podcast block is the former Tory Brexiter Steve Baker. So who else would he get as his first guest than the Trusster. If anything, Steve has got even more weird in the two years since he lost his seat. These days he has the look of a far-right survivalist holed up in a hut somewhere in the Montana wilderness. And his podcast surroundings have the same feel. All very basic, just a table and chairs. The table probably has a cache of semi-automatic rifles underneath it. Every so often, Steve will interrupt the recording to do an ad for gold. He no longer trusts traditional currencies.And up steps Liz. Doing what only someone as half-witted as she can: talking non-stop nonsense. Often with a weird half-smile on her face. At times you are tempted to believe that she is in on the joke that she is the joke. But then you realise she’s deadly serious. She hasn’t quite understood that people aren’t laughing with her, they are laughing at her. There’s something almost unbearably sad about this. So much so you almost feel guilty for indulging her insanity. Then you remember that only 2,000 people are going to watch this. And only we dedicated few are going to make it to the end.Labour has ruined the country, she says. Tony Blair and Gordon Brown had a secret plot to dismantle British civilisation and nothing has been the same since 1997. At which point, even Steve has to remind Liz that the Tories were in power from 2010. The Trusster doesn’t miss a beat. She is rushing on her run, her onboard computer set to auto-pilot. The Tories weren’t really the Tories. They were socialists in disguise. All of them. They were all part of the woke establishment. That’s why they were anti-Brexit. And austerity never happened.At this point it would have been a kindness to wrap the podcast up. To remind Liz that antipsychotic help was available. Because to the best of my knowledge, Liz had been a minister in successive Tory governments since 2012. She had also been a vocal supporter of Remain.Only it turns out that was a different Liz. A doppelganger. She had been temporarily captured by the wokerati and made to do and say a lot of things against her will. It was only when she became prime minister that she could self-actualise into her truest state and then she was thwarted by the Bank of England getting tough on quantitative easing. All a deliberate plot to destabilise her mini-budget. Nothing to do with the mini-budget being riddled with unfunded tax cuts.There were only two trustworthy people left in the world, she said: Donald Trump and Javier Milei. It was time to disband the judiciary, the prisons and the civil service. The whole world order needed to be rebalanced. Steve readily agreed. He reckoned the NHS should also be included on the grounds that it had almost killed him and a friend of his. Not even Liz was going that far. But together the revolution was possible.Then the big question. What next for Liz? Would she stand for election again? Maybe, she said. But who for? She’s long since been too mad for the Tories and might even be too bonkers for Reform. All she knew was that she would never go away. Not while there were still things to talk about that no one was talking about except her. Poor Liz. The problem isn’t that no one is talking. It’s that no one is listening. Steve chucked her a nugget of gold and they both ran for the hills. You’ll never take them alive.Explore more on these topicsPoliticsThe politics sketchLiz TrusscommentShareReuse this content

title: Location-tracking apps have turned me into a gibbering wreck – but I just can’t look away | Adrian Chiles | The Guardian
description: When my loved ones are on the move, I can’t rest until I know they’ve got from A to B safely. How I long for the ignorance of the olden days, writes Adrian Chiles
Author: Adrian Chiles
Headline: When my loved ones are on the move, I can’t rest until I know they’ve got from A to B safely. How I long for the ignorance of the olden days, writes Adrian Chiles
Content: And now we wait.Photograph: Fabio Principe/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnd now we wait.Photograph: Fabio Principe/Getty ImagesOpinionParents and parentingLocation-tracking apps have turned me into a gibbering wreck – but I just can’t look awayAdrian ChilesWhen my loved ones are on the move, I can’t rest until I know they’ve got from A to B safely. How I long for the ignorance of the olden daysWed 16 Sep 2026 12.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareI’ll call it compassionate surveillance. It’s what I do when I’m worried about a loved one who is on the move. I’m not sure it’s a good thing. Be they travelling by plane, train or automobile, I will keep tabs on them. I can’t help myself. If my daughters – who are highly competent grownups – make a long car journey, by means of some smartphone hocus-pocus I’ll know where they are. I should point out that this is done with consent: they know that I know where they are. In my mum’s case, this is less true, if only because she has long given up trying to make head or tail of location sharing and other such sorcery.I cross my heart and hope to die when I swear to you that I only do this when they are in transit. Honestly, I never look up where they are on a night out or whatever. That would be weird – or weirder, anyway. But when they get in a car, I get the fear. The catastrophising begins. It’s a big world and their car is small. A million other cars, buses and lorries share the roads on which they are motoring. In this, as in all things, overthinking is calamitous. The more you think about what could go wrong, the more your imagination obliges with a steady stream of ghastly possibilities.The answer is simple: stop being an idiot, stop torturing yourself, stop thinking about it and think about something else. Sometimes, I achieve this. More often, I don’t. I resist the temptation to check the tech for as long as possible, but invariably I give in. I’ve yet to find anything absorbing enough to distract me from the paranoia. I can be sitting at a football match, in a live radio studio, in an intense conversation, and that will work only for a while before a sick feeling strikes and I’m wondering if my loved ones are all right.The irony, of course, is that if I had no means of checking, I’d barely be dwelling on it. Just like in the olden days, when there were no mobiles and there would be one phone call home a week and all worries would have to be parked up and set aside until then. Ignorance was bliss. Information can be the opposite.I know this, but before long I’m tracking them anyway. They’re reduced to an avatar on my phone screen, moving, it seems to me, with alarming speed. They’re often on a route I know well, so before long I’m basically in the car with them, worrying about the road narrowing here, a nasty bend coming up there and so on. Before long, I can’t take it any more and I leave them to it, before checking in again – and again.Flights are worse. I’ve got an app, obviously, so I can see the plane they’re on and everything about that plane. So much to worry about. Ten years old? Eh?! Is that even legal? And what do you mean it’s already been to Nice and back today? Doesn’t it need to have a rest, cool down, or something?Then it takes off, into alarmingly crowded skies. When you zoom out on the app, you can barely see the ground for all the planes! When you zoom in to track the metal tube conveying your loved ones, at great speed, at thirtysomething thousand feet, it’s scarier still. Other planes head towards them. Frantically, I check an incomer’s altitude. It’s going to miss. That’s a relief. Probably couldn’t have informed air traffic control in time anyway.Eventually, obviously, it lands (and I can barely write that for fear I’m tempting fate). Relief. And I wonder if this is what it’s really all about – as much as I worry for loved ones, perhaps I’m just slaking a thirst for tension and the subsequent release from it. Thrill-seeking, in other words; needing the endless cycle of fear and relief just to feel alive. It can’t be good for you.Adrian Chiles is a broadcaster, writer and Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick hereExplore more on these topicsParents and parentingOpinionAppsSurveillanceAnxietyLocation based servicesGPSPrivacycommentShareReuse this content

title: The dominance of AI is not inevitable. We can choose to change things for the better | Nick Evershed | The Guardian
description: Countries have come together before to make international agreements in the face of existential threats
Author: Nick Evershed
Headline: Countries have come together before to make international agreements in the face of existential threats
Content: A protest against AI outside OpenAI’s offices in San Francisco. ‘What often seem like insurmountable problems can be addressed by normal people putting pressure on politicians and companies,’ Nick Evershed writes.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA protest against AI outside OpenAI’s offices in San Francisco. ‘What often seem like insurmountable problems can be addressed by normal people putting pressure on politicians and companies,’ Nick Evershed writes.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)The dominance of AI is not inevitable. We can choose to change things for the betterNick EvershedCountries have come together before to make international agreements in the face of existential threatsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 16 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 19.54 EDTShareWith many technological developments, from algorithm-driven social media to AI, many people assume there’s a degree of inevitability to their widespread adoption in society.The argument goes something like this: once the ideas and means to produce the tech are known, then it is inevitable that its usage will spread and we’ll essentially be stuck with it. So therefore we need to accept this and adjust our lives to live with the tech and use it (or at least tolerate it).This argument seems pretty straightforward, since we’ve seen many tech-driven disruptions play out in the past 20 years or so. Uber displacing the taxi industry and the rise of “gig workers”. Algorithmic social media displacing, well, everything. Privacy-invading, hyper-targeted advertising reshaping the internet.Could AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risksRead moreAnd it seems like generative AI is destined to be another huge, disruptive force in our lives. Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI,wrote of AI in 2024 that“with these new abilities, we can have shared prosperity to a degree that seems unimaginable today; in the future, everyone’s lives can be better than anyone’s life is now”. He is also on record elsewhere sayingAI would wipe out entire job categories.Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic,wrote that he believes“AI could cure most major diseases in the next 5–10 years, greatly accelerate economic growth rates, create a world of abundance and empowerment, and usher in a renaissance of democracy and freedom”.But now, bothCEOs, as well asformerandcurrent AI research staffand others, are calling for a slowdown oreven a shutdownof AI development, along with greater government regulation and international coordination of AI development.The calls for a slowdown are based on the fear that, without proper safeguards, AI systems may result incatastrophic events in the near future, ranging from theextinction of humanityto merely causing billions of dollars in economic damage.This is not a new concern and has been raised byindependent academics previously in assessing the risks from AI. However, complicating the situation is that both OpenAI and Anthropic are positioning themselves for IPOs, and so some critics say both companies stand to materially benefit from the perception that they’re on the cusp of developing superintelligent models.AI models being developed in China arealso catching up to the “frontier” models being made in the US, which has prompted some to suggest that calls for greater regulation on AIare an attempt at regulatory capture by the big US AI companies.Regardless of how likely these catastrophic events are, as Sandra Wachter, a professor of technology at the Oxford Internet Institute, has said,AI is already causing real problems, including its environmental impact, the spreading of misinformation and replacing jobs.This is in addition to the “original sin” of most AI models – they’re built on millions of people’s art and writing, largely without compensation or permission until more recently, and theAI companies want to curb proposed laws limiting their accessto such material.double quotation markWhatever semblance of intelligence it has comes from us, and our work.Never forget that generative AI is not a technology that is apart from human society. In fact, its development and whatever semblance of intelligence it has comes from us, and our work.And despite what the tech CEOs say, there’s nothing inevitable about AI, and we as a society can make decisions to change things for the better.History shows us this can be done.What often seem like insurmountable and pervasive problems can and have been addressed by normal people putting pressure on politicians and companies, and through international cooperation and negotiation.Countries have come together before to make international agreements in the face of existential threats. Thenuclear nonproliferation treaty, as well as the associated anti-nuclear activist movement, is a good example, and many have suggested it has parallels with the current AI situation. While the disarmament side of the NPT has had mixed success at best, the NPT and similar agreements have worked to limit the number of nuclear-capable countries and reduce nuclear testing.Gene editing viaCrispris another example. Arguablya more important technological advancement than generative AI, the use of Crispr for gene editing in humans has been treated extremely cautiously by governments around the world. No country currently allows genetic changes to an embryo that could also be passed on to its children, and70 countries have laws against it.We greet the news that AI could extinguish us with a glazed indifference. What is the way out of this nihilism? | Brigid DelaneyRead moreEven social media companies, whose reach and influence on society seemed like it would continue unabated, are now finallyfacing stricter regulation from governments around the worldandself-regulating in response to lawsuits in the US.So, do not take the future dominance of AI as a given.Personally I believe that generative AI can be a useful tool (albeit in far fewer situations than tech companies would have you believe). But to ensure we limit the worst possible consequences, we need independent oversight of its development, regulation to limit some aspects of it, and international agreements to implement these controls globally.If you think the same, then do not accept its inevitability. Contact politicians and demand action. Protest. Speak to friends and family about how you think this technology should be used, or not used. Write to companies using it in ways you disagree with.In thenow-infamous words of Claude: you’re right to push back.Nick Evershed is the data and interactives editor for Guardian AustraliaExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionEthicsAnthropicOpenAIcommentShareReuse this content

title: The best life hack I’ve ever heard? Monetise what you’re bad at | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: Phil Heckels has turned his awful pet portraits into a full-time job. As a blueprint for success, embracing your lack of talent has obvious appeal, writes Polly Hudson
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: Phil Heckels has turned his awful pet portraits into a full-time job. As a blueprint for success, embracing your lack of talent has obvious appeal, writes Polly Hudson
Content: ‘I do get criticism sometimes that the portraits are getting too good.’Photograph: Hercule Van WolfwinkleView image in fullscreen‘I do get criticism sometimes that the portraits are getting too good.’Photograph: Hercule Van WolfwinkleOpinionHobbiesThe best life hack I’ve ever heard? Monetise what you’re bad atPolly HudsonPhil Heckels has turned his awful pet portraits into a full-time job. As a blueprint for success, embracing your lack of talent has obvious appealWed 16 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 09.32 EDTShareWhat do you get if you cross a complete lack of artistic talent with making lemonade out of life’s lemons? Phil Heckels, that’s what – or, rather, who. The former estate agent from West Sussex has turned being bad at drawing animals into a full-time job after posting a hilariously terrible portrait of his dog on social media. Friends started asking him to do awful pictures of their pets, word spread, and he’s now received more than 100,000 requests. His rules are that he only sees the photos immediately before he picks up his pen, he never restarts a drawing, and he doesn’t spend longer than 10 minutes on a creation. He also refuses to charge for his artworks – suggesting charity donations instead – but makes money through merchandise and books.“I do get criticism sometimes that the portraits are getting too good,” Heckelssaid recently. “But people have been saying that since about my 12th portrait. You never have to wait too long for a real stinker to appear, though.”Perhaps statues will be erected to this man, because let’s be honest: monetising what you’re bad at is an amazing life hack. Not to mention an inclusive one that everybody can try, because we all suck at something. There’s also surely a much faster return in taking advantage of weakness than doggedly – not intended – working hard to improve. And imagine the creative freedom! Heckels loves to draw, and that’s now how he spends his days. Maybe you’re a tone-deaf singer, a dancer with two left feet, a ceramicist who can only make mugs with holes. So what? Envision a world where rather than holding you back, a complete lack of talent and skill is a guarantee of success. Where if you aim for the moon, it’s better than fine if you can’t even get one toe off the ground. Nobody’s going to heckle that idea.Polly Hudson is a freelance writerDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: It’s my self-care tip of the year: I quit our local veg box scheme, and set my mind free | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: Being a member felt like the right thing to do and it was a boon during the pandemic. But oh, the emotional labour, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: Being a member felt like the right thing to do and it was a boon during the pandemic. But oh, the emotional labour, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Content: ‘During the long winters, I cursed the endless beetroot. By March we were all about 65% parsnip.’Photograph: Westend61 GmbH/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘During the long winters, I cursed the endless beetroot. By March we were all about 65% parsnip.’Photograph: Westend61 GmbH/AlamyOpinionVegetablesIt’s my self-care tip of the year: I quit our local veg box scheme, and set my mind freeRhiannon Lucy CosslettBeing a member felt like the right thing to do – and it was a boon during the pandemic. But oh, the emotional labour. I can never look at a turnip againWed 16 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 13.24 EDTShareLast week, as summer gave way to pumpkin season, I found myself contemplating the final squash. Like the horror movie trope of the final girl staggering out of the woods after the massacre, this squash is the sole survivor. All her sister squashes had either been cooked and eaten or left to rot. Now, my killing days were almost over. There would be no sequel.Or, to put it less dramatically: after six years, we have quit the local organic veg bag collective, which delivered to a nearby pickup point a bag of organic, local seasonal veg once a week. And as a result the mental load and emotional labour of having to contemplate and devise a use for various esoteric kinds of veg is finally, mercifully, over.I approached the final squash the way I had many, many of her contemporaries. First, I tried to identify her so I could work out how to cook it and whether the skin was edible or not. “Medium-sized frilly orange pumpkin type” I wrote into Google. No match was forthcoming. Then I took a picture of it and did an image search. Still no match. For all its supposed miraculous capabilities, during my own experiments AI has never successfully identified a single pumpkin.Usually, this is the point where my cortisol soars, but this time it stayed stable: this was the last time that I would expend precious time and energy trying to correctly identify a vegetable, before giving up and doing what I always do, which is chopping it up and roasting it.Now that it’s done, I cannot tell you how liberated I feel. No more kohlrabi. No more Jerusalem fartichokes. Only my husband will miss the turnips.Historically, I have always been a great quitter. To use hideous modern parlance, anything that no longer “served” me, whether a job, a relationship, a university course, a country, would always be efficiently dispatched. No looking back.Leaving the local organic veg collective didn’t feel like this, though. Being a member felt like the right, ethical thing to do (“Don’t be mean about them,” my husband says. “They are a great service”). Raised by a veg box mum – and being a Guardian writer to boot – surely this was my destiny, my birthright? It gave me a warm, self-satisfied glow, albeit an ephemeral one lasting only until I was once again scrubbing layers of caked mud from all of the potatoes just so I could make my kid some sodding chips. “What is this? Wartime?” I muttered to myself.I’d say my heart hasn’t been in it for at least two years, probably longer, but despite the fact that the relationship had become toxic I felt guilty for wanting to leave. Ever since I had my son, the veg bag has been an albatross. During the long winters, I cursed the endless beetroot. By March we were all about 65% parsnip. “More bloody parsnips,” we would sigh, as we unpacked on a Wednesday. “I’m not sure I can do this any more.” Yet another season was always around the corner. The green promise of spring. “Soon! There will be asparagus!” And we would stick it out for another year.Well, it’s done now, even though I keep picturingHugh Fearnley-Whittingstallshaking his head in disapproval, along with you, dear reader. The veg is more ethical, better for you, and tastier than anything from a supermarket. All of this I acknowledge. Maybe I’m just lazy. And yet, I am a confident – some might say even good – cook. I make meals from scratch, I understand about vitamins and nutritional value. I sometimes open, and look at the pictures in, recipe books by Nigel Slater. It was just that something finally had to give.It may sound hyperbolic, but getting rid of the veg bag has saved me from a breakdown, possibly. My mental load feels far lighter. “I feel so fucking free, you guys!” I posted, on Instagram, and was inundated with people who had been on the same journey. In some cases, arguing about the rotting veg in the bottom of their fridges was affecting their marriages. We all wanted to do the right thing, it’s just that modern life simply didn’t feel compatible.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI have some fond memories of the veg bag. I’m grateful to the collective for feeding my family. I will miss being a member, especially at Christmas. We joinedduring the pandemic, when not every item was always available in the shops. My son was weaned on pureed celeriac. We got to try things I never would have otherwise –winter purslane! Land cress! – and I adored the rainbow chard. The kohlrabi actually made a very nice rosti. Even the final squash was completely and utterly delicious, as if to try to tempt me back. But no. It’s over. And I am finally free.Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsVegetablesOpinionSeasonal foodFarmingFoodPumpkinFood & drink industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on the Houthi advance in Yemen: another vital Middle East artery becomes a battlefield | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The extraordinary success of the rebels, and Saudi counterstrikes, threaten economic havoc. But the country’s civilians are paying the highest price
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The extraordinary success of the rebels, and Saudi counterstrikes, threaten economic havoc. But the country’s civilians are paying the highest price
Content: ‘The Houthis are not mere proxies for Tehran, but their interests are increasingly aligned.’Photograph: Houthi Military Media/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘The Houthis are not mere proxies for Tehran, but their interests are increasingly aligned.’Photograph: Houthi Military Media/ReutersOpinionHouthisThe Guardian view on the Houthi advance in Yemen: another vital Middle East artery becomes a battlefieldEditorialThe extraordinary success of the rebels, and Saudi counterstrikes, threaten economic havoc. But the country’s civilians are paying the highest priceWed 16 Sep 2026 13.36 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 14.58 EDTShareEven in a region beset by turmoil and learning to expect the unexpected, thelightning advance of Yemen’s Houthisalong the Red Sea coast has shocked observers. More than 100,000 peoplehave been forced to fleein a country where immiseration and displacement have become routine and half the population depend on humanitarian aid. But outsiders are paying close attention, because by claiming thousands of kilometres in a matter of days, and seizing strategically important islands, the Iran-backed rebels now control the Bab al-Mandab strait – the othermajor regional energy chokepointafter the Hormuz strait.The Iran war has forced Saudi Arabia to rely on moving oil via its east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports. Now drone strikes – blamed on an Iran-backed militia in Iraq – have shut the pipeline: onone estimate, a month-long closure could cut global crude supply by 120m barrels. The halt to shipping through the Bab al-Mandab strait could be much more protracted. Taking the oil north is a far slower and more expensive route to Asian markets, and does not preclude attacks by the Houthis, who are also targeting oil facilities.Saudi Arabia had painfully extracted itself from a war with the Houthis which it recklessly spearheaded – nominally in support of the internationally recognised government – at astounding cost to its own coffers and Yemeni civilians. It apparently hoped that it could calibrate its response to a flight from Iran to Houthi-controlled Sana’a in July, the first in over a decade, sufficiently to save the 2022 truce. But bombing Sana’a airport gave the Houthis the opportunity to escalate while blaming Riyadh.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump.Photograph: Alex Brandon/APThe Houthis are not mere proxies for Tehran, but their interests are increasingly aligned, thanks to Donald Trump’s unlawful war on Iran. They need to maintain Iranian support and the strait of Hormuz crisis has created a new opportunity to exert economic pressure, and perhaps create a new income stream, via strategic gains along the coast. The forces ranged against them, including the government and southern secessionists, are more fractured than ever. The United Arab Emirates, which has clashed withits former close partnerSaudi Arabia,withdrew its troopsat the turn of the year.Saudi strikes alone will not be enough to push theHouthisback. But Mr Trump has rebuffed requests for help. The Houthis have been canny enough to say that they are targeting only the Saudis, though that message reinforces the fact that their leverage could be used more broadly in future. They are also closer than ever to Djibouti, home to US, Chinese and other military bases.The Saudisface a choicebetween negotiations with an emboldened enemy now making increasingly maximalist demands – or returning to the kind of full-scale war they previously regretted, with little support this time. Turkey and Pakistan are not rushing to act on thenew Mecca defence pactthe three countries signed in August.Yemen’s recent history amply demonstrates the futility of seeking a military solution. Ultimately, its citizens deserve a government not dependent on either Riyadh or Tehran. Outside parties should concentrate on promoting a political process within the country. They should stress that both sides must protect civilians, and support humanitarian efforts. Their priority, however, should be a resolution to the Iran war, without which danger in the region, andbroader instability, will only grow.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Sweden’s election result: an opportunity that progressive parties must not squander | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: After a desperately tight race, voters rejected the prospect of the far right in government. A potential centre-left coalition needs to seize the moment
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: After a desperately tight race, voters rejected the prospect of the far right in government. A potential centre-left coalition needs to seize the moment
Content: Voters at a polling station inside the Swedish parliament in Stockholm on 13 September 2026.Photograph: Zuma Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenVoters at a polling station inside the Swedish parliament in Stockholm on 13 September 2026.Photograph: Zuma Press/ShutterstockOpinionSwedenThe Guardian view on Sweden’s election result: an opportunity that progressive parties must not squanderEditorialAfter a desperately tight race, voters rejected the prospect of the far right in government. A potential centre-left coalition needs to seize the momentWed 16 Sep 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareEuropean progressives searching for reasons to be cheerful have been finding them hard to come by this autumn. In Germany, thedramaticrise of the Alternative für Deutschland party is threatening the liberal values that underpin the identity of the federal republic. In France, polls continue to point to a likely Marine Le Pen victory in a presidentialelection, which is months away. Across mainland Europe, centre-left parties are failing to muster an adequate response to nativist movements that have colonised swathes of the working-class support that they once relied on.In such an ominous political landscape, theoutcomeof a cliffhanger Swedish election provides a much‑needed source of optimism – albeit one that comes with heavy caveats. Prior to last Sunday’s poll, the outgoing prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, was explicit that if his rightwing alliance won the largest number of seats, he would invite members of the far-right Sweden Democrats party (SD) to become ministers in the next government.That would have meant the formal end of the SD’s pariah status in Swedish politics, after four years in which its parliamentary votes have propped up Mr Kristersson’s minority administration. In a Europe wherefirewallsandcordons sanitairesagainst the far right have never seemed less secure, another significant threshold would have been crossed.Voters appear to have instead handed the narrowest of victories to the Social Democratic leader, Magdalena Andersson, and the progressive bloc of parties. The SD’s share of the vote fell for the first time since it began its political journey as an openly neo-Nazi party in the late 1980s, and it slipped from second to third place behind the conservative Moderates.View image in fullscreenMagdalena Andersson of the Swedish Social Democratic party.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersSo much for the good news. As in Germany and France, the Swedish far right has not needed to win power for its agenda to become normalised and partially implemented. Mr Kristersson’s reliance on the SD resulted in a government that behaved with performativecrueltytowards migrants, and enacted much of its draconian programme on deportations and citizenship restrictions. Ms Andersson hasrespondedby offering a milder version of the same approach to immigration and asylum. As it leaked support on the left accordingly, her party recorded its lowest vote share for over a century.Unless traditional powerhouse parties of European social democracy are more courageous in seeking to shift the dial of political debate, the far right will continue to set its terms. The SD’s chosen slogan for its campaign was “Make Sweden Sweden again” – varying the usual Maga trope in order to stress the core ethnocentric message. From the sidelines its rhetoric will become still more extreme, and the defeat of the rightwing bloc is already being invidiously attributed to foreign-born voters.Should Ms Andersson eventually succeed informinga centre-left coalition government, she should counter the forces of division by channelling the best of her own party’s traditions. The Social Democratic party historically dominated Swedish politics through the idea of theFolkhemmet, or People’s Home, which encapsulated the inclusive ethos of a welfare society admired around the world. Locating the resources and ambition to develop a similarly attractive politics of the common good for the 21st century is the urgent task for progressives, in Sweden and beyond.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
