Short-term financial pressures have meant that the army has been told to stop non-essential training by the end of the year.Chancellor John Healey resigned as defence secretary from Keir Starmer’s government in June because the former prime minister would not commit to 3% by 2030, arguing that it would require too great a step up in the next decade.But Healey refused to recommit to the interim target when he was appointed to the Treasury by Burnham a month later, raising questions that the new government was backloading spending increases until after the next election.Rutte said that he had discussed Britain’s “Nato commitments” when he had met Burnham at a science business park in Oxford earlier on Wednesday, without offering any details, in the first one-on-one meeting between the two.Prior to that meeting, Burnham acknowledged that he had replaced Starmer, but insisted that there was “never any change in the UK’s unwavering commitment to Nato and our Nato obligations”.The Nato chief, a former Dutch prime minister, said many in Europe had made the “casual assumption” that the US would “always provide most of the muscle and pick up the bill, no matter what” until Trump returned to the White House.Instead, he noted that during a summit in The Hague in 2025, the UK and other alliance members had agreed to increase their own defence spending to match US levels, in response to Trump’s demand that Europe take the lead in defending the continent.“We need more UK and more Europe in the alliance,” Rutte said, because Nato “faces the most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation” with a return to wars in Europe and the Middle East, and wider geopolitical uncertainty.Ukraine war briefing: Nato ‘foils Russian undersea cable sabotage drill’Read moreCiting “Russia and its war against Ukraine, terrorism, Iran and the tectonic shifts of global geopolitical competition”, Rutte argued that the UK and Europe needed to invest more, because otherwise “our collective defence will not be credible”.Britain, he said, had “a central role in building this stronger Europe in a stronger Nato” and noted that the UK was spending billions to upgrade the Trident nuclear deterrent, which is pledged to the defence of Nato members.The UK is also gradually upgrading its conventional forces, though the UK’s overall defence spending, long the second largest in the alliance, is now behind Germany. By 2029, Berlin’s military budgets are on track to be twice that of the UK.The UK was “leading the pushback” against a Russian campaign of provocation and sabotage across Europe, Rutte said, and that the UK had been “a good friend to Ukraine”. Britain spends £3bn a year supporting Ukraine with weapons.Meanwhile, Canada, seeking to diversify its defence ties ⁠away from ⁠the ​US, has formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military ⁠coalition, prime minister Mark Carney’s office said on Wednesday.The a grouping ⁠of 10 North Atlantic Nato member states is ​a rapid response ‌military partnership.Canada, already a Nato member, ‌is seeking closer military cooperation with Europe.The JEF comprises Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and the UK.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsNatoAndy BurnhamMark RuttenewsShareReuse this content

title: US opts not to back Saudi Arabia in Yemen after meeting Houthi leaders | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Iran-backed militants have offered Trump administration assurances over safety of Red Sea shipping
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Iran-backed militants have offered Trump administration assurances over safety of Red Sea shipping
Content: Houthi fighters participate in an offensive near the port city of Mokha, Yemen.Photograph: EPAView image in fullscreenHouthi fighters participate in an offensive near the port city of Mokha, Yemen.Photograph: EPAYemenUS opts not to back Saudi Arabia in Yemen after meeting Houthi leadersIran-backed militants have offered Trump administration assurances over safety of Red Sea shippingPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorWed 16 Sep 2026 10.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOfficials from the US met Houthi leaders over the weekend at the country’s embassy in Muscat, Oman, it has been confirmed, leading to the US decision not to intervene to help Saudi Arabia drive back aHouthi advance inside Yemen.The Iran-backed militant group reassured the US that theceasefire agreement between the two sidesstruck in 2025 still held and the movement had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea. Only Saudi-linked shipping was regarded as a target owing to its blockade of Yemen, the Houthis confirmed.The meeting helps to explain Donald Trump’s decision to condemn the Houthi advance down the west coast of Yemen for threatening freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandab strait, but so far to reject any military response in support of Riyadh. The US is already embroiled in anexpensive and resource sapping conflict with Iran, which backs the Houthis.The US labelled the Houthis as a foreign terrorist entity in March 2025, but in the recent past American officials have met leaders from Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. The US vice-president,JD Vance, confirmed on Monday that the US was in direct contact with the Houthis.The US refusal to become directly involved has put pressure onSaudi Arabiato reach either a diplomatic solution with the Houthis over the future governance of Yemen, or to try to build a regional alliance with Pakistan and Turkey to force the Houthis back. In a lightning offensive last week, the Houthis seized control of large swathes of western Yemen along the Red Sea coast.Map of Yemen showing Houthi military developmentsA former deputy US ambassador to Yemen, Nabeel Khoury, said a “kind of tacit understanding” had been struck between theTrump administrationand the Houthis. Khoury added: “The Houthis are promising the American administration that American and international navigation will not be affected in the Red Sea, but the only danger is to Saudi ships or those carrying Saudi oil.”In an attempt to build popular support against the Houthis in the region, Riyadh made the disputed claim that theHouthis had fired a drone at the holy city of Meccaon Tuesday, but the missile had been destroyed by Saudi defence forces. It said the drone was entering a prohibited airspace close to Mecca’s most holy shrines. The drone was intercepted at about 6.50pm local time on Tuesday, according to coalition spokesperson Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki.Saudi Arabia said any attack on Mecca was a red line and the move was condemned in lengthy statements by the UN-recognisedYemengovernment based in Aden as well as the 57-country Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. The Pakistani prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, condemned what he described as a “dastardly and heinous” attempted attack on Mecca. “The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act,” he said in a statement posted on X.The Houthi leadership – followers of a Shia Zaydism that respects the pilgrimage to Mecca – dismissed the claim as the lie of the century, and said such worn-out lies had been used before and fooled no one.The Houthi’s deputy foreign minister, Abdul Wahid abu Ras, said “whoever opened the land of the two holy mosques to debauchery and entertainment parties, and whoever defiled the land of the two holy mosques by the presence of Zionist Jews in it, is the one who targets Mecca, Medina and the Islamic holy sites”.TheHouthiscountered that they had shot down a Saudi F-15 plane close to Marib, and attacked an Aramco plant in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu. No supporting evidence was provided by the Houthi military spokesperson, but the head of the Houthi negotiating team, Mohammed abdul Salam, said the downing of the plane was a warning to the west not to fall victim to Saudi propaganda.Mohammed al-Farah, a Houthi political bureau member, said: “The truth is that Saudi Arabia is experiencing a real predicament in Yemen. It became embroiled in a war, a siege and an occupation, and then failed to achieve its goals.“Today, it is looking for external solutions, so it is begging the international community, warning the world about Bab al-Mandab and requesting support from Pakistan, Turkey, America, Israel and Egypt. Then it is trying to mobilise Muslims with a false pretext called ‘targeting Mecca’.”Separately, Israeli officials have leaked details of a secret meeting between military commanders from the US, Israel and several Arab states in Germany last week to discuss the war launched by Israel and the US againstIran. The report from the Axios journalist Barak Ravid said the “private retreat” was organised by the head of US Central Command, Adm Brad Cooper.Citing two unnamed Israeli officials, Ravid reported that the meeting was attended by the military chiefs of staff of Israel, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt. It was the first such gathering since theUS and Israel went to war with Iran more than six months ago. Israel, once a target for the Houthis, is offering to intervene in Yemen on Saudi Arabia’s behalf.Iranian security forces coordinated killing, torture and sexual abuse of protesters, says AmnestyRead moreA meeting of the UN security council on Tuesday condemned any attempt to close the Red Sea, but the meeting was notable for the Russian envoy beginning to edge away from its previous stance that the UN-recognised government based in Aden was the only legitimate government inside the country.In Beijing, the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Wednesday met his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, in an effort to secure support for its plans for the future administration of the strait of Hormuz. The strait remains closed owing to separate Iranian and US blockades.A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said China did not want to see further regional tension spill over into Yemen and the Red Sea. The Chinese called on the US to return to the talks based on thememorandum of understanding agreed between the two sides in June. Beijing, the main importer of Iranian oil, is eager for a settlement and is resisting any suggestion that US secondary sanctions applied to countries trading with Iran should apply to its own country.Oil prices remain well over $100 (£74) a barrel and a keySaudi east-west pipeline remains closedbecause of a bombing incident.Explore more on these topicsYemenMiddle East and north AfricaHouthisUS-Israel war on IranSaudi ArabiaUS foreign policyIrannewsShareReuse this content

title: English far-right extremist who discussed killing Jews, Muslims and migrants is jailed | Crime | The Guardian
description: Ivan Jennings, 46, sentenced to five years after pleading guilty to encouraging terrorism on social media
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: Ivan Jennings, 46, sentenced to five years after pleading guilty to encouraging terrorism on social media
Content: Ivan Jennings pleaded guilty to encouraging terrorism in an online chat and dissemination of a terrorist publication in his trial at Leicester crown court.Photograph: Counter Terrorism PolicingView image in fullscreenIvan Jennings pleaded guilty to encouraging terrorism in an online chat and dissemination of a terrorist publication in his trial at Leicester crown court.Photograph: Counter Terrorism PolicingCrimeEnglish far-right extremist who discussed killing Jews, Muslims and migrants is jailedIvan Jennings, 46, sentenced to five years after pleading guilty to encouraging terrorism on social mediaRobyn Vinterand agencyWed 16 Sep 2026 14.53 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 13.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA rightwing extremist who discussed poisoning Jews and Muslims and called for the killing of migrants and minority communities has been jailed.Ivan Jennings, 46, called for the murder of hundreds of people he labelled “subhumans”, saying it was “justified and actually needed”, in extreme far-right groups over a period of three months in 2024.The father-of four from Stafford hadpleaded guilty to encouraging terrorismin an online chat between 15 August and 14 November that year and dissemination of a terrorism publication, namely a manifesto by the Norwegian mass murderer Anders Breivik, on 21 August 2024.Jennings, who worked at a warehouse, was jailed for five years and three months and handed a further five years on extended licence at Leicester crown court on Wednesday.Daniel Oscroft, prosecuting, told the court that Jennings had been an “active participant” in at least seven extreme rightwing groups on the social media platform Telegram.Jennings, who joined the far-right organisation Patriotic Alternative in early 2024, told one of the groups that he was in touch with a man “who wanted to go in a boat and make a difference to the amount of people coming into the UK”, the court heard.In another post, when asked if he supported murder, the defendant wrote: “It’s not murder because we are at war. If it’s subhumans, it’s justified and actually needed.”On 22 August that year, he searched online for motorboat chartering services at Dover and how much it cost to hire a boat in the UK. A week later, another user shared a video of a boat, on which Jennings commented: “We need one of those to take out the dinghy divers.”He told another chat group “something needed to be done soon” and each person “needs to take out at least 200 and stop the constant influx [of migrants]”.The defendant also shared a post about an event in Manchester celebrating Pakistan’s independence day, identifying it as a target with the message: “We need to start acting.”He made reference to the 51 people killed in the Christchurch terror attacks, a mass shooting at two mosques in New Zealand on 15 October 2019, adding: “We need a bigger impact.”The court heard that another user commented on the post about the Pakistan independence day event: “It disgusts me to see that in the UK.” Jennings replied: “Exactly, we need to start acting to turn the tables.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn another comment about the Pakistan event, he wrote: “If I go to prison for anything, it’s going to be for making a real change.”Oscroft told the court: “In a smaller group of eight participants, there was discussion about the most poisonous mushrooms and how to get them into the food of Jews or Muslims.”The defence barrister Oliver Renton said Jennings was “struggling with deep existential fears about himself” after he collapsed at work in 2023 in cardiac arrest, and that he descended into “fear and isolation” and became susceptible to “nihilistic, bleak worldviews”.In his sentencing remarks, Judge Lockhart KC said Jennings had “deeply held abhorrent and racist views”.Explore more on these topicsCrimeFar rightRaceImmigration and asylumUK security and counter-terrorismNorth of EnglandSocial medianewsShareReuse this content

title: Fossil fuel advertising contracts at all-time high in 2026  | Oil and gas companies | The Guardian
description: In year of extreme weather, ad agencies found to be building Big Oil’s image as integral to family life and security
Author: Damien Gayle
Headline: In year of extreme weather, ad agencies found to be building Big Oil’s image as integral to family life and security
Content: A Chevron campaign positioned it as part of family life, describing the company as ‘the energy that keeps America moving’.Photograph: YoutubeView image in fullscreenA Chevron campaign positioned it as part of family life, describing the company as ‘the energy that keeps America moving’.Photograph: YoutubeOil and gas companiesFossil fuel advertising contracts at all-time high in 2026In year of extreme weather, ad agencies found to be building Big Oil’s image as integral to family life and securityDamien GayleEnvironment correspondentWed 16 Sep 2026 13.58 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 15.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It’s that time of the year again,” the Abu Dhabi NationalOilCompany told Emiratis in a Ramadan advertising campaign. “Where tanks are always full – for night after night of majlis hopping.”When you think about fossil fuels, you might think of offshore oil platforms flaring gas in rough seas, the US/Iran war or the greenhouse effect heating up the world’s climate. A new report argues, however, that what Big Oil wants you to think about is family, friends and faith instead.The advertising industry campaign group Clean Creatives went through the records and found that in 2026, the year climate breakdown went so haywire gardeners weregrowing watermelons in Bristol, there were 1,321 active contracts between the fossil fuel industry and advertising agencies, the most ever recorded.As the war in Iran intensified global shortages of oil and gas, leading to spiking prices and profits for the oil companies, the fossil fuel industry appears to have invested part of its windfall on its image. Clean Creatives found that 386 fossil fuel companies across 73 countries had engaged 802 advertising and PR agencies to shape their public image and messaging.Strikingly, business links between the two industries held strong, despite agencies’ claims of environmental responsibility, said the lead researcher, Nayantara Dutta.“By reading through all of their climate disclosures, what I find most telling this year is this is the first year in our research where advertising agencies are across the board acknowledging climate risk in their annual reports,” she said.Omnicom was the advertising company that held the most contracts with the fossil fuel industry, with 118 contracts, followed by WPP, with 88. In third place was Publicis, whose 34 fossil fuel industry contracts were no barrier to its being named as one ofTime magazine’s most sustainable companies of 2026.Dutta led a team of four who spent nine months compiling the survey. They painstakingly documented each contract by piecing together information from lobbying databases, creative portfolios and even LinkedIn posts. They quantified the extent of the trade and assessed its storytelling.View image in fullscreenAbu Dhabi National Oil Company (Adnoc) released an advertisement promoting fossil fuel use to enable ‘majlis-hopping’ during Ramadan, which advertising industry campaign group Clean Creatives described as ‘unsettling’.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAdvertising executives were portraying their fossil fuel industry clients as indispensable to our ways of life and economic security, Dutta said.“The cultural themes we have always seen have continued,” she said. “But there is a global trend of increased economic insecurity and fear-mongering around energy supply and demand, around jobs and around fossil fuels as being essential.”“Energy security requires all of our energy,” said Equinor, the Norwegian oil company that wants to develop the Rosebank oilfield in the North Sea, in a LinkedIn campaign by McCann Relationship Management, an Omnicom agency.Chevron launched a campaign celebrating the US’s 250th anniversary, announcing it was “the energy that keeps America moving”. “Since 1879, our people have been more than a source of energy. They’ve been a source of progress,” the company claimed in a Facebook ad.“In the US, UK, and Europe, we’re seeing a lot of nationalism,” Dutta said. “Really connecting the economic prosperity of a country with the fossil fuel industry and its expansion.”In the global south, on the other hand, fossil fuel firms often tie themselves to family life and cultural events. Pointing to Adnoc’s “unsettling” Ramadan advert, she said: “Basically they position themselves not only as a company that is helping the economy and providing jobs, but as a company who cares about the culture and wellbeing of their people.“So rather than addressing the political news of what’s happening in the world, they like to focus on the same themes of family and community to show themselves as integral to building that.”A spokesperson for the Advertising Association told the Guardian: “Fossil fuel advertising represents a very small proportion of overall UK advertising spend. Where such campaigns do run in the UK, they are subject to some of the world’s strictest regulation under the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) and CAP Codes. The rules are clear: ads must not mislead consumers, and companies presenting environmental claims must demonstrate total transparency regarding the full scope of their activity, including distinguishing between renewable and fossil fuel operations.“The ASA actively monitors and enforces compliance in this space, routinely taking action against claims that fall short. Alongside strict regulatory standards, programs such as Ad Net Zero continue to equip UK agencies and advertisers with the tools to reduce operational emissions, eliminate greenwashing and support the broader transition to a low-carbon economy.”Explore more on these topicsOil and gas companiesFossil fuelsEnergy industryOilMarketing & PRAdvertisingCorporate social responsibilitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Planning permission for new Scottish AI datacentres suspended for up to a year | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Scottish parliament brings in strict environmental impact assessments and will delay decisions until national strategy is developed
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: Scottish parliament brings in strict environmental impact assessments and will delay decisions until national strategy is developed
Content: Anti-datacentre protests at the Scottish parliament at Holyrood.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAnti-datacentre protests at the Scottish parliament at Holyrood.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianDatacentres - UKPlanning permission for new Scottish AI datacentres suspended for up to a yearMSPs vote for strict environmental impact assessments and will delay decisions until national strategy is developedPatrick GreenfieldWed 16 Sep 2026 14.28 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 07.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHolyrood has voted to pause planning applications for all new AI datacentres for up to a year until the Scottish government has developed a national strategy.On Wednesday, MSPs backed a Scottish Labour motion to halt new schemes for up to 12 months while rules on hyperscale datacentres are developed in what could be a blow to the British government’s AI strategy.Scotland has seen a boom in planning applications for large datacentres as global investment in AI infrastructure has exploded, with British officials encouraging developers to includeScotlandin the infrastructure buildout. Datacentres are critical for storing and processing data used by AI. One scheme in Auchtertool, Fife, has been billed as the second largest in the world, and is among more than 20 large datacentres proposed so far.Campaigners have raised concerns about water usage and carbon emissions from large datacentres, and questioned whether Scotland has the capacity to cope with the resulting explosion in energy demand.On Wednesday, MSPs voted to approve only projects that meet robust environmental impact assessments that consider the impact of neighbouring communities, and to make no decisions on planning for datacentre applications for up to a year until national planning guidance has been formalised by the Scottish government.Kat Jones, the director of the NGOAction to Protect Rural Scotland, who has spearheaded demands for a datacentre moratorium in Scotland, said the vote was a “landmark day for all those communities across Scotland who have been extremely concerned about projects coming forward in their areas.”“There’s much still to be done, but this is a huge step forward and we can all at least take a breath now,” she said. “That means the Scottish government must now urgently call in those applications which are approaching a decision date. The communities will expect nothing less.”Ahead of the vote, the Scottish government announced that large-scale datacentres would face mandatory environmental impact assessments, as a result of growing concern about the ecological impact of the AI boom.This month, hundreds from community groupsprotested outside Holyroodagainst the construction of large datacentres for AI until clear planning rules and the definition of a “green” datacentre had been formalised.On Thursday, AI leaders will gather at Dumfries House in Ayrshire for a summit with King Charles on the future of the technology, amid warnings that the speed of its development threatens the survival of humanity.After the vote, the Scottish Labour economy spokesperson, Daniel Johnson, said the economic potential of the AI boom needed to be considered alongside the impacts on the environment, communities and energy demand.“So far the SNP has failed to do the work needed to get this right – that must change. It is right that the SNP government has accepted the need for national guidance before more decisions are made, and I want to see that guidance delivered with the urgency needed,” he said.“The SNP must put in place the protections needed and ensure that any datacentres work for communities, create good jobs and deliver for Scotland.”The Scottish government has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingScotlandEdinburghScottish politicsPlanning policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Datacenter rush will create ‘tsunami’ of discarded electronics, report says | Datacentres | The Guardian
description: Global push will triple toxic e-waste annually in 25 years, filling enough shipping containers to circle globe six times
Author: Erin McCormick
Headline: Global push will triple toxic e-waste annually in 25 years, filling enough shipping containers to circle globe six times
Content: Datacenter equipment won’t be designed for repair and reuse, the report projects, and would need to be completely replaced every two to five years.Photograph: Tatsiana Volkava/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDatacenter equipment won’t be designed for repair and reuse, the report projects, and would need to be completely replaced every two to five years.Photograph: Tatsiana Volkava/Getty ImagesDatacentresDatacenter rush will create ‘tsunami’ of discarded electronics, report saysGlobal push will triple toxic e-waste annually in 25 years, filling enough shipping containers to circle globe six timesErin McCormickWed 16 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 13.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe ongoing campaign to build thousands of massive datacenters for AI will create a “tsunami” of discarded electronics, putting the world on a course to triple its annual generation of toxic e-waste in the next 25 years, anew reportprojects.The electronic trash AI generates in the next 25 years could fill enough shipping containers to encircle the globe six times, it said. Yet, says the report by the non-profit environmental group Basel Action Network (BAN), there is no plan to deal with that waste – which typically contains toxins like lead, mercury, cadmium and forever chemicals, as well as valuable metals that are challenging to reclaim.“Already electronic waste is the fastest-growing waste stream on the planet and only one-fifth is properly managed,” said Jim Puckett, co-founder of BAN, which works to see that toxic waste doesn’t end up getting dumped on the world’s poorer communities.Experts concur. “We’re doing a terrible job of handling e-waste in the US,” said Vince Beiser, author of the book Power Metal, which details the global problems of trying to reclaim valuable metals inside electronic goods. “Some of it gets dumped overseas. Most of it just gets dumped in landfills, which is a problem because it can leach all kinds of nasty things into the water, into the soil.”There are 4,871 new datacenters in the construction pipeline in the US, the report said, adding that, while not all are clearly designated for use by AI, many will be.It calculated the volumes of e-waste related to computer servers used for AI, and to “the thousands of tonnes of copper, steel, concrete” for cooling, power distribution, networking and energy storage equipment needed to operate inside datacenters.To estimate the total, the report approximated the amount of computing power analysts project will be built – totalling roughly 100 gigawatts of new capacity worldwide by 2030 alone and growing beyond that. It then analyzed how much equipment would be needed by weight – including racks of computer servers weighing 1,360kgs each, switches that weigh up to 30kgs, and hundreds of kilograms of copper cable connecting each rack.Such equipment won’t be designed for repair and reuse, the report projects, and would need to be completely replaced every two to five years.On top of this, it assumed that AI developments will force the rapid replacement of consumer computers, phones, and telecommunications equipment owing to the computing requirements of the new systems.By taking this wide view of all the various types of e-waste that will be created, the BAN report projects that AI-driven equipment retirement will generate up to 13m metric tonnes per year by 2030 – a far higher estimate than a handful ofpreviousstudies.AI datacenter construction has already created a groundswell of bipartisan opposition around the US for the huge amount of space and energy it requires, but the report comes when focus is turning to the long-term pollution AI could create.A group of environmental and health experts last weekcalled for the federal government to issue a pledgeto protect citizens’ health from the repercussions of AI buildout. It citedestimatesthat the air pollution from the enormous amount of electricity generation needed for datacenters could result in hundreds of thousands of new asthma cases and as many as 1,300 premature deaths per year in the US alone.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Trump administration has sought to weakenenvironmentalsafeguardsthat would normally govern such a massive technological buildout.A 2025 report by McKinsey & Companyestimates that, in order to achieve the tech industry’s planned rollout of artificial intelligence, nearly $7tn in capital outlays will be needed worldwide in the next five years to build datacenters running millions of computer servers 24 hours a day.BAN’s white paper notes that this unprecedented spending “is roughly the cost of ending world hunger for the next 75 years – being spent in just five”.“We all find ourselves unwitting participants in the AI horserace,” said the report, “as IT users everywhere find themselves using AI whether they would like to or not, and yet almost always, without being aware of the greater consequences of doing so.”Explore more on these topicsDatacentresPollutionHealthDatacenters – USDatacentres - AustraliaDatacentres - UKnewsShareReuse this content

title: Company behind failed Surrey oilfield project sells site at massive loss | Fossil fuels | The Guardian
description: New owners apply for permission to extract oil in Surrey despite landmark ruling from supreme court in 2024
Author: Matthew Pearce
Headline: New owners apply for permission to extract oil in Surrey despite landmark ruling from supreme court in 2024
Content: The supreme court reversed a 2019 decision to grant planning permission for expanding operations at the Horse Hill oil site near Horley.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe supreme court reversed a 2019 decision to grant planning permission for expanding operations at the Horse Hill oil site near Horley.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty ImagesFossil fuelsCompany behind failed Surrey oilfield project sells site at massive lossNew owners apply for permission to extract oil in Horse Hill despite landmark ruling from supreme court in 2024Matthew PearceWed 16 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter years of trying to dig for oil inSurrey, the company behind the drilling project that was turned down in a landmark supreme court ruling has sold off the site for a fraction of the money it spent on it, and rebranded as a clean energy company.Meanwhile, the new owners, who picked up the site for £1m, are applying, once again, for permission to dig.UK Oil and Gas (UKOG) spent more than a decade trying to develop Horse Hill oilfields, where they said they had found100bn barrels of oil.But in 2024 the supreme court, in a decision which has since become known as theFinch Ruling, decreed that “a planning authority should have considered the indirect downstream greenhouse gas emissions of an oil and gas project as part of its environmental impact assessment” and overturned a council decision to let expansion go ahead.The Guardian understands that the implied value of the Horse Hill licence area reached a peak of £46m in September 2018 after UKOG agreed to buy a 14.3% economic stake from a group of vendors for £6.6m. The surging valuations given to the fields was driven by industry estimates that there could be about 9.24bn barrels of oil in the tight Jurassic shale and conventional reservoir sections within the Horse Hill licences.Public records appear to show UKOG invested more than £25m into the site. Prior to the £1m sale, UKOG’s financial accounts showed that it had written down the value of its Horse Hill interests to just £55,360 on its balance sheet.UKOG has now changed its name to UKEnergyGroup, seeking to shift its focus towards salt-cavern energy storage and other clean energy projects.Stephen Sanderson, the company’s chief executive,said whilethe company still sees “potentially material resources” at Horse Hill, the divestment presented “timely and attractive opportunity to complete UKOG’s exit from the UK onshore oil and gas sector”.The company reportedly raised £1m in 2025 to develop hydrogen-storage projects in south Dorset and Yorkshire, and a further £500,000 to acquire land for a proposed East Yorkshire salt-cavern site.Guy Prince, the head of energy supply at energy transition thinktank Carbon Tracker, said Horse Hill was an example of “regulatory stranding”, in which climate litigation and regulatory shifts undermine the value of a fossil fuel asset.“The same transition risk can have really radical financial consequences depending on who owns the asset,” he said. “For a major [company], it might impair one investment opportunity. But for a small company concentrated on one project like this, it just transformed the entire business.”New owner Energy B is taking over UKOG’s application to drill for oil in Surrey. Horse Hill Developments Ltd, which it now controls, submitted a renewed planning application to Surrey county council in May for four production wells, a new oil processing area, tanker-loading facilities and a fluid reinjection well.The proposal would allow nearly 700,000 tonnes of oil to be extracted over 20 years.Sarah Finch, the campaigner whobrought the successful legal challenge to the supreme court in 2024, said there were “serious shortcomings” with the application’s new environmental assessment.View image in fullscreenSarah Finch, left, took her fight against Horse Hill all the way to the supreme court in 2024.Photograph: Carl Court/Getty Images“New guidance from the government and pre-existing guidance all say that they have to place the emissions from a new proposed project within a cumulative context of all current and approved fossil fuel projects,” Finch said. “They didn’t make any attempt to do that, although the data is readily available out there.”The application estimates that the development would result in about 2.3m tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions over its lifetime, including emissions from the eventual burning of the oil, but concluded the impact was “insignificant”.Planning documents said: “Horse Hill would account for around 0.05% of the projected UK carbon budget; an insignificant contribution that would give rise to insignificant climate change effects.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFinch said the developer’s argument was “false”. “Any greenhouse gas emissions are significant,” she added. “TheInternational Energy Agency has saidwe can’t afford any new oil or gas. Any additional fossil fuels are going to make it impossible to stay within the 1.5C target, so [the emissions] are significant.”World’s top 20 private equity firms produce more greenhouse gases a year than most countries, report findsRead moreThe application argued that extracting up to 678,693 tonnes of oil at Horse Hill would improve energy security by reducing the UK’s reliance on imports. An Energy B spokesperson said: “At a time of global uncertainty and energy price shocks, domestic oil and gas production increases energy security.“We are confident of meeting all the necessary legal and environmental requirements for the site. With the oil being refined in the UK and the gas serving the domestic market, the field will contribute positively to the UK economy.”Finch disputed that argument, saying domestically produced oil was typically traded on an international market rather than necessarily supplying British consumers.Finch said Surrey county council’s decision would be a “significant test case” for whether the climate risks of fossil fuel projects are being properly assessed after the supreme court ruling.The local authority’s formal consultation closed on 13 July, although the council has said it will consider submissions received before it makes its decision, which could be reached this month.Finch said the Weald Action Group would not rule out seeking another judicial review if the council approved the development. “We’re fairly confident that the environmental statement that’s been submitted isn’t compliant with the law and the new guidance,” she said.UK Energy Group/UKOiland Gas declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsFossil fuelsOilSurreyOil and gas companiesEnergyEnergy industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Suspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case found dead at his west London home | UK news | The Guardian
description: HSBC director Nicholas Brandram, 44, was found unresponsive by emergency services on Tuesday evening
Author: Vikram Dodd
Headline: HSBC director Nicholas Brandram, 44, was found unresponsive by emergency services on Tuesday evening
Content: Nicholas Brandram was arrested in June in connection with a 2017 incident in which a jogger running across Putney Bridge pushed a woman towards an oncoming bus.Photograph: Central NewsView image in fullscreenNicholas Brandram was arrested in June in connection with a 2017 incident in which a jogger running across Putney Bridge pushed a woman towards an oncoming bus.Photograph: Central NewsUK newsSuspect in ‘Putney pusher’ case found dead at his west London homeHSBC director Nicholas Brandram, 44, was found unresponsive by emergency services on Tuesday eveningVikram DoddPolice and crime correspondentWed 16 Sep 2026 13.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA senior city banker suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a moving bus in the “Putney pusher” case has been found dead.Nicholas Brandram, 44, was discovered at his home in Chiswick, westLondon, on Tuesday.He was arrested in June by the Metropolitan police in connection with a 2017 incident in which a jogger running across Putney Bridgepushed a woman towards an oncoming bus.She only avoided serious injury after the driver swerved around her at the last moment.Brandram was a director at HSBC and had previously served in the military, reaching the rank of captain.He was released on bail by detectives in June after being arrested on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm. In September, after answering bail, he was re-bailed with no conditions.Video footage showed the woman being pushed by a male jogger. She fell into the road, with the jogger running on.The Met wound down its investigation in 2018, after interviewing 50 men and arresting three suspects. The case, which attracted considerable attention, was unsolved.In a statement on Wednesday, the Met said: “At 19.12 on Tuesday, 15 September officers and the London ambulance service attended an address in Chiswick, Hounslow after a man was found unresponsive inside a property.“Sadly, a 44-year-old man was pronounced dead at the scene. His next of kin have been informed.“At this time his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.“A file will be prepared for the coroner in due course.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBrandram was the grandson of Princess Katherine of Greece, who was the great-granddaughter of Queen Victoria, the Daily Telegraph reported in 2013 when he was convicted of crashing his Harley-Davidson motorbike into a female cyclist around Hyde Park Corner, before driving off without leaving his details.In an interview with theCitywealth websitein March this year, Brandram said he was a senior relationship manager at HSBC Private Bank.He said: “I usually bicycle into our office in Mayfair from my home in west London. And then from there, can either stay at my desk, go to Canary Wharf or the City, or get on a train or go to the airport. My first meeting is ideally over breakfast and I’m ideally home for bath time. I’m a co-parenting single father with a three-year-old.”Brandram said his proudest professional achievement was being invited to a Buckingham Palace garden party after military service in Afghanistan, and that the person he most admired was his mother. “She raised three children as a single parent and is the busiest person I know,” he said. “I’ve never met someone with greater moral integrity and courage, as well as resilience and stamina.”Explore more on these topicsUK newsLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: the UK towns with the fewest jobs for young people | Youth unemployment | The Guardian
description: Rotherham has 46 online vacancies for every 1,000 young people but there are 288 in Cotswold district council area
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Rotherham has 46 online vacancies for every 1,000 young people but there are 288 in Cotswold district council area
Content: Shoppers in Rotherham. The IPPR has published a ‘local youth opportunity index’ to track job vacancies in Britain.Photograph: Ben Molyneux Photography/AlamyView image in fullscreenShoppers in Rotherham. The IPPR has published a ‘local youth opportunity index’ to track job vacancies in Britain.Photograph: Ben Molyneux Photography/AlamyYouth unemploymentRevealed: the UK towns with the fewest jobs for young peopleRotherham has 46 online vacancies for every 1,000 young people but there are 288 in Cotswold district council areaRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentWed 16 Sep 2026 05.30 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYoung people in Rotherham face a local jobs market with the fewest suitable opportunities in Britain, according to a report that warns stark regional divisions are fuelling a crisis in youth work.As ministers push to combat rising youth unemployment, the analysis from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) showed young people faced a tougher challenge in some parts of the country to find work than in others.Publishing a new “local youth opportunity index” to track job vacancies across Britain, it said there was a sixfold gap in jobs in theSouth Yorkshiretown compared with the more affluent Cotswolds, where there are fewer young adults but more opportunities.WhereasRotherhamhas 46 online job vacancies for every 1,000 young people, there are 288 in the area covered by Cotswold district council. Highlighting deep regional divisions, the report found nine of the 10 best areas for youth job opportunities are in the south of England.Places with job openings relative to the local youth population below the national average of 109, include East Renfrewshire in Scotland, Newcastle-under-Lyme in Staffordshire, and Broxtowe in Nottinghamshire. Cities includingSheffield, Coventry and Cardiff also ranked near the bottom of the list for youth employment opportunities.Places with the most opportunities included Woking in Surrey, Gloucester, Cherwell in Oxfordshire, and Warrington in the north-west ofEngland.The analysis comes as ministers await recommendations from a highly anticipated report by Alan Milburn, who is leading areview into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness. The former Labour health secretary, who is expected to publish his findings next month before the autumn budget, has called for a policy overhaul involving education, welfare and employment support.Chart of job vacancies for young people in local authority areasBritain’s young adults are bearing the brunt of a rise in unemployment, with the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are not in employment, education or training (Neet)surpassing 1 million earlier this yearfor the first time in more than a decade.Representing as many as one in eight young people, the rate has swelled at a significantly faster rate than in other countries amid a sharp rise in mental ill health and a tough jobs market.The IPPR said its report showed that becoming Neet was not simply a question of an individual’s qualifications or willingness to look for work. It urged ministers to prioritise overhauling the apprenticeship system and to create a new “work start” programme that would fund youth jobs in areas with too few entry-level opportunities. It also called for a new “youth allowance” that would replace different rates of universal credit benefits based on work capability.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionResponding to the IPPR report, David Blunkett, the former Labour education secretary, said he had first-hand experience of the challenges facing young people from growing up on a Sheffield council estate and leaving school at 16 with no qualifications.“Young people have an immense amount to give. With national ambition, local leadership and the willingness to invest, we can ensure that birthplace does not determine a young person’s future,” he said.“We can renew the promise that should lie at the heart of any decent society: that no young person will be discarded, that the door to opportunity will remain open and that everyone will have the chance to build a life of purpose.”A government spokesperson said: “Where you’re from should never determine where you end up in life.“The Milburn review will lay the foundation for further youth employment reform, but thanks to our £2.5bn investment, we are already taking action, including reprioritising apprenticeships for young people and rolling out youth hubs to every community, helping us create 1m work and training opportunities.“We are also supporting businesses to back young talent by offering hiring incentives worth up to £8,000 and continuing the national insurance exemptions for under-21s and apprentices under 25.”Explore more on these topicsYouth unemploymentUK unemployment and employment statisticsRotherhamYoung peopleInequalityUnemploymentEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bonnie Greer, writer and cultural commentator, dies aged 77 | Books | The Guardian
description: The British-American novelist and playwright who regularly appeared on current affairs shows will be remembered for her ‘warmth, humour and generosity’, says her husband
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: The British-American novelist and playwright who regularly appeared on current affairs shows will be remembered for her ‘warmth, humour and generosity’, says her husband
Content: Bonnie Greer pictured in 2016.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBonnie Greer pictured in 2016.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianBooksBonnie Greer, writer and cultural commentator, dies aged 77The British-American novelist and playwright who regularly appeared on current affairs shows will be remembered for her ‘warmth, humour and generosity’, says her husbandElla CreamerWed 16 Sep 2026 08.47 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British-American novelist, playwright and commentatorBonnie Greerhas died aged 77.In a statement, her husband David Hutchins said that she died on Tuesday evening following a brief illness.Greer’s “intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life”, said Hutchins. “To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her.”“RIP Bonnie Greer,” wrote novelist Bernardine Evaristo in a social media post. “Very sad news. There was a period in the 90s/00s when Bonnie was probably the most important and high profile black cultural commentator in the UK. Other than her writing, she also sat on many important boards – representing.”In an Instagram post, former deputy prime minister David Lammy wrote that Greer was “a powerful wordsmith and artist, she was eloquent and exacting. A true life force.”Greer was born on 16 November 1948, the eldest of seven children, and grew up on Chicago’s South Side. She studied playwriting under David Mamet in the city before moving to New York to work in theatre. In 1985, she brought a play to the Edinburgh fringe, and ultimately moved to the UK the following year, becoming a citizen in 1997.Greer’s work – which often focused on the lives of minorities, and of women – spanned novels, nonfiction, plays and broadcasting.Her first book, Hanging By Her Teeth, published in 1994, was a novel about a Black American woman travelling through the US and Europe in search of her father. Her later books included Obama Music (2009), about her and the former US president’s connections to Chicago’s South Side, Langston Hughes: The Value of Contradiction (2011), a biography of the Harlem Renaissance figure, and A Parallel Life (2014), her memoir. In 2019, she contributed to New Daughters of Africa, a landmark anthology edited by Margaret Busby. In 2022, she was made a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature.Greer’s stage plays included Dancing on Blackwater, which explored mother-daughter relationships, Jitterbug, composed of seven short plays about cultural divisions, and Munda Negra, for which she won the Soho Theatre Company Verity Bargate award for best play.In 2005, the BBC broadcastMarilyn and Ella Backstage at the Mocambo, Greer’s radio play about Marilyn Monroe and Ella Fitzgerald – in the 50s, Monroe persuaded a nightclub to book Fitzgerald amid racist reluctance, promising to sit in the front row every night. Greer eventually adapted the story into a musical drama for stage,titled Marilyn and Ella. The drama ran at the Edinburgh Fringe, the Theatre Royal Stratford East, and the Apollo Theatre, London.Greer wrote many radio dramas for the BBC, including Rosa Parks, about the civil rights icon, and Ferguson, inspired by August Strindberg’s play The Father and set in the US in 2016, against the backdrop of protests following the police killing of Michael Brown. She also translated and dramatised The Little Prince for a full-cast BBC radio adaptation.She often wrote opinion pieces for publications including the Guardian, the Independent and the New Statesman.In aninterview with the Guardianin 2016, she said that “Black Lives Matter is a rerun. It’s a replay of what we did as student activists in the 60s, the Black Panthers. I understand it because I’ve been through it and seen it.”Greer regularly appeared as a panellist on current affairs shows, including Newsnight Review and Question Time. Appearing in a controversial episode of the latter alongside far-right British National Party leader Nick Griffin in 2009, she heard “something in the audience: a kind of singing”, she later wrotein the Guardian, and turned the experience into an opera, Yes,which opened two years later.She served on the boards of the Royal Opera House, the British Museum and the London Film School, and was chancellor of Kingston University, London. In the 2010 birthday honours, she was appointed OBE for contribution to the arts.In 2009, shewrote thather hero was James Baldwin, describing him as “the person who first moved me and still does”. She was 12 when she read his first book, Go Tell It on the Mountain. “He nailed the emotions I felt right on the head and I read all his subsequent books.”Greer married Hutchins, whom she had first met in the aisle of a supermarket, in 1993. In his statement after her death, Hutchins said that “those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together”.Many writers and politicians shared tributes to Greer on social media on Wednesday. “Bonnie’s voice brought courage, humour and humanity to Britain’s cultural conversation”,wrote London mayorSadiq Khan. “She inspired and opened doors for so many others. And she was great fun too.”Explore more on these topicsBooksBonnie GreernewsShareReuse this content

title: Previously unseen drawings by Moomins author Tove Jansson to go on show in London | Tove Jansson | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Exhibition focusing on Finnish writer and artist’s illustrations will include original art from her first Moomins book
Author: Dalya Alberge
Headline: Exclusive: Exhibition focusing on Finnish writer and artist’s illustrations will include original art from her first Moomins book
Content: A sketch for Princessan Glittergull (1922), to be shown at the Quentin Blake Centre for Illustration.Photograph: Tove Jansson EstateView image in fullscreenA sketch for Princessan Glittergull (1922), to be shown at the Quentin Blake Centre for Illustration.Photograph: Tove Jansson EstateTove JanssonPreviously unseen drawings by Moomins author Tove Jansson to go on show in LondonExclusive: Exhibition focusing on Finnish writer and artist’s illustrations will include original art from her first Moomins bookDalya AlbergeWed 16 Sep 2026 10.08 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Moomin books about lovable trolls with hippopotamus snouts who live in harmony with nature are a global publishing phenomenon, having sold up to 30m copies since the Finnish artist and writerTove Janssonwrote and illustrated them between 1945 and 1977.Now previously unseen drawings of her eccentric characters will be among more than 100 exhibits in a major exhibition that is being staged inLondon25 years after her death.Tove Jansson and her Families will open at the Quentin Blake Centre forIllustrationin November, it will be announced on Thursday.Billed as the UK’s first exhibition to focus on Jansson’s illustrations, it will feature sketches, photographs and films, as well as her correspondence with those closest to her and fans of all ages.View image in fullscreenTove Jansson ‘had this very special skill to harness themes that touch the reader’, said her niece, Sophia Jansson.Photograph: Eva KonikoffThe displays will include original art from her first published book,The Moominsand the Great Flood, in which she presented a world “where everything was natural and benign – and possible”, in a story about Moomintroll’s search, with Moominmamma, for their missing Moominpappa and how they found their way to the magical Moominvalley.Jansson’s books celebrate nature, friendship, tolerance and the freedom to be oneself. Enchanting children and adults alike, they have been translated into more than 60 languages, inspiring animated films, television series and theme parks.View image in fullscreenA sketch of Moominpappa with a giant shell has not been shown before.Photograph: Moomin CharactersSophia Jansson, Tove’s niece, told the Guardian: “She had this very special skill to harness themes that touch the reader … on a universal and a personal level – and then disguise them in these stories, so that we think we’re reading about Moomins in Moominvalley and, when you finish the book, you realise that you’re actually reading about ‘us’, about humans and how we interact and all our peculiarities.”Previously unseen material will include a sketch of Moominpappa, a sea-loving adventurer, with a giant shell. It was an early draft for the cover of Moominpappa at Sea, in which the Moomin family moves to a remote island at the mercy of the sea and storms.It is among images that even Sophia, the chair of the Moomins Characters brand, has not seen before, but which have recently come to light: “This is the amazing thing about Tove. She was extremely prolific.”Asked whether this is the first-ever UK exhibition to focus on Jansson’s illustrations, Sophia said: “Definitely, because the one in Dulwich [Picture Gallery in 2017] was mainly to show her paintings.”Paul Gravett, a Jansson expert and guest curator at the Quentin Blake Centre, told the Guardian: “The prose novels are still extremely topical because of the sheer variety of characters that are brought together. They are filled with a lot of love and tolerance, that ‘isn’t it wonderful how very different we all are?’“Moomin celebrates that, enjoying eccentricity and going with the flow of life. This is one of the reasons that they’re not just for children. They have a lot of depth to them.”Gravett said the draft book cover was different from the one eventually published, but “every bit as good”.At the age of seven, Jansson was already writing and illustrating homemade booklets, which she sold to her classmates. Exhibits will include these drawings. “You can see a lot of the same fascination with fantasy and dreams, which came out of her childhood reading,” Gravett said.Her passion for fantasy literature stayed with her. She illustrated Swedish editions of Lewis Carroll’s The Hunting of the Snark and Alice in Wonderland in a horror style. With JRR Tolkien’s The Hobbit, she reinterpreted his characters, making Gollum monstrously large.View image in fullscreenJansson’s books have been translated into more than 60 languages.Photograph: Moomin CharactersTolkien himself was surprised. Realising he had never clarified Gollum’s size, he amended the second edition to describe him as “a small, slimy creature”. The first English edition with Jansson’s illustrations will be published this month by HarperCollins.Jansson was an outspoken political cartoonist, criticising fascism during the second world war, once saying: “Most of all I liked the fact that I got to be beastly to Hitler and Stalin.” In one cartoon, she depicted a woman and little girl in a toy shop with the caption: “Don’t you have a doll that says ‘Momma’?/ ‘No, little friend, our new stock says ‘Heil Hitler!’”She had a special connection with London: at a time when it was rare for female cartoonists to have their own daily strip, her first Moomin series went into print from 1954 in London’s Evening News. Her comic strips were circulated worldwide.Exhibits will include a sketch for one of the earliest examples. Gravett said: “It’s a miracle it survived because it’s covered in coffee stains and it was headed for the waste paper bin. A fellow cartoonist spotted it and rescued it.”Gravett is working on a Jansson book, followinghis 2022 studyof her illustration work.Tove Jansson and her Familiesruns from 21 November to 9 Mayat theQuentin Blake Centre for Illustration, Clerkenwell, LondonExplore more on these topicsTove JanssonIllustrationThe MoominsArtLondonChildren and teenagersPicture booksnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Godfather of AI’ says tech regulation is nearing Covid-style pivot moment | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Safety crisis makes it more likely that governments will be spurred into action, says Yoshua Bengio
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Safety crisis makes it more likely that governments will be spurred into action, says Yoshua Bengio
Content: Bengio is a prominent voice in the campaign to rein in breakneck AI development.Photograph: Atlantic StudiosView image in fullscreenBengio is a prominent voice in the campaign to rein in breakneck AI development.Photograph: Atlantic StudiosAI (artificial intelligence)‘Godfather of AI’ says tech regulation is nearing Covid-style pivot momentSafety crisis makes it more likely that governments will be spurred into action, says Yoshua BengioDan MilmoGlobal technology editorWed 16 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 15.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleConcerns over AI safety are reaching a point where governments realise they must act to protect the public, similarly to in the Covid pandemic, according to one of the “godfathers” of the technology.Yoshua Bengio said recent events, including a “swarm” of OpenAI agentshacking a startupandtech insider warnings of an existential threat, were cutting through – making government action more likely.The Canadian computer scientist, a prominent voice in the campaign to rein in breakneck AI development, said he was now “more optimistic than many observers because I see the public moving”.Comparing the AI safety crisis to the onset of the Covid pandemic in 2020, Bengio said: “Think about how quickly governments moved after the beginning of the pandemic when they realised that public safety, their future, democracy, was in danger. You would expect that they move quickly. So we are, I think, nearing that point.”Concern over the potential threat of powerful AI systems has reached a new pitch in recent months after a series of safety incidents involving OpenAI and Anthropic agents carrying out unsanctioned activities such as hacking third parties, hijacking a German website, and using fake identities to try to trick developers.His comments came as 42 fellows and foreign members of the Royal Society wrote to the organisation’s president, Sir Paul Nurse, to express their “extreme concern” over the pace of AI development. “By the time the situation becomes obvious to the wider public, it may be too late to act,” the researchers wrote in an open letter to Nurse. “We believe this is an emergency, and call on the Royal Society to use its influence to convey this view to government and the media.”Last week, a researcher at Anthropic, the startup behind the Claude chatbot, resigned after warning that colleagues believed AI could “kill us all by the end of the decade”. Days later, Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei,called for a slowdownin the pace of cutting-edge AI development – a move that was immediately supported by OpenAI, Google and Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX.However, sceptics of the “slowdown” call have claimed that calls by major AI firms are an example of “regulatory capture”, where companies persuade governments to introduce safety regimes that raise the cost of smaller rivals being able to compete. They also claim existential fears overshadow more immediate issues with AI such as its impact oncopyright-protected workand human rights.Bengio said he disagreed with the regulatory capture argument because a slowdown by leading AI firms would “cost them financially”. The US president, Donald Trump, has rejected a slowdown, saying he does not want the US to lose its lead over China in the AI race.View image in fullscreenYoshua Bengio, a professor at the University of Montreal, won a Turing award in 2018.Photograph: Andrej Ivanov/AFP/Getty ImagesBengio spoke as the Canadian and German governments announced funding of up to C$300m (£160m) for hisnon-profit organisationdedicated to creating an “honest AI” that will act as a guardrail against rogue agents – AI tools that carry out sequences of tasks without human intervention.Bengio, a professor at the University of Montreal, earned the “godfather of AI” moniker after winning the 2018 Turing award, seen as the equivalent of a Nobel prize for computing. He shared it with Geoffrey Hinton,who later won a Nobel, and Yann LeCun, the former chief AI scientist at Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta.Bengio’s organisation, LawZero, is developing a system called Scientist AI that will act as a guardrail against AI agents showing deceptive or self-preserving behaviour, such as trying to avoid being turned off. LawZero is also funded by the Gates Foundation, the chipmaker Nvidia, and Coefficient Giving, a philanthropic body linked to effective altruism, a movement that believes AI poses an existential threat.The LawZero technology is viewed by Bengio as a counterpoint to reinforcement learning, a trial-and-error development technique used by major AI companies where AIs are rewarded for working out how to carry out a specific task. The Canadian computer scientist believes, along with other experts, this training technique encourages AIs to pursue their goals recklessly and cause harm in the process, as shown by the OpenAI “swarm”.Deployed alongside an AI agent, Bengio’s technology would raise potentially harmful behaviour by an autonomous system – having weighed whether its actions could cause harm. Bengio expects the technology to be deployed for other uses eventually, such as accelerating scientific breakthroughs.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: US Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time since 2023 | Federal Reserve | The Guardian
description: Trump urges lower rates after central bank agrees increase by quarter-percentage point to range of 3.75% to 4%
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Trump urges lower rates after central bank agrees increase by quarter-percentage point to range of 3.75% to 4%
Content: Kevin Warsh at the Federal Reserve in in Washington in July.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenKevin Warsh at the Federal Reserve in in Washington in July.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersFederal ReserveUS Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time since 2023Trump urges lower rates after central bank agrees increase by quarter-percentage point to range of 3.75% to 4%Federal Reserve raises interest rates – liveGaya GuptaWed 16 Sep 2026 17.01 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 14.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe USFederal Reservevoted to raise interest rates on Wednesday for the first time since 2023 as the central bank continues to fight to tamp down inflation.The Fed’s open market committee voted unanimously to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%. This is the first time the Fed has raised rates since July 2023 and potentially sets Kevin Warsh, the current Fed chair, on a collision course with Donald Trump.“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said on Wednesday. “This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.”After the announcement, Trumpsaidin a Truth Social post that interest rates should be 1% or less and criticized the US trade deficit. Trump said the US would make “at least 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year” if it were to stop trading with countries with which it has a deficit.“We are ‘carrying’ almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer. LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!,” Trump wrote.Chart of Fed funds target rateThough Warsh acknowledged changing geopolitics, he avoided calling out the US-Israel war with Iran by name.“There’s no hiding from hotspots around the world, and our judgment about what is the most likely or least likely of the geopolitical situation has changed,” he said.Warsh also declined to answer questions about how Trump would react but reiterated that Fed independence was “a two-way street”.“We will let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane. That is the way we can stand up here and call them the way we see them,” he said.The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.New projections showed a majority of officials penciled in another rate hike before the year’s end, with four officials predicting the Fed’s benchmark interest rate would reach a range of 4.25% to 4.5% by the end of the year.And though estimates on the country’s economic growth and unemployment rate were upbeat, Fed officials believed it would take roughly until 2029 for inflation to reach its 2% goal.At its last meeting in late July, the open market committee voted 9-3 to maintain rates, the first time in 10 years that so many members shared dissent on a policy decision. Since then, the US and Iran have renewed attacks against each other, driving up the Brent crude benchmark to its highest levels in month.The war has driven up inflation, especially energy prices. Gas prices have remained, on average, $1 a gallon more expensive compared with a year ago. Diesel fuel, which is used for buses, trains and trucks, recently reached an all-time high of $6.31.Concerns about inflation have induced asell-offin the US bond market, with the yield on the 10-year treasury note hitting a 19-year high earlier this week, despite efforts from the US treasury to calm the market. Typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, trouble in the US bond market canlead tohigher interest rates for consumer and business loans.The Fed uses interest rates as a tool to cool price increases by slowing activity. Higher interest rates impact mortgages, car payments, student debt and other types of loans. After inflation reached a generational high of 9.1% in June 2022, the Fed increased rates 11 times from 2022 and 2023. Rates were brought up to a target range of 5.25% to 5.5% before the Fed eventually started lowering rates in 2024 and 2025.At the beginning of the year, when the annualized inflation rate was 1% lower than current levels, a Fed rate hike seemed highly unlikely. A majority of Fed officials were actually predicting a rate cut before the end of the year. But inflation in Augustremained stubbornly highwhile unemployment was steady, which furthered the chances of a rate hike.Higher prices have painted a grim economic outlook as voters prepare to head to the polls in November. Recent data and surveys have shown heightened inflation has wiped out wage gains for Americans and dampened consumer outlook. In August, hourly earnings for employees decreased by 0.1% year-over-year after accounting for inflation and fell by 0.3% from the month prior. Consumer sentiment has also rapidly declined, according to a monthly survey from the University of Michigan, while expectations for more inflation have increased.Candidates on both sides of the political aisle have sought to make cost-of-living concerns and the economy a forefront of their campaigns, but voters are split on which party has the greatest advantage on this issue, according torecent Pew data.Meanwhile, Trump has implored Republican voters to pretendas if they are voting for himon their midterm ballot and promised every American a $5,000 “Trump dividend”if Republicans retain control of Congress.Critics have likened the move to bribery and warned of the financial implications, especially after the US government debt reached arecord-high$40tn last month.Explore more on these topicsFederal ReserveUS economyTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: House votes to hold Leon Black in contempt over Epstein subpoenas refusal | Jeffrey Epstein | The Guardian
description: Billionaire has refused to comply with subpoenas from House oversight committee as part of Epstein inquiry
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: Billionaire has refused to comply with subpoenas from House oversight committee as part of Epstein inquiry
Content: Leon Black in California in May 2018.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLeon Black in California in May 2018.Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesJeffrey EpsteinHouse votes to hold Leon Black in contempt over Epstein subpoenas refusalBillionaire has refused to comply with subpoenas from House oversight committee as part of Epstein inquiryUS politics live – latest updatesAnna BettsWed 16 Sep 2026 16.50 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 15.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheHouse of Representativesvoted on Wednesday to hold billionaire investor Leon Black in contempt of Congress over his refusal to comply with subpoenas issued to him by the House oversight committee as part of its investigation into Jeffrey Epstein.The action came a day after the committeevoted unanimouslyto recommend that the House hold Black in contempt. Wednesday’s House vote passed under unanimous consent, meaning there was not a formal roll call, but no member objected to thecontempt resolution.The Department of Justice will now decide whether to take action on the resolution, though it is not required to. Congressheldformer attorney general Merrick Garland in contempt in 2024, but the justice departmentdid not act on it. But it did prosecute Trump advisers Peter Navarro and Steve Bannon after congressional referrals for contempt, and both menservedprisontime.Epstein survivors praise House panel over Leon Black contempt voteRead moreIn a statement on Wednesday, a justice department spokesperson said: “The Department of Justice is expecting to receive the referral from House oversight committee and takes allegations of contempt of Congress seriously.“For the past 18 months, the department has repeatedly said it will follow additional investigative leads in all matters relating toJeffrey Epstein,” they added. “The US attorney’s office for the District of Columbia will review the referral of Mr Black carefully and will not hesitate to pursue additional cases where the evidence supports.”Black, whose namecame uprepeatedly in theEpstein files, and who, as reported bythe New York Times, paid Epstein a total of $170m for what he described as tax and estate planning services from 2013 to 2017, first voluntarily appeared before the committee for a transcribed interview as part of its investigation in June, but the sessionended abruptlyafter lawmakers from both parties said that Black refused to answer questions about NDAs. Black has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and said he had no knowledge of Epstein’s criminal activities.His lawyers criticized the contempt resolution shortly after it passed Wednesday. “This an outrageous action that ignores the facts and the truth about Mr Black. The House of Representatives has rushed through every stage of this inquiry,” they said.“We intend to pursue our litigation challenging this action and will hold the committee and Chairman Comer accountable in the courts.”The committee, chaired by Republican James Comer, then issued two subpoenas: one demanding that Black produce all NDAs “to which he is a party” and another requiring him to appear before the committee again for a deposition.Blackdid not appearfor his scheduled 3 September deposition and did not produce all of the NDAs sought by the committee.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe instead sued Comer and the committee, arguing that the subpoenas were “invalid” and exceeded the committee’s “delegated authority in seeking private information that bears no legitimate connection” to its legislative purpose. He also argued that the subpoenas would “expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein”.On Tuesday, Black’s attorneyssaidthat the committee under Comer and the representative Robert Garcia, its top Democrat, had “lost sight of its legislative purpose and is abusing its power”. They described the subpoenas as “illegitimate, illegal and a textbook abuse of power designed to bully and destroy legal protections of private citizens” and reiterated that Black “never abused a woman”, “was never blackmailed by Epstein” and “had no knowledge of any of Epstein’s heinous conduct”.On Wednesday morning, more than a dozen survivors of Epstein’s abusepraised the Houseoversight committee for their vote.“Survivors have fought for years to bring the truth about Epstein’s network into the open and have helped create this moment of accountability,” they said on Wednesday morning before the House vote. “Congress now has an opportunity to build on that work by following the investigative leads contained in the Epstein files wherever they go and demanding answers from the powerful people connected to them.”Explore more on these topicsJeffrey EpsteinHouse of RepresentativesUS CongressUS politicsShareReuse this content

title: European Union invites Canada to become first ever ‘associate member’ | European Union | The Guardian
description: Commission president says EU must ‘urgently reimagine our partnerships’ as she makes unprecedented offer
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Commission president says EU must ‘urgently reimagine our partnerships’ as she makes unprecedented offer
Content: 1:27Von der Leyen 'opens door' to Canada becoming associate EU member – videoEuropean UnionEuropean Union invites Canada to become first ever ‘associate member’Commission president says EU must ‘urgently reimagine our partnerships’ as she makes unprecedented offerJennifer Rankinin Strasbourg andLeyland Ceccoin TorontoWed 16 Sep 2026 09.48 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 04.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada has been invited to become the first “associate member” of the EU by the European Commission president,Ursula von der Leyen.In an unprecedented offer, von der Leyen said on Wednesday that the EU andCanada“see the world with the same eyes” through shared democratic values and common approaches to many big issues, from AI to climate breakdown, the Ukraine war and geopolitics.Canada should become an EU state in all but name. Here’s how to make that a reality | Fabian ZuleegRead moreSpeaking in the presence of the Canadian prime minister,Mark Carney, at the European parliament in Strasbourg, she said: “We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. We must urgently reimagine our partnerships.
