So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU.”Carney, who is due to address the parliament on Thursday, has called fora “unique alliance” with the EUas Canada seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade.He later tweeted: “Canada and the EU are natural partners, united by shared values.”The EU and Canada are due to hold a summit in late October to develop the future relationship.View image in fullscreenCanada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, attends the annual ‘State of the European Union’ address at the European parliament on Wednesday.Photograph: Pascal Bastien/APCanada and the EU already have a trade deal and numerous bilateral agreements, but have been moving closer since Donald Trump returned to the White House and raised tariffs on both old allies, while repeatedlytalking about Canada becoming the 51st US stateand lambasting the EU.Von der Leyen said the existing EU-Canada trade deal would be upgraded to an “alliance for the future” to create a “common prosperity and economic security space”.She said the two sides would also create a tech alliance, integrate defence industrial bases and make the Arctic a “flagship joint project”. EU officials are especially interested in Canada’s energy and natural resources. Von der Leyen pitched joint work on energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security.The offer of associate membership is certain to raise questions among other EU allies, including the UK, which has long sought a more flexible approach from Brussels.The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, although it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, allowing deep economic integration with these countries, who follow many EU rules.It remains to be seen what associate membership means, including for Canada’s relationship with the EU single market. When theUK was negotiating its departure from the bloc and post-Brexit relationship, EU officials repeatedly said there was no status that enabled a foreign country to be half in and half out of the single market.The phrase itself took EU insiders by surprise since von der Leyen had not used the term when she briefed senior EU diplomats ahead of her speech last Friday.One EU diplomat said member states were “generally very supportive of ambition” in the EU-Canada relationship, but had been slightly worried in recent weeks that von der Leyen was overpromising on Canada. “‘Associate membership’ sounds like a nice headline but in reality 10 member states have still not ratified Ceta,” the person said, referring to the EU-Canada trade agreement that was agreed 10 years ago. A second EU diplomat described associate membership as “an empty phrase”.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Mark Carney; the European parliament president, Roberta Metsola; and Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday.Photograph: Ronald Wittek/EPACarney’s approach to dealing with Trump has however attracted widespread praise among MEPs.Last month, Carney announced he wasbreaking off trade talks with the US, saying Canada would not be subjugated, and then introduced retaliatory tariffs on billions worth of US goods. By contrast, the EU last yearaccepted 15% tariffs on many European goodswhile dropping its own duties to avoid a trade war with Trump.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJavier Moreno Sánchez, a Spanish socialist MEP, who leads the European parliament’s Canada delegation, said “for sure” the EU had lessons to learn from Carney’s approach, because “Trump respects people who are strong”. He added: “Canadians are the most European people outsideEuropeand that is the key point for the development of our relationship.”‘My future is in the EU’: the Ukrainian children who don’t want to go homeRead moreMartin Leng at the Brussels Institute for Geopolitics thinktank said a world in flux was “pushing the EU towards far greater flexibility in its relations with third states”.He said von der Leyen’s speech, with its focus on different sectoral areas of cooperation “points to the ambition and strategic breadth of the associate membership which the parties have in mind but also suggests that, in reality, Canada’s ‘membership’ may consist of ‘plugging in’ to existing programmes and frameworks, such as the European Defence Agency, rather than joining the union in any traditional sense”.Roland Paris, the director of the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa and a foreign affairs adviser to the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, said the term “associate member” has taken too much focus and “doesn’t really matter” in the long term.“My hunch is that von der Leyen was hoping to rally supporters of much closer cooperation with Canada by using that label. In the end, what I expect is that we’re going to see a collection of agreements rather than membership in any institutional sense,” he said.Carney’s decision to formalise close ties with Europe however prompted outrage from Conservatives at home.Pierre Poilievre, the Tory leader,posted on social mediathat he feared Canadians “struggling to pay their rent” would have to pay more taxes “to fund the European Union’s heavy bureaucracy”.“The welder from Welland didn’t elect a Eurocrat to regulate our steel. The farmer from Saskatchewan and the fisher from the Atlantic provinces didn’t choose a Brussels food regulator who has never seen our prairies or our coasts,” he wrote. “We will NEVER be the 51st American state. And we will NEVER be the 28th state of theEuropean Union.”Another, Jamil Jivani,postedthat Conservatives “will NEVER support Mark Carney’s Liberal plan to have Canada join the hopelessly run, over-regulated, and self-destructive EU”.Paris said no Canadian leaders “would be interested in formal EU membership if it involves subordinating Canadian law and regulatory structures” to Europe.“I don’t think that’s on the table right now. There has long been a bipartisan push in Canada to deepen trade connections between Canada and Europe,” he said. “We’re now seeing now is a logical extension of those trade discussions into other areas.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionUrsula von der LeyenCanadaMark CarneyEuropeEuropean CommissionInternational tradenewsShareReuse this content

title: EU moves closer to social media ban for under 13s | Social media bans | The Guardian
description: Ursula von der Leyen announces draft law to stop apps ‘depriving children of their childhood’
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Ursula von der Leyen announces draft law to stop apps ‘depriving children of their childhood’
Content: The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, gives the EU’s annual state of the union address in Strasbourg on Wednesday.Photograph: Pascal Bastien/APView image in fullscreenThe European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, gives the EU’s annual state of the union address in Strasbourg on Wednesday.Photograph: Pascal Bastien/APSocial media bansEU moves closer to social media ban for under 13sUrsula von der Leyen announces draft law to stop apps ‘depriving children of their childhood’Jennifer Rankinin StrasbourgWed 16 Sep 2026 10.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe EU will move forward withplans for an under 13s social media ban, the head of the European Commission has confirmed.Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday that social media apps were “depriving children of their childhood” and big tech platforms needed to prove the safety of their products.She promised a draft law for a totalban on social mediafor under 13s, while children aged 13-15 would be allowed “mini accounts” under parental supervision with time limits on apps.The commission will publish its social media plan on Thursday, which will have to be agreed by the European parliament and 27 EU member states if it is to become law.Von der Leyen also promised that the commission’s Digital Fairness Act, due to be submitted to the European parliament this year, would tackle features such as addictive design, which she said was “harming everyone”.A world map showing where social media bans have been implemented or proposedSocial media bans go global: big tech faces a reckoning after Australia’s crackdownRead moreThe commission president made the comments in Strasbourg as part of her annual state of the union address. In a wide-ranging speech covering the EU’s place in a turbulent world and plans for continent-wide legislation, she also promised a European heatwave plan and committed to an emergency response mechanism to deal with sudden inflows of migrants in response toevents in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in August.Von der Leyen also made an unprecedentedinvitation to Canada to become an “associate member” of the EU, and pledged to set out ideas for a European security council involving Canada, Norway, Ukraine and the UK.The former German defence minister said the EU needed its version ofNato’s article 4– an “emergency security protocol” that means all member states would convene at the request of another in response to a hybrid attack.“Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook,” she said. “We urgently need a consensus on how to respond to certain incidents – those which fall below armed aggression but clearly threaten our national security.”Nato’s article 4, which is separate from the collective defence clause, article 5, means members of the alliance can consult when one of them believes their territorial integrity, political independence or security is threatened.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEuropean nations have recently faced a series of hostile acts attributed to Russia, including sabotage, incursions by jets into European airspace anda drone attack on Leipzig airport.Warning that Ukraine faced a tough winter, von der Leyen suggested the EU may have reached its limits on economic restrictions against Russia. “What is needed is not necessarily new sanctions, but above all the enforcement of existing sanctions,” she said.After 21 rounds of measures, EU member states have found it increasingly difficult to agree sanctions on the Kremlin’s war machine, wary of the cost to their own economies.Von der Leyen also touched on Europe’s divisions over whether or not to introduce restrictions on trade with Israel and itsillegal settlements in the West Bank. The commission has declined to publish a proposal to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements, though several EU member states and allies including France, Canada and the UK have moved in this direction.“When Europe is divided, it cannot change the course of events,” she said.Explore more on these topicsSocial media bansEuropean UnionEuropean CommissionUrsula von der LeyenSocial mediaDigital mediaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Sunderland gets its Kicks: Nissan to invest £170m to build new hybrid SUV | Nissan | The Guardian
description: Latest attempt to secure future of Britain’s biggest car factory may be subject to UK weakening EV sales mandate
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Latest attempt to secure future of Britain’s biggest car factory may be subject to UK weakening EV sales mandate
Content: The Nissan plant in Sunderland.Photograph: Nissan/PAView image in fullscreenThe Nissan plant in Sunderland.Photograph: Nissan/PANissanSunderland gets its Kicks: Nissan to invest £170m to build new hybrid SUVLatest attempt to secure future of Britain’s biggest car factory may be subject to UK weakening EV sales mandateAlex DanielWed 16 Sep 2026 06.38 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNissan has said it will invest £170m to build a new SUV at its factory in Sunderland – but said the move was subject to the UKweakening its electric vehicle sales mandate.The new hybrid model, the Kicks, is Nissan’s latest attempt to secure the future of the plant, which employs 6,000 people in Tyne and Wear and is Britain’s biggest car factory.Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s head in Europe, Asia, Africa and Oceania, said the move would not bring new jobs but waspart of “securing and maintaining” jobs at the site, which has been running at 50% capacity.On long road back from Brexit, north-east’s recovery rides on survival of Nissan’s ‘shining star’ plantRead moreThe Kicks will be the fourth Nissan model produced at theSunderlandplant, which already makes the Qashqai, Juke and Leaf. It is already sold in more than 70 markets but has never been built in Europe.The announcement is a boost to Britain’s automotive sector, which was last week hit by the news thatJaguar Land Rover will cut 4,000 jobs.Carmakers have come under pressure from US tariffs,competition from Chinese rivalsand high industrial energy costs in recent years.Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, said the investment and new car model was “a huge vote of confidence in the UK’s manufacturing expertise and automotive future”.However, it also came with an apparent warning from Messina, who said: “Of course we’re going to keep discussing with the UK government because large part of this is subject to the ZEV [Zero Emission Vehicles] mandate amendment.”The government isconsulting on cutting the UK’s electric vehicle sales targetsfor manufacturers. Under the ZEV mandate, carmakers ensure a percentage of the cars they sell each year are zero-emissions, with the target rising each year to reach 80% by 2030.But after heavy lobbying pressure from manufacturers, the government said last month that it was considering cutting that figure to as little as 50% by the end of the decade, which it is consulting on until late October.When pressed on whether Nissan would still make the investment if the targets were not weakened, Messina said: “We try to assess always if this is more likely than unlikely.”He added that the company was pushing for a cut to 50% of sales needing to be EVs. “I just want to think that this is done,” he said. “For me, yes, it’s going to happen.”Nissan is separately in talks to share production with the Chinese carmaker Chery, which is looking to build its own cars in the UK, to bring the site closer to full capacity again.Messina said he was putting “pressure internally and externally” to complete the deal which wasannounced in June. “We are ready to go. We are waiting just that Chery finalises volume and lineup.”Separately, LEVC, the maker of London’s black cabs, said on Wednesday that it will launch its next-generation taxi model next year, built at its factory in Ansty, near Coventry. The Chinese company, owned by Geely, said the new taxi would replace the currentall-electric TX range introduced in 2018.Nissan is also lobbying Brussels over the EU’s “Made in Europe” rules, which wouldrequire cars to be built within the blocto qualify for subsidies and public procurement.The company has previously said that itcould be forced to close Sunderlandif the rules go ahead as currently drafted.Messina said: “You might imagine how much time I’m spending on this to secure that this comes together in order to have Sunderland and the UK part of it.“There are good indications that this will be achieved. We believe strongly, regardless what will be the outcome, that UK cannot be left anyway outside.”Mike Hawes, the chief executive of the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, said the investment was “a major boost for Nissan Sunderland, the thousands of highly skilled jobs it supports and the wider local supply chain”.On Wednesday, McLaren announced it wouldinvest £500m in its UK operations,including a new factory, 1,000 jobs and its first SUV.Explore more on these topicsNissanAutomotive industryElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsManufacturing sectorSunderlandMotoringTravel and transportShareReuse this content

title: Ladbrokes owner prepares to cut 400 jobs weeks after profit boost | Gambling | The Guardian
description: Entain, which also owns Coral and BetMGM, starts consultation process over customer care roles
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Entain, which also owns Coral and BetMGM, starts consultation process over customer care roles
Content: The Ladbrokes owner, Entain, is headquartered in London and employs more than 28,000 people worldwide.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Ladbrokes owner, Entain, is headquartered in London and employs more than 28,000 people worldwide.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/ReutersGamblingLadbrokes owner prepares to cut 400 jobs weeks after profit boostEntain, which also owns Coral and BetMGM, starts consultation process over customer care rolesBusiness live – latest updatesLauren AlmeidaWed 16 Sep 2026 05.44 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheLadbrokesowner, Entain, has said it is preparing to cut 400 jobs, only weeks after the FTSE 100 business reported better than expected profit in its first half of the year.The gambling group, which also owns Coral and BetMGM, has started a consultation process that could remove one in five of its 2,000 customer care jobs.Its chief executive, Stella David, said the proposed changes were made to ensure the “business remains competitive, financially resilient, and well positioned for the future as our sector faces an increasingly challenging operating environment.“This decision has not been made lightly, and our immediate priority is to support those of our colleagues who may be impacted through this transition.”It comes only weeks after the company revealed its underlying operating profit had hit £479m in the six months to the end of June – 2% below the same period in the year prior but ahead of what investors had expected.Entain blamed the job cuts partly on higher taxes in the UK, as the sector also braces for a mooted increase to machine games duty in the budget.The chancellor, John Healey, is reportedly looking at increasing the levy in his inaugural budget on 28 October, in a way that could target betting shops and adult gaming centres (AGCs).AGCs, which offer 24-hour gambling machines, have grown rapidly across UK high streets in recent years,disproportionately targeting economically deprived areas.Whileonline casinos were hit with a tax increasein Rachel Reeves’s budget last year, duty on physical slot machines in AGCs were not affected.Doubling machine games duty could increase the tax take from “category B” £2-a-spin slot machines by between £275m and £458m, on top of the £600m they currently pay,according to research by the Social Market Foundation thinktank.David wrote to Andy Burnham last week, arguing that doubling the standard rate of machine games duty from 20% to 40% would add about £100m to the cost of running Entain’s retail business in the UK, and claiming that could result in 1,470 betting shop closures in the UK and 15,900 job losses.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBurnham has previously backed aproposal by Gordon Brownto pay for an end to the two-child benefit cap by tapping the gambling industry for more tax.Entain, which is headquartered in London and employs more than 28,000 people worldwide, started as GVC Holdings in 2004 under Kenny Alexander. It has grown into one of the biggest betting businesses in the world, and includes brands such as BetCity and Eurobet as well as gaming brands Foxy Bingo, Gala and PartyCasino.Shares in the company, which will be demoted to the mid-cap FTSE 250 index from 21 September, are down by about 36% in the year to date. They fell 1% in early trading on Wednesday.Explore more on these topicsGamblingLadbrokesJob lossesnewsShareReuse this content

title: McLaren to build SUVs geared towards Formula One fans with children | Automotive industry | The Guardian
description: Model comes as part of £500m UK investment by firm’s new Abu Dhabi owner that will also fund new factory
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Model comes as part of £500m UK investment by firm’s new Abu Dhabi owner that will also fund new factory
Content: McLaren will create 1,000 jobs, adding to its existing workforce of 2,500 people, after a £500m investment by its new Abu Dhabi owner.Photograph: Stan PapiorView image in fullscreenMcLaren will create 1,000 jobs, adding to its existing workforce of 2,500 people, after a £500m investment by its new Abu Dhabi owner.Photograph: Stan PapiorAutomotive industryMcLaren to build SUVs geared towards Formula One fans with childrenModel comes as part of £500m UK investment by firm’s new Abu Dhabi owner that will also fund new factoryAlex DanielWed 16 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMcLaren is gearing up to build an SUV for the first time in its 63-year history, betting that the glamour of itsall-conquering Formula One teamcan sell cars to wealthy fans who do not own its supercars.The model, which does not yet have a name, comes as part of a£500m investment by McLaren’s new Abu Dhabi ownerthat will also create 1,000 jobs, adding to the existing workforce of 2,500 people.It will also fund a new factory, with Sheffield, home to McLaren’s existing carbon-fibre plant, understood to be the preferred site over the company’s headquarters in Woking.Nick Collins, the carmaker’s chief executive, said the recent success of the McLaren racing team had created an “untapped love” for the brand among people who have never bought its cars.The SUV would open the door to more buyers for whom two-seater sports cars were a limitation, he said. “It’s quite difficult if you have to decide which one of your kids you want to leave behind at home.”The new model is part of a turnaround plan at McLaren Automotive, which was bought from the Bahraini sovereign wealth fund Mumtalakat last year by CYVN Holdings, an Abu Dhabi government-owned investment company.View image in fullscreenMcLaren Automotive has been a dedicated road carmaker since 2010.Photograph: Stan PapiorCYVN has vowed to invest $2bn (£1.4bn) in the loss-making group over five years. McLaren also merged with the British electric vehicle startup Forseven Holdings last April.However, McLaren has no immediate plans to build an EV of its own, despite agovernment mandatesaying all new cars in the UK must be zero-emission by 2035. “[Customers] are not asking us, and we’re not doing one,” Collins said.Founded in 1963 by the racing driver Bruce McLaren, the company built racing cars, and later the McLaren F1 supercar in the 1990s, before spinning off McLaren Automotive as a dedicated road carmaker in 2010.But it has struggled in recent years amidmounting debts and falling sales, before last year’s takeover by CYVN.European luxury carmakers have faced tough trading conditions after acollapse in demand in China, a key market, which has already forced job losses at rivals Aston Martin and Bentley.Michael Straughan, McLaren’s chief operating officer, said the SUV was a “critical” moment for the company, adding that he could “quite easily see us doubling” sales, which now stand at about 3,000 cars a year, through the new model.He said the new factory was likely to be built in Sheffield, calling it “the jewel in the crown” for the company’s manufacturing capability, though no final decision has been made.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt comes amid a bumper period for sister company McLaren Racing, which haswon the last two Formula One constructors championshipsand is also based in Woking. Mumtalakat still has majority control of McLaren Racing, while CYVN has a minority stake.Straughan said: “There’s no doubt there’s people who are F1 fans … who would never purchase a McLaren sports car, but would definitely consider a McLaren SUV.”He would not be drawn on the exact price of the new vehicle, but expects it to compete with the Bentley Bentayga, Aston Martin DBX and Lamborghini Urus, models that all start above £200,000.“I think the trick here is conquest of other brands’ customers,” Straughan added – though not before seeing a Ferrari F40 drive past the window of McLaren’s technology centre in Woking.The prime minister, Andy Burnham, welcomed the investment, saying it showed the company was “doubling down on Britain”.The growth of SUVs has come against the backdrop of warnings over “carspreading” and safety. Research has showncars have grown 1.2cm longer, 0.5cm taller and 0.5cm wider each year on average since 2000, and that potential SUV buyers areundeterredby warnings they are more likely to kill pedestrians.Explore more on these topicsAutomotive industryManufacturing sectorMcLarenFormula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We thought death could do with a bit of dancing’: welcome to Sondering, the arts festival with its own funeral march | Festivals | The Guardian
description: A brush with mortality inspired sisters Sophia and Camilla Minden to create a unique event featuring a funeral procession, wild swimming … and an ‘emoshpit’
Author: Claire Potter
Headline: A brush with mortality inspired sisters Sophia and Camilla Minden to create a unique event featuring a funeral procession, wild swimming … and an ‘emoshpit’
Content: ‘Fun is allowed’ … Sophia, left, and Camilla Minden, organisers of The Sondering festival in the Lake District.Photograph: Sheenah AlcockView image in fullscreen‘Fun is allowed’ … Sophia, left, and Camilla Minden, organisers of The Sondering festival in the Lake District.Photograph: Sheenah AlcockFestivals‘We thought death could do with a bit of dancing’: welcome to Sondering, the arts festival with its own funeral marchA brush with mortality inspired sisters Sophia and Camilla Minden to create a death-themed event featuring live bands, wild swimming … and an ‘emoshpit’Claire PotterWed 16 Sep 2026 08.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 09.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRaised in theLake Districton “music, moss and macaroni cheese,” Sophia and Camilla Minden were mindful of death from a very early age. The sisters shared a bed and played in the woods behind their house, frequently bringing home injured and dying birds, frogs and a rat they named Adrian and fed pate and pork pie. “Everything we’d learned about their diet, we learned from Wind in the Willows,” admits Sophia. The creatures rarely survived, but the death of each one was respectfully honoured with a burial in the garden, words spoken, singing and a stone or flower placed on the grave.What they didn’t expect was that little more than a decade later, they’d be planning Camilla’s own funeral. Diagnosed with late-stage Hodgkin’s lymphoma just after her 20th birthday, she was given an 80% chance of survival, but the other 20% made her investigate her local undertakers (“dated, impersonal and expensive”) and work out what she wanted at her funeral (“spag bol and quite a lot of Michael Jackson”). Navigating “shit wigs” and people’s awkwardness around the subject of dying, she says that she spent a lot of time “bargaining with God”, promising that if she made it through, she’d live life to the full and appreciate every single day.Now 37 and 40, the sisters have retained that mindset, and after initially exploring setting up their own progressive funeral directors, landed on the idea of creating a death-themed festival that would be as much a celebration of life as an exploration of mortality. So unlike other more conference-style or town-based death events, the Sondering, which debuts this weekend, is unashamedly an arts festival where “fun is allowed”. With live music, theatrical performances and a variety of creative workshops from clowning to shroud-making – plus a splash of guided wild swimming in Rydal Water – the programme has been designed to give people the opportunity to participate and express themselves in ways that might be sorrowful or joyful. “It’s OK to cry and ask for a cup of tea, it’s OK to laugh and dance,” says Sophia.View image in fullscreen‘The Lake District is magical, healing’ … Coffin route sign.Photograph: Sophia MindenLocated on a working farm with a capacity of just 300 to create an intimate feel, the festival site was chosen for its proximity to particular geographical features. “The Lake District is stunning, magical, healing,” says Sophia. “And we want to share it in a way that brings the landscape and local history alive,” adds Camilla. At sunset on Saturday evening, a cappella groupMouthfulwill be performing and leading a singing session inside Rydal Cave, making the most of its natural acoustics. And on Sunday, festival-goers will be invited to walk in a slow communal procession with a willow coffin along the old Coffin Route from Rydal to Grasmere. Up until the mid-1800s, this scenic two-and-a-half-mile footpath was how people carried their dead to church to be buried. The coffin – which will be collectively woven on site over the weekend and filled with personal notes of remembrance – will be taken right inside St Oswald’s Church, where there will be a musical performance from kora player John Haycock with Dan Bridgwood-Hill, featuring clarinet, guitar, violin and fiddle. “This is as close to a funeral as we get at the festival,” says Camilla. “We’re not afraid of ritual.”Aimed equally at those who are simply death-curious and those who are grieving the loss of a loved one, most of the music at the festival has been chosen for its “emotion and energy” and includes folk, reggae, opera, electro-punk and an uplifting DJ set on the Saturday night with an “emoshpit” where emotions good, bad and messy can be released.Other acts have an direct connection to death. The improvised singing ofLaurel Morganis inspired by the Celtic tradition of keening, where wails and wordless sounds are used to lament the dead. And sound artistJack McNeillwill be doing a performance with disassembled clarinets and words from poems written by his wife in response to losing three close family members in the same year. “It’s so easy to feel isolated in grief because it’s so rarely explored other than through a lens of sympathy,” he says. “I’d love people to feel less alone, more connected, and I think music does that better than most things.”Sophia and Camilla say some have questioned whether a music and arts festival isn’t romanticising or trivialising death. But they say they’re acutely aware the topic is “too big and too hard” for that. “We’re not saying death isn’t scary or painful or tragic,” says Sophia. “We’re asking if facing up to death together in this way can bring us closer to life and each other?” The ultimate aim of the festival is to encourage people to live as richly and compassionately as they possibly can: “Live like they’re going to die.” Even as children with a garden full of wild animal graves, they tell me their house was always full of dancing, laughter, warmth, generosity and love. “We thought death could do with a bit of that,” says Camilla.The Sondering is atRydal, Lake District, from 18-21SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFestivalsTheatreCraftDeath and dyingLake DistrictfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Your mission, Tom Cruise, is to improve at interviews. And please keep sending the cakes | Movies | The Guardian
description: He risks his life for entertainment, but getting an anecdote out of him is a trickier matter. Happily, Cruise is no stranger to knuckling down and pulling off the impossible
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: He risks his life for entertainment, but getting an anecdote out of him is a trickier matter. Happily, Cruise is no stranger to knuckling down and pulling off the impossible
Content: Acting again … Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in Digger.Photograph: Warner BrosView image in fullscreenActing again … Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in Digger.Photograph: Warner BrosMoviesYour mission, Tom Cruise, is to improve at interviews. And please keep sending the cakesHe risks his life for entertainment, but getting an anecdote out of him is a trickier matter. Happily, Cruise is no stranger to knuckling down and pulling off the impossibleStuart HeritageWed 16 Sep 2026 06.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 06.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy now, we’ve grown used to watchingTom Cruiseexcel at everything he does. Running in films? The best. Risking his life in action scenes so preposterously dangerous that audiences need to have their sphincters manually unclenched with a crowbar? Absolutely, none better. Singlehandedly ensuring that theatrical exhibition didn’t go extinct after Covid? The man deserves all the praise in the world for that.But nobody is perfect. Live long enough and a few flaws will worm their way to the surface. This is as true for Tom Cruise as it is for anyone else. And while I realise that thismight do me out of a cake this Christmas, the following really needs to be said: Tom Cruise isn’t very good at interviews.As you will be aware, Cruise’s new film Digger comes out soon. The film is a risk. It is his first original, non-sequel, non-action film in which he co-stars since2007’s Lions for Lambs. It is also, if the trailers are any indication, palpably batshit. This means that Cruise has to reintroduce himself to the world as an actor, rather than the guy who just flings himself off a variety of increasingly berserk surfaces. And this means promotion. Until this week, that promotion has involved either World Cup-themed promos filmed in character or interviews where the subject matterwas almost exclusively limited to lens choice.However, yesterday Cruisesubjected himself to a rare longforminterview opposite GQ’s Zach Baron. On paper, it couldn’t have been easier. Baron was a perfectly chosen interviewer for the job, understanding exactly when to flatter and when to needle. However, Tom Cruise’s defences are foot-thick and watertight, and the majority of Baron’s questions simply bounced off him.This resulted in a fairly unsatisfactory 30-minute stalemate in which Tom Cruise talked and talked and said nothing at all. No matter how hard Baron probed, he was met with a fat wedge of waffle. The clickbait industrial complex has done its best to pick the bones of the interview for a news peg, but the best it seems to have come up with is a variation of “Tom Cruise admits that he can be intense on set”.Which, well, duh.Aside from that, we simply got a rehash of all the old talking points from every junket he’s done for a decade. He’d rather talk about cinematography than himself. He is constantly trying to learn new skills. He writes down his dreams and how to accomplish them. None of this is new information. It’s all highly frustrating. But it does make sense. As brilliant as he is on screen, behind the scenes Cruise is a carefully managed enigma. This may well be because, the last time he allowed his own self to parade before the press, it ended with couch-jumping and excruciatingly testy interviews about Scientology. It seems unthinkable now, but that press run went so badly that Sumner Redstone ended upeffectively firing Cruise from Paramount over it.It took Cruise years to build himself back up from that, and the results have been spectacular. The Mission: Impossible films have been some of the greatest of his career. Top Gun: Maverick saved Hollywood. He is now in a position of enormous power and authority. So going back out in front of an interviewer is bound to be a risk for him. But one thing is certain. The Digger promotional cycle cannot just be variations of the GQ interview, because too many opaque soundbites will simply end up boring potential audiences rigid. There will be more interviews – he’s thought to be hitting the podcast circuit soon – so he needs to adapt his strategy.The good news is that one thing Cruise did say in his GQ interview is that, when he sets a goal, he writes down all the steps necessary to accomplish it. This is exactly what he should do here. If his dream is doing press that will make people want to watch Digger, then he knows he will need to work up some new anecdotes – long enough to filibuster, but twisty enough to entertain – while developing a persona that appears to welcome scrutiny while wriggling out from underneath it.It can be done. Robert Downey Jr is an actor with many areas of his past he would rather not touch in print, and he has built up an incredibly charming suit of armour that allows him to breezily bat questions away when they get too personal. This is exactly what Tom Cruise should be learning to do. Or perhaps not; after all, he has made hundreds of millions of dollars by revealing scarcely anything about himself for a decade. Maybe that’s an option, too.But, hey, this is Tom Cruise. When he sets his mind on something, he achieves it. With that in mind, expect a dramatic upward turn in the quality of his interviews from this moment onwards. Thanks for reading. Please still send cakes.Explore more on these topicsFilmTom CruiseDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Liberation review – Carrie Coon joins all-female cult in unsettling drama | Toronto film festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Director Guy Nattiv draws on personal experience for an 80s-set tale of a woman abandoning her family for a creepy commune
Author: Benjamin Lee
Headline: Director Guy Nattiv draws on personal experience for an 80s-set tale of a woman abandoning her family for a creepy commune
Content: Carrie Coon as Rita in The Liberation.Photograph: Bleecker StreetView image in fullscreenCarrie Coon as Rita in The Liberation.Photograph: Bleecker StreetFirst look reviewToronto film festival 2026ReviewThe Liberation review – Carrie Coon joins all-female cult in unsettling dramaToronto film festival:Director Guy Nattiv draws on personal experience for an 80s-set tale of a woman abandoning her family for a creepy communeBenjamin Leein TorontoWed 16 Sep 2026 14.22 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 15.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWe remain fascinated and horrified by the hows and whys of cult narratives, how someone could be so seduced by something so unknown and why they would then risk everything for it. Oscar-winning writer-director Guy Nattiv has been personally affected by these questions for most of his life, his grandmother joining a cult when he was a child and never coming back.A Talent for Murder review – Helen Mirren is a viperous Patricia Highsmith in hit-and-miss thrillerRead moreHis attempt to try to understand who she was and why she acted in such a way has led to unsettling drama The Liberation, a fictionalised tale that acts as a form of therapy for him and a mostly successful antidote to more sensationalist cult stories for us. Enough Netflix docuseries and schlocky horror movies have given us a more extreme and often violent idea of how cults infect and destroy vulnerable people but Nattiv opts for a more thoughtful slow-burn. He’s recruited a suitably thoughtful actor in Carrie Coon, no stranger to this particular psychology having broken out in The Leftovers, one of the more intelligent cult dramas in recent years.It’s a rare big-screen lead for Coon, an actor who made a name for herself a little later than most, and she tears into it, working hard to try to bring us into the mindset of someone who would do something so unimaginable. We might never truly understand or even like her all that much but we believe her and like Nattiv, we’re haunted by her actions.Like his grandmother, the character is called Rita, a wife, mother and assistant bank manager living in early 80s New Jersey. Her life is small and undeniably average but not unhappy, her husband (played warmly by Coon’s real-life spouse Tracy Letts) is loving and she is close to her two daughters (played by Odessa Young and a tenacious Bella Ramsey). But Rita has a past that won’t let her fully relax into her life: she grew up in Poland and endured the horrors of the Holocaust, her family taken from her at a young age. Like the most susceptible of us, she’s an open wound, something quickly realised by the charismatic, raven-haired Ricky (Lily James), who invites her to join a group of friends at the beach. Rita is baffled by the offer and by Ricky in general but also flattered, an attractive younger woman suddenly flooding her with attention and compliments.The film flips back and forth between the gradual, awful grooming process as Rita spends more and more time with Ricky’s heart-over-head all-female troupe, dancing and appreciating nature, and then much later when her concerned daughters track her down to a remote compound. I don’t know if the timeline-switching really adds all that much, a common complaint at the moment, but it’s less distractingly gimmicky and more inconsequential.The cult is very much rooted in its time, those who believe in nature and love and spirituality rallying against the gluttony of overconsumption as the 70s starts to give way to a decade of greed and excess, but it’s also one that feels horribly relevant today. There areMahaechoes in how Ricky bloviates about the rot of modern medicine (she calls doctors “barbaric predators”) and how much more qualified she is to treat any ailments the women have. (Who needs insulin when you can have concentrated mistletoe extract and fenugreek?) Nattiv gets that, for all of her flowery slogans (which again could just come directly from a vapid contemporary LA influencer), Ricky, like many cult leaders, is just a garden-variety narcissist who believes she knows better than any system or expert and her professions of love inevitably turn into demands for money. James isn’t always an actor who convinces me – there can be something a little reticent about her performances – but she’s bewitchingly sinister here. Words like witch and possessed are thrown around, and Nattiv often shoots scenes as if we’re watching a horror film unfold, but things are kept at a simmer.For the most part at least, because for all of the unusual elements – a female cult leader, relatively few mentions of religion, questions over answers – Nattiv ultimately lands in pretty standard cult movie territory. What started out as Rita’s story becomes anyone’s as familiarity takes over with an underbaked subplot involving an undercover member and a conventional race-against-time finale. At just under two hours, things also start to sag a little before a strangely rushed ending wraps things up in haste. The pre-credits text, informing us of what happened to the real Rita, is grim and shocking, but it’s that which stays with us over anything we have seen in the last act. Coon’s performance endures, an actor we typically associate with strength showing how convincingly fragile she can be. Rita might remain a maddening enigma but it’s easy to understand and appreciate the vastness of what Coon can do.The Liberation is screening at theToronto film festivaland will be released later this yearExplore more on these topicsToronto film festival 2026First look reviewToronto film festivalFestivalsDrama filmsLily JamesBella RamseyreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Resident Evil review – Zach Cregger’s rebooted action horror is a wild rollercoaster ride | Horror films | The Guardian
description: The Weapons director delivers a seat-edge thriller with a standout lead performance from Austin Abrams as an everyman navigating chaos
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: The Weapons director delivers a seat-edge thriller with a standout lead performance from Austin Abrams as an everyman navigating chaos
Content: Austin Abrams in Resident Evil.Photograph: Dušan Martinček/Dušan Martinček/2026 CTMG, Inc. All Rights Reserved.View image in fullscreenAustin Abrams in Resident Evil.Photograph: Dušan Martinček/Dušan Martinček/2026 CTMG, Inc. All Rights Reserved.Horror filmsReviewResident Evil review – Zach Cregger’s rebooted action horror is a wild rollercoaster rideThe Weapons director delivers a seat-edge thriller with a standout lead performance from Austin Abrams as an everyman navigating chaosJesse HassengerWed 16 Sep 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 12.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTypically horror fans react to blatant on-screen stupidity with vocal derision. Don’t go in there! Girl, get out of the house! Guys, ignore that distress signal! But genre aficionados may find themselves falling a little bit in love with Bryan (Austin Abrams), the hapless de facto hero of the new horror filmResident Evil. It’s not that Bryan is traditionally hunky, or even a caricatured version of a square-jawed warrior, like Bruce Campbell in his later Evil Dead outings. But Abrams is in possession of a Campbell-ish charm, even in the face of his character’s repeated blundering, as well as an everyman relatability that makes this wild carnival-ride movie play a little closer to the ground.Resident Evil at 30: how Capcom’s horror opus has survived and thrivedRead moreBryan is a courier – a glorified Postmates driver, in his own estimation – who postpones the end of his shift to take one last night-time run, driving an important item from one hospital to another in a snowstorm without the proper tires or four-wheel drive. After all, the distance and urgency means double pay. When he hits a mysterious woman who emerges suddenly on to a slick road, he’s drawn into a hellish outbreak that will look familiar to fans of the Resident Evil video game series (or maybe the previous six-movie Milla Jovovich franchise, which apparently drifted afield from the games’ storylines).The key to Abrams’s winning performance as a perpetual loser is in how the actor and cowriter-director Zach Cregger take care to show Bryan stumbling his way through sloppy versions of doing the right thing. When he hits the clearly zonked woman, Bryan attempts to take her along on his hospital run. When he’s quickly pulled over by a cop, he makes little attempt to weasel out of his situation, attempting to prioritize his medical task. The man tries, even if some of his efforts in certain areas are lamentably weak (supporting his unseen girlfriend in a non-outbreak-related couple crisis) or understandably incompetent (wielding a firearm against undead creatures). His oscillations between overconfidence and panic make him a particularly fresh point-of-view character for a zombie/monster movie.In short, he’s not unlike a guy who’s been dropped into a video game before learning the proper controls – in keeping with Cregger’s reported desire to replicate the experience of the game without adapting any of its stories directly. Abrams manages to humanize this unspoken and potentially arch conceit of an avatar learning the rules as he goes. It’s tempting to compare his many scenes without other human characters to silent comedy – only he’s not quiet enough to qualify, unleashing a hilarious symphony of profane and frustrated muttering. At one point, well after his life has been endangered multiple times, he can be heard complaining about his wet socks.Good as Abrams is, alone and when playing opposite skeleton-crew supporting cast, he’s not exactly a one-man show, either; the guy behind the camera is his constant scene partner. Cregger, who has become a horror brand name on the strength of the similarly inventive Barbarian and Weapons, orchestrates the mayhem with expert command of pacing, comic-horrific timing, and even that old standby, the lowly jumpscare. (There’s at least one genuinely masterful version here.) The movie’s comic side isn’t quite Sam Raimi broad (or bold), but Cregger’s sketch-comedy roots are just as delightfully visible here as they were in Barbarian, without the aid of that movie’s clever shifts in timeline or perspective.Indeed, Resident Evil has a streamlined single-mindedness, and as it barrels through its gamified plot, the tension and entertainment value never flag. Cregger only falters in the tail end, and it’s more a sin of omission than a big misstep. Resident Evil flirts with becoming a full-on monster movie where its cinematic predecessors tended to keep circling back to zombie action (at least in terms of their horror elements; let’s not discount Jovovich’s action bona fides). Cregger’s monster-mashier shift is a welcome one, and presumably closer in spirit to the games. But he doesn’t bring the movie close enough to whatever line separates monstrousness and the humanity that might be lurking underneath.It could be that there’s not supposed to be any – in which case the movie more or less just screeches to a halt before it gets too thorny. Weapons had acreepy, evocative aversionto simple metaphorical reads that ultimately increased its effectiveness; the same isn’t quite true here. Resident Evil foregrounds one obvious bit of character change for Bryan, but after doing a great job making us care about him for more than 90 minutes, Cregger seems to abandon him a few steps shy of completing any real journey. Is he awaiting a level up that never arrives? Hard to say. But maybe bringing a video game sensibility to the big screen while keeping any gamer cheesiness on the margins is journey enough.Resident Evil is in cinemas on 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsHorror filmsResident EvilAction and adventure filmsScience fiction and fantasy filmsThrillersGamesreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Smile at Last review – photo-love-story style parable of a teen abandoned at a tough Soviet youth facility | Movies | The Guardian
description: With handheld camerawork, this unsentimental rite of passage film follows Mari, who tries to escape from a residential home in Estonia
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: With handheld camerawork, this unsentimental rite of passage film follows Mari, who tries to escape from a residential home in Estonia
Content: Shy, unhappy … Smile at Last, 1985.Photograph: KlassikiView image in fullscreenShy, unhappy … Smile at Last, 1985.Photograph: KlassikiMoviesReviewSmile at Last review – photo-love-story style parable of a teen abandoned at a tough Soviet youth facilityWith handheld camerawork, this unsentimental rite of passage film follows Mari, who tries to escape from a residential home in EstoniaPeter BradshawWed 16 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 10.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis intriguing 1985 film fromEstoniauses nonprofessionals and handheld camerawork, which brings faces looming up to the screen. It is directed by Leida Laius and Arvo Iho and based on the YA novel Stepmother by Estonian author Silvia Rannamaa. The Estonian title Naerata Ometi is translated here as Smile at Last; perhaps it should be Give Us a Smile as it is what a boorish, bullying guy tells a shy, unhappy young woman.It is at one level a kind of coming-of-age story, but entirely without that genre’s usual, sentimental sense of something finally learned or gained from an emotional rite of passage – something finally to smile about, in fact. Actually, it is more of a mysterious parable, couched in the language of soap opera or photo-love story, depicting the Soviet state and its gruesome pretension to be caring or nurturing.Mari (Monika Raide) is a teenager whose mum has died and whose feckless dad has taken up with another woman; Mari has been packed off to a residential youth care facility somewhere between an orphanage and a state boarding school. She tries to run away and winds up spending the night at a police station, where a photo of Lenin frowns down from the walls. Back in the home, unhappy Mari is lost in a tough world where many of the young women are single mothers whose kids are bullied; one is literally locked in a drier and left to tumble. She soon learns that the top dog is Robi (Hendrik Toompere Jr), the swaggering, preening tough guy with a retinue of submissive boys and girls. He is the one who tells Mari to “smile”. But there is also Tauri (Tauri Tallermaa), a more caring and sensitive guy who has a talent for music, and a rumoured connection to Robi. He seems to like Mari, but Mari is to realise that Robi is not what he seems.There is a dreamlike quality to the action, despite its ostensible kitchen-sink realism. It is almost a kind of pastoral: the young people in this institution apparently have no school lessons, they seem free to just drift around, playing games, pursuing crushes, quarrels and intrigues, until it all turns sour. But there is a curious kind of acceptance; has Mari become institutionalised, just as the head teacher predicted, when she brought Mari back from the police station? A strange, bittersweet vignette.Smile at Last is on Klassiki from 19 September.Explore more on these topicsFilmRomance filmsDrama filmsFilm adaptationsEstoniareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Slow Horses season six review – it gets harder to enjoy Gary Oldman’s spy thriller every year | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The show’s creator has gone, it’s been retooled as a conventional thriller and it feels like it’s starting to run out of ideas – even if it’s as slick and confident as ever
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: The show’s creator has gone, it’s been retooled as a conventional thriller and it feels like it’s starting to run out of ideas – even if it’s as slick and confident as ever
Content: Rather whiny … Jack Lowden with Gary Oldman in Slow Horses season six.Photograph: Jack English/AppleView image in fullscreenRather whiny … Jack Lowden with Gary Oldman in Slow Horses season six.Photograph: Jack English/AppleTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewSlow Horses season six review – it gets harder to enjoy Gary Oldman’s spy thriller every yearThe show’s creator has gone, it’s been retooled as a conventional thriller and it feels like it’s starting to run out of ideas – even if it’s as slick and confident as everJack SealeWed 16 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis is a new Slow Horses: season six is the first not to be guided by Will Smith, a writer whose previous work on The Thick of It and Veep explained why this espionage saga had an unusually sharp comic tongue. The absence of Smith’s drollery is discernible in a more straight-faced new story, but the bigger problem is one of a creative work naturally eroding over time.Slow Horsesis now old.It’s always been a difficult, delicate proposition. The staff of Slough House, a purgatorial spin-off of MI5 where misfits and screw-ups are given boring work when it would make more sense to just fire them, regularly outstrip supposedly elite spies despite being shambling losers. Leading the field agents is River Cartwright (Jack Lowden), who has the good looks of a spy hero and some of the skills, but is also a brittle, luckless and rather whiny wretch, who regularly has to be saved from ignominious death. The jokes have helped us suspend our disbelief that River and the rest haven’t yet been riddled with bullets, and the relocation of traditional spy thrills to decaying urban settings is still a tonic, but enjoying this conjuring trick gets harder every year.View image in fullscreenStill a tonic … Kristin Scott Thomas in Slow Horses.Photograph: Jack English/AppleThe crisis descended in season five, Smith’s last, with a flat story powered by generic terrorists delivering blowback for British crimes abroad. Slow Horses also began to suffer from the curse of the celebrated supporting character: when you know you have failsafe comic relief in your cast, the temptation to promote them can be irresistible, but they don’t always survive the exposure. That happened to showboating virgin Roddy Ho (Christopher Chung), who had previously snarked from in front of his computer but was now given a pivotal role, in which he soon became unbearable. Even the star of the show,Gary Oldman, might have been better staying in the background as the physically disgusting but intellectually unbeatable Slough House boss, Jackson Lamb: he’s a brilliantly conceived and perfectly performed cartoon, but in season five he started to burn out.So, new lead writer Gaby Chiappe – who didThe LevelandThe Beast Must Die, two lean and underrated dramas – is pushing buttons on a desk that has several red lights blinking. She responds by making the new Slow Horses more of a conventional thriller, with complex geopolitical machinations almost entirely on mute; for the Slough House mob themselves, old friends unexpectedly reappear.Someone is bumping off past team members, which at first means a cruelly brief comeback for Struan Loy (Paul Higgins), who meets a horrible end in the typically desolate Slow Horses milieu of a shipping container parked on a dull expanse of estuary mud. When it becomes clear that the two frighteningly confident, black-clad killers – played by MyAnna Buring and Kyle Soller – are not going to be satisfied with slaughtering spooks from season one whom we barely remember, the whole gang ends up on the run.View image in fullscreenImmediately improves everything he’s in … Lenny Rush with Christopher Chung in Slow Horses.Photograph: Jack English/AppleAs well as the re-emergence of a more important character from long ago, recent apparent departures are reversed: Rosalind Eleazar is back as Louisa, Joanna Scanlan is back as Moira, and Hugo Weaving is back as Frank, the bleakly amoral mercenary who is also, a bit implausibly, River’s dad, and whose narrative seemed to have played out perfectly well back in season four. None of them makes an unwelcome return, but cycling back to familiar faces does feel like something that might be done by a show that finds itself short of ideas.The main issue, though, is the plot, which boils down to a long chase. The killers keep coming and the slow horses, mainly River, chaotically run away – which often requires the murderers to suddenly become incompetent in order for the story not to end prematurely. With the vicious banter not quite as piercing as it used to be and the parallels to real political issues also not as piquant – besides some stuff about Russia – it becomes more noticeable when tropes like trained killers who can’t shoot straight creep in. Having cast actors of the calibre of Buring and Soller to play the new foes, the show inexplicably never gets round to getting to know them. Also struggling to make an impact is Harry Lloyd, who looks as if he could be superb as a malevolent media mogul who is blackmailing MI5 boss Diana Taverner (Kristin Scott Thomas), but never gets a proper chance to show us.Slow Horses is still slick and confident enough, and it helps itself by casting Lenny Rush, an actor who immediately improves anything he’s in, as a civilian caught in this year’s crossfire. But it might have run its course.Slow Horses is on Apple TV now.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionSlow HorsesDramaJack LowdenGary OldmanKristin Scott ThomasreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I thought I would lose my career’: Orville Peck on addiction and creating his best album yet | Music | The Guardian
description: Though the masked country singer has a No 1 album and duets with superstars under his belt, his demons and mental health caught up to him
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Though the masked country singer has a No 1 album and duets with superstars under his belt, his demons and mental health caught up to him
Content: ‘It’s hard for someone like me because it takes not just admitting to yourself that you have a problem - I also had to reckon with my phobia of conforming.’Photograph: Courtesy of Warner RecordsView image in fullscreen‘It’s hard for someone like me because it takes not just admitting to yourself that you have a problem - I also had to reckon with my phobia of conforming.’Photograph: Courtesy of Warner RecordsMusicInterview‘I thought I would lose my career’: Orville Peck on addiction and creating his best album yetJason LamphierThough the masked country singer has a No 1 album and duets with superstars under his belt, his demons and mental health caught up to himWed 16 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 09.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOrville Peck was in the middle of a soundcheck when he found out that his idolDolly Partonhad died. It was late August and the masked, pseudonymous country singer was due to perform an intimate set at London’s Rough Trade East in half an hour. The news hit him like a truck. With no chance to process it, he decided to grieve in real time, on stage, before a roomful of fans.“I’m a little bit of a mess right now,” Peck told the audience, perched on a stool with an acoustic guitar. “Dolly was my hero,” he continued, his voice cracking. “As a gay man coming into country music and feeling sort of alone, I think the thing that always felt comforting is, like, just knowing Dolly existed in country. It made me feel like I had a friend there.” He then launched into a rendition of Parton’s iconic hit I Will Always Love You.From Jolene to Islands in the Stream: Dolly Parton’s 10 best recordingsRead more“It felt like an impromptu memorial,” Peck recalls on the sofa of his New York City hotel room three days later, having touched down the night before to promote his new album, Mule. “I had to work through it with 400 strangers. We all got to sort of mourn together. I definitely think everyone there will remember that forever.”Mortality has been on Peck’s mind a lot lately. Mule is a brutally honest chronological account of what he describes as “the most important year of my life”, a period marred by profound heartache and self-destruction during which he split up with his partner of four years, overdosed and nearly died. Its opening track envisions his own memorial – what would have happened if he hadn’t come back from the brink.Prologue (Eulogy of a Man Turned Mule)is an a cappella hymn sung not by Peck, but byEmmylou Harris, Allison Russell and Noah Cyrus, a trio of country muses from different generations whom he compares to the witches of Macbeth or a Greek chorus. “Come walk through the fire, come stand with the few / Who break their own hearts to be saved,” they intone. “But the heart can’t be saved from the wretched and blue / Here lies a man turned mule.”While country has beendominatingthe top spots of the Billboard Hot 100 this summer, Peck emerged from Toronto during 2019’s “yee-haw moment”, as artists likeKacey MusgravesandLil Nas Xwere turning some pop listeners’ ears to the genre, injecting it with disco and hip-hop beats and a modern, queer sensibility. His face obscured, Peck kept his true identity a mystery, but he was open about his sexuality, and undeniably sexy, out of the gate (he recently posed forPlaygirl). That he had a baritone croon that evoked Roy Orbison and Elvis Presley made his arrival all the sweeter. Over the next few years, Peck would duet withElton John,Kylie Minogueand another one of his major inspirations,Willie Nelson, who dueted with him on acoverof the gay country classic Cowboys Are Frequently Secretly Fond of Each Other, score a No 1 album on the UK country charts and scoop up Glaad’s Vito Russo award for elevating LGBTQ acceptance and visibility. In 2025, he made his Broadway theater debut as the Emcee in the vibrant revival of Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club.The 38-year-old musician’s previous records – 2019’s Pony, 2022’s Bronco and 2024’sStampede– were laced with metaphor, at times unspooling like the dusty tales of an omniscient, enigmatic gunslinger. While the bluegrass-inflected Mule is more literal, like an unvarnished memoir, he couldn’t abandon the high drama completely. “I still wanted to add some kind of theatrical element,” says Peck. Today, he wears a white tank, chunky Wrangler x Cherry knit jacket, faded jeans, cowboy boots and a cream-colored Stetson. His penetrating blue eyes peek through a simple suede mask, but his trademark disguise, a black leather upper with a fringed veil, sits behind him on the bed, its golden tassels cascading over the edge of it. His right hand and wrist are wrapped in a thick bandage.“I thought, We’ll start with the most bleak thing possible,” Peck continues. “If I had died in 2023, if that was my legacy, what would these three witches be singing about?”Peck is not afraid to contemplate his own demise, nor is he afraid to be sitting now in the same hotel where he tried to take his own life. “It’s like when people ask me, ‘Oh, do you regret any of your tattoos?’” he says, chuckling at the slight absurdity of the analogy. “And I’m like, Well, I have some that are really shitty, but I would never get rid of them or wish I hadn’t gotten them, because I feel like it’s part of my story.”He would not deny, however, that his overdose may be the darkest chapter of that story. The night it happened, in June 2023, he was preparing to kick off his tour for Bronco with a sold-out concert at the Theater at Madison Square Garden. He went out to celebrate, got hammered, bumped into his ex at a club and spiraled. His management found him the next morning and gave him an ultimatum: he would cancel the tour and get help, or they’d cut ties with him. After rallying to play the packed show that evening, he announced that he was postponing his remaining tour dates to focus on his mental and physical health. Then he flew back home to Los Angeles and checked into a rehabilitation center.View image in fullscreenOrville Peck.Photograph: Aidan KlimenkoWhile he could acknowledge that he was leaning too much on booze, cocaine and prescription pills, he entered the facility begrudgingly. “I was like, I’ll be fine. I’ll play along with the parts that I don’t really think I need, and I’ll just kind of roll my eyes at the stuff I’m entitled to be annoyed about,” Peck says. “I believed that I had it under control.”He details his dismissive outlook and resentment – which he now realizes was just blinding denial – in the first half of Mule. He refers to rehab as “the slammer” and deems it a waste of time in the mockingAlready Gone. In the next track, the clever, ragtime-y Rehab Blues, the reality of his surroundings sets in: watchful eyes, sad sharing circles, stifling seclusion. “So catch me on the evenin’ news: Dumb fag dies from the rehab blues,” he sings sardonically, later confessing, “I hate it here, I don’t care and I wanna die.”‘People think fame is a magic wand’: Jarvis Cocker on old songs, young fans and his granny’s verdict on PulpRead morePeck left the center about a month later, knowing full well that he’d continue to use. He told himself that he wasn’t like the others he’d met there. He wasn’t an addict. “There’s a term for it: We call it terminal uniqueness,” Peck says. “Where a part of you is actually seeing that it’s totally you, but then a massive part of you is going, But I’m different. I can stop.”The root of his resistance, he thinks, was an inveterate aversion to following the herd. Growing up queer and closeted in South Africa and Canada, he had supportive parents – his father was a glam-rock sound engineer and his mother is an artist and a seamstress – but he says he felt alienated from his peers. “That’s where this otherness came from”, he says. “At first, it was put on me … and it was unbearable.” To escape, he turned to ballet and musical theater. He discovered punk and the renegade country of Nelson andJohnny Cash. He found himself drawn to outsize characters like Parton andJohn Waters. His reaction, eventually, was to wear his outsiderness as a badge of honor. That is where Orville Peck, the masked lone ranger, was born.View image in fullscreenOrville Peck performing at music festival Oya in Oslo, 2019.Photograph: Gonzales Photo/Alamy“It’s hard for someone like me because it takes not just admitting to yourself that you have a problem – I also had to reckon with my phobia of conforming,” he says of his struggle to get sober. “In a situation like that, I choose to remove myself in a way that’s like, I don’t need this shit. I’m not the same.” He’d been carving out his own path for most of his life to protect himself. With his successful stage persona, he explains, a defense mechanism to shield his vulnerability had become his superpower. But by 2023, it had become his downfall.After rehab, the partying and blackouts continued. He was still reeling from his breakup at the beginning of that year. Solo and shattered in his house in the Hollywood Hills, he tried filling the void with tricks and flings, including, as he reveals in the song Ring the Bell, an affair with a linebacker for the Las Vegas Raiders. (He remains coy when pressed for specifics, telling me only: “I snogged him and it was hot.”)His recklessness escalated until he woke up one morning that November, after a particularly brutal night, terrified. “I was like, You are gonna lose any chance of getting your relationship back. You’re gonna lose your career. You could lose your life,” Peck recalls. “It scared the absolute shit out of me.”He knew things had to change. “Finally, I was able to drop all of the traumas and the hang-ups and the defenses and the patterns, and all the things that we all walk around with all muddled up, and look at myself in the mirror and say, ‘Get your shit together.’” He pauses. “I have not taken a drink since.”‘I’m trying to figure out where I’m supposed to be’: singer Momo Boyd on making space for herselfRead moreSobriety brought clarity, and a desire to dig deeper. He came to understand that his battle with addiction stemmed, at least partly, from the pressures that accompanied newfound stardom, particularly the tug-of-war between Peck the performer and the man behind closed doors. Mule’s penultimate song, War of the Worlds, tackles this duality. “The dilemma I have on this album is not me versus this character that I’ve created, or whatever people think,” Peck says. “The dilemma is, I am an incredibly sensitive, hurt person who’s carrying around a lot of shit that I have to work on – and then my job requires me to also navigate thousands of people’s opinions of every single breath I take. That creates a dichotomous life, regardless of if Orville Peck is my birth name.”Peck’s attempt to reconcile his two identities – the famous Orville he’d become and the pre-fame dreamer of his youth – gives the album its title, and the name of its closing track. Mules are half horse, half donkey, and they cannot reproduce, he explains. Perhaps they, like him, feel trapped somewhere in between, unsure where they belong, always a little alone. He is quick to clarify that he’s not looking for pity. He just knows he has to figure most of this out on his own.View image in fullscreenOrville Peck’s album art for Mule.Photograph: Warner RecordsWhen he was drinking and on drugs, Peck says, he had “pretty much no ability” to reckon with his past or cope with the bumps in the road. His relationships, friendships and wellbeing suffered because of it. “I had this insane fear of abandonment,” he says. He couldn’t fathom being unlovable or unwanted, so he’d stay in terrible, even abusive situations. He doesn’t do that anymore. “I was just so, so hurt,” he says. “I still hurt sometimes,” he adds, “but now I think I have the courage to face it.”As he approaches three years of sobriety, Peck seems to be riding high. Despite its grim subject matter, Mule is often funny, knowing and buoyant. It’s his best album yet (or at least his catchiest). While he never got to meet or collaborate with Parton, a bucket-list item for him, he did achieve another one of his big career goals, making his Grand Ole Opry debut in July – the first song he performed that evening was, coincidentally, I Will Always Love You. He has become a hero in his own right, showing queer kids that Nashville’s once-conservative country scene may actually have a place for them. And he’s found love again.As our interview wraps, I ask Peck why his hand is bandaged. He laughs, clearly embarrassed, and tells me that he punched his new partner’s mostly finished birthday cake as a joke and fractured his finger on the table beneath it. I look incredulous, but he laughs again and waves it away. “It’s a long story,” he says. His smile suggests it is ultimately a happy one.Mule is out on 18 SeptemberIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14.
