title: David Bowie: The Shel Talmy Recordings review – these unheard 60s tunes are actually pretty flimsy | David Bowie | The Guardian
description: On this new compilation of his mid-60s Davie Jones years, Bowie can’t distinguish himself from the era’s other bands – and ends up hedging his bets
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: On this new compilation of his mid-60s Davie Jones years, Bowie can’t distinguish himself from the era’s other bands – and ends up hedging his bets
Content: David Bowie in 1965, aged 19, then styled as Davie Jones.Photograph: Smith Archive/AlamyView image in fullscreenDavid Bowie in 1965, aged 19, then styled as Davie Jones.Photograph: Smith Archive/AlamyDavid BowieReviewDavid Bowie: The Shel Talmy Recordings review – these unheard 60s tunes are actually pretty flimsy(Parlophone)On this new compilation of his mid-60s Davie Jones years, Bowie can’t distinguish himself from the era’s other bands – and ends up hedging his betsAlexis PetridisWed 16 Sep 2026 05.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1973,David Bowiereleased Pin Ups, a loving if slightly over-wrought collection of covers from the mid-60s: the moment when the previous driving forces of British pop, Merseybeat and the blues revival started giving way to something noticeably weirder, noisier and more expansive. In an accompanying promotional interview, he waxed lyrical about his memories of seeing the Pretty Things, the Who, the Creation and the nascent Pink Floyd “with dear old Syd” in impeccable mod lingo (“up the Windmill or the Elephant, get blocked, bust over to Richmond”) but tactfully neglected to mention that he was more than an amphetamine-fuelled fan: he’d wanted to be a participant, and had recorded a handful of mid-60s singles inspired by his idols.That elision shows what a strained relationship Bowie had with his pre-fame material. For most of his career, he simply tried to ignore it, although it doggedly refused to go away: his former labels kept re-releasing it, usually in sleeves that attempted to fool the buyer that it was current. Then, in his 50s, he seemed to reconsider, revisiting his 60s oeuvre on Toy, a 2001 album that was rejected by his then-label EMI – a baffling decision, if you buy the posthumous rewriting of Bowie’s history that insists his Glastonbury performance in 2000 utterly reinvigorated his career and made him as revered as he was in his peak years.View image in fullscreenCover art for David Bowie: The Shel Talmy RecordingsPhotograph: ParlophoneThat Glastonbury performance actually did nothing of the sort – as with his 90s releases, the next couple of albums continued to receive respectful but not ecstatic reviews and sold well rather than extraordinarily so – but Bowie’s history often gets rewritten like this, to the point where he is deemed an unimpeachable genius who released nothing but masterpieces, and the muted contemporary reception afforded some of his work was simply a matter of said masterpieces being misunderstood. This makes his career seem vastly less interesting than it really was, with its astonishing artistic peaks and troughs, where Bowie seemed uninspired or lost or wrong-headed before marshalling his talent and producing something extraordinary after years in the doldrums.But the mindset that he could do no wrong has resulted in The Shel Talmy Recordings, in which the era that produced two flop singles released by Bowie when he was still Davie Jones – one with the Mannish Boys and the other with The Lower Third – is re-examined with a 21-track compilation that comes with its own range of merchandise: four different T-shirts, a hoodie, a baseball cap, a tote bag, a commemorative mug and a pair of socks.It also comes with a quote fromthe late Talmy, best known as the producer of the Kinks and the Who: “He and I were about six years ahead of the market.” It’s difficult to know what this is supposed to mean, given that the music on The Shel Talmy Recordings couldn’t conceivably be more redolent of 1965, the year of the Yardbirds’ Heart Full of Soul, the Sorrows’ Take a Heart, the Rolling Stones’ Satisfaction and Get Off of My Cloud and the Who’s explosive trio of early singles.The latter in particular hang over the compilation’s contents. A year away from Bowie writing his first truly great songs – Can’t Help Thinking About Me and The London Boys – the actual material, some of which has never been officially released, is pretty flimsy.Take My Tip is a straight-up impersonation of Georgie Fame, Baby Loves That Way an uptempo re-write of Smokey Robinson’s You Really Got a Hold on Me, and I Pity the Fool a wan blues riff with a bit of Slim Harpo’s I’m a King Bee in its DNA. You’ve Got a Habit of Leaving and I Want Your Love, meanwhile, might have been B-sides by the Swinging Blue Jeans or the Dave Clark Five. What interest there is lies in the arrangements, which erupt into distortion and noise, or frantic drum rolls, or guitar solos that squeal a little more painfully than would have been permissible 12 months previously. The only thing worth noting about the instrumental Keeping Up With the Jones is the crunching guitar riff that opens it, a fair forgery of Dave Davies’ work on the Kinks’ breakthrough singles.As a document of British rock in transition – the sound of middling bands nevertheless alive to some cutting-edge developments – it’s fine, although there’s something telling about a handful of demos that strike out in noticeably different musical directions: Walker Brothers-influenced balladry on Today, very vaguely Dylan-ish folksiness on Bars of the County Jail, the dreamy easy-listening pop of I Want My Baby Back. It’s as if Bowie realised that his efforts weren’t up to the standards set by the bands he loved and sought to hedge his bets as a result. At their most intriguing, the demos throw up I Live in Dreams, which – with a spit and a polish – might conceivably have ended up on Bowie’s eponymous post-Space Oddity album in 1969: it doesn’t really sound like anything else, which isn’t something you can say about everything else here.Ten years after his death, is David Bowie’s musical legacy at risk of fading from view?Read moreWere they judged on quality alone, rather than Bowie’s involvement, the songs on The Shel Talmy Sessions would be filler for collections of obscure 60s freakbeat, with the real purchasing incentive provided by superior, if similarly unsuccessful, peers: the Syndicats’ deranged Crawdaddy Simone, the Eyes’ When the Night Falls, or Leaving Here by Ronnie Wood’s mid-60s mob the Birds, the latter a single so tough and potent it provided a lifelong touchstone for the musical approach of Motörhead frontman Lemmy. That they’re instead deemed to warrant special treatment – an exclusive red vinyl collectors’ edition, 8,000 words of excellent sleevenotes by 60s rock historian Alec Palao, and indeed an accompanying pair of socks – tells you less about their quality than about the posthumous rewriting of Bowie’s history, and the industry it fuels.David Bowie: The Shel Talmy Recordings is released 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsDavid BowiePop and rockalbum reviewsShareReuse this content

title: Redwood by Ben Macintyre review – a superbly wrought tale of cold war defection | History books | The Guardian
description: This story of Soviet agent and his MI6 handler in revolutionary Iran is a page-turning masterpiece
Author: Oliver Bullough
Headline: This story of Soviet agent and his MI6 handler in revolutionary Iran is a page-turning masterpiece
Content: Posters of Ayatollah Khomeini during the 1979 Iranian revolution .Photograph: Kaveh KazemiView image in fullscreenPosters of Ayatollah Khomeini during the 1979 Iranian revolution .Photograph: Kaveh KazemiBook of the dayHistory booksReviewRedwood by Ben Macintyre review – a superbly wrought tale of cold war defectionThis story of Soviet agent and his MI6 handler in revolutionary Iran is a page-turning masterpieceOliver BulloughWed 16 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBen Macintyre uses the acronym MICE to describe the reasons people betray their countries: Money, Ideology, Coercion or Ego. In the set-piece that opens his latest work of true-espionage, we discover a new reason: erectile dysfunction.Stressed, drinking too much, under constant surveillance, furious about the corruption of his colleagues and frustrated with his home life, the KGB’s Vladimir Kuzichkin is offering to betray the secrets of his homeland and its Iranian allies, if only a British doctor can help him have sex again.If you have read Macintyre before, you’ll recognise a classic example of his style: the journalist’s eye for salacious detail combined with a historian’s rigour. The rest of Redwood lives up to the attention-grabbing opening scene; I devoured it in a single sitting.If you haven’t read him, he is the author of a hatful of bestselling books about war, politics and secrecy, several of which have been adapted for the screen, and one of which – Operation Mincemeat – has become a West End and Broadway musical. They are sometimes derided as “dadlit”, the kind of nonfiction read by golf club bores and armchair colonels. But Redwood is as far above yet-another-book-about-the-second-world-war as a George Smiley novel is above Jack Reacher.The setting is the immediate aftermath of the 1979 revolution that brought Iran’s ayatollahs to power. The west was on the back foot, having lost a key ally, with the Americans particularly discomfited by Islamists having seized their embassy and taken its staff hostage. The Soviets, meanwhile, thought they had an opportunity to spread their influence south, to a strategic and oil-rich country with warm water ports.Kuzichkin’s job was to further this aim by distributing money, arms and encouragement to the Tudeh party, an orthodox communist movement led by a Stalinist who had spent the previous few decades in exile in East Germany. He ran his operation out of the huge Soviet embassy, where his mostly useless colleagues celebrated even the smallest of successes with vast quantities of vodka, and he really hated it.Literally across the street, in the equally large British embassy, was Ian McCredie, a young MI6 operative who had recently arrived in Tehran with a wife and baby in tow, his task to re-establish a British intelligence presence after the entire team had been forced to leave. He didn’t drink as much as Kuzichkin, but he did discover 50 crates of whisky that a predecessor had imported as a present for the Shah and left in a garage, so was able to ride out the revolutionaries’ ban on alcohol quite well.The relationship between the two men, which becomes one of handler and double agent, is the backbone of the book. It is set against the ever-present risk of discovery by the Revolutionary Guard, and given added poignancy by the fact that neither one realises their actions are taking place amid a geopolitical tectonic shift, in which the communists are slipping into irrelevance and the Islamists rising to take their place.This is demonstrated most starkly when, after Kuzichkin has been safely exfiltrated to the UK for debriefing, his controllers send him to Pakistan to share his intelligence about the communists with the Iranian authorities. They hoped this would win them favour in Tehran, but instead it unleashes an orgy of violence and torture against Tudeh supporters which further entrenches the Islamic Republic’s control and does nothing to help the west.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut such weighty matters are leavened throughout by witty turns of phrase: an antiquated coding machine is “not so much user-unfriendly, as overtly hostile”; the head of Britain’s mission in Tehran is “a master of the art of thinking twice before saying nothing”; McCredie’s wife Lucy had nothing to fear from living under an oppressive regime because “she had been educated in an English girls’ boarding school”. So, by all means give Redwood to your father for Christmas, but make sure you read it yourself first: it’s superb.Redwood by Ben Macintyre is published by Viking (£25). title: Safe Spaces by Tice Cin review – a kaleidoscopic vision of precarity, music and grief | Fiction | The Guardian
description: Part spoken-word poem, part journalistic meditation, this is an inventive, tender novel of a songwriter’s journey through love and loss in London
Author: Sana Goyal
Headline: Part spoken-word poem, part journalistic meditation, this is an inventive, tender novel of a songwriter’s journey through love and loss in London
Content: Shape-shifting perspectives … Tice Cin.Photograph: Eric Aydin BarberiniView image in fullscreenShape-shifting perspectives … Tice Cin.Photograph: Eric Aydin BarberiniFictionReviewSafe Spaces by Tice Cin review – a kaleidoscopic vision of precarity, music and griefPart spoken-word poem, part journalistic meditation, this is an inventive, tender novel of a songwriter’s journey through love and loss in LondonSana GoyalWed 16 Sep 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTice Cin’s philosophical and poetic new novel about a young Turkish-Cypriot songwriter and music producer extends the preoccupations of her prizewinning debut, 2021’sKeeping the House. This intimately told sophomore novel, again a story of friendship, precarity and community, is at once an elegy, a spoken-word poem and a journalistic meditation, repeatedly asking readers: “So, are you listening?”For our unnamed narrator, “hurts come in different shapes each time”: from the childhood scars of her father’s abandonment, to sexism in the creative scene and the difficulties of navigating short-lived flatshares on universal credit (“If you don’t know about being money dry, if you don’t know loss – you don’t get it. If you know, you know”). Her journey of personal discovery is mapped on to the contemporary travails of London’s wider working-class inner-city diaspora communities as she calculates her life by doorways, “walking past each one” without a roadmap for her personal and professional goals.At the centre of the novel is the loss of the narrator’s closest confidante, referred to as “My Favourite Person”. As his untimely death becomes fodder for gossip, she addresses those questioning how he died: “You’re asking for information but to me it’s the loop, the scaffolding, never comes down, this con of process, all dying to know how he died.” Meanwhile, she remembers their late-night phone calls, continues to leave him unheard voicemails: “Don’t want to do it all without you on my team.”double quotation markOn dance floors, in therapy sessions, the grieving narrator attempts to articulate herself creatively and emotionallyHow to survive in a world darkened by an unshakeable loss? “Memories are a bit like a messy laundry cupboard. Whenever you brush past the door, all the items inside are falling out… Jamming the door doesn’t help because everything is still messy inside.” Through love affairs and short-term jobs, in DJ booths or on dancefloors of local raves, in therapy sessions and beauty parlours, the grieving narrator attempts to articulate herself creatively and emotionally. “Sometimes my head feels like the city, ambulances going past 24/7 but we still hear nothing. In a way it’s a type of growth, to feel the wrong things less.”In Cin’s dexterous hands, form meets content to kaleidoscopic effect. Told in the first person and without character names, most vignettes are additionally prefaced with a clarification of who is being addressed, or doing the addressing: “The ‘you’ is reading me. The ‘me’ is still me.” “The ‘she’ is all of us, me.” “I am ‘her’ and ‘you’.” With a protagonist deep in the world of music, these shape-shifting perspectives give the impression of a DJ spinning tracks.In the narrator’s own safe space, she is “a marshmallow gravity genie who sleeps facefront on a soft cloud”, floating away from earthly human concerns. This is a tender novel looking for a foothold in an alienating world.Safe Spaces by Tice Cin is published by Granta (£14.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com.
