title: Michelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for serving dessert topped with ants | South Korea | The Guardian
description: Prosecutors sought jail term for chief executive of Evett after insects not approved for consumption were on menu
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: Prosecutors sought jail term for chief executive of Evett after insects not approved for consumption were on menu
Content: Ants are used as an ingredient in the US and Europe, and the restaurant appeared not to have realised they were not permitted in South Korea, the judge said.Photograph: Patrick SeanView image in fullscreenAnts are used as an ingredient in the US and Europe, and the restaurant appeared not to have realised they were not permitted in South Korea, the judge said.Photograph: Patrick SeanSouth KoreaMichelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for serving dessert topped with antsProsecutors sought jail term for chief executive of Evett after insects not approved for consumption were on menuRaphael Rashidin SeoulWed 16 Sep 2026 05.09 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA South Korean court has fined the operator of one of Seoul’s most celebrated restaurants and its chief executive for serving a dessert topped with ants, an insect not approved for consumption under local food safety law.The operator of Evett, a two-Michelin-star restaurant in the affluent Gangnam district, was fined 10m won (£5,400) and its chief executive 15m won,Newsis reported.Prosecutors had soughta one-year prison term for the chief executive and a 20m won fine for the company.The judge at Seoul’s western district court, Lee Se-chang, said the offence was “by no means light”, citing the length of time the dishes had been sold for, the restaurant’s use of them to promote itself and tests that found heavy metals above permitted levels in the ants.View image in fullscreenProsecutors said the restaurant imported dried ants from the US and Thailand by post and served three to five of them on a sorbet made with sikhye, a sweet Korean rice drink.Photograph: Patrick SeanHe said he had taken into account that the defendants admitted the offence, that the chief executive had no previous criminal record under the food safety law, that the number of ants served appeared lower than prosecutors had calculated and that the restaurant no longer used ants.Ants are used as an ingredient in the US and Europe, and the restaurant appeared not to have realised they were not permitted in South Korea, he said.Both sides have seven days to appeal. The Guardian contacted Evett for comment.Evett was founded by the Australian chef Joseph Lidgerwood, who has appeared on the Netflix cooking competition Culinary Class Wars and is the restaurant’s public face. He was not a defendant and was not charged.Under South Korean food safety law, the legal duties fall on the person registered as operating the business. Ginny Kim, Lidgerwood’s wife, is registered as the company’s chief executive and was named as a defendant, alongside the company that operates the restaurant.Only 10 insect species are approved as food ingredients in South Korea, including grasshoppers, mealworms and silkworm pupae.Businesses wishing to use an unapproved insect must obtain temporary approval from the ministry of food and drug safety, a step the restaurant did not take. Violating the law carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison or a 50m won fine.The ministry launched its investigation after seeing mentions of the ant dishes in blog posts and social media.Prosecutors said the restaurant imported dried ants from the US and Thailand by post from April 2021, and served three to five of them atop a sorbet made with sikhye, a sweet Korean rice drink, until January 2025.View image in fullscreenLawyers said in court that only about 60% of customers accepted the ant topping when it was offered.Photograph: Patrick SeanThey estimated the dessert was served to 12,274 customers, using 49,096 ants, for total revenue of about 120m won.Lawyers disputed that figure in court, arguing that only about 60% of customers accepted the ant topping when it was offered.The restaurant also noted that only a small number of dishes on their 15-course menu included ants, and that restaurants in countries including Denmark, the UK and Australia use ants as an ingredient.Insect-eating is neither new nor unusual in South Korea. Beondegi, steamed silkworm pupae, has been sold from street carts for decades and remains a nostalgic popular snack for children.Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreaFoodRestaurantsAsia PacificFood safetyKorean food and drinknewsShareReuse this content

title: How to turn excess olive brine into a lipsmacking salad dressing – recipe  | Food | The Guardian
description: The liquid from a jar of olives is naturally chock-full of savoury flavour, so why should it go to waste? It’s perfect for sprucing up a salad
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: The liquid from a jar of olives is naturally chock-full of savoury flavour, so why should it go to waste? It’s perfect for sprucing up a salad
Content: Tom Hunt's olive brine vinaigrette.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt's olive brine vinaigrette.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notFoodHow to turn excess olive brine into a lipsmacking salad dressing – recipeThe liquid from a jar of olives is naturally chock-full of savoury flavour, so why should it go to waste? It’s perfect for sprucing up a saladTom HuntWed 16 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOlive brine is a simple byproduct that has so much flavour, and it elevates a classic salade nicoise dressing while keeping things colourful, elegant and relatively simple.Salade nicoise with olive-brine vinaigretteThough this one-bowl wonder began life as a simple tomato and anchovy salad with olive oil, it has become more elaborate over time, and the addition of cooked green beans, eggs and even tuna all make sense to me. What’s worth preserving, though, is its Mediterranean simplicity, and the olive-brine dressing adds a lot of flavour without needing loads of extra ingredients.In the spirit of simplicity, this vinaigrette keeps to just three wonderfully flavourful ingredients: olive brine for salt and depth of flavour, red-wine vinegar for acidity and olive oil for substance and piquancy. It won’t hold a stable emulsion in the way a mustard dressing does, so give it another good shake just before it goes on the salad. I buy whole olives with the pits in and pit them myself. They, and the brine, taste so much better that way.Serves4For the vinaigrette2 tbsp brine from a jar of olives1 tbsp red-wine vinegar6 tbsp extra-virgin olive oilBlack pepper, to tasteFor the salad6eggs200g green beans, topped200g cocktail tomatoes, or cherry tomatoes1 red pepper, stalk, seeds and pith removed, flesh sliced into rings½ medium cucumber, skin on and seeds in, cut into large chunks4 spring onions, cut into 1cm lengths (white and green parts)1 small jarblack olivesAnchovy fillets, (optional) to taste; I used a whole standard 50g tin1 small handful basil leaves, to finishPut the olive brine, vinegar and extra-virgin olive oil in a jar, and add a grind of black pepper to taste. Screw on the lid and shake until the mixture emulsifies. It won’t stay emulsified for long, so shake again just before you’re ready to eat. The dressing will now keep in the fridge for up to a week.Put the eggs in a pan of cold water and bring to a boil. Once boiling, add the green beans, bring back to a boil and cook for four minutes. Drain, then put the eggs and beans in a bowl of iced or cold water. Once cooled, drain again and put the beans to one side (they can be left whole or cut into pieces). Peel and halve the eggs.Cut the tomatoes in half, then arrange all the vegetables on a platter. Scatter over the stoned olives and drained anchovy fillets to taste, then finish with the halved eggs, some torn basil leaves and the freshly shaken dressing. Eat straight away.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteSauces and graviesSaladFrench food and drinkMain courseStarterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Squid ink tomato pasta and honey and fig semifreddo: Chris Leach’s Italian recipes for the end of summer | Food | The Guardian
description: Cooking at this time of year is all about low-effort, maximum-impact options. This savoury dish comes together quickly but looks striking, while the dessert showcases figs at their most flavoursome
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cooking at this time of year is all about low-effort, maximum-impact options. This savoury dish comes together quickly but looks striking, while the dessert showcases figs at their most flavoursome
Content: Chris Leach’s squid ink spaghetti with anchovies, cherry tomato and pangrattato.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.View image in fullscreenChris Leach’s squid ink spaghetti with anchovies, cherry tomato and pangrattato.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.FoodSquid ink tomato pasta and honey and fig semifreddo: Chris Leach’s Italian recipes for the end of summerCooking at this time of year is all about low-effort, maximum-impact options. This savoury dish comes together quickly but looks striking, while the dessert showcases figs at their most flavoursomeChris LeachWed 16 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe secret to late-summer/early autumn cooking is to keep things relatively low-effort, not least to assuage those back-to-work/school blues. And that rule applies across the board, whether you’re making a midweek meal, entertaining or serving up a long, slow Sunday lunch. The sauce for this pasta dish, for example, comes together while the pasta is cooking, while the semifreddo pudding makes the most of ripe figs when they are at their absolute best.Squid ink spaghetti with anchovies, cherry tomatoes and pangrattatoThe contrast between the black pasta, the red tomatoes and the golden crumbs is really something else, as are the flavours.Prep15 minCook30 minServes4For the pangrattato150g day-old sourdough or country bread3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil2 garlic cloves, peeled and finely sliced3 sprigs thyme, leaves pickedFine sea salt and black pepperFor the pastaSea salt400g squid ink spaghetti4 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, plus extra to finish3 garlic cloves, peeled and thinly sliced300g ripe cherry tomatoes6 anchovy fillets in oil75ml dry white wineFinely grated zest and juice of ½ unwaxed lemon1 small handful picked flat-leaf parsley, finely choppedBlack pepperFirst make the pangrattato. Tear the stale bread into rough pieces, then pulse in a food processor to make coarse, uneven breadcrumbs. Put the oil in a large frying pan on a medium heat, add the sliced garlic and cook gently, stirring, for a minute or two, until fragrant but not coloured. Add the thyme leaves, cook for a further 30 seconds, then stir in the breadcrumbs and cook, stirring regularly, for eight to 10 minutes, until evenly golden and crisp all over. Season with a pinch of sea salt and a little black pepper, then transfer to a plate to cool completely.Bring a large pan of well-salted water to a boil, then cook the squid ink spaghetti according to the packet instructions, until al dente.While the pasta is cooking, put the oil in a large frying pan on a medium heat, then add the sliced garlic and cook gently, stirring, for two minutes, until fragrant and just beginning to colour. Add the whole cherry tomatoes and cook, stirring, for three to four minutes, until they begin to soften and burst, then stir in the anchovy fillets and press them into the pan with the back of a spoon so they dissolve into the oil. Pour in the white wine, turn up the heat and leave to bubble and reduce by about half.Use tongs or a spider sieve to lift the cooked pasta directly into the tomato pan (alternatively, drain the pasta, saving some of its water), then add a splash of the cooking water, and toss and stir until the sauce lightly coats the pasta. Finish with the lemon zest, a squeeze of lemon juice and the chopped parsley, then taste and adjust the seasoning, adding black pepper and more lemon as needed.Divide the pasta between bowls and finish each serving generously with about 50g of the pangrattato (store any excess in an air-tight container and savefor another use: it’s especially good on salads and in other pasta dishes) and a final drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil.Honey, thyme and fig semifreddoView image in fullscreenChris Leach’s honey, thyme and fig semifreddo.Take this out of the freezer about 10 minutes before slicing and serving. Serve with warm honey, fresh figs and toasted seeds for a simple but very special finish.Prep20 minCook45 min, plus coolingFreeze8 hr+Serves6For the thyme cream300ml double cream3 sprigs fresh thymeFinely grated zest of ½ unwaxed lemonFor the honey sabayon3 large egg yolks75g chestnut honey, or good-quality floral honey1 pinch fine sea salt20g brown butter– that is, melted and browned, then left to cool (optional, but recommended)For the fig ripple200g fig jam1 tbsp aged balsamic vinegarTo finish4 fresh figs, quartered2 tbsp warm honey1 pinch toasted poppy seeds1 pinchfennel seeds, toasted and lightly crushedA few picked thyme leaves1 pinch flaky sea saltFirst, infuse the cream. Put the cream and thyme in a small pan and heat until just below boiling. Take off the heat, stir in the lemon zest and leave to infuse and cool for 20-30 minutes. Once cool, strain, then chill thoroughly before whipping to soft peaks.For the honey sabayon, put the egg yolks, honey and salt in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water, making sure the base of the bowl doesn’t touch the water. Whisk for six to eight minutes, until the mixture is pale, thick and has tripled in volume. Take off the heat, keep whisking for two to three minutes more, until the mix is just warm, then fold in the cooled brown butter, if using.Now for the fig ripple. Warm the fig jam, balsamic vinegar and a tablespoon of water until the mix is smooth enough to ripple through the semifreddo, then take off the heat and leave to cool completely.Fold a third of the thyme-infused whipped cream into the sabayon to loosen it, then, taking care not to knock out the air, gently fold in the remaining cream until well incorporated.Now to assemble the semifreddo. Line a small loaf tin with baking paper, leaving plenty of overhang on all sides. Spoon in a third of the semifreddo mixture, drizzle over some of the fig ripple, then use a knife gently to swirl into the mix and make a marbled effect. Repeat twice more with the remaining semifreddo mix and fig ripple, finish with a final swirl of the knife, then cover with the overhanging paperand freeze for at least eight hours, and ideally overnight.Take the semifreddo tin out of the freezer 10-15 minutes before you want to serve it. Once it’s softened a little, lift it out of the tin, using the paper overhang to help you, then place on a board and cut into six slices. Arrange the fresh fig halves around it, top with the warm honey, and finish with a sprinkling of toasted poppy seeds, toasted crushed fennel seeds, a few thyme leaves and a small pinch of flaky sea salt.Chris Leach is chef and co-founder ofManteca, London EC2Explore more on these topicsFoodItalian food and drinkPastaMain courseStarterDessertTomatoesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘It sits at the meeting point of science and the humanities’: should you study psychology? | Psychology | The Guardian
description: Psychology has become one of the most popular courses at university. That’s no surprise as the insights it gives to our behaviour can help in a huge variety of careers
Author: Tess Reidy
Headline: Psychology has become one of the most popular courses at university. That’s no surprise as the insights it gives to our behaviour can help in a huge variety of careers
Content: Psychology offers the chance to ‘make a positive difference to people’s lives’.Photograph: Maskot/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPsychology offers the chance to ‘make a positive difference to people’s lives’.Photograph: Maskot/Getty ImagesUniversity Guide 2027Psychology‘It sits at the meeting point of science and the humanities’: should you study psychology?Psychology has become one of the most popular courses at university. That’s no surprise as the insights it gives to our behaviour can help in a huge variety of careersTess ReidyWed 16 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor Niamh Mulcahy, 21, graduating with a psychology degree from the University of Bath has already paid off. After navigating a competitive graduate jobs market this year, she secured a sales role with a FTSE 100 company starting in September.“My degree involved a lot of data analysis, which has been really useful in job applications,” she says. “The course felt very current. We covered everything from neuroscience to forensic psychology, and my dissertation was on ‘incels’. I’ve always been fascinated by human behaviour and why people make the decisions they do.”Mulcahy is not alone. Psychology has become one of the UK’s top subjects at university and is now thesecond most popular A-levelchoice after maths. It consistently ranks among the most searched subjects in the Guardian’s University Guide, behind medicine, law and economics.According to Ucas, applications for psychology courses were up 4.9% in January 2026 compared with the previous year.So what explains psychology’s enduring appeal? At its core, the subject is about understanding how people think, feel and behave. But academics argue its popularity goes far beyond a growing interest in mental health.Heather Cleland Woods, from the School of Psychology andNeuroscienceat the University of Glasgow, believes the subject is booming because it develops skills that are becoming increasingly valuable in the age of AI. “Psychology teaches communication, critical evaluation and collaboration,” she says. “Those are absolutely key skills.”James Ainge, head of psychology and neuroscience at the University of St Andrews, says the discipline’s breadth is one of its biggest attractions. “It sits at the meeting point of science and the humanities,” he says. “At one end of the spectrum you’re asking people about their opinions and feelings. At the other, you’re studying neuroscience and computational models.” That combination also teaches students how to weigh evidence from multiple sources and think critically, he adds, abilities that are becoming more important than ever.There is also growing interest among young people in subjects that feel relevant to the challenges they see around them. “Students are interested in real-world issues,” says Jess Lomas, recruitment lead for psychology at the University of Sheffield.Psychologygives them a framework for understanding topics like the climate crisis, AI, smartphone use and mental health, while also offering the chance to “make a positive difference to people’s lives”.The degree’s versatility is another major draw. Graduates go on to careers in healthcare, professional psychology, research, teaching and academia, but also into marketing, government, consultancy, HR and the corporate world. “It sets you up well for a huge range of careers,” says Ainge.For prospective students, choosing between courses is important. Psychology is usually offered as either a BA or a BSc at undergraduate level. The key thing is to look at where psychology sits within the university. Is it part of the psychology department, or the social sciences faculty or health sciences faculty? That will give you a sense of the course’s emphasis. Many universities also offer joint honours degrees, allowing students to combine psychology with subjects such as education or statistics. What A-levels you need depends on the university: a science or maths A-level would generally be seen as an advantage for a competitive BSc course, and psychology A-level would give access to both routes.Andrew Welchman, professor of neuroinnovation at the University of Birmingham, also recommends looking for courses accredited by the British Psychological Society. Accreditation ensures programmes meet consistent national standards and cover the core content required for graduates who may later want to train as professional psychologists.Explore more on these topicsPsychologyUniversity Guide 2027Higher educationSocial sciencesUniversitiesStudentsYoung peopleNeurosciencefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Barclaycard sent me a bill for someone else’s account | Money | The Guardian
description: It told me a year ago I had applied for a credit card – now it is it telling me my payment is overdue
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: It told me a year ago I had applied for a credit card – now it is it telling me my payment is overdue
Content: Barclaycard is sending bills for a credit card that was never applied for.Photograph: Michael Melia/AlamyView image in fullscreenBarclaycard is sending bills for a credit card that was never applied for.Photograph: Michael Melia/AlamyConsumer championsMoneyBarclaycard sent me a bill for someone else’s accountIt told me a year ago I had applied for a credit card – now it is it telling me my payment is overdueAnna TimsWed 16 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA year ago I got an email from Barclaycard stating that my “application was successful” for a credit card.I had made no such application. I immediately reported thisto Barclaycard. More emails arrived and I made repeated phone calls to customer service.I was assuredit was a simple typo rather than fraud, and that my email address would be removed.However, I’m now receiving notifications that the latest account payment is overdue.Thecustomer who holds this account has the same name as me but with aslightlydifferent spelling.Can you convince Barclaycard to delete my email address and give my namesake a bell?PG, ManchesterSuch a small mistake, so easy to fix, so unnerving for you as the payment reminders become more urgent. The other PG is also affected by Barclaycard’s incompetence since you have his email address and know that he is in debt.Barclaycard blames “human error” and removed your email from the account exactly 13 months after you reported it. It apologised for the delay and offered £200 for the “inconvenience”.We welcome letters but cannot answer individually. title: Sali Hughes on beauty: lip gloss is back in vogue and these new formulas have me hooked | Beauty | The Guardian
description: Personally I’ve never been a fan of painting on the gloss but thanks to a range of fresh formats in sophisticated shades and textures, my head – and lips – have been turned
Author: Sali Hughes
Headline: Personally I’ve never been a fan of painting on the gloss but thanks to a range of fresh formats in sophisticated shades and textures, my head – and lips – have been turned
Content: Photograph: Kellie French/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Kellie French/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.BeautySali Hughes on beauty: lip gloss is back in vogue and these new formulas have me hookedPersonally, I’ve never been a fan of painting on the gloss, but thanks to a range of fresh formats in sophisticated shades and textures, my head – and lips – have been turnedSali HughesWed 16 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m deeply suspicious of people who never change their minds. To be so completely sure of anything as to be permanently entrenched in any position isn’t something I admire, which is why I shove an olive into my mouth every couple of years and hope it finally takes.I do the same with lip gloss, with historically similar results. Fashion has, until recently, been on my side. Less sophisticated than lipstick, overshadowed by TikTok trending lip oils, less effortless cool-girl than tinted lip balm, gloss has barely had a look-in these past few years, but new formulas steal from other formats for a better user experience and, well, like everything eventually, lip gloss is back in vogue.The launch of Nars’Afterglow Lipshine(£28.50) was what first gotmehooked. Its smooth, unsticky texture, lack of scent and lasting moisture make it a pleasure, and a characteristically thoughtful colour range makes the whole lineup feel as adult and sophisticated as lipstick.double quotation markThe high street comes into its own with lip gloss, but even so, Maybelline’s Lifter Gloss is a standoutSmooth Talk, a cool, sheer cocoa brown, was my most worn lip colour of last winter (either alone or over lipstick) and will soon see me through another. I’ll be adding in Nympho, an unusual cool taupe. Abbey Road, a golden, shimmering (who even am I?) bronze has lived in my handbag all summer, alongside a nude lip liner and … not one lipstick.Sali Hughes on beauty: will social media bans for teens mean the return of grownup skincare?Read moreMore recently, Chanel has relaunched its Rouge Coco lip glosses asRouge Coco Hydra Gloss(£39), a more moisturising, thinner, unsticky version of its bestseller in interesting but wearable shades. Icing looks as it sounds – a translucent, milky pink, wet glaze that looks gorgeous on its own (it’s a perfect lip for a natural bridal look) or over another lip colour to make it more muted.Accessoire – a neutral, classic Chanel beige – is my other everyday favourite. Naturally, the packaging looks beautiful pulled out of a handbag, and even when the gloss is carelessly slicked on, lips stay moisturised for a good couple of hours.The high street comes into its own with lip gloss, but even so, Maybelline’sLifter Gloss(£8.99) is a standout. If you ignore the scent (sweet, warm) and needlessly chunky packaging, the product itself is indistinguishable from many luxury lip glosses. This is a not-at-all-sticky, very comfortable, easy-to-use gloss in some very pretty, wearable shades. Stone (008), a neutral peachy taupe, is my favourite that would suit anyone. Toast is a glorious reddish brown that makes me long for autumn knits.Explore more on these topicsBeautyWomenLipstickfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The other side of Croatia: ‘a landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany’ | Croatia holidays | The Guardian
description: Weekenders from Zagreb head to the rolling green Samobor Hills for nature, vineyards, delicious local food and Habsburg-era architecture
Author: Mary Novakovich
Headline: Weekenders from Zagreb head to the rolling green Samobor Hills for nature, vineyards, delicious local food and Habsburg-era architecture
Content: Vineyards in Croatia’s Plešivica wine region.Photograph: Ilija Ascic/AlamyView image in fullscreenVineyards in Croatia’s Plešivica wine region.Photograph: Ilija Ascic/AlamyCroatia holidaysThe other side of Croatia: ‘a landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany’Weekenders from Zagreb head to the rolling green Samobor Hills for nature, vineyards, delicious local food and Habsburg-era architectureMary NovakovichWed 16 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘You’re going to Samobor? You must trykremšnita,” my Dubrovnik friends told me before I set off on my trip north. “But I’ve already hadkremšnitain Zagreb,” I told them. They do it better inSamobor, they insisted. I wasn’t about to get embroiled in a battle of the cream cakes in a region where Croatians, Slovenes and Austrians all like to celebrate their own versions of this decadently thick, fat custard slice topped with puff pastry and icing sugar. But I was more than willing – happy, even – to follow everyone’s suggestions to trykremšnitain Hotel Livadić’sKavana Livadić, in Samobor’s main King Tomislav Square, a mere half-hour drive west of Zagreb.View image in fullscreenThe excellentkremšnitaat Kavana Livadić, Samobor.Photograph: Mary NovakvoichIt lived up to the hype – delicately rich, creamy and with a light touch. After spending a few weeks in sun-bleached Venetian Dalmatia, amid the scrubby, limestone Dinaric Alps, I had swapped empires and was firmly in Habsburg Croatia. Here, inZagreb County’sprettiest town, handsome baroque houses in pastel shades of buttery yellow, apricot and pistachio, festooned with stucco, line narrow King Tomislav Square, whose umbrella-shaded cafe terraces were filled with Croatians getting their morning fix of coffee and chatter.The lush green Samobor Hills overlook the medieval town, through which the Gradna – part river, part stream – flows and ripples under wooden bridges adorned with flowers. One of these bridges led to the onion-domed church of Saint Anastasia; another, with a fairytale wooden roof, took me to one of Samobor’s many green spaces, dotted with free red deckchairs, which had the slogan “Volim Samobor” (“I love Samobor”) written in white. In front of them, the stately former home (now thetown’s museum) of one of Croatia’s foremost 19th-century composers, Ferdo Livadić, added to the air of gentle refinement, of culture worn lightly. It was easy to visualise Livadić entertaining his artistic friends, including Franz Liszt, in this august setting.double quotation markHandsome baroque houses in pastel shades of buttery yellow, apricot and pistachio line narrow King Tomislav Square in SamoborAs well as the graceful architectural legacy of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy, this rolling green landscape is crisscrossed with forested trails, particularly within theŽumberak nature park, about 16 miles (26km) west of Samobor, where weekenders from Zagreb come to hike and bike in woods of hornbeam, oak and beech with bubbling waterfalls. Not having time for a full-on hike, I could still drive to Potočna dolina Slapnica, near the Vranjak waterfalls, and scramble up the path beside a series of cascades each more impressive than the last.Closer to Samobor, the hilltop ruins of Okić castle rose to nearly 500m above sea level, one of the best-preserved romanesque fortifications in the country. The Mongols couldn’t defeat it, nor could the Ottoman Turks. Sadly, it defeated me when I attempted to hike to the top. Not realising there was a newer, easier path, I ended up on one that was little else but vertical tree roots. With a newly healed ankle and no phone signal, I thought it unwise to continue. But it’s on my list for next time.View image in fullscreenThe mist-shrouded ruins of Okic castle.Photograph: Ivan Smuk/AlamyA much easier path to take was along the Plešivica wine road, where more than three dozen wineries were scattered on a heart-shaped route between the village of Plešivica (10 miles south-west of Samobor) and the town of Jastrebarsko. In a harmonious landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany, vineyards clung to steep slopes between forested hills, many producing the sparkling wine Plešivica is renowned for. I met Martina and Krešimir Ivančić, whose ancestors were given a noble title and coat of arms by the Austrian empress Maria Theresa in 1759. The griffin on the family crest inspired the name of theGriffin Winery, which came about when a Hungarian count gave them a licence to plant a vineyard in 1773.View image in fullscreenRudarska grebalica: a salty, stuffed pastry from Nikl in Rude.Photograph: Pixsell/AlamyMartina took me to the covered patio of a wooden hut above the vineyards, a suitably bucolic place to taste an elegant and lightly fruity sparkling rose made from red portugieser grapes. We carried on in the extremely stylish tasting room, where plates of cured meats and cheeses accompanied glasses of full-bodied chardonnay.I was also offeredcopanjek, a thin savoury pastry pie of cheese and greens. “They’re very portable, so workers would take them to the vineyard,” Martina told me. This looked like the winemaker’s version ofrudarska greblica, which I had tasted that morning in the village of Rude, about a 10-minute drive west of Samobor, and liked so much I had to have two. Filled with cheese and walnuts, carrots or greens, these used to be made by the wives of Rude’s long-gone miners. They’re such an integral part of the region that they have their own festival every July and have been given EU protected status. AtPekarnica Nikl, in Rude, I met Jelena and Andrejas Nikl, the only authorised bakers of this much adored speciality. Jelena acknowledged the responsibility of keeping up this tradition ofrudarska greblica, especially with the paperwork that came with legal protection – but, she said, it was worth it.View image in fullscreenThe sunny terrace at Korak winery and restaurant.Photograph: Mary NovakovichAll around the Samobor Hills, people were holding fast to their heritage and infusing it with life. The Korak family is one of the most illustrious, with its Michelin-starredKorak winery and restaurantin Plešivica. Not a whiff of Michelin stuffiness or pretentiousness here, just the fourth and fifth generations of a family producing superb wine and making beautiful food in a serene setting facing the vineyards. Brother Bernard is chef (and has worked with Massimo Bottura of Italy’s Osteria Francescana and Ana Roš of Slovenia’s Hiša Franko); sister Vera is front of house; and parents Velimir and Mirjana tend the vines – even the siblings’ grandparents are still making cheese andpršut(prosciutto) for the restaurant.Bernard grows as much as he can – the rest comes from local producers, including the farmer whose pigs are fed on scraps from Bernard’s kitchen. And if it’s not in season, it’s not on the plate. My June visit rewarded me with a truffle tagliatelle, and clams and green beans in a caviar sauce, among other delicious dishes in a five-course tasting menu at €118 (a very reasonable price, and in keeping with the region’s overall lower prices).I could only imagine what delights autumn will bring, especially during the annualWine Daysfestival in Jastrebarsko from 25-27 September. The Samobor Hills will be teeming with autumn truffles and mushrooms, and welcoming the change in season the best way they know – on the plate.Explore more on these topicsCroatia holidaysEurope holidaysFood and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A moment that changed me: I felt hugely self conscious about my skin - until I had a revelation | Comedy | The Guardian
description: For years, my vitiligo controlled my life, and I was constantly trying to disguise it. But one day, I realised I could take a very different and extremely liberating approach
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: For years, my vitiligo controlled my life, and I was constantly trying to disguise it. But one day, I realised I could take a very different and extremely liberating approach
Content: Natalie Ambersley, pictured in 2025.Photograph: Courtesy of Natalie AmbersleyView image in fullscreenNatalie Ambersley, pictured in 2025.Photograph: Courtesy of Natalie AmbersleyA moment that changed meComedyA moment that changed me: I felt hugely self conscious about my skin - until I had a revelationFor years, my vitiligo controlled my life, and I was constantly trying to disguise it. But one day, I realised I could take a very different and extremely liberating approachNatalie AmbersleyWed 16 Sep 2026 01.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe microphone felt heavier than I expected. As I stood on stage at a London comedy club last December, I looked out at a room full of strangers sitting quietly, waiting for me to make them laugh. It felt nerve-racking and surreal. I had spent years hiding my vitiligo, hoping people wouldn’t notice it. Now I was about to joke about it in my set.I was three years old when I developed my first patch of vitiligo on the back of my hand, which later spread to my arms, legs, face and other parts of my body. By the time I was six years old, 70% of me was covered. I was too young to understand what was happening.Despite this, I had a happy childhood because I was unaware then that being different was something that was viewed negatively. I went swimming, wore shorts and T-shirts, and barely gave my skin much thought. My parents taught me it was part of me and that it wasn’t something that had to hold me back. However, what I couldn’t foresee was how others would perceive me later in life.View image in fullscreen‘I got a buzz from the idea of dong something so far outside my comfort zone.’Photograph: Charlotte StevensMy teenage years were by far my hardest. I became painfully self-conscious and increasingly aware that I was different. I struggled with swimming lessons because I was worried about wearing a swimsuit, and during the summer I’d wear clothes that kept me covered because I was embarrassed about how I looked. I wore thick foundation on my face to cover the patches around my eyes and mouth, and excessive layers of fake tan on my body. My skin had complete control of my life.Then, in November 2025, I signed up for a six-week comedy class. I was nervous, but I got a buzz from the idea of doing something so far outside my comfort zone. During the first few sessions, we had to think about subjects that we could joke about. The one thing that kept coming back to me was vitiligo.I had spent years trying to disguise it, because I was worried about being judged or spoken about negatively. But as I got older, things started to change. I spent years working on my mindset, and blocking out negative thoughts and the pressure to look a particular way. I connected with the global vitiligo community online, which made me realise that I wasn’t alone, and started publicly advocating and raising awareness. I created an Instagram page calledGifted Skinwhere I started to share my journey, to help others living with the condition.The thought of writing a seven-minute comedy sketch about a skin condition that had hugely knocked my confidence when I was growing up felt strange. I wanted people to laugh with me, rather than feel as though I was making light of something that might still be very painful for others. I worried that my material could offend or upset someone in the audience – or simply fall flat.But the more I thought about the issues around dating with a skin condition, the struggle to form relationships, growing up mixed race with vitiligo, my time at school and how society judged me, the more material I found.View image in fullscreenAmbersley on stage at 21 Soho, London.Photograph: Courtesy of Natalie AmbersleyThe course sped by and, before I knew it, it was the night of the performance at 21 Soho in central London. When my name was called, I walked up to the stage, acting confident but feeling far from it. I didn’t start with the vitiligo jokes. I wanted to warm up the crowd and earn myself some laughs first.A moment that changed me: I had a panic attack on public transport – and it led me to a horrifying secretRead moreAfter a few minutes, I introduced my first joke. I started by telling the audience that I had vitiligo and asking if anyone else in the room did too. There was silence. “Thought as much,” I said, “out here on my own again.” The room filled with laughter and I instantly felt at ease. It was like I was inviting the audience to look into my world with vitiligo, but on my terms. I felt as if I was in control – and it was nerve-racking, funny and unexpectedly liberating.Some jokes focused on my dating experiences and the unfiltered ways children react to my skin, while others focused on the responses I’ve given when people have asked inappropriate questions. The cheers felt like the biggest sign of approval; as if I was educating the audience and advocating for vitiligo while standing under a spotlight and owning it.Although I haven’t performed again since, I am keen to explore more open-mic nights. I learned so much about myself that evening but, most of all, I realised that the little girl who wanted to disappear and wished she looked “normal” had become a woman who was proud of who she was. I had chosen to make myself visible in an empowering way. I was never going to shrink myself again.Explore more on these topicsComedyA moment that changed meHealthHealth & wellbeingBeautyBody imagefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘My future is in the EU’: the Ukrainian children who don’t want to go home  | Global development | The Guardian
description: Thousands of children in state care were evacuated when Russia invaded. Kyiv wants them back – but many resist
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Thousands of children in state care were evacuated when Russia invaded. Kyiv wants them back – but many resist
Content: Evelina’s foster mother speaks to the 18-year-old, who spent two years with her in Sicily. After being repatriated to Ukraine, Evelina says she begged to go back to ItalyView image in fullscreenEvelina’s foster mother speaks to the 18-year-old, who spent two years with her in Sicily. After being repatriated to Ukraine, Evelina says she begged to go back to ItalyUkraine in depthGlobal development‘My future is in the EU’: the Ukrainian children who don’t want to go homeThousands of children in state care were evacuated when Russia invaded. Kyiv wants them back – but many resistSupported byAbout this contentStefania D'Ignoti. Photographs by Camilla MinnozziWed 16 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 12.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen he first arrived in his new home in a small village in the Italian Alps in March 2022, 15-year-old Denys* says he felt homesick and confused. He had been put on an overnight bus and relocated along with more than 100 other children from his orphanage in Berdiansk, in easternUkraine, which was one of the first areas to be invaded by Russian troops.“Ukraine was all I knew,” says Denys. “I had never left it my whole life.”But after he began going to school, making friends and integrating into Italian life, Denys says he no longer wanted to go back home. “I started to realise there was a different way of life I could be living,” he says. “One that didn’t involve airstrikes and poverty, and that could give me better opportunities for my future.”Thousands of Ukrainian social orphans – children given up to the state or taken away from parents considered unable to care for them – were evacuated overseas after Russia’s invasion in 2022. The relocation was meant to be temporary, but even after the situation stabilised in parts of Ukraine, many of them, such as Denys, refused to return.Ukrainian officials have repatriated most of the children, but more than 1,500 remain elsewhere in Europe. Some – like Denys – have been aided by Italian courts after their foster parents in Italydefied Kyiv’s repatriation order, citing concerns regarding the children’s wellbeing in a war-torn country with heavily damaged social welfare and public infrastructure.For Ukraine, already battling aplummeting birthrateand theloss of children abducted by Russia in occupied territories, the failure of some juveniles to return home has become a crisis.Kateryna Rashevska, a legal expert on war crimes against childrenin Ukraine, says: “We are losing those who should’ve been the future citizens of our nation. If these children ever actually return to Ukraine, they will have limited Ukrainian language, culture, history and identity, which also poses a threat to our future heritage and demography.”View image in fullscreenUkrainian teenagers at schools in Rota d’Imagna have weekly online Ukrainian language classes, which is a requirement of the authorities in KyivThe situation escalated in April after a 15-year-old boy who had been evacuated to Italy in 2022 was legally adopted by an Italian family, despite having parents and two sisters back in Ukraine who wanted him to return home. A court in Italy overruled Ukrainian laws – in May 2022, shortly after the war started, Ukraine hadsuspended international adoptionsto prevent trafficking or wrongful adoptions.Yuliya Donnichenko, a Ukrainian national based inItalywho has overseen evacuations to southern Italy and repatriations back to Ukraine for about 100 orphans, says there have been many childless couples who she sensed were taking advantage of the unstable situation to bypass strict international adoption laws and get a Ukrainian child.“I know that they meant the best for these kids, that they became attached to them and wanted the best for their future, away from a war-torn nation. But what they don’t understand is that by [seeking adoption] they’re putting at risk an already fragile situation,” she says.“It might not seem like a lot – just a few more hundreds compared with the already 20,000 lost to Russia – but to us every child counts. It’s the future of our nation.”Some accuse Ukraine of not being prepared to offer stable conditions and a fair future to a new generation, with the reality of return for many of the children different from what they were promised.Evelina, now 18, was repatriated after almost two years spent with an Italian foster family in Sicily, and was assigned to an adoptive Ukrainian family on the border with Romania. The family already had several foster children under their care, making her living conditions “not much different from living in an orphanage”, she says.Evelina says that when she returned home, she had her phone confiscated for more than a year, as she was not allowed to be in touch with the Italian family who hosted her throughout her stay there.“I was confined at home and didn’t go to school. I would only leave my room for an English class once a week or church on Sunday,” she says. “I felt very depressed; I didn’t understand why they made me return to live like this.”View image in fullscreenAlmost 100 Ukrainian orphans were evacuated to Rota d’Imagna, in Bergamo, northern ItalyWhen she was finally given a new phone in autumn 2024, Evelina says she managed to open a Telegram account and spent hours talking to her Italian foster mother – the only mental escape from otherwise long, boring days. “I missed her. I constantly begged her to come pick me up and bring me back to Sicily,” she says.Evelina says her new family would record videos of her going up and down the street outside her home, as proof of her doing a minimum amount of exercise and getting out of the house. After she shared her concerns with the Italian family, Evelina’s phone was confiscated again, and her WhatsApp and Telegram accounts were permanently deleted.Now she is 18, Evelina says she cannot wait to leave Ukraine and return to the EU: “It made no sense to force our return since most of us had planned to leave anyway after turning 18, thanks to the connections we developed inEurope.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“After all,” she says. “It was unfair to pretend we’d just get a quick taste of freedom in Europe and then head back to a place that can’t offer us as much as an EU country can right now.”Denys says he and almost 100 orphans evacuated to Rota d’Imagna, in the hills of Bergamo, received their repatriation order from Kyiv in August 2024. He was 17 at the time of the call to return, which meant that setting foot in Ukraine for him – as well as other boys in his age range – could mean being drafted into the war. “I was utterly frightened, but the authorities didn’t listen to our concerns,” he says.Russia has network of 200 camps for ‘brainwashing’ Ukrainian children – reportRead moreDuring one-on-one meetings in Italy with the orphans supposed to return, Denys says Ukrainian social workers would use “intimidating language and even swearwords if we showed any signs of resistance”, with younger ones “promised candies and PlayStations on their arrival in Ukraine”.He says: “They would use any possible, misleading argument to convince us to accept the return. They promised us we’d be adopted or reunited with family relatives we still had back home. All fake promises they couldn’t guarantee for sure.”With the help of Italian courts, Denys managed to stay in Italy, where he now works as a waiter and hopes to remain for the foreseeable future. He says those who ended up returning tell him they regret the choice, and that many stay not with adoptive parents but at institutions where there is no running water or electricity, and where up to six people live in the same room.View image in fullscreenDiego Mosca, who supervised the group of Ukrainian orphans in Rota d’Imagna, says the children had been ‘tossed around like a tennis ball between two sides’He says they regularly have to hide in bunkers, as even western provinces in Ukraine are targeted by Russian attacks. “This proves that they didn’t have our best interests and safety at heart,” he says.Maksym, another orphan from the Rota d’Imagna group, said he reluctantly accepted repatriation, only to move to Germany three months later when he turned 18. “Ukraine changed too much over the past few years. There’s nothing for us young people there. My future is in the EU.”Diego Mosca, who supervised the group of Ukrainian orphans in Rota d’Imagna, says the children had been “tossed around like a tennis ball between two sides” by the repatriation dispute.“This situation has traumatised them and will forever leave wounds on their psyche. Providing mental health support to those who returned should be a priority over demographic needs.”* Name changed to protectidentityExplore more on these topicsGlobal developmentUkraine in depthUkraineItalyChildrenEuropeAdoptionFosteringfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The women saving Borneo: battling fire, patriarchy and super El Niño on Indonesia’s peatland frontlines | Indonesia | The Guardian
description: Fire threatens Kalimantan’s rainforests. On the peatland frontlines, a group of local mothers is defending their community
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fire threatens Kalimantan’s rainforests. On the peatland frontlines, a group of local mothers is defending their community
Content: Ratinah, a member of the Power of Mama team, joined the group in 2023.Photograph: Garry Lotulung/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRatinah, a member of the Power of Mama team, joined the group in 2023.Photograph: Garry Lotulung/The GuardianIndonesiaThe women saving Borneo: battling fire, patriarchy and super El Niño on Indonesia’s peatland frontlinesFire threatens Kalimantan’s rainforests. On the peatland frontlines, a group of local mothers is defending their community.Words and Photography: Garry LotulungTue 15 Sep 2026 21.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 02.24 EDTShareIrma puts on her heavy rubber boots as she prepares for a volunteer firefighting shift in her village of Sungai Putri, on the Indonesian side of Borneo island.Dressed in full safety gear she heads into fire zones on her motorbike, the air thick with toxic smoke.The 39-year-old is a member of the Power of Mama, Indonesia’s first-ever all female firefighting team, formed to protect one of the most biodiverse regions on the planet.View image in fullscreenMembers of the Power of Mama team educate local residents at agricultural land while patrolling in Sungai Putri village“Because we are housewives, we are the ones that feel its effects most,” Irma says of what motivated her to join, “I thought I had to do something about it.”The group is made up of 146 women, aged between 20 and 58, from 10 villages in her area of West Kalimantan, in Indonesian Borneo. Formed in 2022 by an NGO called YIARI, the group’s members receive rigorous training, from firefighting to operating surveillance drones, and conducting essential community outreach.An aerial view shows a fire burning in Sungai Putri villageFrom 10am until 4pm the group’s volunteers patrol high-risk areas, recording locations and alerting the Manggala Agni forestry brigade, a specialised brigade under the forestry ministry, when they identify hotspots.They scour plantation and forest boundaries areas, record coordinates, take photographs, and enter the information into the special monitoring app.It’s sometimes gruelling work in tough conditions.View image in fullscreenSuriati (R) and RatinahView image in fullscreenTop: Suriati (R) and Ratinah, members of the Power of Mama team, rest while patrolling the forest. Below: Members of the Power of Mama team restBut members say the hardest part has been convincing people in their community not to “slash and burn,” or illegally clear the land by burning it, a common practice in Indonesia, and a cheap and effective way to clear land for crops such as oil palm.That, and breaking down the village patriarchy.Irma says the group faced criticism from men at first, but now they work hand-in-hand with the community.“The men of the village would tease us: ‘Are women really patrolling?” Irma recalls, “‘Why do women have to patrol? Don’t you have any other duties to perform?’”View image in fullscreenA member of the Power of Mama team shows a map and coordinates of detected fires on a smartphone in Sungai Putri village, Ketapang Regency, West Kalimantan province, Indonesia, 20 August, 2026.“The biggest challenge we face is how the public reacts,” agrees Suriati another Power of Mama member.“Sometimes they think we are showing off. They say, ‘What do mother folk know?’ When we ask them not to burn land carelessly, they can be stubborn. With older people especially, we have to be gentle.”When the team identifies someone clearing land for palm oil, they explain the harmful effects, says Ratinah, who joined the group in 2023.“We say, ‘We’re not stopping you from clearing the land, but could you please control the fire, so it doesn’t spread?’ We help them understand how the smoke can harm their children and families.”Drone footage of a fire in West Kalimantan provinceThis year, the Power of Mama has its work cut out for it.Thousands of hotspots in Kalimantan have so far burned 57,081.33 hectares, according to news outlet Harian Kompas.The worst blazes have occurred on peatland, which are notoriously difficult to extinguish and can burn underground for weeks.“It is very difficult to put out peatland fires since the fire is below the surface,” says YIARI director Karmele Llano Sanchez. “You can’t see the flames, but the burning goes on, and often a light breeze is sufficient to rekindle the fire.”This year also coincides with a“super” El Niño, which could exacerbate the fires.View image in fullscreenMembers of the Power of Mama team patrol the forest on foot to search for undetected fires in Sungai Putri village, Ketapang Regency, West Kalimantan province.Mark Parrington, a senior scientist at Copernicus, the European Union’s Earth observation programme, says the trends this year already points to a bad fire year.“For Indonesia, seasonal fire emissions and regional haze are already higher than normal and we will be keeping a close watch on the situation to understand how the fires and their impact on air quality are changing,” he noted in a recent report.Irma says it hasn’t rained in Sungai Putri since late June, which is adding pressure to an existing water shortage.View image in fullscreenAn aerial view shows a fire burning on peatland and forest in Sungai Putri village.“The small ditches and even the rivers have dried up,” she says, “Which makes it extremely hard for us to put out the fires.”“Our only option is to gather with the locals at the edges of the plantation or the forest to keep a constant watch on the fire’s progress. I am terrified the flames will reach residential areas. It is extremely dangerous.”Erly Marlina, a 46-year-old schoolteacher, says she was inspired to join the Power of Mama after seeing the terrible fires in 2019.View image in fullscreenA motorist drives past a burning palm oil plantation in Sungai Putri village“I joined so that I might have a platform through which to express my love for environmental conservation and could take direct action in the field,” she says.Recalling a night operation from that year, Ely says their team played a crucial role.“Houses were about 100 metres away. We began putting out the fire after Isha evening prayer and brought it under control by 11pm,” she says. “The operation took four to five hours. As volunteers, we stay on guard continuously during the dry season; residents really depend on this team.”View image in fullscreenIt hasn’t rained in Sungai Putri since late June, adding pressure to an existing water shortage.Power of Mama is also making an impact outside Borneo, in 2023 winning the Indonesian Clean Air Championship.“Protecting the forest is one of our main objectives,” says YIARI’s Sanchez. “This isn’t just about putting out fires. It’s about seeing these women become more confident, and taking their rightful, powerful role in society.”
