title: ‘We are prey’: discovery of seven women’s bodies fuels anger over femicide in South Africa | South Africa | The Guardian
description: String of female murder victims found near Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: String of female murder victims found near Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week
Content: A police cordon around a woman’s body found on Tuesday in KwaThema, south-east of OR Tambo airport in Gauteng, South Africa.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenA police cordon around a woman’s body found on Tuesday in KwaThema, south-east of OR Tambo airport in Gauteng, South Africa.Photograph: APSouth Africa‘We are prey’: discovery of seven women’s bodies fuels anger over femicide in South AfricaString of female murder victims found near Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past weekRachel Savagein JohannesburgWed 16 Sep 2026 11.02 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe discovery of the bodies of eight women around Johannesburg’s international airport, including five in the past week, has prompted an outpouring of fear, grief and anger over a lack of progress in tackling femicide.When Elizabeth “Tsontso” Moselakgomo did not return after going for a run on 9 September, her eight-year-old daughter alerted relatives, who contacted police. The 38-year-old’s body was found on Saturday and identified by relatives on Monday. The news of her disappearance had gone viral.Police said in a statement on Saturday that four women’s bodies had been found since 15 July in Kempton Park, across the highway from OR Tambo international airport. All were half-naked and with visible bruising.On Monday and Tuesday, two more bodies were found in the town of Olifantsfontein about 15 miles north of Kempton Park. On Tuesday, police said another woman’s body had been found 25 miles to the south-east, naked and decomposed. The acting police minister, Firoz Cachalia, said on Wednesday that another woman’s body found in Olifantsfontein on 7 September, was being added to the investigation.“In this country we are prey,” Sakane Mokoena posted on Instagram after confirmation of the death of her friend and fellow runner Moselakgomo.Elizabeth Moselakgomo was abducted and killed while out for a run on 9 September.South Africa has one of the highest rates of femicide in the world. Women were killed at a rate of 12.2 per 100,000 people in 2022, nearly six times the global rate, according to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime.For years, women have called on the South African government totake gender-based violence seriously. Afterhundreds of women protestedon the eve of the G20 summit in Johannesburg in November 2025, President Cyril Ramaphosa declared it a national crisis.However, the lack of a concrete plan or action has frustrated campaigners – and women keep being killed.The latest deaths are being investigated by specialist officers, who said on Saturday: “Women in and around Kempton Park are urged not to walk or run alone, particularly in isolated areas. They should avoid secluded spaces, remain vigilant and, where possible, travel or exercise in groups.”South African women responded with anger at the idea that they had to be responsible for their own safety, with many runners noting they already took precautions, such as sharing routes. “We are tired of being told to be vigilant when women are already doing everything possible to stay alive,” said the advocacy groupWomen For Change.“It should not take a missing woman, a desperate family, runners and communities searching, and a case going viral, before an area is searched with this intensity,” the group said.Detectives said on Saturday that they were examining a serial killer angle. However, on Monday, a police spokesperson, Athlenda Mathe,told reporters: “For now, nothing tells us that we’ve got a serial killer.”Mathe added that a suspect in the killing in July of the first woman, her boyfriend, was in custody.Ramaphosa said on Tuesday that he had directed police authorities to prioritise the ongoing murder investigations.Although the gender of the suspect or suspects in the other killings has not been confirmed, campaigners called on men to take responsibility for violence against women and children.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long WaveNesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA protest against femicide in Johannesburg last November. South Africa has one of the highest murder rates for women in the world.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images“When some of these things happen in our presence, most of us men tend to look the other way,” said Bafana Khumalo, a co-executive director of SonkeGenderJustice.“You have excuses like ‘No, it’s not my business’. We feel strongly that violence against women is our business. We need, as men, to begin to face each other squarely and hold each other accountable.”The identification of Moselakgomo’s body has triggered an outpouring of grief.Mokoena met her about two years ago, when Moselakgomo joined a running club so she did not have to train alone on Saturdays.“She’s an amazing woman,” said Mokoena. “She always spoke about her daughter. Tsontso always said ‘Bye guys, I have to go, I have to go to my child’.“That’s just an example of how close she was with her baby girl. And she was a really light-spirited, funny and joyful woman, who was kind – very, very kind.”Running clubs around SouthAfricaorganised events to remember Moselakgomo and Mokoena said she hoped this would help push the government and police to do more to protect women.She added: “I’m just happy that the world, or at least our country, was standing still for a moment to acknowledge what is happening. Let’s get this out there and figure out exactly what is happening to women.”Explore more on these topicsSouth AfricaWomenFemicideAfricaViolence against women and girlsGendernewsShareReuse this content

title: US to bar some South Africans over claims of anti-white discrimination | South Africa | The Guardian
description: Announcement of visa restrictions follows Trump’s false claims of ‘white genocide’ taking place in South Africa
Author: Rachel Savage
Headline: Announcement of visa restrictions follows Trump’s false claims of ‘white genocide’ taking place in South Africa
Content: Afrikaners in Pretoria showing support for Donald Trump after he signed an executive order granting them refugee status in the US in February 2025.Photograph: Kim Ludbrook/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAfrikaners in Pretoria showing support for Donald Trump after he signed an executive order granting them refugee status in the US in February 2025.Photograph: Kim Ludbrook/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockSouth AfricaUS to bar some South Africans over claims of anti-white discriminationAnnouncement of visa restrictions follows Trump’s false claims of ‘white genocide’ taking place in South AfricaRachel Savagein JohannesburgWed 16 Sep 2026 08.35 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 06.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US has announced visa restrictions on some South Africans as Donald Trump’s administration continues to claim that South Africa’s government racially discriminates against white minority Afrikaners.Theannouncementdid not specify individuals who were barred from the US. Trump has spent his second term falsely claiming there is a “white genocide” in South Africa and railing against its affirmative action policies.Since the start of last year, the US has cut aid to South Africa, barred it from this year’s G20 summit in Miami and set up a refugee programme for Afrikaners and other South African racial minorities. Meanwhile, theTrump administrationhas been dismantling refugee and asylum programmes for people fleeing war and persecution.“The South African people are being failed by a government that is destroying its economy through an obsessive pursuit of racial grievance against the Afrikaner minority,” the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio,said in a post on X.“The South African government has consistently failed to adequately address rural crime, violent and dehumanising rhetoric, and race-based discriminatory policies against Afrikaners and other minority populations.”View image in fullscreenMarco Rubio said the restrictions would target those who ‘enact or enable policies that promote race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation’.Photograph: Saul Loeb/ReutersThe US visa restrictions would target “foreign nationals who enact or enable policies that promote race-based discrimination, incite violence, or enable land confiscation without compensation in South Africa”, Rubio added.The US ambassador to South Africa, the conservative media activistLeo Brent Bozell III, saidon X: “As has been made absolutely clear, the time for endless ‘dialogue’ has run its course … This visa restriction policy is only the first step in a series of escalatory measures that will show America’s firm resolve in this matter.”South Africa’s foreign ministry said in response that its policies were being misrepresented. “The announcement, once again, aligns with the mischaracterisation of South Africa’s domestic policies by fringe groups who wrongly portray themselves as representatives of “minorities” and Afrikaners in general,” the ministry spokesperson Chrispin Phirisaid in a statementthat was first published in Afrikaans.Phiri added: “It is our sovereign right to put in place laws that address the nation’s concern over centuries of racial injustice … South Africa respects that the United States may hold different views regarding particular measures and their implementation.”View image in fullscreenAfrikaner farmers in Pretoria demonstrate their support for Donald Trump in February 2025.Photograph: Kim Ludbrook/EPA-EFE/ShutterstockAfrikaners, who are descended from Dutch and French settlers, ruled South Africa during apartheid. The regime discriminated against and repressed the country’s black majority, while keeping white people safe and wealthy.Since Nelson Mandela took office as South Africa’s first black president in 1994, South African governments have tried to redress the country’s racial inequality, including through Black economic empowerment policies and buying land to redistribute.These efforts have had limited impact. White South Africans typically have 20 times the wealth of Black people, according toa 2023 article in the Review of Political Economy, an economic journal.Nonetheless, some white South Africans claim they are now the victims of racial discrimination, allegations that US conservatives have long promoted.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump shows Cyril Ramaphosa articles purporting to show violence against white minority during a meeting in the Oval Office.Photograph: Evan Vucci/APRubio’s visa restrictions announcement criticised land expropriation without compensation. South Africa introduced a law last year that allows the government to seize land without paying for it in specific circumstances, including if it is abandoned or only held for speculation. There is no large-scale expropriation of land.Among white South Africans who think they are discriminated against, many cite the far-left opposition leader Julius Malema’s repeated use of apartheid-era chant “Kill the Boer”, Boer being another word for Afrikaner. A video featuring the chantwas played by Trumpwhen he met South Africa’s president, Cyril Ramaphosa, in the Oval Office last year.The ruling African National Congress party has disavowed the chant, which South African courts have ruled is not meant literally and is therefore not hate speech.Explore more on these topicsSouth AfricaUS immigrationTrump administrationMarco RubioDonald TrumpUS foreign policyAfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Al-Qaida and IS-linked violence in Africa’s Sahel belt set to hit record levels this year | Africa | The Guardian
description: Twenty-five years after 9/11, figures compiled by conflict monitor underline how Sahel region has become centre of Islamist terror
Author: Jason Burke
Headline: Twenty-five years after 9/11, figures compiled by conflict monitor underline how Sahel region has become centre of Islamist terror
Content: Three armed al-Shabaab fighters in Mogadishu, Somalia in 2008 – the al-Qaida-linked group is one of Africa’s deadliest.Photograph: Farah Abdi Warsameh/APView image in fullscreenThree armed al-Shabaab fighters in Mogadishu, Somalia in 2008 – the al-Qaida-linked group is one of Africa’s deadliest.Photograph: Farah Abdi Warsameh/APAfricaAl-Qaida and IS-linked violence in Africa’s Sahel belt set to hit record levels this yearTwenty-five years after 9/11, figures compiled by conflict monitor underline how Sahel region has become centre of Islamist terrorJason BurkeInternational security correspondentWed 16 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIslamist extremist violence in Africa’s Sahel region is set to reach historic highs after a series of sweeping offensives by groups linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State, according to new figures compiled by the conflict monitorAcled.As the US marks the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks launched by al-Qaida against targets in Washington and New York, the statistics underline the continued expansion of the veteran organisation in parts ofAfrica– in stark contrast with its relative weakness elsewhere.Compiled by Acled, which stands for Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, the statistics focus on the centre of Islamic militancy in three countries – Mali,Burkina Fasoand Niger – which together comprise a huge and hotly contested zone at the heart of the strategic Sahel region.According to the respected non-profit organisation, incidents of violence with jihadist groups present in the three countries have soared from 63 in 2016 to 2,845 in 2025. So far this year, 2,145 events have already been logged. If current trends continue in coming months, an annual total of well over 3,000 events appears likely.Sahel violence chartThough total deaths from terrorism globally have fallen to theirlowest level since 2008, those in the Sahel have risen sharply.“Terrorism has become more geographically concentrated: the Sahel continued to record some of the world’s highest terrorism death tolls, with the UN recording more than 9,000 deaths from security incidents across Burkina Faso, Mali andNigerin 2025,” the 2026 report of the Global Peace Index noted earlier this year.View image in fullscreenScreenshot of a video filmed by JNIM fighters in Mansila, Burkina Faso, in 2024.In April, a joint offensive in Mali launched by the al-Qaida-linked groupJama’at Nusrat ul-Islam wa al-Muslimin(JNIM) and the Tuareg-dominated rebel group Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) targeted strategic towns, government forces and theirRussian auxiliarieswith ambushes, car bombs, drones and raids, inflicting significant casualties.Mali’sdefence ministerdied in a suicide attack on his residence in the garrison town of Kati, 9 miles north-west of the capital, Bamako, and the head of military intelligence was killed.Other attacks hit Mali’s international airport, while rebels seized control of the strategic city of Kidal, a former stronghold of the FLA, after soldiers fled and a force of Russian mercenaries surrendered. The defeat reversed a key symbolic victory won by the junta inMalithree years ago.Since then, JNIM has continued to expand areas under its control in Mali, killing more soldiers and Russian mercenaries in recent weeks, and broadening its operations in some neighbouring countries.Much of the violence involves fighting with rival groups. The conflict has also included multiple killings by government armed forces and Russian mercenaries.View image in fullscreenThree Russian mercenaries, on right, in northern Mali.Photograph: French Army/APIn Burkina Faso, JNIM has claimed more than 130 attacks in 2026, striking closer to Ouagadougou, the capital. In Niger, the group claimed at least 17 attacks but remained significantly less active than its rival Islamic State in the Greater Sahara, according to a recentUnited Nationsreport based on intelligence supplied by member states.Experts said JNIM had distanced itself from al-Qaida’s historic objectives of striking the US and its allies.How rampant violence made Nigeria an insecurity hotspot in the Sahel – mappedRead more“In the Sahel,Islamic Stateand al-Qaida now command big areas but these are very localised groups. Not a single attack in Europe or the US has been planned in the Sahel,” said Ulf Laessing, a senior analyst at the Konrad Adenauer foundation in Berlin.The other main group in sub-Saharan Africa with links to al-Qaida is al-Shabaab, which has dominated much of Somalia’s rural areas for many years.“In east Africa, al-Shabaab remains one of the continent’s deadliest groups, with Acled recording more than 10,000 reported deaths in al-Shabaab-related violence over the past 18 months,” said Peter Bofin, Acled’s senior analyst for south-east Africa. “Despite some degradation of its extortion in Mogadishu, its revenue streams stretch across the country, and the region.”Militant groups linked loosely to IS are active in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Mozambique,Chadand Nigeria, where they were targeted byUS airstrikeslast year.The continuing expansion in sub-Saharan Africa has been welcomed in al-Qaida’s propaganda, but experts point out the continent barely featured in the group’s strategic planning until recent years. “Twenty-five years ago it was all about Afghanistan and then Iraq … Africa wasn’t really of interest then. Now its the main area of operations,” said Laessing.View image in fullscreenA Somali police officer at the site of an al-Shabaab attack in Mogadishu in 2023.Photograph: Feisal Omar/ReutersThough sectarian and ethnic conflict, bitter competition over resources, poor governance, endemic instability and other factors make Africa a fertile ground for Islamic militant recruiters, territory in places like Mali and Somalia has major limitations as a base for campaigns elsewhere in the world or for long-range terrorist attacks.At its peak in the years after the 9/11 attacks, al-Qaida affiliates posed a significant threat to authorities across much of the Middle East, with thousands convinced by the group’s call for a global uprising against the US, Israel and local regimes.Al-Qaidawas also able to inspire and direct a series of lethal attacks in Europe that killed hundreds.However, the recent UN report described al-Qaida senior leadership as “marginalised” and noted that the group’s capability and intent to conduct external operations remained “unclear”.Analysts point out there has been no formal declaration of a successor to Ayman al-Zawahiri, the veteran Egyptian militant killed in Kabul by the US in 2022.View image in fullscreenThere has been no declaration of who will succeed Ayman al-Zawahiri, seen here with Osama bin Laden in 2001, as al-Qaida leader since his death in 2022.Photograph: Daily Dawn/ReutersInstead, the de facto leader is believed to be 66-year-oldSaif al-Adel,who is thought to have been in Iran since 2002 and has yet to make any public statement. Other leaders are likely to be based in Afghanistan, where the group has been able to rebuild a limited infrastructure, western intelligence services believe.The most potent al-Qaida affiliate outside Africa is the Yemen-based Al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which the UN report described as “the vanguard of the global al-Qaida movement” and one of the few affiliates committed to continuing al-Qaida’s decades-old campaign against the US.In May, AQAP’s media channels released a new video calling on Muslims in Europe and the US to carry out local attacks and to fight on “behalf of the [Islamic community] in any way possible”.But though AQAP continues to maintain an estimated 2,000 fighters, largely entrenched in the mountains between Abyan and Shabwa,the group’s activity fell by approximately 70%,from 63 events in the first seven months of 2025 to 19 during the same period in 2026, according to Acled.Some analysts have contrasted the high numbers of militants currently mobilised by groups such as JNIM and al-Shabaab, which number in the tens of thousands, with the much more limited manpower available to al-Qaida before the 9/11 attacks. Others stress the very different intentions and capabilities of the group now and 25 years ago.Explore more on these topicsAfricaSahelIslamic StateAl-QaidaSeptember 11 2001MaliBurkina FasonewsShareReuse this content

title: Slave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research finds | Slavery | The Guardian
description: Dozens of Bank of England directors and founding subscribers invested in trafficking of enslaved Africans
Author: David Conn
Headline: Dozens of Bank of England directors and founding subscribers invested in trafficking of enslaved Africans
Content: The scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged.Composite: Guardian/Diana EjaitaView image in fullscreenThe scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged.Composite: Guardian/Diana EjaitaEnslaving nationSlaverySlave-trade wealth was embedded in Britain’s financial system, research findsDozens of Bank of England directors and founding subscribers invested in trafficking of enslaved AfricansDavid ConnInvestigations correspondentWed 16 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTShareTheBank of Englandand the British financial system were for centuries deeply involved in the enslavement and transatlantic trafficking of millions of African people, according to new research on Britain’s slavery history.Research by historians compiling theRegister of British Slave Tradershas found that the scale of the financial system’s involvement in enslavement is greater than previously known or acknowledged. The Bank of England, the central bank owned by the government since nationalisation by Clement Attlee’s Labour administration in 1946, had dozens of financiers involved in its foundation who were also significant investors in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans.Dr Michael Bennett of the University of Sheffield, who has conducted extensive research on the Bank’s historical involvement in enslavement, has found that 24 directors were investors in the trafficking of enslaved African people. Four were among the London elites who were founding directors of the Bank in 1694. The other 20 were in office at Threadneedle Street over the next century.The last, Christopher Puller, was a shipper of weapons for the slave trade and co-owner of a 1786 voyage that trafficked enslaved people from the Gambia to Jamaica, according to the register. Puller was a director for 11 years before he died in 1789. Nine of the 24 were also governors of the Bank.View image in fullscreenWealth generated from the slave trade formed part of the Bank of England’s initial capital, according to Dr Michael Bennett.Photograph: Alexander Spatari/Getty ImagesBennett also researched the founding subscribers to the Bank of England, finding that at least 30 invested in the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. At their head were the king and queen of the day, William III and Mary II, who held shares in the Royal African Company. It is clear, Bennett said, that wealth generated from the slave trade formed part of the Bank’s initial capital.“Slave traders and their wealth were firmly embedded within Britain’s, especially London’s, private banks and financial corporations during the 17th and 18th centuries. They shaped the development of the financial system,” he said. “Banks and other institutions, like insurers, provided the financial services that supported, and made great wealth from, the transatlantic slave economy.“The Bank of England supported this system throughout, and directly provided financial services to the slave trade. Its clients included the Royal African Company and the South Sea Company.”An archetypal example of a Bank of England director in the register is John Rudge,the MP for Evesham. He was a director of the Bank between 1699 and 1740, and governor in 1713-15. Rudge was also a shareholder and assistant (director) in the RAC and deputy governor of the South Sea Company.The findings of the register add to the research carried out by historians behind theLegacies of British Slavery(LBS) archive at University College London, which documents owners of enslaved people on plantations. That research found that 16 past governors of the Bank of England and 26 directors had a financial interest in the ownership of enslaved people and plantations in the period before abolition in 1833. The Bank itself, and the Treasury, were centrally involved in paying out £20m, the equivalent of £23bn today according to one method of calculation, in “compensation” to enslavers under the abolition legislation. Nothing was paid to the people who had been enslaved and trafficked.View image in fullscreenThe Black Lives Matter protests in 2020 prompted several high street banks and financial institutions to acknowledge their historical involvement in slavery.Photograph: pawopa3336/Getty Images/iStockphotoThe Black Lives Matter protests of 2020 prompted several high street banks and financial institutions toacknowledge their historical involvement in slavery. Dr Nicholas Draper, who led the LBS research, was also a lead investigator for the register and he discovered many more historic slave traders who were founders of private banks and other financial organisations.Research by Bennett after the BLM protests found that the Bank of England hadowned 599 enslaved peopleon two plantations.An exhibition at the Bank in 2022 included the names of the enslaved people. Most of the men, women and children listed had European names such as Pierre, Catherine and Alexandre, with no information about the country from which they were taken.The Bank also acknowledged andapologised forpast governors and directors having been involved in the slave trade.Humphry Morice, a longtime director and governor from 1727-29,was also an MPand defrauded the Bank to fund his trafficking operations.Morice was described by Prof Matthew David Mitchell, in an articlepublished on the Bank’s website, as “the biggest London-based trafficker of enslaved human beings from Africa to the British colonies in America.” Morice was responsible for equipping about 110 ship voyages between 1704 and 1732, transporting more than 30,000 enslaved men women and children to Jamaica, Barbados, Virginia and elsewhere in America, Mitchell wrote. “This was his principal commercial activity, and it is for this that he must chiefly be remembered.”While the Bank has acknowledged this history and apologised, the Treasury has not publicly done so. This is in line with the government’s position of resisting the discussion of reparations and not acknowledging culpability for the centuries of trafficking and enslaving.Bennett’s further findings will increase the pressure on the government to do so, which is buildingfrom Caribbean and African countries.A Bank of England spokesperson said it had explored its connections to enslavement in depth in its 2022 exhibition, adding: “We are grateful for Dr Bennett’s collaboration on that work.”In 2023, the Scott Trust, the Guardian’s sole owner, published research showing that the founder of the Manchester Guardian and his backers profited from the enslavement of African people in Jamaica and the US. In response, the Scott Trust launched the Cotton Capital series and the Legacies of Enslavement programme, a 10-year restorative justice initiative.

title: Battle of Chile director Patricio Guzmán dies aged 85 | Movies | The Guardian
description: Passionate documentary maker won international acclaim for unsparing but poetic films exploring the impact of the Pinochet regime in Chile
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Passionate documentary maker won international acclaim for unsparing but poetic films exploring the impact of the Pinochet regime in Chile
Content: Patricio Guzmán (right) filming Nostalgia for the Light.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPatricio Guzmán (right) filming Nostalgia for the Light.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockMoviesBattle of Chile director Patricio Guzmán dies aged 85Passionate documentary maker  won international acclaim for unsparing but poetic films exploring the impact of the Pinochet regime in ChileAndrew PulverWed 16 Sep 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatricio Guzmán, the film-maker who chronicled Chile’s bloody 1970s political strife and its subsequent social and political turmoil in films such as The Battle of Chile and Nostalgia for the Light, has died aged 85.According to Chilean news outlet Emol, Guzmán died on Tuesday in Paris after a cardiorespiratory arrest.Guzmán’s chief preoccupation throughout his career was the carnage unleashed by Augusto Pinochet’s coup in 1973 against Salvador Allende, Chile’s elected president.He later told the Guardian: “I’m a film-maker who was very marked by the ways of the dictator. It has remained with me for ever. I cannot leave it behind.” However, he resisted the idea that he was an activist, political film-maker, adding: “I’m not a sociologist. Neither am I a politician. I make films that are metaphorical and poetic; I interpret reality through my own personal way of looking.”Andy Beckett salutes The Battle of ChileRead moreBorn inChilein 1941, Guzmán initially worked in advertising before studying film, first in Chile and then in Madrid. On his return to Chile, Guzmán responded to the febrile political atmosphere after Allende’s election in 1970, eventually completing the mammoth Battle of Chile documentary that chronicled Pinochet’s ultimately successful attempt to overthrow Allende, resulting in the latter’s suicide. Guzmán did not shrink from the brutality of the period, even including footage shot by camera operator Leonardo Henrichsen as he is shot dead by the soldier he is filming.View image in fullscreenA still from The Battle of Chile.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyGuzmán was helped in the endeavour by French film-maker Chris Marker, who supplied film stock and connections that proved vital to make the film. Guzmán himself was arrested but eventually released, but the film’s cinematographer Jorge Müller was not so lucky – along with his girlfriend Carmen Bueno, he wasarrested, tortured and “disappeared” in 1974.Guzmán completed The Battle of Chile outside the country, releasing each of its three parts – The Insurrection of the Bourgeoisie (1975), The Coup d’État (1976) and Popular Power (1979) – through the rest of the 70s. Described by the Guardian as “an outstandingly photographed example of a newsreel film that captures the drama and volatility of the period”, it has continued to attract acclaim since then. Guzmán revisited the film in the mid-90s with Chile, Obstinate Memory, in which he returned to the country after a quarter-century of exile. In 2001 he completedThe Pinochet Case, after the Chilean former dictator wasarrested in Londonin 1998.Patricio Guzmán, Chile's master of documentary, focuses on the starsRead moreThe director moved on to more metaphysical subjects with a trilogy of films starting in 2010:Nostalgia for the Light,The Pearl ButtonandThe Cordillera of Dreams. They sought to explore Chile’s traumatic past by absorbing the country’s magnificent natural landscapes. His final film,My Imaginary Country, was premiered in 2022 and coveredChile’s dramatic 2019 street protests.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsChileAugusto PinochetAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: People protecting nature and land set up self-defence units amid threat of murder | Indigenous peoples | The Guardian
description: Defenders of forests and rivers killed at rate of one every three days in 2025, with 85% of deaths in Latin America
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Defenders of forests and rivers killed at rate of one every three days in 2025, with 85% of deaths in Latin America
Content: Asháninka Indigenous people dance and sing during an annual celebration recognising the Asháninka territory. In July, Asháninka leaders on the Brazilian border with Peru petitioned the government for help after armed and masked men entered their homes.Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/APView image in fullscreenAsháninka Indigenous people dance and sing during an annual celebration recognising the Asháninka territory. In July, Asháninka leaders on the Brazilian border with Peru petitioned the government for help after armed and masked men entered their homes.Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/APIndigenous peoplesPeople protecting nature and land set up self-defence units amid threat of murderDefenders of forests and rivers killed at rate of one every three days in 2025, with 85% of deaths in Latin AmericaJonathan WattsWed 16 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 01.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNature and land defenders were murdered at the rate of one every three days last year, prompting many communities to set up self-defence units, according to the latest annual death toll by the independent watchdog Global Witness.Organised crime groups or professional killers were implicated in more than a third of the 124 killings of defenders in 2025 as narco-trafficking activities overlapped with intrusions into indigenous territories and environmental crime, such as illegal logging and wildcat gold mining.This was particularly true in Latin America, which accounted for 85% of last year’s deaths of people trying to protect forests, rivers and other ecosystems.Colombia had the highest toll with 39 killings, followed by Brazil with 26 and Honduras with 12. In Asia, the most dangerous country for defenders was thePhilippines, with 12 killings – many during crackdowns by state security forces.View image in fullscreenAsháninka territory in Brazil sits along the winding Amônia River. Many defenders are now exposed to more organised crime with less assistance from the international community.Photograph: Jorge Sáenz/APSince Global Witness began compiling statistics in 2012, the overallglobal tallyis now 2,375 deaths and disappearances – on a par with a small-scale war.On a more positive note, the headline figure has declined over the last two years, from 196 in 2023 and 142 in 2024, though the report authors say this is likely to be an underestimate because data collection is difficult in war zones and authoritarian regimes.Many countries and companies are also carrying out nonlethal attacks on defenders, including criminalisation and online smear campaigns.Many defenders are now exposed to more organised crime with less assistance from the international community, partly as a result of cuts by the Trump administration. “The dismantling of USAID, which previously supported initiatives forIndigenous peoplesto steward their own land, has had particularly serious implications for defenders,” the report says.Almost three-quarters of the killings documented in 2025 were of Indigenous people and small-scale farmers targeted for defending their land. With less outside help, an increasing number of these communities are establishing their own territorial defence mechanisms.The report highlights the example of the Kakataibo Indigenous Guard in the Peruvian Amazon. Six of the community’s leaders have been killed since 2020 amid growing incursions into the forest by criminal groups. Starting in 2022 with a few dozen recruits, the guard now has more than 150 volunteers in its 10 bases.Segundo Ispón, the commander of the organisation, said the self-defence groups provided a global benefit: “Defending our territory is important to us as a community and as a people, and we’re proud to support the climate that we all depend on. In our culture, the work of defending our resources and territory is taught from an early age. But for this next generation coming up, the work is more dangerous than ever.”At least a dozen other communities in Peru have organised self-defence units. Similar bodies have existed for some years inColombiaand Brazil. But it is risky. Last year, seven Indigenous guards were murdered. In at least five of these cases, the killings were linked to organised crime.Many forest communities report the narco-threat is growing closer. In July, Asháninka leaders on the Brazilian border with Perupetitioned the government for helpafter armed and masked men entered their homes, apparently in search of assassination targets.In the Ucayali basin on the other side of the border, Global Witness said there was a 600% increase in coca production between 2019 and 2023. This is pushing gangs to expand smuggling networks, including through the opening of illegal roads and trails through the forest. Corruption further adds to the risks facing forest protectors who stand in their way because many local politicians and police are in the pay of the traffickers.View image in fullscreenAn Indigenous person looks out over Apurímac River valley in Peru. Local leaders, environmental defenders and human rights activists have been threatened after calling for a more effective state presence across affected countries.Photograph: Ernesto Benavides/AFP/Getty ImagesForest communities want help from governments to ease these pressures but there are concerns the opposite may be happening. Under US leadership, many rightwing governments are pursuing military crackdowns on coca growers and drug traffickers, which is pushing narco-gangs further into remote regions and indigenous territories.Ricardo Soberón, a former head of Peru’s anti-narcotics office, said many communities were also affected on the border of Peru and Colombia. “We are in a situation where transnational criminal groups have appropriated the daily life of the Huitoto, Quichua, Bora, Secoya Indigenous people, who live along the Putumayo basin,” he said.Of particular concern, he added, were the threats against local leaders, environmental defenders and human rights activists who call for a more effective state presence. He fears the newly elected rightwing governments in affected countries will make matters worse by militarising the conflict in line with the “America shield” priorities of the Trump administration.Global Witness has urged the authorities to respect and work with nature and land defenders rather than making their role more difficult.Toby Hill, the lead author of the report, said: “Defenders are the world’s eyes and ears on the ground. It’s thanks to them that we know when ecosystems are being destroyed, where forests are being cleared or rivers polluted. We can’t forget the thousands of defenders around the world who are working every day to protect their territories and cultures under increasing pressure.”Explore more on these topicsIndigenous peoplesPeruBrazilOrganised crimeAmericasAmazon rainforestDrugs tradenewsShareReuse this content

title: Michelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for serving dessert topped with ants | South Korea | The Guardian
description: Prosecutors sought jail term for chief executive of Evett after insects not approved for consumption were on menu
Author: Raphael Rashid
Headline: Prosecutors sought jail term for chief executive of Evett after insects not approved for consumption were on menu
Content: Ants are used as an ingredient in the US and Europe, and the restaurant appeared not to have realised they were not permitted in South Korea, the judge said.Photograph: Patrick SeanView image in fullscreenAnts are used as an ingredient in the US and Europe, and the restaurant appeared not to have realised they were not permitted in South Korea, the judge said.Photograph: Patrick SeanSouth KoreaMichelin-starred Seoul restaurant fined for serving dessert topped with antsProsecutors sought jail term for chief executive of Evett after insects not approved for consumption were on menuRaphael Rashidin SeoulWed 16 Sep 2026 05.09 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA South Korean court has fined the operator of one of Seoul’s most celebrated restaurants and its chief executive for serving a dessert topped with ants, an insect not approved for consumption under local food safety law.The operator of Evett, a two-Michelin-star restaurant in the affluent Gangnam district, was fined 10m won (£5,400) and its chief executive 15m won,Newsis reported.Prosecutors had soughta one-year prison term for the chief executive and a 20m won fine for the company.The judge at Seoul’s western district court, Lee Se-chang, said the offence was “by no means light”, citing the length of time the dishes had been sold for, the restaurant’s use of them to promote itself and tests that found heavy metals above permitted levels in the ants.View image in fullscreenProsecutors said the restaurant imported dried ants from the US and Thailand by post and served three to five of them on a sorbet made with sikhye, a sweet Korean rice drink.Photograph: Patrick SeanHe said he had taken into account that the defendants admitted the offence, that the chief executive had no previous criminal record under the food safety law, that the number of ants served appeared lower than prosecutors had calculated and that the restaurant no longer used ants.Ants are used as an ingredient in the US and Europe, and the restaurant appeared not to have realised they were not permitted in South Korea, he said.Both sides have seven days to appeal. The Guardian contacted Evett for comment.Evett was founded by the Australian chef Joseph Lidgerwood, who has appeared on the Netflix cooking competition Culinary Class Wars and is the restaurant’s public face. He was not a defendant and was not charged.Under South Korean food safety law, the legal duties fall on the person registered as operating the business. Ginny Kim, Lidgerwood’s wife, is registered as the company’s chief executive and was named as a defendant, alongside the company that operates the restaurant.Only 10 insect species are approved as food ingredients in South Korea, including grasshoppers, mealworms and silkworm pupae.Businesses wishing to use an unapproved insect must obtain temporary approval from the ministry of food and drug safety, a step the restaurant did not take. Violating the law carries a maximum penalty of five years in prison or a 50m won fine.The ministry launched its investigation after seeing mentions of the ant dishes in blog posts and social media.Prosecutors said the restaurant imported dried ants from the US and Thailand by post from April 2021, and served three to five of them atop a sorbet made with sikhye, a sweet Korean rice drink, until January 2025.View image in fullscreenLawyers said in court that only about 60% of customers accepted the ant topping when it was offered.Photograph: Patrick SeanThey estimated the dessert was served to 12,274 customers, using 49,096 ants, for total revenue of about 120m won.Lawyers disputed that figure in court, arguing that only about 60% of customers accepted the ant topping when it was offered.The restaurant also noted that only a small number of dishes on their 15-course menu included ants, and that restaurants in countries including Denmark, the UK and Australia use ants as an ingredient.Insect-eating is neither new nor unusual in South Korea. Beondegi, steamed silkworm pupae, has been sold from street carts for decades and remains a nostalgic popular snack for children.Explore more on these topicsSouth KoreaFoodRestaurantsAsia PacificFood safetyKorean food and drinknewsShareReuse this content

title: Health officials in turmoil over 11th-hour backflip on aged care algorithm override powers, emails reveal | Aged care | The Guardian
description: Ministers given emergency briefing about changes to algorithm decisions just three days before tool rollout
Author: Melissa Davey
Headline: Ministers given emergency briefing about changes to algorithm decisions just three days before tool rollout
Content: While assessors had been reassured they would be able to override IAT decisions on aged care funding, the way legislation had been drafted did not make this possible.Photograph: Constantinis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWhile assessors had been reassured they would be able to override IAT decisions on aged care funding, the way legislation had been drafted did not make this possible.Photograph: Constantinis/Getty ImagesAged careHealth officials in turmoil over 11th-hour backflip on aged care algorithm override powers, emails revealMinisters given emergency briefing about changes to algorithm decisions just three days before tool rolloutFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastMelissa DaveyMedical editorWed 16 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 17.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSenior health department officials were in turmoil before the rollout of an algorithm to determine funding packages for older Australians, after discovering legislation had been drafted so rigidly that the tool could not legally be overridden by aged care assessors.Emails published under freedom of information (FoI) by the Department ofHealth, Disability and Ageing show that, despite assessors long receiving reassurance from the department that they would have powers to change incorrect algorithm decisions, officials realised at the 11th hour this would violate proposed regulations.It prompted an emergency briefing of the aged care minister, Sam Rae, and health minister,Mark Butler, just three days before the rollout of the algorithm. In an email, they were warned by senior department staff that removing the human override function from the aged care assessment tool for support at home (SaH) packages carried risk.View image in fullscreenThe federal minister for health, Mark Butler.Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAPIn the email sent on 29 October, three days before the 1 November algorithm rollout, the ministers were told: “There is a risk that this late change in messaging to assessment organisations may not filter through to assessor behaviour.“In public statements, including responses to media enquiries, the department has regularly indicated that there will be an ability for assessors to override the … classification algorithm recommendation. In accordance with this position, an override functionality has been built into the relevant systems.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailHowever, the ministers were told the Aged Care Rules 2025 legislation had been drafted in a way that provided “no legal discretion for assessors or assessment delegates to override the recommendation of the algorithm for a SaH classification”.It meant the manual for using the algorithm and the assessment tool it was part of – known as the Integrated Assessment Tool (IAT) – needed to be updated ahead of the rollout to make it clear to assessors that they could not override outcomes.“Assessment organisations (including state and territory governments) or individual assessors may criticise this position as being inconsistent with previous government statements,” the email said.The IAT involves an assessor asking an older person questions about their physical, social and personal circumstances before the algorithm uses this data to determine how much government-funded home support and funding they are eligible to receive.The algorithmic decision cannot be overridden by the assessor even if they believe the older person has been allocated a lower level of support than needed.On 24 October an assistant secretary at the department, Rachel Blackwood, wrote to deputy secretary of aged care Greg Pugh about the legal issues that had come to light around allowing assessors to override the algorithm.Quick GuideContact us about this storyShowThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know.If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods.Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don't already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.SecureDrop, instant messengers, email, telephone and postIf you can safely use the Tor network without being observed or monitored, you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Illustration: Guardian Design / Rich CousinsWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The Aged Care Rules 2025 “have been drafted to provide no discretion for assessors or assessment delegates to do anything other than accept the recommendation of the SaH algorithm,” her email said.Blackwood wrote that the department had “consistently indicated that assessment delegates would have the discretion to use their clinical judgement to override the recommendation of the SaH algorithm”.“It is clear that the inclusion of an override has been regarded by many staff … as a settled position.”She presented a list of solutions and risks, all of which were redacted in the FoI documents. On 26 October, Pugh responded that the solution he had chosen “… may not be your preferred approach”.“However I am comfortable that this decision is the best available in light of all contextual circumstances, including proximity to 1 November and having a clear and workable pathway to address it,” he wrote. “A big thanks for working through this tricky issue and for providing your frank and open advice.”On 27 October, Blackwood wrote to Pugh: “We have been working hard to build credibility with assessment organisations and other stakeholders, and want to avoid doing things that will undermine our working relationship at a critical time.“We have a responsibility to provide guidance to delegates to exercise their powers with integrity, accuracy and honesty,” she wrote.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenGuardian Australia previously reported that people already on support packages who needed reassessment because of increased needs were routinely being recommended for less support by the algorithm.Photograph: The Good Brigade/Getty ImagesIt is unclear why the department chose to remove assessor override from the instruction manual, rather than change the legislation to allow override. The department of health did not respond to requests for comment.Within days of the algorithm rollout, Blackwood was emailing other senior department officials to say complaintswere coming in from distressed assessorsthat the algorithm was routinely under-assessing vulnerable older Australians, leaving them without adequate support.In an email to senior department staff sent on 20 November Blackwood wrote: “The majority of Aged Care Needs Assessment Organisations (including State and Territory Governments) have raised concerns about the inability to override the IAT classification algorithm.”“Assessment organisations have provided details of cases in which assessors believe the algorithm has generated an outcome that does not align with client needs,” she wrote.Dementia patients warned off seeking home care in case Australia’s aged care algorithm cuts fundingRead moreSeparatedocuments released to Guardian Australiaunder FoI show state health officials were keeping logs of hundreds of cases of underassessment,sending these to their federal counterparts.“Approving classifications and assessment outcomes that they [aged care assessors] do not agree with does not align with their professional ethics and they are concerned this has possible legal impacts,” one of those emails, sent on 14 November, said.Guardian Australiapreviously reported that people already on support packageswho needed reassessment because their needs had increased were routinely being recommended for lower support packages by the algorithm.FoI documents also reveal that when the department discovered the tool was under-assessing people despite the government’spublic promises and policy that older Australians would be “no worse off”under the aged care reforms, a workaround was implemented.When an aged care assessor clicked “accept” on the algorithm’s downgraded package recommendation, the portal temporarily kept the client’s old package dollar amount active while quietly logging a lower clinical classification on their permanent record, the documents show.The shadow aged care minister, Anne Ruston, said the Coalition had introduced legislation to restore human decision-making to the assessment process and accused Labor from blocking it.She described it as “a practical, overdue fix that has passed the Senate but remains blocked by Labor from even being debated in the House”.Ruston said while restoring the override was necessary, it was nowhere near sufficient on its own to fix an aged care system she described as “broken”.Do you know more? title: ‘Made in Europe’ law threatens UK plans for reset with EU | European Union | The Guardian
description: Government sources say legislation aimed at China poses a risk to British businesses and must be addressed
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Government sources say legislation aimed at China poses a risk to British businesses and must be addressed
Content: A UK government source said ‘Made in Europe should be on the table’ in reset negotiations with the EU.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAView image in fullscreenA UK government source said ‘Made in Europe should be on the table’ in reset negotiations with the EU.Photograph: Andy Rain/EPAEuropean Union‘Made in Europe’ law threatens UK plans for reset with EUGovernment sources say legislation aimed at China poses a risk to British businesses and must be addressedLisa O’CarrollandJessica ElgotWed 16 Sep 2026 15.39 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK government’s EU reset summit will be delayed again unless the bloc agrees to discuss legislation that could lock British business out of parts of EU industry, government sources have said.The“Made in Europe” legislation– formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act – is designed to curb China’s increasing presence in European industry, but was not onthe reset plan agreed by the former prime minister Keir Starmerand the European Commission chief, Ursula von der Leyen, in London in May 2025.A follow-up summit was due to be held in July this year, but wascancelled after Starmer’s resignation. The government is now looking to change the roadmap, with one source saying that “Made in Europe should be on the agenda”.It is understood that Hamish Falconer, the new cabinet minister with responsibility for the reset, told the EU’s trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, this was the UK’s new priority when the pair met last week.The trade minister, Anas Sarwar, told a gathering of UK business leaders on Tuesday they needed to let their EU partners know the risks posed by Made inEurope, which will prioritise EU suppliers in key industries including car manufacturing and defence.Ministers have privately expressed fears that the reset has lost significant momentum since Andy Burnham became prime minister, with his focus on the domestic agenda. Agreements have yet to be reached on several key issues, includingwhat tuition fees will be paid by EU students coming to the UKon a mooted “youth experience” programme.View image in fullscreenKeir Starmer and Ursula von der Leyen set out plans for a UK-EU reset in London in May 2025.Photograph: Carl Court/PAUK sources say that whilea food and drink dealand a youth mobility scheme are still on the agenda, the government will not agree to a new summit date until the bigger issues of the Industrial Accelerator Act are included in discussions.There was talk in London and Brussels that a meeting could be convened on 6 November, but it is understood this could now be pushed backuntil the end of November or beyond.One government source said: “Weare willing to negotiate on the things that matter to them, but they have to be able to negotiate the thing that matters to us. Made in Europe should be on the table, definitely.”The UK fears the Made in Europe laws could jeopardise billions of pounds worth of trade if British goods are not categorised as European, locking it out of key contracts on the continent.France, which conceived the Made in Europe laws, is pushing to have the legislation passed by the end of the year, deepening fears that British manufacturing could be left behind.It is thought that France is sympathetic to the UK’s position, but believes increasing competition from China makes it more important to get the legislation on the books now, and make allowances for third countries later, a process that could take years.View image in fullscreenA Chinese-made electric bus on the streets of Copenhagen, Denmark.Photograph: Francis Joseph Dean/Dean Pictures/AlamyOne EU diplomat said that there was substantial backing among key member states for the UK to be included in Made in Europe, though not all agreed. “The problem is the benefits are seen as asymmetrical,” the diplomat said. “The UK gets more out of it than the EU.”It is understood the Netherlands, Germany, Poland and Italy are all in favour of the UK’s inclusion, but France remains unconvinced.The government’s newly assertive approach could give the UK some leverage in negotiations over concessions on youth mobility, something that is a political priority for many EU capitals.Another UK source said a deal on Made in Europe would be “a good faith demonstration that we can find answers and almost everything else”.A government spokesperson said: “The UK is a close and trusted European partner, committed to our shared security and economic cooperation.“We will continue to engage with the EU on Made in Europe and work together, as like-minded partners, to boost growth and open up trade.”The UK’s desire for a deal on manufacturing rules comes at time when the EU is under pressure from industry across the bloc to loosen China’s growing presence in supply chains.Last week, manufacturing bosses warned of apotential loss of 300,000 jobs this yearunless incentives were put in place to make European products more attractive than cheaper parts from China.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe EU’s deficit with China is now running at €1bn a day, with fears thatEuropean companies are being cannibalised from within.Fears of new China shock as EU industry’s reliance on imports growsRead moreIn her state of the union address to the European parliament on Wednesday, von der Leyen said the EU needed to grow non-Chinese supplies of rare earths and critical minerals vital to manufacturing.Hersurprise offer of an associate membership deal with Canadademonstrated how far Brussels can go to court third-country partners.Speaking in the presence of the Canadian prime minister,Mark Carney, the EU chief said: “We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. We must urgently reimagine our partnerships.”The EU andCanadaare to hold a summit in late October to develop their future relationship. The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, though it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, enabling deep economic integration with these countries, which follow many EU rules including free movement – a red line for the UK.Carney, who is to address the European parliament on Thursday, has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU, as his country seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade.View image in fullscreenMark Carney and Andy Burnham in Liverpool on Wednesday night.Photograph: John Clifton/Action Images/ReutersBurnham met Carney at a football match in Liverpool on Wednesday night, where the two Everton fans watched their team in theEFL Cup. Burnham is also due to meet the US president, Donald Trump, for the first time at the UN general assembly in New York next week.The potential new alliance between the EU and Canada will worry UK ministers that the bloc’s priorities are shifting. Should Burnham fail to complete a food and drink deal that was already on Starmer’s reset agenda, it could have implications for October’s budget, as the economic effects of easing trade with the EU is priced in as part of growth calculations.The Conservatives criticised the UK-EU reset on Wednesday, saying a future Tory government would build a wholly independent regulatory system.Alex Burghart, the party’s deputy leader, and Victoria Atkins, the shadow environment secretary, warned the plans would make Britain less competitive.Speaking at the Policy Exchange thinktank, Burghart said: “Labour’s EU reset is the worst of both worlds and will leave Britain unable to take advantage of our country’s future growth potential.“The next Conservative government would not be bound by this arrangement and will begin work now on a genuinely independent regulatory system.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionBrexitAndy BurnhamUrsula von der LeyenForeign policyMark CarneyCanadanewsShareReuse this content

title: Is EU’s offer to Canada a blueprint for Britain – or a reminder it is out in the cold? | European Union | The Guardian
description: Ursula von der Leyen has opened door for Canada to become associate member to deepen links in ‘openly hostile world’
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Ursula von der Leyen has opened door for Canada to become associate member to deepen links in ‘openly hostile world’
Content: Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, and Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, in Strasbourg, France.Photograph: Justin Tang/The Canadian Press/APView image in fullscreenCanada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, and Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, in Strasbourg, France.Photograph: Justin Tang/The Canadian Press/APEuropean UnionAnalysisIs EU’s offer to Canada a blueprint for Britain – or a reminder it is out in the cold?Lisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentUrsula von der Leyen has opened door for Canada to become associate member to deepen links in ‘openly hostile world’Wed 16 Sep 2026 14.57 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTShareCanada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, has been advocating closer alignment with “middle powers” since January in the face of recklessness in Washington.But what should worry another middle power, the UK, is that it was Brussels that came up with Wednesday’s big reveal in Strasbourg.To a standing ovation at her State of the Union address, Ursula von der Leyen said she wanted toopen the door to Canada becoming the EU’s first “associate member”in a push to forge new ⁠links among allies in “an openly hostile world”.The European Commission president’s deal could be seen as an “earthquake” offersaid Joël Reland, of UK in a Changing Europe,though it remains “deliciously vague”.But it also sets Canada apart from the UK, which could, once upon a time, have had some sort of associate membership with the EU were it not for the drive for a clean-break Brexit.The last time associate membership of the EU was mooted was in relation to Ukraine as an off-the-books novel way of bringing Kyiv closer to the bloc without become a fully fledged member state.New partnerships, von der Leyen said, were needed “in the cold fragility of today’s world” and in the face of an increasingly assertive China.Just moments earlier she spoke about the need for the EU to diversify urgently its supply of critical raw materials (CRM) and rare earths currently dominated by China, allowing it to follow Japan and stockpile said minerals needed for everything from the car to the defence industries.It is not a new subject – after all the EU has been grappling with China’s export surplus since 2023 and it introduced the Critical Raw Materials Act as far back as 2024.The prospect of an enhanced relationship with Ottawa is one that Keir Starmer might have dreamed of.Canada has something the EU desperately needs – rich supplies of CRM and rare earths – and the EU has something Canada urgently wants: new markets for products it can no longer sell into the EU in the face of a trade war with Donald Trump.Speaking before von der Leyen’s speech, Tobias Cremer, a German social democrat MEP, said a new deeper relationship between the EU and Canada could be a blueprint for other countries, including the UK.Bernd Lange, the influential chair of the European parliament’s international trade committee, said associate membership could “become a model for close transcontinental partnerships with democratic countries against the new model of the law of the strongest”.After Iceland’s rejection of membership of the EU, Fabian Zuleeg, the chief executive and chief economist of the European Policy Centre, suggestedit was time that the EU developed new models, beyond the European Economic Area, that might offer “partial, gradual or associated membership options”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionReland said the vagueness of the offer extended to Canada could be promising for the UK’s hopes for a similar offer.“Any deep Canadian integration into the EU market would take some very heavy work to negotiate a defined set of treaty-bound rights and obligations, and so it seems more likely that – at least in the short term – cooperation will focus on more vaguely constructed alliances for ‘prosperity’ and ‘security’,” which aligns with the UK government’s desires, Relandwrote on Wednesday.In the current political climate in the UK, it is difficult to envisage a world in which Andy Burnham would encourage any associate membership of the EU. He has a steely focus on domestic issues and is keen to avoid going down any Brexit wormholes.The UK is seeking a reset with the EU, but the goals in the first year were modest and have yet to be achieved.The offer to Canada suggests the bigger ambitions for relations with the EU the better.Additional reporting: Jennifer RankinExplore more on these topicsEuropean UnionEuropeCanadaUrsula von der LeyenCritical mineralsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Former French culture minister goes on trial over corruption charges | Rachida Dati | The Guardian
description: Rachida Dati accused of lobbying for carmaker Renault-Nissan when she was member of European parliament
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Rachida Dati accused of lobbying for carmaker Renault-Nissan when she was member of European parliament
Content: Rachida Dati arriving at court in Paris on Wednesday.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersView image in fullscreenRachida Dati arriving at court in Paris on Wednesday.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersRachida DatiFormer French culture minister goes on trial over corruption chargesRachida Dati accused of lobbying for carmaker Renault-Nissan when she was member of European parliamentAngelique Chrisafisin ParisWed 16 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRachida Dati, a former French culture minister, has gone on trial in Paris on corruption charges linked to dealings with the Renault-Nissan carmaking group.Dati, 60, is accused of illegal lobbying when she accepted €900,000 (£770,000) in lawyer’s fees from a Netherlands-based subsidiary of Renault-Nissan while she was a member of the European parliament. The court will have to decide what the money was for.Dati’s legal team denied all corruption allegations, saying she worked “exclusively” as a lawyer for the Renault-Nissan subsidiary. French prosecutors argue that she was instead paid to lobby for the carmaking group, an activity that is banned for members of the European parliament. Prosecutors said there was a lack of evidence to show Dati had carried out legal work.Dati was placed under investigation in 2019 on suspicion of illegally lobbying for Renault-Nissan between October 2009 and February 2013, when she was an MEP.Dati is on trial withCarlos Ghosn, the disgraced former Renault-Nissan chief, who will be tried in absentia. Ghosn, 72, was detained in Japan in November 2018 amid allegations of financial misconduct in a separate case involving a plot to falsify records about his personal pay in order to enrich himself. He dodged trial in Japan after escaping to Lebanonin an audio equipment case. He has denied all wrongdoing in the Japan case as well as in the Dati case.French prosecutors argue that a legal services contract signed in 2009 between Dati and Ghosn, in which Dati was paid an annual fee of €300,000, was used to disguise lobbying work. Investigators obtained the contract in 2019 during a search of Renault’s headquarters after Ghosn’s arrest in Japan.Dati, 60, who is the district mayor of the 7th arrondissement in Paris, is one of the most prominent figures on the French right. She was the first woman of north African and Muslim heritage to hold a major French government post when she was appointed justice minister by the rightwing president Nicolas Sarkozy. She returned to government under Emmanuel Macron, as culture minister.Dati redefined political celebrity in France, and has said growing up as the second of 11 children on a low-income housing estate on the outskirts of Chalon-sur-Saône in Burgundy gave her a greater understanding of the French electorate. Sheran for mayor of Parisearlier this year, but lost to the SocialistEmmanuel Grégoire.If convicted, Dati faces up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to €450,000. She could also face a five-year ban on holding public office.Dati’s lawyers said: “Unfounded allegations of influence peddling in the European parliament stem from an artificial intellectual construct devised by the prosecution.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn a separate investigation, Dati has been accused of accepting nearly €300,000 in undeclared payments from the energy group GDF Suez, also while an MEP. Prosecutors said last year they were looking into reports Dati failed to declare jewellery and watches worth €420,000 upon taking ministerial office.She has denied any wrongdoing in all cases.Explore more on these topicsRachida DatiFranceEuropeRenaultNissanAutomotive industryCarlos GhosnnewsShareReuse this content

title: Sweden voted against more power for the far right – but are centrists listening? | Sweden | The Guardian
description: Even as the ‘extremist’ AfD seeks further election gains in Germany, Europe’s leaders can learn from Sweden’s dangerous embrace with far-right ideology
Author: Katherine Butler
Headline: Even as the ‘extremist’ AfD seeks further election gains in Germany, Europe’s leaders can learn from Sweden’s dangerous embrace with far-right ideology
Content: Social Democrats react to the presentation of an exit poll during the party's election night watch party in Stockholm, Sweden, 13 September 2026.Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/EPAView image in fullscreenSocial Democrats react to the presentation of an exit poll during the party's election night watch party in Stockholm, Sweden, 13 September 2026.Photograph: Jonas Ekstromer/EPAThis Is EuropeSwedenSweden voted against more power for the far right – but are centrists listening?Even as the ‘extremist’ AfD seeks further election gains in Germany, Europe’s leaders can learn from Sweden’s dangerous embrace with far-right ideologyDon’t get This Is Europe delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereKatherine ButlerAssociate editor, EuropeWed 16 Sep 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 18.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEurope’s focus turned nervously to Sweden on Sunday, after an explosive election in Germany justa week earlierplaced a far-right party, officially classed as “extremist”, on the brink of power in a German state for the first time since the Nazi era. A party with neo-Nazi roots has been pulling the government’s strings in Sweden for the last four years. Would the country’s general election put the far right formally in government? Or would enough Swedes opt for a gear change, having seen the Sweden Democrats’ hardline (somewould say poisonous) agenda in action?Votes were still being counted on Wednesday but it was immediately clear that the far-right Sweden Democrats hadsuffered a setback; their first loss of support among voters since entering parliament for the first time 16 years ago. The party slipped from being the country’s second biggest party to its third.The centre-left Social Democrats appear poised for a return to power, although it could take months for their leader, Magdalena Andersson, to form a coalition. Strong results for the left and green parties gave her left bloc a wafer-thin, three-seat majority.Is the far right’s regression, however modest, a turning point? Have Swedes reached the limits of a taboo-busting experiment with populist, nationalist rightwing prescriptions? And is there a message formainstream leaders across Europe, many of whom seem fatalistic about a continent-wide far-right surge? France goes to the polls in April while governments in Italy, Spain and Poland, all face their electorates later next year.The Dutch political scientist Cas Mudde says elections in one country are a poor guide to what will happen in another. Specific local factors in Sweden, including a scandal, may have dented the far right’s support. For Mudde, the scale of the AfD’s win in Saxony Anhalt, however, was “a black day for Europe” – and with far-right ideas gaining ground, he warned mainstream politicians that “today’s key fight is for democracy, rather than for party or power”.This is whereSwedenoffers a cautionary tale. Its political establishment had “fully normalised” the far-right party, Mudde said. “Its nativism is now shared by all the major parties, albeit in lighter form, from the Moderates on the right to the Social Democrats on the left.”But the decline in the far right’s support, for now, he thinks, “at the very least creates space for mainstream parties to focus on issues other than immigration”.Ann-Cathrine Jungar, a professor of political science at Södertörn University in Stockholm, is very sure that the Sweden Democrats are not on the way out. Electoral rankings go up and down, she said, and the party’s influence will endure. More important now is how the mainstream parties respond.“We focus a lot on the extreme and radical right parties, but the key to their influence is what the other parties do. Why have Sweden’s mainstream parties adopted the far right’s policies? The Social Democrats have co-opted their ideas, even though they are counter to the country’s needs. In Sweden, we need competent, talented people who want to come and live here, we need labour for health and social care. Yet nationalism seems to be the prevailing ideology now.”In a widely readGuardian essayheadlined How Sweden lost its soul – and stopped being Sweden, published before the vote, Martin Gelin documented his country’s transformation after 2022. Rightwing parties that year signed a Faustian pact with the Sweden Democrats, buying its support for a minority rightwing government. The deal? The far right party was given a direct hand in shaping policy. “A new Sweden has emerged, cruel and cold for migrants”, wrote Gelin, with xenophobic and ethno-nationalist ideas “now comfortably embedded in the political mainstream”.Most shockingly, Andersson’s Social Democrats, modelling themselves on their hardline Danish counterparts, had bought into the far right’s framings on crime and immigration.Will Sweden’s Social Democrats now learn from their worst performance in more than 100 years, and embrace an agenda that does not involve deporting toddlers to Iran,people with dementia to the UK, or locking up 14-year-olds?Jungar is sceptical. “When it comes to linking crime and immigration, this is the new normal,” she said. “The Social Democrats will not pursue policies that are more liberal.”Yet the political centre in Sweden could articulate a clear alternative to the far right, Mudde says. The Left and the Greens did significantly better among young voters in this week’s election. “This reflects a development we see acrossEurope, namely that young people prefer outspokenly leftwing parties over centre-left parties.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGhosts of grievanceView image in fullscreenUlrich Siegmund (centre), head of the AfD state parliamentary group in Saxony-Anhalt, celebrates his party’s election win with parliamentary leaders Alice Weidel (left) and Tino Chrupalla (right).Photograph: Michael Kappeler/DPA/APLike Giorgia Meloni’s party, Brothers of Italy, and Marine Le Pen’s National Rally in France, the Sweden Democrats have “deradicalised” in selective ways, to broaden their appeal, Jungar told me.By contrast, what was striking in Germany, was how the AfD doubled its score to 44% of the vote, on what Constanze Stelzenmullerin the FTcalled “a programme of stunning malevolence”.Two further regional elections this Sunday in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania will be closely watched, including by the AfD’s American boosterssuch as Elon Musk. Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania has economic and demographic conditions comparable to Saxony Anhalt.For those struggling to understand the appeal of the AfD in eastern Germany, Carolin Würfel’s essayoffered an original insight. Born in the former East Germany, Würfel believes that many voters there don’t actually know or care about the AfD’s detailed policies. But the party had tapped into a legacy of grievance about the economic impact of reunification in the 1990s. “Villages and small towns that had been hollowed out, some of them ghostly and depopulated, were suddenly told again: you matter. Everyone else may have left you behind, but I, we, the AfD, care.” The AfD won’t improve life in east Germany, Würfel wrote, “but that was never the point”.As in Sweden, thepolitical centre in Germanyis now being warned that time is running out to offer a credible democratic alternative to the far right.
