As Florian Ranft of the Das Progressive Zentrum thinktankwrote: “Waiting for the AfD to fail is not a strategy.”To receive the complete version of This Is Europe in your inbox every Wednesday,please subscribe here.Explore more on these topicsSwedenThis Is EuropeEuropenewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Key House Democrat refuses to clear Trump’s $2.8bn arms sale to Israel | US foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Pro-Israel Gregory Meeks raises concerns over threat to civilian lives from package of 40,000 one-ton bombs
Author: Joseph Gedeon
Headline: Pro-Israel Gregory Meeks raises concerns over threat to civilian lives from package of 40,000 one-ton bombs
Content: Gregory Meeks at a rally on the 63rd anniversary of the March on Washington in August.Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenGregory Meeks at a rally on the 63rd anniversary of the March on Washington in August.Photograph: Bonnie Cash/UPI/ShutterstockUS foreign policyKey House Democrat refuses to clear Trump’s $2.8bn arms sale to IsraelPro-Israel Gregory Meeks raises concerns over threat to civilian lives from package of 40,000 one-ton bombs‘An antidote to Trumpism’: Our politics team answered your questions on Democrats’ midterms hopesJoseph Gedeonin WashingtonWed 16 Sep 2026 16.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee has thrown up a roadblock to one of thelargest US arms transfersof Trump’s second term, refusing to clear a $2.8bn sale of 2,000lb bombs to Israel.Gregory Meeks announced the hold on Tuesday on a package of 40,000 of the bombs, among the most destructive conventional munitions in the US arsenal.“TheTrump administrationhas not provided sufficient assurances that these weapons will be used by the Netanyahu government in accordance with US law and with appropriate protections for civilians,” he said. “I therefore will not clear this sale at this time.”The deal, funded through US Foreign Military Financing, covers 20,000 MK-84 bombs, 20,000 BLU-117 bombs and 20,000 I-2000 penetrator warheads.Meeks cannot single-handedly veto the $2.8bn arms transfer, but his leverage comes from the informal custom of “tiered review”. Under this practice, the state department submits major weapons packages to top foreign affairs lawmakers for an informal sign-off before triggering a formal notification to Congress. Killing the sale outright would need a veto-proof joint resolution of disapproval in both chambers, a bar Congress has not cleared. A similar push by Senator Bernie Sanders failed along party lines in April.In 2025, the secretary of state, Marco Rubio,declared a national security emergencyto bypass congressional review and fast-track nearly $3bn in weapons, including more than 35,000 heavy bombs and 4,000 bunker-buster warheads. With a separate $6.67bn package in January, the administration has now cleared or expedited over $12bn in arms for Israel since Trump took office. Meeks has said the pace has outrun oversight, accusing officials of skipping briefings and rushing sales while raising alarms over Israeli conduct in the occupied West Bank and Lebanon.The hold also lands amid longstanding accusations that Israel has used American weapons unlawfully. The Leahy laws bar US assistance to foreign military units credibly linked to extrajudicial killings and serious abuse; the state department in 2024 flaggedat least five Israeli unitson those grounds before the war in Gaza even began, including one battalion tied to the death of a Palestinian American at a West Bank checkpoint.The Geneva conventions, meanwhile, bar arming a party where there is a clear risk of war crimes – a standard a UN commission of inquiry cited last year in finding Israel’s Gaza campaign amounted to genocide and calling on the US and other states to halt weapons transfers. In 2024, Bidenadministration lawyers, including some at the state department, had concluded it was reasonable to assess that Israel had violated international humanitarian law and Leahy laws by using American weapons in Gaza, even as the administration publicly avoided making that determination.Meeks, long known for his strong pro-Israel views, emphasized that the hold was not a break with the country itself.“This decision does not diminish congressional support for Israel’s legitimate defense needs,” he said. “It reflects Congress’s responsibility to ensure that US-funded weapons are used lawfully, responsibly and with meaningful safeguards for human life.”The state department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Explore more on these topicsUS foreign policyDemocratsTrump administrationIsraelUS politicsMiddle East and north AfricaUS militarynewsShareReuse this content

title: More Republicans are turning on Iran war as midterms come into view | Republicans | The Guardian
description: Three more GOP members voted for war powers resolution to force withdrawal from the conflict as election looms
Author: Chris Stein
Headline: Three more GOP members voted for war powers resolution to force withdrawal from the conflict as election looms
Content: Heavy structural damage at a destroyed residential building on Qeshm Island, Hormozgan province, Iran, on 11 September 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenHeavy structural damage at a destroyed residential building on Qeshm Island, Hormozgan province, Iran, on 11 September 2026.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesRepublicansAnalysisMore Republicans are turning on Iran war as midterms come into viewChris SteinThree more GOP members voted for war powers resolution to force withdrawal from the conflict as election loomsUS politics live – latest updatesWed 16 Sep 2026 13.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 14.21 EDTShareAs theUS war with Irandrags on, the ranks ofRepublicanssignaling the conflict is a liability for their party continues to grow.When theHouse of Representativeson Tuesday evening considered its sixth war powers resolution intended to force Donald Trump to withdraw troops from the conflict, three Republicans who had not supported the previous efforts broke with their party to vote this one to passage. Earlier that day, a Republican who had lost his primary after repeatedly clashing with Trumpproposed impeachingthe US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, alleging a variety of constitutional transgressions including prosecuting the war against Iran without congressional authorization.House speaker sending lawmakers home early ahead of US midterm election recessRead moreThe rebellions in the GOP are thus far mostly symbolic – Trump has ignored the sole war powers resolution to make it through both the House and Senate, and the prospects of Hegseth’s impeachment are unclear. But they underscore the growing nerves among both the party’s most vulnerable and most disobedient lawmakers over continuing a conflict that appears to have accomplished little other than play into the hands of Democrats, who have spent the entirety of Trump’s second termarguingthat only they can be trusted to lower costs for Americans.“I said it in March: the mission had to stay focused and limited, because Americans do not want another forever war. I will not vote to keep our soldiers in an open-ended war, with Iowans paying too much at the pump,” said the congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks, one of the trio ofRepublicanswho for the first time supported a war powers resolution.She was joined by another Iowa Republican, Zach Nunn, who justified his vote by noting his state “has already paid a devastating price” in the conflict, with two Iowans among the US soldiers killed by Iranian attacks as the war began.“Congress owes them, their families, and every American in uniform clear objectives and constitutional oversight. With the negotiating window closed, sustained combat operations now require congressional authorization,” the congressman said.“Having deployed multiple times and flown over 700 combat hours in the Middle East, I will not support another open-ended war. We can defend Americans, pressure Iran and pursue peace while ensuring Congress fulfills its constitutional responsibility.”Since the US joined Israel in attacking Iran at the end of February, Democrats have wielded war powers resolutions as a cudgel to get Republicans on the record about a conflict that polls indicate isnot popularwith the public. Their first three attempts failed, but in June, the fourthpassedwith the votes of two libertarian-minded Republicans – Thomas Massie of Kentucky and Warren Davidson of Ohio – along with Tom Barrett of Michigan and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, both of whom occupy battlefield districts.The Senate laterapprovedthat measure, but Trump refused to abide by it. In July, the same lineup in the Housepasseda fifth war powers resolution, before Nunn, Miller-Meeks and Nancy Mace of South Carolina expanded the ranks of Republican objectors to seven in Tuesday’s vote.The two Iowans are among the Republicans considered most at risk of losing re-election in the November midterms, with Miller-Meeks having won her race two years ago by fewer than 800 votes. They also represent areas of a state where the market impacts of the war with Iran are pronounced, as Iowa farmersstrugglewith higher prices for diesel, gasoline and fertilizer, all of which have been compounded byTrump’s tariff regime.Iowa has drifted consistently to the right over the past decade, but this year, Democrats believe thecircumstances are rightfor them to oust not just Miller-Meeks and Nunn, but also to win a Senate seat, the governor’s mansion and potentially more congressional districts in the state.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt’s far from the only state where Democrats are on the offensive. The House vote took place on the same day the New York Times and Siena University releasedpollingthat showed likely voters preferred Democrats over Republicans for Congress by nearly nine percentage point, a finding that lines up withother surveys.Democrats are helped in their quest to retake the House by the fact that Republicans control it with a tiny majority that may be exceedingly hard to defend in November, and has also enabled Republicans like Massie to seize on splits within the party to embarrass Trump and his ally the House speaker, Mike Johnson.Last year, Massie banded together with Democrats and a handful of Republican dissidents to force passage of a bill requiring the release of files related to the disgraced financier and former Trump associate Jeffrey Epstein.That intensified the president’s ire towards him, and Massie lost his primary to the Trump-endorsed Republican Ed Gallrein earlier this year. Now with even less to lose, the congressman appears to be trying to seize on splits within the House GOP to retaliate against Hegseth, who campaigned for Gallrein.Massie proposed the resolution on Tuesday, and House rules appear to require it be voted on by Thursday. The chamber was scheduled to be in session that day for the last time before the 3 November midterm elections, but on Wednesday morning, House Republican leaders canceled votes scheduled for Thursday, sending lawmakers home early to face their constituents.Explore more on these topicsRepublicansUS midterm elections 2026US-Israel war on IranHouse of RepresentativesUS SenateUS CongressUS militaryanalysisShareReuse this content

title: At least 21 killed after Israeli-hit building in Gaza City collapses | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Rescue workers say search for dozens of people hampered by lack of heavy machinery
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: Rescue workers say search for dozens of people hampered by lack of heavy machinery
Content: A search operation taking place in the rubble of the collapsed multistorey building in Gaza City.Photograph: Saeed MMT Jaras/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA search operation taking place in the rubble of the collapsed multistorey building in Gaza City.Photograph: Saeed MMT Jaras/Anadolu/Getty ImagesGazaAt least 21 killed after Israeli-hit building in Gaza City collapsesRescue workers say search for dozens of people hampered by lack of heavy machineryLorenzo Tondoin Jerusalem,Seham Tanteshin Gaza and agenciesWed 16 Sep 2026 12.36 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 06.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA building housing about 100 displaced Palestinian families has collapsed inGazaCity, killing at least 21 people in their sleep, including 11 children, forcing rescuers to dig through the rubble with their bare hands as they search for dozens of people believed to be trapped.A rescue team from Gaza’s civil defence said they had recovered the bodies of five children among the victims, while 25 injured people were taken to hospital. Medical sources said rescuers could hear the voices of people trapped beneath the rubble as they tried to reach them.The bombed-out multistorey building, which contained four apartments on each floor, had previously been hit by Israeli strikes during the war, leaving its structure badly weakened and at risk of collapse. When it gave way on Wednesday, it fell on to tents beside it housing displaced families, witnesses said.1:31Emergency crews rush to free families from building collapse in Gaza – videoThe collapse highlights the continuing danger facing tens of thousands of Palestinians living in an estimated 2,000 buildings damaged by Israeli airstrikes across Gaza.Mohammed Abu Dan, a superviser with the civil defence team recovering victims, said more than 10 families had been living in the building and displaced people had been forced to stay there because no other shelter was available.“Search and rescue operations are being carried out under extremely difficult conditions due to a lack of the necessary equipment and resources,” he said.View image in fullscreenRescue workers remove the body of a victim from the collapsed building in south-western Gaza City.Photograph: Hamza ZH Qraiqea/Anadolu/Getty ImagesPalestinian and UN officials have blamed Israeli restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery in the territory. Israel says its restrictions are intended to prevent equipment from reaching militant groups.US set to deliver 2,000lb bombs to Israel as part of vast arms dealRead moreA video obtained by Reuters showed rescue workers trying to pull two people from beneath a collapsed wall. Another video circulating on social media showed Gaza’s civil defence spokesperson, Mahmoud Basal, carrying a young girl wrapped in a bloodstained scarf.Raed al-Dahshan, the director of Gaza City’s civil defence service, said: “We are still hearing voices from under the rubble, so there is still hope to find people.”Alessandro Mrakic, the head of the UN Development Programme’s Gaza office, said rescuers from UN agencies were taking part in the operation, which he described as extremely difficult because of the lack of appropriate machinery. Egypt’s relief agency was also involved.“There are actually people that are digging with their bare hands. We need to prepare [for more deaths],” Mrakic said.Tents belonging to displaced families had been erected along the road beside the building because there was nowhere else for them to shelter.View image in fullscreenThe search for survivors and the dead in the rubble continued on Wednesday.Photograph: Hamza ZH Qraiqea/Anadolu/Getty ImagesSimilar incidents have occurred repeatedly over the past two years, with dozens of homes and buildings damaged during the war later collapsing, trapping people and causing further deaths and injuries.With few other options, many Palestinians have returned to partly destroyed homes or moved into abandoned buildings, clearing small spaces among the rubble despite the danger. Soaring rents and the cost of vacant land have made finding safer accommodation increasingly difficult.Hundreds of thousands of displaced Palestinians also remain unable to return to neighbourhoods near theso-called yellow line, forcing families to find whatever space they can elsewhere. In May, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu,ordered the military to seize 70% of Gaza.Damaged roofs, walls and supporting columns can collapse without warning, particularly during strong winds, heavy rain or further bombardment. Asked whether they feared for themselves and their children, people living there said: “Yes, we are afraid, but where can we go? This is better than staying out on the street.”Israeli strikes on Gaza have continued despite the ceasefire. According to Gaza’s health ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025.This year, an independent UN inquiry found Israel had continued to commit genocide bydeliberately targeting Palestinian childrenin Gaza.View image in fullscreenCivil defence and municipal teams conduct search and rescue operations.Photograph: Saeed MMT Jaras/Anadolu/Getty ImagesSeparately, a video from the Sheikh Radwan neighbourhood of Gaza City showed the aftermath of an Israeli drone strike that killed Mohammed al-Zinati, 15, and wounded several other people. Al-Zinati had been trying to recover the body of a man killed in an earlier strike.Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said on Wednesday that it was only a matter of time before Israel resumed full-scale war in Gaza and moved to force out its Palestinian population.Katz, responding to criticism from another rightwing politician before the 27 October elections, said 70% of Gaza had already been emptied of its population during Israel’s offensive launched after the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023 that killed more than 1,200 people, the deadliest attack against Israel, according to official Israeli figures.He added that the Israel Defense Forces were prepared “to finish the job so that we can also implement the migration plan”.Since the war began, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the health ministry.Explore more on these topicsGazaIsrael-Gaza warPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahuInternally displaced peopleIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: US opts not to back Saudi Arabia in Yemen after meeting Houthi leaders | Yemen | The Guardian
description: Iran-backed militants have offered Trump administration assurances over safety of Red Sea shipping
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Iran-backed militants have offered Trump administration assurances over safety of Red Sea shipping
Content: Houthi fighters participate in an offensive near the port city of Mokha, Yemen.Photograph: EPAView image in fullscreenHouthi fighters participate in an offensive near the port city of Mokha, Yemen.Photograph: EPAYemenUS opts not to back Saudi Arabia in Yemen after meeting Houthi leadersIran-backed militants have offered Trump administration assurances over safety of Red Sea shippingPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorWed 16 Sep 2026 10.56 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOfficials from the US met Houthi leaders over the weekend at the country’s embassy in Muscat, Oman, it has been confirmed, leading to the US decision not to intervene to help Saudi Arabia drive back aHouthi advance inside Yemen.The Iran-backed militant group reassured the US that theceasefire agreement between the two sidesstruck in 2025 still held and the movement had no intention of attacking US shipping in the Red Sea. Only Saudi-linked shipping was regarded as a target owing to its blockade of Yemen, the Houthis confirmed.The meeting helps to explain Donald Trump’s decision to condemn the Houthi advance down the west coast of Yemen for threatening freedom of navigation through the Bab al-Mandab strait, but so far to reject any military response in support of Riyadh. The US is already embroiled in anexpensive and resource sapping conflict with Iran, which backs the Houthis.The US labelled the Houthis as a foreign terrorist entity in March 2025, but in the recent past American officials have met leaders from Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. The US vice-president,JD Vance, confirmed on Monday that the US was in direct contact with the Houthis.The US refusal to become directly involved has put pressure onSaudi Arabiato reach either a diplomatic solution with the Houthis over the future governance of Yemen, or to try to build a regional alliance with Pakistan and Turkey to force the Houthis back. In a lightning offensive last week, the Houthis seized control of large swathes of western Yemen along the Red Sea coast.Map of Yemen showing Houthi military developmentsA former deputy US ambassador to Yemen, Nabeel Khoury, said a “kind of tacit understanding” had been struck between theTrump administrationand the Houthis. Khoury added: “The Houthis are promising the American administration that American and international navigation will not be affected in the Red Sea, but the only danger is to Saudi ships or those carrying Saudi oil.”In an attempt to build popular support against the Houthis in the region, Riyadh made the disputed claim that theHouthis had fired a drone at the holy city of Meccaon Tuesday, but the missile had been destroyed by Saudi defence forces. It said the drone was entering a prohibited airspace close to Mecca’s most holy shrines. The drone was intercepted at about 6.50pm local time on Tuesday, according to coalition spokesperson Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki.Saudi Arabia said any attack on Mecca was a red line and the move was condemned in lengthy statements by the UN-recognisedYemengovernment based in Aden as well as the 57-country Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. The Pakistani prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, condemned what he described as a “dastardly and heinous” attempted attack on Mecca. “The people of Pakistan are saddened and perturbed by this outrageous act,” he said in a statement posted on X.The Houthi leadership – followers of a Shia Zaydism that respects the pilgrimage to Mecca – dismissed the claim as the lie of the century, and said such worn-out lies had been used before and fooled no one.The Houthi’s deputy foreign minister, Abdul Wahid abu Ras, said “whoever opened the land of the two holy mosques to debauchery and entertainment parties, and whoever defiled the land of the two holy mosques by the presence of Zionist Jews in it, is the one who targets Mecca, Medina and the Islamic holy sites”.TheHouthiscountered that they had shot down a Saudi F-15 plane close to Marib, and attacked an Aramco plant in the Red Sea port city of Yanbu. No supporting evidence was provided by the Houthi military spokesperson, but the head of the Houthi negotiating team, Mohammed abdul Salam, said the downing of the plane was a warning to the west not to fall victim to Saudi propaganda.Mohammed al-Farah, a Houthi political bureau member, said: “The truth is that Saudi Arabia is experiencing a real predicament in Yemen. It became embroiled in a war, a siege and an occupation, and then failed to achieve its goals.“Today, it is looking for external solutions, so it is begging the international community, warning the world about Bab al-Mandab and requesting support from Pakistan, Turkey, America, Israel and Egypt. Then it is trying to mobilise Muslims with a false pretext called ‘targeting Mecca’.”Separately, Israeli officials have leaked details of a secret meeting between military commanders from the US, Israel and several Arab states in Germany last week to discuss the war launched by Israel and the US againstIran. The report from the Axios journalist Barak Ravid said the “private retreat” was organised by the head of US Central Command, Adm Brad Cooper.Citing two unnamed Israeli officials, Ravid reported that the meeting was attended by the military chiefs of staff of Israel, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan and Egypt. It was the first such gathering since theUS and Israel went to war with Iran more than six months ago. Israel, once a target for the Houthis, is offering to intervene in Yemen on Saudi Arabia’s behalf.Iranian security forces coordinated killing, torture and sexual abuse of protesters, says AmnestyRead moreA meeting of the UN security council on Tuesday condemned any attempt to close the Red Sea, but the meeting was notable for the Russian envoy beginning to edge away from its previous stance that the UN-recognised government based in Aden was the only legitimate government inside the country.In Beijing, the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, on Wednesday met his Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, in an effort to secure support for its plans for the future administration of the strait of Hormuz. The strait remains closed owing to separate Iranian and US blockades.A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said China did not want to see further regional tension spill over into Yemen and the Red Sea. The Chinese called on the US to return to the talks based on thememorandum of understanding agreed between the two sides in June. Beijing, the main importer of Iranian oil, is eager for a settlement and is resisting any suggestion that US secondary sanctions applied to countries trading with Iran should apply to its own country.Oil prices remain well over $100 (£74) a barrel and a keySaudi east-west pipeline remains closedbecause of a bombing incident.Explore more on these topicsYemenMiddle East and north AfricaHouthisUS-Israel war on IranSaudi ArabiaUS foreign policyIrannewsShareReuse this content

title: Iranian security forces coordinated killing, torture and sexual abuse of protesters, says Amnesty | Global development | The Guardian
description: Leaked documents and testimony reveal extent of regime’s crackdown in 2022 and how it paved the way for more brutal killings of protesters this year
Author: Deepa Parent
Headline: Leaked documents and testimony reveal extent of regime’s crackdown in 2022 and how it paved the way for more brutal killings of protesters this year
Content: A young woman in Bukan, Iran, without a hijab during nationwide protests, September 2022.View image in fullscreenA young woman in Bukan, Iran, without a hijab during nationwide protests, September 2022.Rights and freedomGlobal developmentIranian security forces coordinated killing, torture and sexual abuse of protesters, says AmnestyLeaked documents and testimony reveal extent of regime’s crackdown in 2022 and how it paved the way for more brutal killings of protesters this yearSupported byAbout this contentDeepa ParentWed 16 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIranian security forces “coordinated” the killing, torture and sexual abuse of hundreds of people who took part in the women-led nationwide protests in September 2022, according to leaked state documents and interviews.Tens of thousands of people, including children,took to the streets of towns and cities across Iranafter the death in custody of Mahsa Amini, a 22-year-old Kurdish woman, after her arrest by the “morality” police for allegedly not complying with the country’s hijab regulations.In response, the Iranian state instigated a brutal crackdown. Official statements and leaked documents cited by Amnesty reveal instructions for a “firm and severe” response. One leaked order instructed forces to “respond mercilessly and go as far as causing death”.The rights group has now investigated and verified the deaths of 377 protesters and bystanders, including 56 children. It also documented the cases of 16 people who were reportedly subjected to rape while arbitrarily detained in connection with the uprising, who included six women, seven men, a 14-year-old girl and two boys aged 16 and 17.TheAmnesty reportsaid: “State agents penetrated women and girls vaginally, anally and orally, while men and boys were penetrated anally. Victims were penetrated with wooden and metal batons, glass bottles, hosepipes and/or the sexual organs and fingers of agents.”The harrowing findings echo testimonies gathered by the Guardian during and after the crackdown. In aGuardian report from December 2022medics said security forces were shooting female protesters in the faces, breasts and genitals, and warned that the severity of the injuries could leave hundreds of young Iranians with permanent damage.View image in fullscreenAn X-ray of a woman shot in the crotch during Iran protests in 2022, with about 200 metal balls embedded in her upper thigh and pelvic area.Photograph: suppliedIn testimony published in 2023,a 25-year-old protester told the Guardianshe had been blindfolded and sexually assaulted during interrogation by security agents. Similar testimonies involving sexual assault and torture were reported by people interviewedfollowing the anti-regime protests that took place in January 2026.Amnesty’s report says years of impunity for the violent crackdown paved the way for the even more brutal crackdown on the nationwide anti-government protests in January 2026, which culminated in thedeaths of thousands of protestersover 48 hours on 8 and 9 January.Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s secretary general, said: “This investigation exposes the layers of command and coordination behind the Iranian authorities’ deadly protest crackdowns. The agents on the streets operated within a hierarchical and coordinated chain of command linking them to officials who directed, enabled, facilitated and supported crimes committed on a massive scale.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAmnesty identified 87 Iranian officials, including the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, and Mohammad Bagheri, the former chief of the general staff of the armed forces, killed in an airstrike in June 2025, who it said should be investigated for “crimes against humanity”.Amnesty also named the then minister of interior, Ahmad Vahidi, who has since become the general commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and the then deputy minister of interior for police and security, Majid Mirahmadi.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentRights and freedomIranMiddle East and north AfricaProtestHuman rightsAmnesty InternationalArab and Middle East unrestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Climate crisis likely behind devastating Nepal-Tibet floods that killed more than 1,300, first study finds | Climate science | The Guardian
description: Scientists say global heating was a destabilising factor in collapse of 200,000 sq metre glacier in August
Author: Damien Gayle
Headline: Scientists say global heating was a destabilising factor in collapse of 200,000 sq metre glacier in August
Content: Devighat Bazaar, a Nepalese town devastated by last month’s flash flooding.Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAPView image in fullscreenDevighat Bazaar, a Nepalese town devastated by last month’s flash flooding.Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAPClimate scienceClimate crisis likely behind devastating Nepal-Tibet floods that killed more than 1,300, first study findsScientists say global heating was a destabilising factor in collapse of 200,000 sq metre glacier in AugustDamien GayleWed 16 Sep 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClimate breakdown probably weakened the glacier that collapsed causing catastrophic floods and killing hundreds of people in Nepal andTibetlast month, the first scientific study of the disaster has found.Researchers identified unusually warm conditions beforethe glacier’s collapse, which sent an avalanche of 110m cubic metres (3,885 cu ft) of snow and ice into the valley below. This triggered flash floods on an almost unprecedented scale,hitting communities downstreamwithout warning.How the deadly Nepal and Tibet flash flood unfolded – a visual guideRead more“Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,” said Dr Friederike Otto, a climate science professor atImperial College London, which carried out the study.“When warming destabilises the roof of the world, no amount of local adaptation can fully shield vulnerable people downstream from this scale of destruction. Without much faster action to transition to zero fossil fuel emissions we will inevitably see more disasters of this scale occurring in the years to come.”View image in fullscreenA impromptu memorial in Kathmandu commemorates some of the people killed in the flooding.Photograph: Narendra Shrestha/EPAMore than 1,300 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing after a massive section of overhanging glacier and rock measuring roughly 200,000 sq metres (2,153,000 sq ft) fell from Langtang Lirung mountain on 26 August.It dropped about 1,400 metres (4,660ft), slamming into the valley floor with such intensity that it registered as an earthquake, liquidising ice and sparking a freezing flood that careened downriver at speeds exceeding 110 mph.The devastating flood of water, ice, rock and sediment swept away families, homes, settlements, roads, bridges and other infrastructure, leaving survivors stranded and cut off.“Rock avalanches of this size are rare, with annual frequency estimates of approximately one event this size every 1,000–10,000 years,” the study said. “This event shows that limits to adaptation are already being reached.”The research was unlike previous studies by Otto and her team at World Weather Attribution (WWA) – a collaborative project between Imperial and other climate specialists worldwide – in that the role of climate breakdown could not be ascribed to one particular weather event.Instead, the researchers found the disaster was the result of a compound crisis, with a number of factors made worse by decades of atmospheric heating as a result of greenhouse gas pollution.Dr Ben Clarke, who researches extreme weather and climate change at Imperial, said the “fingerprints of climate change” were clear in the long-term changes that happened around the glacier before its catastrophic collapse.View image in fullscreen‘Communities in Nepal are paying with their lives for a crisis driven by fossil fuel emissions thousands of miles away,’ said Dr Friederike Otto.Photograph: Suryams Upreti/AAPAmong the study’s key findings were:skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the region where the collapse happened, climate breakdown has caused about 2C of warming since pre-industrial times, and about 1.5C of warming in July and August specifically;July and August 2026 were the warmest on record locally, reaching 5C above the 30-year average in the days before the collapse;The freezing threshold in the Himalayas has risen by about 100 metres per decade since the 1980s, with higher and longer thaw temperatures weakening mountain slopes shaped by permafrost;The warming temperature had already driven substantial glacier recession, removing stabilising ice from around the site where the collapse occurred and contributing meltwater;A 7.8 magnitude earthquake in 2015further contributed to slope failure, though its specific contribution to the disaster in August could not be confirmed.Otto, Clarke and the WWA team said their study did not directly ascribe climate breakdown as the fundamental cause of the catastrophe. Instead, it was best understood as a destabilising factor on the existing geology.Clarke said: “We found that climate change is transforming the high mountain environment, influencing many of the possible drivers of this collapse.”View image in fullscreenA major earthquake in Nepal in 2015 may also have contributed to the glacier’s collapse.Photograph: Ishwar Rauniyar/The GuardianNepal has filed a formal request with the UN loss and damage fund for financial support to address the destruction caused by the flood, a process that requires proof of a link to the climate crisis. The country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, has also demanded that top emitting nations such as China and India“wake up” and accept shared responsibilityfor the disaster.Madhab Uprety, senior technical advisor for the Red Cross Red Crescent Climate Centre, which is part of WWA, said only aggressive cuts to global emissions could begin to address the “losses and damages faced by vulnerable frontline communities”.He added: “In addition to the human tragedy on an unimaginable scale, the cost of recovery for this disaster is substantial. For a nation that’s done virtually nothing to contribute to this problem, it underlines the need to find fairness in helping climate vulnerable nations cope with the problems they have not unleashed.”Explore more on these topicsClimate scienceNepal-Tibet flood disasterClimate crisisFloodingNepalTibetExtreme weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: English far-right extremist who discussed killing Jews, Muslims and migrants is jailed | Crime | The Guardian
description: Ivan Jennings, 46, sentenced to five years after pleading guilty to encouraging terrorism on social media
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: Ivan Jennings, 46, sentenced to five years after pleading guilty to encouraging terrorism on social media
Content: Ivan Jennings pleaded guilty to encouraging terrorism in an online chat and dissemination of a terrorist publication in his trial at Leicester crown court.Photograph: Counter Terrorism PolicingView image in fullscreenIvan Jennings pleaded guilty to encouraging terrorism in an online chat and dissemination of a terrorist publication in his trial at Leicester crown court.Photograph: Counter Terrorism PolicingCrimeEnglish far-right extremist who discussed killing Jews, Muslims and migrants is jailedIvan Jennings, 46, sentenced to five years after pleading guilty to encouraging terrorism on social mediaRobyn Vinterand agencyWed 16 Sep 2026 14.53 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 13.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA rightwing extremist who discussed poisoning Jews and Muslims and called for the killing of migrants and minority communities has been jailed.Ivan Jennings, 46, called for the murder of hundreds of people he labelled “subhumans”, saying it was “justified and actually needed”, in extreme far-right groups over a period of three months in 2024.The father-of four from Stafford hadpleaded guilty to encouraging terrorismin an online chat between 15 August and 14 November that year and dissemination of a terrorism publication, namely a manifesto by the Norwegian mass murderer Anders Breivik, on 21 August 2024.Jennings, who worked at a warehouse, was jailed for five years and three months and handed a further five years on extended licence at Leicester crown court on Wednesday.Daniel Oscroft, prosecuting, told the court that Jennings had been an “active participant” in at least seven extreme rightwing groups on the social media platform Telegram.Jennings, who joined the far-right organisation Patriotic Alternative in early 2024, told one of the groups that he was in touch with a man “who wanted to go in a boat and make a difference to the amount of people coming into the UK”, the court heard.In another post, when asked if he supported murder, the defendant wrote: “It’s not murder because we are at war. If it’s subhumans, it’s justified and actually needed.”On 22 August that year, he searched online for motorboat chartering services at Dover and how much it cost to hire a boat in the UK. A week later, another user shared a video of a boat, on which Jennings commented: “We need one of those to take out the dinghy divers.”He told another chat group “something needed to be done soon” and each person “needs to take out at least 200 and stop the constant influx [of migrants]”.The defendant also shared a post about an event in Manchester celebrating Pakistan’s independence day, identifying it as a target with the message: “We need to start acting.”He made reference to the 51 people killed in the Christchurch terror attacks, a mass shooting at two mosques in New Zealand on 15 October 2019, adding: “We need a bigger impact.”The court heard that another user commented on the post about the Pakistan independence day event: “It disgusts me to see that in the UK.” Jennings replied: “Exactly, we need to start acting to turn the tables.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn another comment about the Pakistan event, he wrote: “If I go to prison for anything, it’s going to be for making a real change.”Oscroft told the court: “In a smaller group of eight participants, there was discussion about the most poisonous mushrooms and how to get them into the food of Jews or Muslims.”The defence barrister Oliver Renton said Jennings was “struggling with deep existential fears about himself” after he collapsed at work in 2023 in cardiac arrest, and that he descended into “fear and isolation” and became susceptible to “nihilistic, bleak worldviews”.In his sentencing remarks, Judge Lockhart KC said Jennings had “deeply held abhorrent and racist views”.Explore more on these topicsCrimeFar rightRaceImmigration and asylumUK security and counter-terrorismNorth of EnglandSocial medianewsShareReuse this content

title: Nato leader warns of ‘most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation’ | World news | The Guardian
description: Mark Rutte asks UK and Europe to ‘provide hard power Nato needs’ in face of geopolitical uncertainty
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Mark Rutte asks UK and Europe to ‘provide hard power Nato needs’ in face of geopolitical uncertainty
Content: NATO secretary general Mark Rutte discussed Britain’s Nato commitments with Andy Burnham during their first one-on-one meeting.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenNATO secretary general Mark Rutte discussed Britain’s Nato commitments with Andy Burnham during their first one-on-one meeting.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAWorld newsNato leader warns of ‘most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation’Mark Rutte asks UK and Europe to ‘provide hard power Nato needs’ in face of geopolitical uncertaintyDan SabbaghDefence and security editorWed 16 Sep 2026 14.46 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNato needs “more UK and more Europe” to deal with the most dangerous security environment faced by the west in a generation, the secretary general of the 32-country military alliance said this afternoon on a visit to the UK.Mark Rutte praised Britain for promising to increase defence spending in line with US demands after a meeting prime ministerAndy Burnham– but argued that the military and financial effort must continue into the future.“It is essential that your armed forces continue to provide the hard power Nato needs,” Rutte said in a speech to a specialist audience at Ditchley Park, a wartime retreat used by Winston Churchill in Oxfordshire.It was a plea for the UK to make progress towards an alliance-wide target demanded by Donald Trump of spending 3.5% of GDP by 2035, about £30bn in real terms, money that has to be found from extra taxation, borrowing or reducing other spending.Russian warship fires flares at Danish helicopter as Nato jets shoot down drone over LithuaniaRead moreBritain has so far only budgeted to increase defence spending to 2.7% of GDP by the end of the next decade. Short-term financial pressures have meant that the army has been told to stop non-essential training by the end of the year.Chancellor John Healey resigned as defence secretary from Keir Starmer’s government in June because the former prime minister would not commit to 3% by 2030, arguing that it would require too great a step up in the next decade.But Healey refused to recommit to the interim target when he was appointed to the Treasury by Burnham a month later, raising questions that the new government was backloading spending increases until after the next election.Rutte said that he had discussed Britain’s “Nato commitments” when he had met Burnham at a science business park in Oxford earlier on Wednesday, without offering any details, in the first one-on-one meeting between the two.Prior to that meeting, Burnham acknowledged that he had replaced Starmer, but insisted that there was “never any change in the UK’s unwavering commitment to Nato and our Nato obligations”.The Nato chief, a former Dutch prime minister, said many in Europe had made the “casual assumption” that the US would “always provide most of the muscle and pick up the bill, no matter what” until Trump returned to the White House.Instead, he noted that during a summit in The Hague in 2025, the UK and other alliance members had agreed to increase their own defence spending to match US levels, in response to Trump’s demand that Europe take the lead in defending the continent.“We need more UK and more Europe in the alliance,” Rutte said, because Nato “faces the most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation” with a return to wars in Europe and the Middle East, and wider geopolitical uncertainty.Ukraine war briefing: Nato ‘foils Russian undersea cable sabotage drill’Read moreCiting “Russia and its war against Ukraine, terrorism, Iran and the tectonic shifts of global geopolitical competition”, Rutte argued that the UK and Europe needed to invest more, because otherwise “our collective defence will not be credible”.Britain, he said, had “a central role in building this stronger Europe in a stronger Nato” and noted that the UK was spending billions to upgrade the Trident nuclear deterrent, which is pledged to the defence of Nato members.The UK is also gradually upgrading its conventional forces, though the UK’s overall defence spending, long the second largest in the alliance, is now behind Germany. By 2029, Berlin’s military budgets are on track to be twice that of the UK.The UK was “leading the pushback” against a Russian campaign of provocation and sabotage across Europe, Rutte said, and that the UK had been “a good friend to Ukraine”. Britain spends £3bn a year supporting Ukraine with weapons.Meanwhile, Canada, seeking to diversify its defence ties ⁠away from ⁠the ​US, has formally applied to join the British-led Joint Expeditionary Force military ⁠coalition, prime minister Mark Carney’s office said on Wednesday.The a grouping ⁠of 10 North Atlantic Nato member states is ​a rapid response ‌military partnership.Canada, already a Nato member, ‌is seeking closer military cooperation with Europe.The JEF comprises Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden and the UK.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsNatoAndy BurnhamMark RuttenewsShareReuse this content

title: Prisoners to ‘double up’ in one-person prefab cells, leaked documents show | Prisons and probation | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Ten category C prisons in England and Wales asked to add second beds, in breach of safe occupancy limits
Author: Rajeev Syal
Headline: Exclusive: Ten category C prisons in England and Wales asked to add second beds, in breach of safe occupancy limits
Content: An example of an existing category C prison cell.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenAn example of an existing category C prison cell.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyPrisons and probationPrisoners to ‘double up’ in one-person prefab cells, leaked documents showExclusive: Ten category C prisons in England and Wales asked to add second beds, in breach of safe occupancy limitsRajeev SyalHome affairs editorWed 16 Sep 2026 14.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Prison Service has drawn up plans to “double up” hundreds of prisoners in temporary prefabricated cells built for one person, at the request of the Ministry of Justice, leaked documents show.Amid an ongoing overcrowding crisis inEnglandand Wales, governors of 10 category C prisons have been asked to sign off the installation of second beds in “rapid deployment cells [RDCs]”.The units, some of which measure 2.9 metres by 3.4 metres and include a bed, toilet and shower, were placed in the grounds of more than 15 prisons as a temporary solution to past overcrowding problems.Estimated to have a 15-year lifespan, the steel-framed “pods” can be stacked to be two storeys and are usually occupied by low-risk prisoners, some of whom have been allowed to move into them as a reward for good behaviour.According to leaked emails, the planned doubling-up suggested by Ministry of Justice officials would increase the overall capacity of the prison estate by 476.Responding to the leaked documents, governors and prison officers said the numbers being proposed by Whitehall could breach health and safety laws and make jails unsafe for prisoners, staff and the public.Map of prisons where ‘doubling up’ has been proposedThe plans were disclosed in an email sent on 27 August by a senior Prison Service executive to governors.“As you are aware, maximising available prison capacity is of high ministerial interest, and HMPPS [His Majesty’s Prison and Probation Service] have been asked to explore the viability of crowding Rapid Deployment Cell accommodation,” the executive wrote.“The physical viability of installing a second bed in these units has been worked through at pace, and the assessment … is that ground floor units only are suitable to install a second bed.“Given continued high population growth, and less supply coming online than anticipated, it is important that all potential capacity is identified quickly, and as such the panels need to take place over the next few days.”The email was sent three days before Andy Burnham announced a substantialnarrowing of prisoners’ eligibility for the government’s early release scheme, blocking hundreds of violent criminals from being freed.What is Burnham doing to the early prison release scheme and why?Read moreAccording to a second leaked document, the doubling up plans would include beds being added to temporary cells in the following prisons: Wayland, in Norfolk (43 beds); Littlehey, in Cambridgeshire (60); Erlestoke, in Wiltshire (66); and Rochester, in Kent (60).Other prisons asked to find extra capacity in temporary cells include The Verne, in Dorset; Wymott, in Lancashire; Channings Wood, in Devon; Whatton, in Nottingham, which is a prison for people convicted of sexual offences; The Mount, in Hertfordshire; and Huntercombe, in Oxfordshire.The second document also shows that the doubling up proposals would breach “operational capacity”, putting the number of prisoners above safe occupancy levels.Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the Prison Officers Association, said capacity breaches could prompt industrial action by his members. “By law our members cannot strike, but I know they would walk out on health and safety grounds if asked to oversee prisons which cannot cope with the numbers being proposed,” he said.“Creating more space increases the pressure on an already overcrowded prison estate and risks the stability of prisons. If the government are convinced that early release schemes are sufficient, you have to ask why they are now insisting prisons source every available bit of spare capacity.”Tom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors Association, said a full risk assessment would have to be carried out on each prison to ensure the public and staff remained safe if doubling up occurred.“RDCs are amongst the least secure accommodation in the prison estate and prisoners located in them will have to be risk assessed. If you don’t do this, the prison won’t be sufficiently safe or secure,” he said.“Increasing the operational capacity of a prison isn’t as simple as putting bunk beds in cells. There needs to be staff available to supervise the additional prisoners and there needs to be additional regime activities.”Andrea Coomber, the chief executive of the Howard League for Penal Reform, said the proposal was an act of desperation.“Rapid deployment cells were themselves meant to be a short-term response but, ironically, they have come to be seen as being among the more positive parts of the prison estate, with fewer issues related to violence, debt and drug misuse. The risk now is that all this will be undermined as more and more people get crammed in,” she said.There are 87,111 people in prison in England andWales. Under the Ministry of Justice’s own definition of safety and decency, the prison estate should not hold more than 81,616 people.Reacting to the leaked documents, a ministry spokesperson said the department was investing up to £4.7bn creating 14,000 new prison places.“As the public would expect, we’re pulling every lever available to ensure there is always space to lock up dangerous offenders,” the spokesperson said.“Cells are only doubled up where it is safe to do so, and no final decision has been taken on these units.”Explore more on these topicsPrisons and probationEnglandWalesUK criminal justicenewsShareReuse this content

title: Planning permission for new Scottish AI datacentres suspended for up to a year | Datacentres - UK | The Guardian
description: Scottish parliament brings in strict environmental impact assessments and will delay decisions until national strategy is developed
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: Scottish parliament brings in strict environmental impact assessments and will delay decisions until national strategy is developed
Content: Anti-datacentre protests at the Scottish parliament at Holyrood.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAnti-datacentre protests at the Scottish parliament at Holyrood.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianDatacentres - UKPlanning permission for new Scottish AI datacentres suspended for up to a yearMSPs vote for strict environmental impact assessments and will delay decisions until national strategy is developedPatrick GreenfieldWed 16 Sep 2026 14.28 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 07.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHolyrood has voted to pause planning applications for all new AI datacentres for up to a year until the Scottish government has developed a national strategy.On Wednesday, MSPs backed a Scottish Labour motion to halt new schemes for up to 12 months while rules on hyperscale datacentres are developed in what could be a blow to the British government’s AI strategy.Scotland has seen a boom in planning applications for large datacentres as global investment in AI infrastructure has exploded, with British officials encouraging developers to includeScotlandin the infrastructure buildout. Datacentres are critical for storing and processing data used by AI. One scheme in Auchtertool, Fife, has been billed as the second largest in the world, and is among more than 20 large datacentres proposed so far.Campaigners have raised concerns about water usage and carbon emissions from large datacentres, and questioned whether Scotland has the capacity to cope with the resulting explosion in energy demand.On Wednesday, MSPs voted to approve only projects that meet robust environmental impact assessments that consider the impact of neighbouring communities, and to make no decisions on planning for datacentre applications for up to a year until national planning guidance has been formalised by the Scottish government.Kat Jones, the director of the NGOAction to Protect Rural Scotland, who has spearheaded demands for a datacentre moratorium in Scotland, said the vote was a “landmark day for all those communities across Scotland who have been extremely concerned about projects coming forward in their areas.”“There’s much still to be done, but this is a huge step forward and we can all at least take a breath now,” she said. “That means the Scottish government must now urgently call in those applications which are approaching a decision date. The communities will expect nothing less.”Ahead of the vote, the Scottish government announced that large-scale datacentres would face mandatory environmental impact assessments, as a result of growing concern about the ecological impact of the AI boom.This month, hundreds from community groupsprotested outside Holyroodagainst the construction of large datacentres for AI until clear planning rules and the definition of a “green” datacentre had been formalised.On Thursday, AI leaders will gather at Dumfries House in Ayrshire for a summit with King Charles on the future of the technology, amid warnings that the speed of its development threatens the survival of humanity.After the vote, the Scottish Labour economy spokesperson, Daniel Johnson, said the economic potential of the AI boom needed to be considered alongside the impacts on the environment, communities and energy demand.“So far the SNP has failed to do the work needed to get this right – that must change. It is right that the SNP government has accepted the need for national guidance before more decisions are made, and I want to see that guidance delivered with the urgency needed,” he said.“The SNP must put in place the protections needed and ensure that any datacentres work for communities, create good jobs and deliver for Scotland.”The Scottish government has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - UKAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingScotlandEdinburghScottish politicsPlanning policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Greens just four points behind Labour in urban areas, poll reveals | Green party | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: UK’s Green parties could take 40 seats if result replicated at next election, according to Labour-linked thinktank
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: UK’s Green parties could take 40 seats if result replicated at next election, according to Labour-linked thinktank
Content: Zack Polanski, leader of the Green party of England and Wales, is standing for parliament in Keir Starmer’s former constituency.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenZack Polanski, leader of the Green party of England and Wales, is standing for parliament in Keir Starmer’s former constituency.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAGreen partyGreens just four points behind Labour in urban areas, poll revealsExclusive: UK’s Green parties could take 40 seats if result replicated at next election, according to Labour-linked thinktankKiran StaceyPolicy editorWed 16 Sep 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Greens are just four points behindLabourin urban constituencies across the UK, putting them within touching distance of taking as many as 40 seats if the result was replicated at the next election, according to new polling by a Labour-linked thinktank.The survey by ThinkLabour, which has extensive links to Andy Burnham’s government, finds that urban voters have moved in large numbers towards the UK’s Green parties since the 2024 general election. The research highlights the challenge Labour faces inholding on to the Holborn and St Pancras seatin the face of a challenge from Zack Polanski, the party leader in England and Wales, at next month’s byelection.The study’s authors warn that evidence from previous electoral battles between the two parties suggests Labour politicians should dial down direct attacks on the Greens for fear of looking as if they are “kicking a puppy”.Christabel Cooper, one of the report’s authors, said: “The previous administration [under Keir Starmer] had always banked on the fact that Labour would be able to say to people who vote Green that they would get Nigel Farage as prime minister.“But in the 40 seats that we have identified, that is no longer the case – the Greens can claim to be the progressives’ party of choice.”She added that evidence from other elections where the party has gone head to head with Labour suggests that progressives dislike aggressive attacks on the Greens.“The sorts of people who would consider voting Labour consider attacking the Greens like kicking a puppy. They think, we are all supposed to be nice and liberal, why are we having a go at the Greens?”The findings, which have been discussed with strategists in No 10 as they look to solidify separate polling gains made in Burnham’s early weeks as prime minister, show Labour faces a difficult task winning back urban progressives who helped the party win the last election.ThinkLabour’s former chief executive Alison Phillips is now Burnham’s chief of staff, while other alumni of the organisation have senior roles across government.The research was carried out as Burnham was about to take office in Downing Street, meaning it will not have captured the full effect of the “Burnham bounce”, which has seen Labour gain ground with progressive voters and pull level with Reform UK.The poll shows that support for the Greens has increased by 12 points in major cities since the general election, while Labour’s vote share has fallen by 20 points, leaving Labour only 4 points ahead in some of its most reliable strongholds.It found that the move from Labour to the Greens has been more pronounced among voters who are financially struggling, undermining the stereotype of Green voters as affluent liberals.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘We can win here’: Zack Polanski presses the flesh in Holborn and St PancrasRead moreThe report warned that urban voters felt they did not know what Labour’s values were, in part because of some of the counterintuitive measures taken by Starmer in his early days as prime minister, such as cutting winter fuel payments.It also warns that winning these voters back will mean focusing immigration reforms on tackling small boat crossings rather than wider measures to tackle legal migration.Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is bringing in measures to make it harder for legal migrants to achieve settled status, which haveproved controversialwith Labour MPs and activists.The report said: “On divisive areas such as immigration, where liberals and social conservatives can agree on some outcomes – reducing small boat crossings, for example – it should primarily focus on these.“Where its policies appear tough or restrictive, Labour must be able to make a convincing progressive case for them, showing how they solve practical problems rather than simply signalling to the right.”The researchers also found that attacks on the Greens over foreign policy had the most effect with the voters Labour is trying to win back, in part because they found these more credible than other criticisms.While urban voters did not like Green policies on legalising drugs – which Labour focused on during the failed campaign to win the Gorton and Denton byelection – they did not view them as a particularly credible threat.Personal attacks on Polanski, meanwhile, went down badly among those considering voting Green, who viewed criticisms of his CV and his past as a hypnotherapist as especially non-credible.The Green leader has previously come under fire fortelling a journalistin 2013 he could enlarge women’s breasts with hypnotherapy – comments he has since said he regrets.Explore more on these topicsGreen partyLabourZack PolanskiHolborn and St Pancras byelectionImmigration and asylumnewsShareReuse this content

title: LA homelessness non-profit workers arrested over alleged corruption and bribes | Los Angeles | The Guardian
description: Pair accused of misappropriating millions in taxpayer dollars and using money for personal gain
Author: Cecilia Nowell
Headline: Pair accused of misappropriating millions in taxpayer dollars and using money for personal gain
Content: The Skid Row neighborhood of downtown Los Angeles.Photograph: Apu Gomes/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Skid Row neighborhood of downtown Los Angeles.Photograph: Apu Gomes/AFP/Getty ImagesLos AngelesLA homelessness non-profit workers arrested over alleged corruption and bribesPair accused of misappropriating millions in taxpayer dollars as Trump officials target alleged fraud in blue statesCecilia NowellWed 16 Sep 2026 19.34 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 17.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFederal law enforcement officers havearrested two employeesof California-based homelessness non-profits on corruption charges, alleging that they misappropriated millions in taxpayer dollars.The US justice department has arrested Michael Young, a founder of the Culver City-based nonprofit Home At Last, and Lakiya Malone, an employee of the Los Angeles-based Special Service for Groups. The two are expected to appear in court on Wednesday.Young is charged with wire fraud in a scheme to embezzle more than $7.5m from contracts with Los Angeles county and other publicly funded agencies, which he used to open a high-end restaurant, nightclub and bingo hall.Malone is charged with taking more than $180,000 in bribes and kickbacks from the director of another homelessness non-profit, Alexander Soofer, who has agreed to plead guilty in a separate case.The justice department is also seeking to arrest Donye Mitchell, the CEO of the Los Angeles-based nonprofit The Big Blue Umbrella. Mitchell is charged with wire fraud in a case that alleges he fraudulently obtained $1.2m in public grant funding, which he allegedly used for personal expenses, including his own bail bonds, credit card debt and PlayStation charges“My message to every fraudster who steals from the vulnerable is clear: we will track you down, bring charges where the evidence leads, and work relentlessly to reclaim every taxpayer dollar you stole,” said assistant attorney general Colin M McDonald of the National Fraud Enforcement Division.The investigation was led by the homeless fraud and corruption taskforce, which US attorney Bill Essayliformed last yearto “investigate fraud, waste, abuse, and corruption involving funds allocated toward the eradication of homelessness within the seven-county jurisdiction of the central district of California”.Los Angeles mayor Karen Bass said in a Wednesday statement: “My administration has zero tolerance for fraud – period.“Any misuse of taxpayer funds meant to help unhoused Angelenos should be met with the full force of the law. We appreciate the efforts of the Department of Justice in protecting public funds and working towards recovering dollars meant to serve Angelenos experiencing homelessness.”The arrests come amid growing Trump administration-backed efforts to root out “fraud” in blue states, such asCalifornia.In April, Donald Trumpnamed JD Vance his “fraud czar”, with a focus on investigating “those blue states where crooked Democrat politicians … have had a ‘free for all’ in the unprecedented theft of taxpayer money”. Months prior, hefrozefederal childcare funding to Minnesota over accusations of such fraud, and halted more than a quarter-billion dollars in Medicaid funds to the state as part of efforts to ensure it was a “good steward of the American people’s tax money”.This summer, the Trump administrationsuspendedfederal funding to Los Angeles’s homelessness agency, Lahsa, pending an investigation citing allegations of fraud. At the time,about 8% of Lahsa’s budgetcame from federal funding.And earlier this week, 12 people in southern California were charged with fraudulently collecting $10m in government childcare payments, despite allegedly caring for few or no children.“If you fail the taxpayer, if you fail our cities, if you fail our shared mission of ending homelessness, there will be consequences and we will cut you off,” housing and urban development secretary Scott Turner said at a press conference.Explore more on these topicsLos AngelesCaliforniaUS politicsWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: US lawmakers pass bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia and its enablers | Trump tariffs | The Guardian
description: Act divides Democrats and Republicans, with some saying it gives president power that could be turned against US allies
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Act divides Democrats and Republicans, with some saying it gives president power that could be turned against US allies
Content: Buildings heavily damaged following a Russian missile attack in Sloviansk, Donetsk region, UkrainePhotograph: Cameron Jones-Manley/Zuma Press/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenBuildings heavily damaged following a Russian missile attack in Sloviansk, Donetsk region, UkrainePhotograph: Cameron Jones-Manley/Zuma Press/ShutterstockTrump tariffsUS lawmakers pass bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia and its enablersAct divides Democrats and Republicans, with some saying it gives president power that could be turned against US alliesAndrew RothWed 16 Sep 2026 18.41 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe US Congress has passed a sweeping bill allowingDonald Trumpto raise tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy and issue other punishing sanctions against the Kremlin following a pitched battle between lawmakers backing Ukraine and sceptics worried the bill gives the president too much power.The Lindsey O Graham SanctioningRussiaand Iran Act of 2026 passed in a 262-159 vote on the last day before Congress goes on recess ahead of the midterm elections. Graham, who died earlier this year, co-authored and submitted the bill more than a year and a half ago.The long delay in the vote was widely considered to be scepticism from theTrump administration, which had opposed additional sanctions and then recently changed its stance to support tabling the bill as efforts to negotiate with the Kremlin to end the war have yielded few results.However the bill faced last-minute hurdles in Congress as members of the Republican party’s isolationist wing were joined by Democrats who warned that Trump could use the bill’s new tariffs authority against allies instead.The bill would mandate new sanctions on Russian political and military officials, and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. It would also target Russia’s so-called fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite sanctions on its energy exports.It would also allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian energy, including China, as well as other countries helping the Kremlin evade sanctions.Senior Democrats voiced opposition to the bill during a heated floor debate. “Why in the world would this Congress give this president additional authority to visit that kind of economic harm on the American people?” said Hakeem Jeffries, the leading Democrat in the House, during a speech on Wednesday, adding he would vote against the bill.Democratic staffers supporting the bill said that it offered a “last chance” to increase sanctions on Russia before Ukraine entered a “long winter”. Russia has improved the drone technology it has used to strike Ukrainian infrastructure as Kyiv has suffered a shortage of anti-air missiles, leaving the country in a dire position.Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican supporting the bill, called it the US Congress’ “Churchill vs Chamberlain Moment on Russia”.“Choking off the money funding a war of conquest in Europe is exactly what that authority should be used for, and Congress deciding to do that is Congress doing its constitutional job,” he said, rejecting arguments by Democrats that the bill gave Trump too much authority to slap tariffs on foreign countries.The bill passed the Senate last month in a landslide 86-11 vote. However it faced more pushback in the House of Representatives. A Tuesday rule vote allowing consideration of Senate amendments to the bill passed by just 214-211, with two renegade Democrats joining Republicans to vote in favour of what they said was an act of support for Ukraine. That vote led to senior Democrats holding terse talks with their fellow party members.“I’m proud to represent one of the largest Ukrainian communities in America – people who have lost fathers, mothers, sons and daughters in the fight to defeat fascism,” wrote Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, one of the two Democrat representatives, in a statement on Tuesday.“I’ll always stand with my community’s values, and am grateful for the 86 senators who voted to send this bill to the House. My vote today gets us one step closer to enacting these sanctions into law and I look forward to voting tomorrow to cut off the flow of Russian oil money fuelling this war.”The Ukrainian government has said it supported the bill, and hundreds of pro-Ukrainian activists calling for tougher sanctions on Russia held advocacy talks in Washington DC in the days leading up to the vote.“We support any initiative that is in the interest of Ukraine and Ukrainians,” said Denys Sienik, the Chargé d’Affaires at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington DC. “So if we are talking about the possibility of putting more pressure on Russia so that it holds the Russian war machine, of course, we are there, and we are grateful to every senator, to every congressman and congresswoman for their voice and, and for their support.”Explore more on these topicsTrump tariffsDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS CongressUS politicsTariffsRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: US Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time since 2023 | Federal Reserve | The Guardian
description: Trump urges lower rates after central bank agrees increase by quarter-percentage point to range of 3.75% to 4%
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Trump urges lower rates after central bank agrees increase by quarter-percentage point to range of 3.75% to 4%
Content: Kevin Warsh at the Federal Reserve in in Washington in July.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenKevin Warsh at the Federal Reserve in in Washington in July.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersFederal ReserveUS Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time since 2023Trump urges lower rates after central bank agrees increase by quarter-percentage point to range of 3.75% to 4%Federal Reserve raises interest rates – liveGaya GuptaWed 16 Sep 2026 17.01 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 14.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe USFederal Reservevoted to raise interest rates on Wednesday for the first time since 2023 as the central bank continues to fight to tamp down inflation.The Fed’s open market committee voted unanimously to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%. This is the first time the Fed has raised rates since July 2023 and potentially sets Kevin Warsh, the current Fed chair, on a collision course with Donald Trump.“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said on Wednesday. “This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.”After the announcement, Trumpsaidin a Truth Social post that interest rates should be 1% or less and criticized the US trade deficit. Trump said the US would make “at least 1.5 Trillion Dollars a year” if it were to stop trading with countries with which it has a deficit.“We are ‘carrying’ almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer. LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!,” Trump wrote.Chart of Fed funds target rateThough Warsh acknowledged changing geopolitics, he avoided calling out the US-Israel war with Iran by name.“There’s no hiding from hotspots around the world, and our judgment about what is the most likely or least likely of the geopolitical situation has changed,” he said.Warsh also declined to answer questions about how Trump would react but reiterated that Fed independence was “a two-way street”.“We will let people that do trade policy and fiscal policy stay in their lane. That is the way we can stand up here and call them the way we see them,” he said.The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.New projections showed a majority of officials penciled in another rate hike before the year’s end, with four officials predicting the Fed’s benchmark interest rate would reach a range of 4.25% to 4.5% by the end of the year.And though estimates on the country’s economic growth and unemployment rate were upbeat, Fed officials believed it would take roughly until 2029 for inflation to reach its 2% goal.At its last meeting in late July, the open market committee voted 9-3 to maintain rates, the first time in 10 years that so many members shared dissent on a policy decision. Since then, the US and Iran have renewed attacks against each other, driving up the Brent crude benchmark to its highest levels in month.The war has driven up inflation, especially energy prices. Gas prices have remained, on average, $1 a gallon more expensive compared with a year ago. Diesel fuel, which is used for buses, trains and trucks, recently reached an all-time high of $6.31.Concerns about inflation have induced asell-offin the US bond market, with the yield on the 10-year treasury note hitting a 19-year high earlier this week, despite efforts from the US treasury to calm the market. Typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, trouble in the US bond market canlead tohigher interest rates for consumer and business loans.The Fed uses interest rates as a tool to cool price increases by slowing activity. Higher interest rates impact mortgages, car payments, student debt and other types of loans. After inflation reached a generational high of 9.1% in June 2022, the Fed increased rates 11 times from 2022 and 2023. Rates were brought up to a target range of 5.25% to 5.5% before the Fed eventually started lowering rates in 2024 and 2025.At the beginning of the year, when the annualized inflation rate was 1% lower than current levels, a Fed rate hike seemed highly unlikely. A majority of Fed officials were actually predicting a rate cut before the end of the year. But inflation in Augustremained stubbornly highwhile unemployment was steady, which furthered the chances of a rate hike.Higher prices have painted a grim economic outlook as voters prepare to head to the polls in November. Recent data and surveys have shown heightened inflation has wiped out wage gains for Americans and dampened consumer outlook. In August, hourly earnings for employees decreased by 0.1% year-over-year after accounting for inflation and fell by 0.3% from the month prior.
