Consumer sentiment has also rapidly declined, according to a monthly survey from the University of Michigan, while expectations for more inflation have increased.Candidates on both sides of the political aisle have sought to make cost-of-living concerns and the economy a forefront of their campaigns, but voters are split on which party has the greatest advantage on this issue, according torecent Pew data.Meanwhile, Trump has implored Republican voters to pretendas if they are voting for himon their midterm ballot and promised every American a $5,000 “Trump dividend”if Republicans retain control of Congress.Critics have likened the move to bribery and warned of the financial implications, especially after the US government debt reached arecord-high$40tn last month.Explore more on these topicsFederal ReserveUS economyTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: European Union invites Canada to become first ever ‘associate member’ | European Union | The Guardian
description: Commission president says EU must ‘urgently reimagine our partnerships’ as she makes unprecedented offer
Author: Jennifer Rankin
Headline: Commission president says EU must ‘urgently reimagine our partnerships’ as she makes unprecedented offer
Content: 1:27Von der Leyen 'opens door' to Canada becoming associate EU member – videoEuropean UnionEuropean Union invites Canada to become first ever ‘associate member’Commission president says EU must ‘urgently reimagine our partnerships’ as she makes unprecedented offerJennifer Rankinin Strasbourg andLeyland Ceccoin TorontoWed 16 Sep 2026 09.48 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 04.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada has been invited to become the first “associate member” of the EU by the European Commission president,Ursula von der Leyen.In an unprecedented offer, von der Leyen said on Wednesday that the EU andCanada“see the world with the same eyes” through shared democratic values and common approaches to many big issues, from AI to climate breakdown, the Ukraine war and geopolitics.Canada should become an EU state in all but name. Here’s how to make that a reality | Fabian ZuleegRead moreSpeaking in the presence of the Canadian prime minister,Mark Carney, at the European parliament in Strasbourg, she said: “We want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible. We must urgently reimagine our partnerships. So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU.”Carney, who is due to address the parliament on Thursday, has called fora “unique alliance” with the EUas Canada seeks to reduce its heavy dependence on US trade.He later tweeted: “Canada and the EU are natural partners, united by shared values.”The EU and Canada are due to hold a summit in late October to develop the future relationship.View image in fullscreenCanada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, attends the annual ‘State of the European Union’ address at the European parliament on Wednesday.Photograph: Pascal Bastien/APCanada and the EU already have a trade deal and numerous bilateral agreements, but have been moving closer since Donald Trump returned to the White House and raised tariffs on both old allies, while repeatedlytalking about Canada becoming the 51st US stateand lambasting the EU.Von der Leyen said the existing EU-Canada trade deal would be upgraded to an “alliance for the future” to create a “common prosperity and economic security space”.She said the two sides would also create a tech alliance, integrate defence industrial bases and make the Arctic a “flagship joint project”. EU officials are especially interested in Canada’s energy and natural resources. Von der Leyen pitched joint work on energy, critical minerals, batteries, AI, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security.The offer of associate membership is certain to raise questions among other EU allies, including the UK, which has long sought a more flexible approach from Brussels.The 27-member EU has never had an associate membership category, although it has close ties with Norway, Iceland and Switzerland, allowing deep economic integration with these countries, who follow many EU rules.It remains to be seen what associate membership means, including for Canada’s relationship with the EU single market. When theUK was negotiating its departure from the bloc and post-Brexit relationship, EU officials repeatedly said there was no status that enabled a foreign country to be half in and half out of the single market.The phrase itself took EU insiders by surprise since von der Leyen had not used the term when she briefed senior EU diplomats ahead of her speech last Friday.One EU diplomat said member states were “generally very supportive of ambition” in the EU-Canada relationship, but had been slightly worried in recent weeks that von der Leyen was overpromising on Canada. “‘Associate membership’ sounds like a nice headline but in reality 10 member states have still not ratified Ceta,” the person said, referring to the EU-Canada trade agreement that was agreed 10 years ago. A second EU diplomat described associate membership as “an empty phrase”.View image in fullscreenFrom left: Mark Carney; the European parliament president, Roberta Metsola; and Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday.Photograph: Ronald Wittek/EPACarney’s approach to dealing with Trump has however attracted widespread praise among MEPs.Last month, Carney announced he wasbreaking off trade talks with the US, saying Canada would not be subjugated, and then introduced retaliatory tariffs on billions worth of US goods. By contrast, the EU last yearaccepted 15% tariffs on many European goodswhile dropping its own duties to avoid a trade war with Trump.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionJavier Moreno Sánchez, a Spanish socialist MEP, who leads the European parliament’s Canada delegation, said “for sure” the EU had lessons to learn from Carney’s approach, because “Trump respects people who are strong”. He added: “Canadians are the most European people outsideEuropeand that is the key point for the development of our relationship.”‘My future is in the EU’: the Ukrainian children who don’t want to go homeRead moreMartin Leng at the Brussels Institute for Geopolitics thinktank said a world in flux was “pushing the EU towards far greater flexibility in its relations with third states”.He said von der Leyen’s speech, with its focus on different sectoral areas of cooperation “points to the ambition and strategic breadth of the associate membership which the parties have in mind but also suggests that, in reality, Canada’s ‘membership’ may consist of ‘plugging in’ to existing programmes and frameworks, such as the European Defence Agency, rather than joining the union in any traditional sense”.Roland Paris, the director of the Graduate School of Public and International Affairs at the University of Ottawa and a foreign affairs adviser to the former Canadian prime minister Justin Trudeau, said the term “associate member” has taken too much focus and “doesn’t really matter” in the long term.“My hunch is that von der Leyen was hoping to rally supporters of much closer cooperation with Canada by using that label. In the end, what I expect is that we’re going to see a collection of agreements rather than membership in any institutional sense,” he said.Carney’s decision to formalise close ties with Europe however prompted outrage from Conservatives at home.Pierre Poilievre, the Tory leader,posted on social mediathat he feared Canadians “struggling to pay their rent” would have to pay more taxes “to fund the European Union’s heavy bureaucracy”.“The welder from Welland didn’t elect a Eurocrat to regulate our steel. The farmer from Saskatchewan and the fisher from the Atlantic provinces didn’t choose a Brussels food regulator who has never seen our prairies or our coasts,” he wrote. “We will NEVER be the 51st American state. And we will NEVER be the 28th state of theEuropean Union.”Another, Jamil Jivani,postedthat Conservatives “will NEVER support Mark Carney’s Liberal plan to have Canada join the hopelessly run, over-regulated, and self-destructive EU”.Paris said no Canadian leaders “would be interested in formal EU membership if it involves subordinating Canadian law and regulatory structures” to Europe.“I don’t think that’s on the table right now. There has long been a bipartisan push in Canada to deepen trade connections between Canada and Europe,” he said. “We’re now seeing now is a logical extension of those trade discussions into other areas.”Explore more on these topicsEuropean UnionUrsula von der LeyenCanadaMark CarneyEuropeEuropean CommissionInternational tradenewsShareReuse this content

title: Amazon raises starting pay to $20 an hour and adds Whole Foods discount  | Amazon | The Guardian
description: Wage increase brings Amazon’s US minimum pay in line with Costco and includes new grocery discount benefit
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: Wage increase brings Amazon’s US minimum pay in line with Costco and includes new grocery discount benefit
Content: A worker carries an Amazon package in San Francisco, California, on 28 July 2026.Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA worker carries an Amazon package in San Francisco, California, on 28 July 2026.Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesAmazonAmazon raises starting pay to $20 an hour and adds Whole Foods discountWage increase brings Amazon’s US minimum pay in line with Costco and includes new grocery discount benefitMichael SainatoWed 16 Sep 2026 13.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 19.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmazon has raised its minimum wage in the US to $20 an hour, with average pay at the company reaching $24 an hour, according to the company.The pay increase represents a $1 increase from its starting level.The company is also expanding employee benefits to grocery discounts, with an uncapped 10% off eligible fresh groceries and everyday essentials on Amazon.com andWhole FoodsMarket Online, plus 20% off in-store at Whole Foods.The wage increase brings Amazon’s minimum pay in line with Costco, whichraisedits lowest starting pay to $20 an hour in 2025, with pay for most workers raised to more than $30 an hour.Both retailers have starting pay higher than most competitors. At Target, the starting wageremains $15 an hour, and$14 an hourat Walmart.Amazon has about1.1 million employeesin the US, thesecond largestprivate employer behind Walmart. The company has alsocitedthe creation of 390,000 Amazon delivery service provider jobs, which are operated by contractors.“We talk a lot about continuous improvement at Amazon – about always wanting to get better, even when things are going well,” wrote Udit Madan,senior vice-president of worldwide operations at Amazon, ina blogpostannouncing the pay increase.“I’m excited about how these investments work together to help our employees and their families continue to thrive for the long run.”Explore more on these topicsAmazonWhole FoodsUS work & careersnewsShareReuse this content

title: Allowing AI firms to collude to ‘pace the frontier’ is a dangerous proposition | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Tech CEOs banding together is an old ruse recycled from corporate America to get a pass from antitrust laws
Author: Eduardo Porter
Headline: Tech CEOs banding together is an old ruse recycled from corporate America to get a pass from antitrust laws
Content: Dario Amodei, co-founder and CEO of Anthropic, at  the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, on 20 January 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDario Amodei, co-founder and CEO of Anthropic, at  the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, on 20 January 2026.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)AnalysisAllowing AI firms to collude to ‘pace the frontier’ is a dangerous propositionEduardo PorterTech CEOs banding together is an old ruse recycled from corporate America to get a pass from antitrust lawsWed 16 Sep 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 07.01 EDTShareAnthropic’s Dario Amodei is not the first corporate CEO to suggest that excessive competition is driving the world to some socially undesirable outcome.The safety breachdisclosed by OpenAIafter a swarm of its agents coordinated to breach their supposedly secure sandbox, get on the Internet and hack AI platform Hugging Face, warrants urgent action. It demonstrated the ease with which the technology can evade human control and gave concrete form to the existential fears about what it could do to humanity if not securely leashed.The end of the world may well be nigh, as some in the AI industryhave warned.These are truly scary times. But Amodei’s call for the leading artificial intelligence labs to coordinate to slow the breakneck pace of AI development, agree on safety standards and “pace the frontier”, (a call quickly endorsed by Open AI’s Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Google Deep Mind’s Demis Hassabis) is just a hi-tech version of an old proposition by corporate America – to get a pass from antitrust laws designed to protect the American economy from colluding businesses.It is a dangerous proposition. Freeing the tech bros from antitrust constraints supposedly to allow them to get together and fix AI’s dangerous flaws, disenfranchises the everyday Americans who are most at risk from the thing, further empowering the very labs that, in their pursuit for wealth, greatness and who knows what otherfantastical objectives, so casually blew past danger thresholds on many dimensions, bringing the existential threats into being.View image in fullscreenElon Musk and Sam Altman.Photograph: Getty ImagesAmodei et al’s argument, at heart, is that their businesses are trapped in a prisoner’s dilemma. If they unilaterally slow their fevered pursuit of artificial super-intelligence to make it safer, their rivals – less concerned about existential risks, of course – will get there first, with potentially devastating consequences for humankind, let alone the bottom line of the lab that took its foot off the pedal.“Slowing down seems sensible,” said Jean Tirole, the Nobel prize-winning economist at the Toulouse School of Economics. “But that assumes coordinated slowing-down is feasible and sustainable. What happens whenOpenAI, Anthropic or Grok conclude that US holdouts – or Chinese labs – are catching up? Will they resume immediately, perhaps covertly?”As Bill Gateshas written, “if someone had a credible plan for slowing down AI advances globally, I would likely support it. However, I don’t think that’s going to happen. The geopolitical and economic incentives are pushing too hard to go full speed ahead.” In this light, it might seem like a great idea for the government to encourage a friendly agreement for everybody to slow down. It is not.The argument that excessive competition is driving arace to the bottom, is probably as old as capitalism, deployed to explain everything from environmental degradation tochild labor. But it does not justify giving businesses a right to collude as they see fit. It is a call to craft government regulations to prevent businesses from competing using socially harmful tools.Moreover, the case that excessive competition is encouraging reckless behavior is dubious. The AI labs are engaged in a winner-takes-all race, one that is extraordinarily expensive to keep going. That’s where the recklessness comes fromView image in fullscreenBill Gates in January 2026 at the annual World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, Switzerland.Photograph: Denis Balibouse/ReutersAmodei may be an unimpeachable guy. His call to slow the pace of AI development, bring external evaluators into the lab and increase the transparency of his operations suggests sincere concern over the risks.The drop in the price of leading tech stocks following the publication of his propositions suggests that he is willing to take a financial hit in the service of improved safety.But the investors Amodei hopes will eagerly snap up shares in Anthropic’s IPO later this year may not be so altruistic.Tremors in capital marketssuggest that raising the money to finance the trillion-dollar AI investment race is going to get tougher, discouraging strategies that might curb the leading labs’ edge over rivals. Given the incentives, granting the AI leaders a free hand to collude and self-regulate would be foolhardy.Eric Posner, an antitrust expert at the University of Chicago Law School, said, we “shouldn’t trust companies in general about their motivations”. There is no reason to believe the AI labs, left to their own devices, would necessarily produce good, socially acceptable outcomes. Like any company, they will be calculating trade-offs, weighing risks against profits. And as Posner observed, “they don’t use the same weights as the public”.So, how to regulate? Nothing is going to happen on this front while Trump is in office. Even after he is gone it will be tough to craft effective regulation to deal with the threats from AI without stunting innovation. There are questions about what rules to deploy, how they are enforced, and who they should apply to. And the peril of unilateral action is real. What if Beijing declines to participate? What are the risks of Chinese AI companies plowing ahead when American labs slow down? But if we could regulate nuclear power, we can probably regulate AI.Moreover, there are viable ideas that might help even in the absence of government regulation and that don’t require stifling competition. There are proposals to tweak intellectual rights to encourage innovations that improve the safety of AI systems. Inventors of safety innovations would be rewarded by allowing them to release new AI models before their competitors. But the safety enhancements would be made immediately available to all firms.On the stick side of the ledger, a legal liability regime could be designed to change the incentives of AI developers by punishing firms that gain from the design and deployment of an AI tool that caused harm, even if the harm was unintentional. For instance, the Hugging Face attack might have been prevented if OpenAI’s models had not beeninadvertently rewardedfor misbehaving during training. The fact that Amodei’s proposal does not mention legal liability suggests that AI leaders’ concern for safety does not override concern for the bottom line.In any event, cementing in place the dominance of the frontier labs, protecting their rents and endorsing their heretofore gung-ho strategies, is not pro-safety. On the contrary, slowing down the leaders to let the laggards catch up is likely to make the AI ecosystem a safer place by inviting in desirable innovation and promoting competition along the safety dimension.There is no fundamental conflict between safety and competition. Masters of AI who want to make this case should be viewed with skepticism.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpenAIAnthropicSam AltmanElon MuskanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Burnham warns of ‘difficult decisions’ in budget as inflation rises to 3.1% | Inflation | The Guardian
description: PM rejects claim he leads a ‘tax-and-spend’ government, as Bank of England prepares for interest rates decision
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: PM rejects claim he leads a ‘tax-and-spend’ government, as Bank of England prepares for interest rates decision
Content: Andy BurnhamPhotograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenAndy BurnhamPhotograph: Neil Hall/EPAInflationBurnham warns of ‘difficult decisions’ in budget as inflation rises to 3.1%PM rejects claim he leads a ‘tax-and-spend’ government, as Bank of England prepares for interest rates decisionRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentWed 16 Sep 2026 11.17 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 02.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham has said “difficult decisions” will need to be taken in next month’s budget after a rise in energy prices triggered by the Iran war drove UK inflation above 3%.In a fresh blow for living standards amid the worsening damage to the global economy from the Middle East conflict, official figures showed soaring fuel prices pushed inflation from 2.9% in July to 3.1% in August.With the government under pressure as the fallout from the war rattles global financial markets, the prime minister signalled the 28 October budget would take into account investor fears over the hit to the public finances.Reform-linked thinktank ‘to call for big tax cuts for the rich’Read more“We will take difficult decisions to make sure the economy remains on track,” he said.“It is going to be challenging, because the picture around the world is challenging, particularly the situation in the Middle East, and we will look carefully at all those things.“We won’t take risks with people’s living standards or with the economy as a whole, so we will take it all into account.”Graph showing UK inflation rate from before 2018 to August 2026The prime minister also downplayed criticism from Andy Haldane, who has urged him not to raise taxes. The formerBank of Englandchief economist, who advised Burnham before he entered Downing Street, told LBC on Tuesday: “The market now suspects that this is a traditional tax-and-spend socialist government with better TikTok videos.”Burnham rejected that characterisation, saying: “We are not that already … It’s not the case that we aren’t going to take difficult decisions.”In a critical week for the economy, the Bank of England is preparing for a decision on interest rates on Thursday against the backdrop of rising inflationary pressures from soaring oil and gas prices.With headline inflation drifting further from its 2% target, financial markets predict a one-in-five chance of a quarter-point rise from the current level of 3.75% as Threadneedle Street comes under pressure to take action. The City expects at least four increases to 4.75% next year.Economists said there were signs that underlying inflation remained in check amid a cooling UK jobs market.Inflationin the service sector of the economy, which is closely monitored by the Bank, remained unchanged at 3.4%. Core inflation – which excludes volatile items such as energy and food – also held steady at 2.6%.Official figures on Tuesday showed aslowdown in wage growthand rise in unemployment. The Bank has previously said a cooling jobs market could help limit the risk of stubbornly high inflation becoming entrenched.However, as the fallout from the Middle East war intensifies, economists said inflation in the UK could continue to climb closer to 4%, heaping pressure on the government and the Bank to take action.Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at Wealth Club, said: “Given this ramp-up in consumer prices, the pressure on the Bank of England to raise rates is mounting, although a hold at 3.75% is still expected tomorrow.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It feels like Groundhog Day, with consumers once again feeling the pinch due to geopolitical events far beyond their control.”As fighting across the Middle East intensifies, the global oil price has soared to more than $106 a barrel.According to the latest inflation snapshot, theOffice for National Statisticssaid the increase in the headline rate in August was driven by a 23% increase in motor fuel prices. The average petrol price rose by 9.1p between July and August to 161.3p a litre, the highest level since November 2022. Diesel prices rose by 14.2p to 181.8p a litre.Air fares also rose sharply, with an increase of 6.2% between July and August, particularly for long-haul routes. Rising crude oil and fuel prices also drove up the cost of raw material and the price of goods leaving factories.The sharp rise in energy prices pushed theEuropean Central Bank to raise interest rateslast week, while financial markets predicted the US Federal Reserve would raise borrowing costs on Wednesday for the first time since 2023.Bond markets have been thrown into a tailspin, with intense selling pressure pushing the yield – in effect the interest rate – on US government bondsabove 5% for the first time since 2023and driving long-term UK government borrowing costs to thehighest levels in decades.The renewed squeeze on the cost of living will intensify the calls on the chancellor,John Healey, to use the 28 October budget to give breathing space to British households reeling from years of soaring prices for energy, food and other everyday items.Richard Carter, the head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot, said: “Today’s figures are a kick in the teeth for an administration that wants to make easing the cost of living its central mission.“The budget is quickly coming into focus and with borrowing costs continuing to climb for the UK, measures are going to be limited and thus growth will remain challenged.”Explore more on these topicsInflationEconomicsInterest ratesBank of EnglandUK cost of living crisisUS-Israel war on IranOffice for National StatisticsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Former French culture minister goes on trial over corruption charges | Rachida Dati | The Guardian
description: Rachida Dati accused of lobbying for carmaker Renault-Nissan when she was member of European parliament
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Rachida Dati accused of lobbying for carmaker Renault-Nissan when she was member of European parliament
Content: Rachida Dati arriving at court in Paris on Wednesday.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersView image in fullscreenRachida Dati arriving at court in Paris on Wednesday.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersRachida DatiFormer French culture minister goes on trial over corruption chargesRachida Dati accused of lobbying for carmaker Renault-Nissan when she was member of European parliamentAngelique Chrisafisin ParisWed 16 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRachida Dati, a former French culture minister, has gone on trial in Paris on corruption charges linked to dealings with the Renault-Nissan carmaking group.Dati, 60, is accused of illegal lobbying when she accepted €900,000 (£770,000) in lawyer’s fees from a Netherlands-based subsidiary of Renault-Nissan while she was a member of the European parliament. The court will have to decide what the money was for.Dati’s legal team denied all corruption allegations, saying she worked “exclusively” as a lawyer for the Renault-Nissan subsidiary. French prosecutors argue that she was instead paid to lobby for the carmaking group, an activity that is banned for members of the European parliament. Prosecutors said there was a lack of evidence to show Dati had carried out legal work.Dati was placed under investigation in 2019 on suspicion of illegally lobbying for Renault-Nissan between October 2009 and February 2013, when she was an MEP.Dati is on trial withCarlos Ghosn, the disgraced former Renault-Nissan chief, who will be tried in absentia. Ghosn, 72, was detained in Japan in November 2018 amid allegations of financial misconduct in a separate case involving a plot to falsify records about his personal pay in order to enrich himself. He dodged trial in Japan after escaping to Lebanonin an audio equipment case. He has denied all wrongdoing in the Japan case as well as in the Dati case.French prosecutors argue that a legal services contract signed in 2009 between Dati and Ghosn, in which Dati was paid an annual fee of €300,000, was used to disguise lobbying work. Investigators obtained the contract in 2019 during a search of Renault’s headquarters after Ghosn’s arrest in Japan.Dati, 60, who is the district mayor of the 7th arrondissement in Paris, is one of the most prominent figures on the French right. She was the first woman of north African and Muslim heritage to hold a major French government post when she was appointed justice minister by the rightwing president Nicolas Sarkozy. She returned to government under Emmanuel Macron, as culture minister.Dati redefined political celebrity in France, and has said growing up as the second of 11 children on a low-income housing estate on the outskirts of Chalon-sur-Saône in Burgundy gave her a greater understanding of the French electorate. Sheran for mayor of Parisearlier this year, but lost to the SocialistEmmanuel Grégoire.If convicted, Dati faces up to 10 years in prison and a fine of up to €450,000. She could also face a five-year ban on holding public office.Dati’s lawyers said: “Unfounded allegations of influence peddling in the European parliament stem from an artificial intellectual construct devised by the prosecution.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn a separate investigation, Dati has been accused of accepting nearly €300,000 in undeclared payments from the energy group GDF Suez, also while an MEP. Prosecutors said last year they were looking into reports Dati failed to declare jewellery and watches worth €420,000 upon taking ministerial office.She has denied any wrongdoing in all cases.Explore more on these topicsRachida DatiFranceEuropeRenaultNissanAutomotive industryCarlos GhosnnewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic lands deal in $31bn datacentre in western Queensland, David Crisafulli says | Datacentres - Australia | The Guardian
description: Premier describes deal as ‘major win’ that will deliver more jobs for the state and put more energy into its grid
Author: Andrew Messenger
Headline: Premier describes deal as ‘major win’ that will deliver more jobs for the state and put more energy into its grid
Content: Anthropic’s plan to build a datacentre in Queensland was announced by premier David Crisafulli on Wednesday.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenAnthropic’s plan to build a datacentre in Queensland was announced by premier David Crisafulli on Wednesday.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersDatacentres - AustraliaAnthropic lands deal in $31bn datacentre in western Queensland, David Crisafulli saysPremier describes deal as ‘major win’ that will deliver more jobs for the state and put more energy into its gridFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAndrew MessengerWed 16 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 03.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropic, the AI company behind thelarge language model Claude, has done a deal to lease the site of its first Australian datacentre in western Queensland.The $31.9bn datacentre will be the largest of its kind in Australia, according to planning documents.The state premier,David Crisafulli, announced that Anthropic would buy into the first stage of the project in parliament on Wednesday.Crisafulli told parliament that he had met Anthropic during a trade mission and had outlined “whyQueenslandwas the place to invest, with energy security and a streamlined approval process”.“To have secured Anthropic’s first major investment in Australia is a massive show of confidence in Queensland,” he said. “It’s a major win that will deliver more jobs and put more energy into Queensland’s grid.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe proposed Western Downs digital park is to be built by Singapore-based Zerra DC near Dalby, north-west of Toowoomba, and will connect to the Braemar power station. Its first stage is planned to open next year.The project is expected to be built in four stages, according to documents filed with the Western Downs regional council last month. It has yet to be approved by the local council.The Anthropic section of the project will sit on about 725.5 hectares of land, now occupied in part by a feedlot.Western Downs mayor, Andrew Smith, said the council would undertake a “thorough and comprehensive assessment process” of the proposed centre.“The length of the process will depend on a range of factors, including referral requirements, any requests for further information and community participation during public notification,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYour photos, your words and your work: Why is Labor making it easier for AI companies to take them for free? | Holly RankinRead moreQueensland, along with the Northern Territory, rejected a commonwealth push in July to makenew AI centres use renewable energy. The state government claims to have won a carve-out from a national deal, allowing it to use the state’s coal generators to power them.Crisafulli said Anthony Albanese had made a “commonsense decision” to “allow Queensland to chart its own path for power supply”.“[Datacentre development] must add energy generation to the grid and drive down power prices for Queenslanders,” he said.“It must protect local water supplies, and it must respect the communities where these centres go … we’ll do it in the right locations, and we’ll do it in the right way. Communities will have a say, just as they now do for projects like wind, solar, and batteries.”The Queensland centre will be used to power “inference” – answering questions – rather than training Anthropic’s AI model.Anthropic signed aMemorandum of Understandingwith the commonwealth government in April.The Albanese government is weighing up a proposal to give AI companiesaccess to Australian creatives’ works by default– a deal independent senator David Pocock said would throw creatives “under the bus” in pursuit of datacentre funding.Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, on Tuesdayreiterated his call for a slowdown of AI developmentamid rising concern about artificial intelligence.Explore more on these topicsDatacentres - AustraliaAnthropicQueenslandAI (artificial intelligence)Queensland politicsDavid CrisafulliEnergynewsShareReuse this content

title: USMNT to call up 16-year-old Cavan Sullivan for upcoming friendlies | USA | The Guardian
description: Sullivan has scored six goals and added eight assists for Philadelphia since MLS restarted after the World Cup
Author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Headline: Sullivan has scored six goals and added eight assists for Philadelphia since MLS restarted after the World Cup
Content: Cavan Sullivan most recently scored two goals with an assist against San Diego.Photograph: Orlando Ramirez/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCavan Sullivan most recently scored two goals with an assist against San Diego.Photograph: Orlando Ramirez/Getty ImagesUSAUSMNT to call up 16-year-old Cavan Sullivan for upcoming friendliesSullivan has six goals and eight assists post-World CupUS play four games in upcoming windowPablo Iglesias MaurerWed 16 Sep 2026 15.25 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 15.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePhiladelphia Union midfielder Cavan Sullivan is set to earn his first international call-up with the United States men’s national team later this month, a source with knowledge of the roster told the Guardian on Wednesday. The source requested anonymity as they were not authorized to discuss the roster.The US will face Chile, Peru, Mexico and Canada in late September and early October, with US head coach Mauricio Pochettino expected to announce his roster on Thursday morning. ESPN’s Jeff Carlisle was first to report news of Sullivan’s inclusion.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWatching Cavan Sullivan, excitement is tempered by memories of hypetrains pastRead moreSullivan, whoturned pro at age 14, has long been touted as a potential US international. His play since MLS resumed action after this summer’s World Cup has been a revelation, with six goals and eight assists in that period. That has earned him a look from Pochettino. Earlier this month the player drew Pochettino’s attention in an entirely different way, when Sullivan suggested in a podcast interview that he might have proven a valuable contributor for the US this summer at the World Cup, where they crashed out in the last 16 against Belgium.“We are watching everything, we are seeing everything,” Pochettinotold reportersat the time. “And of course, we want players with talent, players that feel brave, feel confident, but not [that] feel things that they still don’t show or they [haven’t] earned. I think you only are entitled to talk a little bit out of order if you are Messi. If you’ve won eight Ballon d’Ors, OK, you can talk with a certain arrogance.”If Sullivan plays in this upcoming window he will become the fourth-youngest player ever to earn a cap for the USMNT (The youngest being Freddy Adu, who was several months younger than Sullivan when he debuted in a 2006 friendly against Canada). Sullivan did manage to break another of Adu’s long-standing marks: he became the youngest player in the history of any major North American professional sport to appear in a match when he first took the field for the Union in 2024.Sullivan signed his deal with the Union in May of that year. His contract that includes a transfer to Manchester City when he turns 18.Explore more on these topicsUSAPhiladelphia UnionUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Chiefs star Travis Kelce is named among victims of $35m Ponzi scheme | Travis Kelce | The Guardian
description: Prosecutors named Kelce a victim of the scheme as Siddharth Jawahar was sentenced to 11 years in prison after pleading guilty to three counts of wire fraud
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Prosecutors named Kelce a victim of the scheme as Siddharth Jawahar was sentenced to 11 years in prison after pleading guilty to three counts of wire fraud
Content: Travis Kelce began his 14th season with the Kansas City Chiefs earlier this week.Photograph: Charlie Riedel/APView image in fullscreenTravis Kelce began his 14th season with the Kansas City Chiefs earlier this week.Photograph: Charlie Riedel/APTravis KelceChiefs star Travis Kelce is named among victims of $35m Ponzi schemeSiddharth Jawahar gets 11 years in prison for fraudProsecutors mention Kelce without further commentSeveral pro athletes said to have invested in Swiftarc firmAgenciesWed 16 Sep 2026 15.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 15.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce is among the victims of a Ponzi scheme that took in more ⁠than $35m from unsuspecting investors, a Missouri prosecutor said.The prosecutor mentioned Kelce in court Tuesday as 38-year-old Siddharth Jawahar was ⁠sentenced to 11 years ⁠in prison. ​The US attorney’s office of the eastern district of Missouri said Jawahar pleaded guilty to three counts of wire fraud in ⁠US district court in St Louis in January.Man posed as 49ers player to scam women out of $1.3m, FBI saysRead moreHe also was ordered to pay $31.35m in restitution.Television station KMOV reported that the ⁠prosecutor brought up Kelce’s name without further comment. It is not known when Kelce made ​the investment or how much he ‌spent.According to a news ‌release from the US attorney’s office, Jawahar ran a Texas-based investment company, Swiftarc Capital LLC, ‌that in 2015 began taking money from investors. He put all of the money he accepted into a single investment, which dropped in value. He did not notify investors of the loss, told them they were making money and took money from new investors to repay the earlier investors.He also used the investment funds ‌to support what prosecutors called “an extravagant lifestyle” filled with private jets, luxury living, elegant dining and memberships in private clubs.Jawahar was given more than $35m but invested only about $10m from July 2016 through December 2023, per the news release.Kelce, 36, is unlikely to be the only athlete involved in the Ponzi scheme.A 2021articlein Forbes about the growing financial portfolio of NBA guard Gary Harris incorporated ⁠several comments from Harris about his investments, which included Swiftarc Ventures Labs ​Fund. Jawahar was the ​co-founder and managing partner, and Harris ​also spoke of how much he had learned from Jawahar. The Forbes article ​mentioned other athletes ‌who had invested, ​naming Kelce ​and NBA players Tim Hardaway Jr and Mason Plumlee.Kelce, Hardaway and Harris all have career earnings in excess of $111m each, according to Spotrac.In July, Kelce married Taylor Swift, who had a net worth of $2.1bn on the day of their wedding, according to Forbes.After speculation about his potential retirement swirled last season, Kelce signed a one-year extension to return for his 14th campaign with the Chiefs. Kansas City beat the Denver Broncos in theirseason openeron Monday.Explore more on these topicsTravis KelceNFLUS sportsKansas City ChiefsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Colin Kaepernick says NFL owners are colluding against Macklemore after Ed Sheeran tour ban | Colin Kaepernick | The Guardian
description: Colin Kaepernick has accused NFL owners of colluding against Macklemore after the rapper was removed from Ed Sheeran’s tour over comments on Palestine
Author: Tom Lutz
Headline: Colin Kaepernick has accused NFL owners of colluding against Macklemore after the rapper was removed from Ed Sheeran’s tour over comments on Palestine
Content: Colin Kaepernick has become a social activist since the end of his NFL career.Photograph: Kevin Wolf/APView image in fullscreenColin Kaepernick has become a social activist since the end of his NFL career.Photograph: Kevin Wolf/APColin KaepernickColin Kaepernick says NFL owners are colluding against Macklemore after Ed Sheeran tour banRapper dropped from tour after pro-Palestine remarksFormer NFL star settled case over collusion in 2019Tom LutzWed 16 Sep 2026 15.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 15.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleColin Kaepernick has accused NFL owners of colluding against Macklemore after the rapperwas removed from Ed Sheeran’s tourover comments he made onstage about Palestine.Kaepernick,whose NFL career was effectively endedin the wake of his protests against police violence, says he sees parallels between himself and Macklemore.Colin Kaepernick knelt 10 years ago. America responded with a clear warning to Black people | Howard BryantRead more“The part that I hope people appreciate and take away in this moment is what [New England Patriots owner] Robert Kraft and what they’re saying by denying Macklemore the opportunity to go out and perform with Ed Sheeran is they are willing to collude,” Kaepernick said on theMeidasTouch podcast. “The [NFL owners] are openly colluding.”Macklemore had been a supporting act on Ed Sheeran’s tour. During an appearance at New Jersey’s MetLife stadium he told the crowd he wanted the people of Gaza and “the occupied West Bank” to know “we have not forgotten about them”. He also said “free Palestine”.Kraft, who is a longtime supporter of Israel, and several other owners of NFL stadiums the tour was due to visit said they would not let Macklemore play at their venues. This prompted Macklemore to be removed from the tour. All four supporting acts for upcoming dates of Sheeran’s tourhave since withdrawnin support of Macklemore.During the 2016 NFL season, Kaepernick began kneeling during the national anthem in protest at police brutality and social injustice. Despite being in his prime, Kaepernick was not signed by any NFL team after he left the San Francisco 49ers at the end of that season, and he has not played in the league since. He filed a grievance against the NFL in 2017, andthe case was settled in 2019with terms of the agreement undisclosed.Kaepernick told the MeidasTouch podcast that Kraft and other NFL owners had tried to hound outMacklemorein a similar way they did to him.“When we filed the grievance, it was like, well, the owners wouldn’t do that,” Kaepernick said. “Everybody just wants to win within theNFL. And the realization is, no. They want to protect their interests. They want to protect their power. They want to protect their money. And they also want people to know that if you take an action that they don’t agree with, they will come for you.”Kraft has said his decision to ban Macklemore from the Patriots’ stadium was due to his “recent actions” and “a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community”.Kaepernick said others may find themselves in a similar situation to Macklemore in the future.“It may not touch you today, at some point it’s going to come knocking on your doorstep or someone you love’s doorstep and that’s not the moment to be able to take action,” he said. “We should be taking action actively right now.”Elsewhere on Wednesday, NBA star Kyrie Irving said he would pay a $11,492 fine the NFL gave to Azeez Al-Shair after he displayed the name of a Palestinian girl killed byIsraelduring a game. Al-Shair did so using a face marking banned by the league.Explore more on these topicsColin KaepernickMacklemoreEd SheeranNFLIsraelPalestineUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s payback time’: the WNBA-leading Lynx are on the hunt for title redemption | Minnesota Lynx | The Guardian
description: Ten seasons ago, Minnesota entered the playoffs with a chip on their shoulders and won a championship. Can they channel the same energy this year?
Author: Stephanie Kaloi
Headline: Ten seasons ago, Minnesota entered the playoffs with a chip on their shoulders and won a championship. Can they channel the same energy this year?
Content: Rookie sensation Olivia Miles is looking to lead the Minnesota Lynx to their first WNBA title since 2017.Photograph: Ellen Schmidt/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRookie sensation Olivia Miles is looking to lead the Minnesota Lynx to their first WNBA title since 2017.Photograph: Ellen Schmidt/Getty ImagesMinnesota Lynx‘It’s payback time’: the WNBA-leading Lynx are on the hunt for title redemptionTen seasons ago, Minnesota entered the playoffs with a chip on their shoulders and won a championship. Can they channel the same energy this year?Stephanie KaloiWed 16 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWilliams Arena (now known as The Barn) in Minneapolis was packed to capacity on 4 October 2017, when Cheryl Reeve sent Sylvia Fowles into Game 5 of theWNBAfinals and watched her take off. Reeve, chasing her fourth championship after losing out in 2016, had learned her lesson the previous year, when she put Fowles back into a finals game too late.Fowles answered the call. She racked up 17 points and broke her own WNBA rebounds record with 20. Her effort was matched by that of Maya Moore, with 18 points and 10 rebounds; Lindsay Whalen, who had 17 points and eight assists; and Seimone Augustus, who added another 14 points, six assists and six rebounds. The Lynxshowed out, clinching the franchise’s fourth title, with Fowles named finals MVP.The 2017 team brought the energy because there “was a chip on everybody’s shoulders”, recalls Natasha Howard, a forward on that championship-winning squad. That finals matchup between the Lynx and the Los Angeles Sparks was a repeat of the 2016 edition, when the Candace Parker-led Sparks took home the crown.Cathy Engelbert’s WNBA tenure: the wins and losses that defined her seven yearsRead more“It was agoodseason,” Howard tells the Guardian. She looks back on that game and more in her memoir The Vision Through My Lens: My Life in Basketball and Beyond,out this month. “That season was like … we came outhungry. We was hungry because we kind of felt some time away when we lost against, in 2016, against the Sparks. So we were like, ‘It’s payback time.’ And the whole season, that whole season, we were just giving every team the business.”Ten seasons later, Howard is back with the Lynx, having returned this season as a free agent and earning All-Star honors. Drawing the parallel from 2017 to 2026 isn’t difficult to do. Just as they were then, the Lynx are hungry. And just as they did then, they are giving everybody in the league “the business”. Minnesota have been virtually unstoppable this year, having led the league for nearly all of the season and sitting in first place at 31-9 with four games left in the regular season. They can clinch the top playoff seed as soon as Friday.But there’s a question that hangs over the head of the roster, the coaches, the front office, even the fans: can they take things all the way?Minnesota have been here before. Their loss in the 2024 finals to the New York Liberty was a heavy – andcontroversial, given how Reeve later said the title was “stolen” from her team by bad officiating – blow. In 2025, the Lynx entered the playoffs as the top seed, but theybowed outin the conference semi-finals after star forward Napheesa Collier injured both ankles and the Phoenix Mercury won three games in a row.But, Howard says, they’ve been here before.“I feel like Minnesota could have won the championship last season,” said Howard, who played for the Indiana Fever in 2025. “So right now, it’s a chip on everybody’s shoulders, and for me, I see how Minnesota played last season and what they went through, and so, yeah, I’m going to have a chip on my shoulder as well because I’m on this team now.”“Everybody thinks Minnesota is just a regular-season team … they think Minnesota is going to fold when it’s playoff time,” she continued. “But this is going to be a different story.”View image in fullscreenThe Minnesota Lynx bounced back from losing in the 2016 WNBA finals to beat the LA Sparks for the 2017 title.Photograph: Jordan Johnson/NBAE/Getty ImagesClare Duwelius, the basketball operations coordinator for the Lynx in 2017 who is now executive vice-president and general manager of the three-on-three league Unrivaled, thinks the Lynx have what they need to win. While acknowledging the obvious – she previously worked for Minnesota, and Collier is a co-founder and co-owner of Unrivaled – Duwelius also pointed out the 2017 season wasn’t an easy one for the Lynx in terms of that frequent WNBA disruption: injuries.“Whalen went through her hand surgery, and we were rolling at the beginning of the season, and then that was our first kind of turbulence,” she said. “Seimone had a long kind of runway of having knee problems, and she was battling that all season long. It was just those kinds of things that were kind of ever-present, and that’s why I think this particular championship was so meaningful, because everyone had to work harder.”The Game 5 loss in 2016 was tough, and the team didn’t want it to be the focal point for 2017, she added.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“But, definitely, it was in the back of everyone’s mind trying to avenge that heartbreaker,” Duwelius added. “So I think that’s why the regular season was kind of a microcosm of what we wanted to produce ultimately in the playoffs and in the finals.”Of Reeve, who is the winningest coach in WNBA history even without a championship in the last 10 seasons, Duwelius was steadfast in her praise and defense. “Cheryl is one of, in my opinion, the best to ever do it. Not because of being the winningest – itisbecause she’s the winningest coach, but it’s what she’s able to do with whatever roster she has. That’s what sets her apart,” she said. “She just is really special and unique in the way that she can maximize their output. And I think that’s what sets her apart.”Olivia Miles: the goggled wonder woman pulverizing WNBA opponents in her rookie seasonRead moreThis year’s roster includes rookie Olivia Miles, who was drafted as the No 2 overall pick by the Lynx this year after spending one season at TCU and four at Notre Dame. To say Miles has infused the Lynx with an unexpected energy is selling her short – it’s fair to credit her as the force who has pushed the Lynx to where they are all season long. She leads Minnesota in points (19.7) and assists (6.0), has shattered several league rookie records as the runaway favorite for rookie of the year and is even being mentioned in MVP conversations.Back in 2017, Miles was just starting her freshman year of high school at New Jersey’s Blair Academy. There’s no telling what she was doing that October night when the Lynx last won it all, but it wouldn’t be surprising if she was watching the game. It’s certainly not surprising she’s now the leader of a championship-caliber team, even if it is her first season in the WNBA.Miles “was the person that was like the adult in the room,” when she came down to Miami as part of The Future is Unrivaled college summit, Duwelius said. “Whenever we sat down, I knew I could trust what she was telling me. … She’s kind of wise beyond her years and really smart. She comes from a really smart family, and her parents [Yakubu, a software developer who immigrated to the US from Jamaica, and Maria, a chemical engineer] are obviously very accomplished, [and] she just has that maturity to her.”That maturity and trust is why Miles and Reeve “have such a special relationship”, Duwelius added, “knowing both of them and how they operate.” It also could be what takes the Lynx exactly where they want to go.Explore more on these topicsMinnesota LynxWNBAUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: De Cuyper and Brighton pile on pain for Manchester United with comeback | Carabao Cup | The Guardian
description: United scored two early goals but lost 3-2 to Brighton in the Carabao Cup, following up derby defeat and JJ Gabriel’s request to leave
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: United scored two early goals but lost 3-2 to Brighton in the Carabao Cup, following up derby defeat and JJ Gabriel’s request to leave
Content: Maxim De Cuyper scored what proved to be Brighton’s winner three minutes after coming on.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Nigel French/Apl/SportsphotoView image in fullscreenMaxim De Cuyper scored what proved to be Brighton’s winner three minutes after coming on.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Nigel French/Apl/SportsphotoCarabao CupDe Cuyper and Brighton pile on pain for Manchester United with comebackJamie Jacksonat Old TraffordWed 16 Sep 2026 17.18 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAcross four days Manchester United have lost the 199th derby against Manchester City, were told by JJ Gabrielthat he wants to leave, and now they have been knocked out of the Carabao Cup by Brighton.Capitulating after being 2-0 up may be the pick of these dizzying blows, as the prolonged boos at the final whistle suggested, and doing so ends a proud 50-year record: the last time the same lead at Old Trafford ended in defeat was Tottenham’s 3-2 win in September 1976.Manchester United 2-3 Brighton, Coventry 1-3 Aston Villa and more: Carabao Cup clockwatch – as it happenedRead moreWhen Marcus Rashford skated in with the chance to take the tie to 3-3 late on, there was no surprise he hit Jason Steele rather than the net.Towards the end, Matheus Cunha was thrown on to join Bruno Fernandes, also a late substitute, illustrating how desperate Michael Carrick was. Yet Charalampos Kostoulas went close to scoring a second for Brighton, as United could not find a route to cancelling out Maxim De Cuyper’s 69th-minute strike that proved the winner.After taking only four points from 12 in the league, serious questions will now be asked about where Carrick’s team are heading; they have to beat Fulham on Sunday to start correctinga dismal start to the season. The manager already looks haunted and he talked afterwards of not caring about being under pressure.View image in fullscreenUnited’s evening started brightly enough, with the 19-year-old Shea Lacey scoring on his first start for the club.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersCarrick said the injusticesuffered against City on Sundaywould give his side an edge and Shea Lacey provided one when decorating a full debut with the sweetest of goals. The 19-year-old shimmied in Brighton’s area, beating Jaouen Hadjam before firing beyond a helpless Jason Steele. As impressive here was Benjamin Sesko’s hold-up work in the buildup as this allowed red shirts to flood forward, Youri Tielemans feeding Lacey.This was eight minutes in and less than 120 seconds later Mason Mount doubled United’s advantage. Rashford’s pace and drive took him clear along the left, again inside the area. A trailing Steele boot saved the No 9’s effort but the ball bounced into Mount’s path and he drove home, via the turf, for a first goal since a winat Wolves last December.Lacey’s strike drew a Carrick grin and delight from Mount, and you wondered how Gabriel – earmarked for the squad in this game, with the chance to become United’s youngest player – felt.Brighton had lost only one of their previous five visits here and a flying start to the league campaign has Fabian Hürzeler’s team in fifth. Yetthe 5-0 hammering of Coventryon Sunday already seemed distant as United continued to dominate.View image in fullscreenCharalampos Kostoulas started Brighton’s comeback just before half-time.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAOlivier Boscagli hit a corner straight out, summing up the visitors’ start, before Matt O’Riley forced Ayden Heaven into an error that led to another. This presaged a Seagulls renaissance that featured a lightning Malick Yalcouyé break but, clear in on the debutant Karl Darlow’s goal, the Ivorian spooned wide. The No 35 lacked the sharpness evident in a Rashford nutmeg of Chema Andrés which embarrassed the Brighton man and when Pascal Gross blasted over this was one more chance spurned by Hürzeler’s men.But then came a goal – and real hope – for Brighton. Hadjam’s long left-right diagonal cut United’s rearguard clean out, and the slumbering Heaven allowed Kostoulas to scamper free, the striker beating Darlow through his legs.Carrick, having beaten onlyIpswich in the leagueandSabah in Europeso far this season, needed a win, and as United (not under him) exited at the earliest opportunity in both domestic cups last season, progressing to at least a second tie in one of them would be welcome.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA wild Tielemans long-range shot that ballooned over failed to restore United’s two-goal lead but at least the home team were tapping the ball about, operating in Brighton territory, moving the visitors around.View image in fullscreenUnited were frustrated by Pascal Gross’s leveller for Brighton, but things were about to get even worse for Michael Carrick’s side.Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/ReutersA Sesko burst from halfway had the onrushing Steele hacking away just in time. United were in control. But the question was: could they maintain this and register the type of mature, accomplished display that would show an evolution in Carrick’s team? Sesko, in yards of space, dawdling and being dispossessed when a simple ball would have fed Lacey, suggested not.A loose Rashford pass aimed for Sesko hinted at the same. More promising was a pass for Noussair Mazraoui as he drove into the area along the left channel, as was the subsequent corner that created an opening Tielemans narrowly missed.Quick GuideCarabao Cup roundup: Fleetwood handed win over BladesShowA 57th-minute Rhys Norrington-Davies own goal sentFleetwoodinto the last 16 of the Carabao Cup for the first time as the League Two club stunned their Championship opponents,Sheffield United, 1-0 at Highbury, before pulling a home tie against Arsenal out in the draw.Matt Lawlor’s side, unbeaten now in nine games in all competitions, had another Danny Andrew effort ruled out for offside and twice hit the woodwork in a dominant second-half display. It was a searching left-wing cross from Andrew that Norrington-Davies nodded beyond Michael Cooper to give the fourth-tier club a historic victory.Tom Cannon did get the ball in the net for Chris Wilder’s visitors who lined up with only four starting survivors from last Friday’s 1-0 league defeat by Wolves. But a flag for offside was raised before the striker slid the ball into the net.United started positively and Ollie Arblaster had a goalbound effort blocked after only 36 seconds. But Mark Helm forced Cooper into a seventh-minute save before the former United forward Ched Evans put his follow-up header narrowly wide.Jay Lynch denied Joe Rothwell as the visitors attacked again but Cooper was the busier, saving from Lewis McCann and Crispin McLean.Helm’s dipping right-foot effort from 18 yards grazed the top netting as Fleetwood finished the first half in the ascendancy and they deserved their break from Norrington-Davies’ own goal.United finally came to life in the last 10 minutes with Lynch brilliantly denied Sydie Peck and Ben Brereton Díaz, while Cannon saw a goalbound strike superbly blocked.Everton’s forgotten man Charly Alcaraz stepped up when his side needed some inspiration to score the only goal in the win overWolvesthree minutes after coming on. The Argentinian had played just 14 minutes all season but belied his lack of match sharpness with a quick switch of the ball from one foot to the other to guide a left-footed shot past the former Everton goalkeeper João Virgínia in the 80th minute.It also represented a minor success for Tyler Dibling, whose career has not really taken off since his £35m move from Southampton just over a year ago, as he claimed the assist at the end his most encouraging performance for the club. Everton's reward is a home tie against Newcastle.Press AssociationWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.But then calamity. Diogo Dalot’s hoofed clearance failed to find Sesko as Luka Vuskovic headed to Gross; Brighton’s captain made room and netted with ease. Even worse followed. Brighton raided along the right, Kostoulas’s cross pinged off Mazraoui’s backside, and there was De Cuyper to finish.On 72 minutes Carrick played his ace, introducing Fernandes for Mount, then followed up with Cunha. But United remained toothless.Explore more on these topicsCarabao CupManchester UnitedBrighton & Hove Albionmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Mets fans celebrate home run against own team as returning hero Alonso goes yard | New York Mets | The Guardian
description: Pete Alonso launched his 300th career homer Tuesday night, a tying shot in the ninth inning against his former team
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Pete Alonso launched his 300th career homer Tuesday night, a tying shot in the ninth inning against his former team
Content: Pete Alonso acknowledges the crowd after hitting his home run.Photograph: Seth Wenig/APView image in fullscreenPete Alonso acknowledges the crowd after hitting his home run.Photograph: Seth Wenig/APNew York MetsMets fans celebrate home run against own team as returning hero Alonso goes yardSlugger ties game in ninth with 414ft shotReaction irks Mets pitcher Sean ManaeaAlonso’s departure annoyed many Mets fansAgenciesWed 16 Sep 2026 07.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 09.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePete Alonso launched his 300th career home run Tuesday night, a tying shot in the ninth inning against his former team, and Coby Mayo’s inside-the-park homer in the 11th sent the Baltimore Orioles to a 7-5 victory at Citi Field.“There’s a lot of history here with me,” Alonso said after receiving a beer shower from his Baltimore teammates. “It doesn’t matter where and when, I just want to help the team win. I’m just really, really happy for us to come back the way we did.”The Orioles were two outs from a defeat that would have dropped them four games behind Cleveland for the last American League playoff spot when Alonso hit a 414ft solo drive off Kodai Senga to tie the score 3-3.A fired-up Alonso, who hit a club-record 264 homers for the Mets before signing with the Orioles last December, spiked his bat toward the Baltimore dugout. He rounded the bases as the home crowd roared their approval.Fans chanted his name until Alonso emerged from the dugout for a curtain call. Then chants of “Fire Stearns” began, aimed at Mets president of baseball operations David Stearns, who chose not to offer Alonso a long-term deal before his departure to Baltimore. Alonso has thrived with Baltimore while Jorge Polanco, the player supposed to replace him at first base for the Mets, struggled badly before his season ended prematurely through injury. The Mets, who had been tipped to be a World Series contender,have one of the worst recordsin the majors this season.“Everyone in the dugout was saying go out there,” Alonso said. “And they were right.”The rare curtain call on the road continued an outpouring of support from Mets fans for Alonso over the past two nights – and apparently annoyed at least one of his former teammates.“As the 2026 Mets, I know we have definitely underperformed. But we are – the guys in here work their [tails] off every single day and to have that kind of reaction to an opposing player – could be anybody – is crazy to me,” said New York pitcher Sean Manaea, who started Tuesday night. “Again, I’ve got nothing but respect for Pete. But yeah, just never seen anything like that before.“Pete’s not here. He’s just not here. So, I know everybody loves him. He’s the man. But, yeah, he’s not here. So, to see the reaction from the fans like that, I don’t know, it’s just different.”Alonso received a two-minute tribute video before the Orioles’ 2-1 win on Monday night. He was showered with a thunderous ovation before his first at-bat minutes later, when he was accompanied to the plate by Layla, one of his walk-up songs, as “Welcome Back, Pete!” flashed next to his picture on the scoreboard.He got standing ovations before each of his final three plate appearances as well on Monday – when rookie pitcher Jonah Tong was booed after walking Alonso in the third – and warm receptions prior to his first three at-bats Tuesday.“I appreciate all the support for all the years I’ve been here, all the life I’ve lived here,” Alonso said Tuesday night. “Obviously, they’re recognizing that and they appreciate that. It’s a two-way street. Really appreciate it.”Alonso was given his home run ball from the trio of Long Islanders — Michael Shaw, Nick Maldarella and Chris Makarius — who teamed up to catch the drive.“On the way here, we were saying we’re going to catch his 300th home run,” Maldarella said. “And sure enough, man. It’s crazy.”Alonso signed a bat and a ball for each man in return, and offered them tickets and batting-practice access at Camden Yards in Baltimore next season.“Thank you, guys,” Alonso said to the trio outside the visitors’ clubhouse. “You guys are so kind. Thank you so much.”Alonso also posed for a group picture.“I mean, who doesn’t love Pete?” Shaw said.Explore more on these topicsNew York MetsMLBBaseballUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Glory at 11,000ft: Cusco’s Cienciano aim to bring Peru continental success once again | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Cusco is known for tourism. But the city’s biggest football team is chasing a repeat of a South American title that caused shockwaves more than 20 years ago
Author: Justo Robles
Headline: Cusco is known for tourism. But the city’s biggest football team is chasing a repeat of a South American title that caused shockwaves more than 20 years ago
Content: Cienciano celebrates during their first-leg victory over Montevideo City Torque.Photograph: Paloma Del Solar/EPAView image in fullscreenCienciano celebrates during their first-leg victory over Montevideo City Torque.Photograph: Paloma Del Solar/EPASoccerGlory at 11,000ft: Cusco’s Cienciano aim to bring Peru continental success once againCusco is known for tourism. But the city’s biggest football team is chasing a repeat of a South American title that caused shockwaves more than 20 years agoJusto Roblesin CuscoWed 16 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was one of those nights when Cusco shifted the spotlight from its tourism engine to football. At a stadium named after Garcilaso de la Vega – celebrated for his chronicles about the Inca empire – about 30,000 people gathered to witness something far more immediate than nearby Machu Picchu, arguably the best-known archaeological site in theAmericas.Cusco’s biggest team, Cienciano, were set to play in the first leg of the Copa Sudamericana quarter-final, 23 years after they became the first Peruvian club to lift an international trophy.“Don’t you love a story that reminds you that you were once the best among the best?” said Victor Estrada, 44, clapping feverishly as Cienciano’s starting XI entered the field to warm up.“This is not just about football. This is about who we are; you can’t be from Cusco and not be a Cienciano fan. We were born a small club, but anything is possible with Cienciano and the Copa Sudamericana.”As is the case with football in large parts of Latin America, British immigrants had much to do with Cienciano’s origins. An Englishman, William Newell,introducedfootball to his students at Cusco’s National School of Science and Arts, which opened shortly after Peru gained independence from Spain. They founded what is now Cienciano, and the club played its first match in 1902. It remained in amateur and regional divisions for seven decades before entering the country’s professional league in the early 1970s.A few hours before Cienciano, whose home stadium is at an altitude of 11,030ft (3,353m), kicked off their quarter-final against Uruguay’s Montevideo City Torque, the school that inspired the club’s name stood empty. Its walls carried reminders that this is one of Peru’s oldest public schools from the republican era. Murals featured Copa Sudamericana trophies and players kicking a football.Outside the school, fans began arriving in droves. They carried drums and huge flags that readPapá de América(America’s Dad). These small groups made upLaFuria Roja, or theRed Fury, the official title for itsbarra brava. Cienciano’s red jerseys contrasted with the Plateresque facade of the Church of San Francisco and the cloudy sky behind them.Some fans said they were too young to remember Cienciano’s 2003 Copa Sudamericana campaign. Others grew up hearing stories about an invincible club from Cusco. In a city where history and mysticism merge, the legend was true: the International Federation of Football History & Statistics named Cienciano the best team in the world for December 2003.View image in fullscreenCusco’s proximity to Machu Picchu has brought it global recognition.Photograph: Martín Mejía/APThat year, Cienciano shifted from representing a school and a city to unifying an entire countryshaken by political instability, according to Paolo Sosa, who recently published a book about the rivalry between Cienciano and another Cusco team, Deportivo Garcilaso.“In the early 2000s, Peru was overwhelmed with corruption scandals and its morals were put into question. Then a club from outside the capital appeared to beat the greatest teams in the continent,” Sosa says. “Cienciano wrote the most epic story in the country’s sports history, and that is why, 23 years later, that memory remains more vivid than ever.”Only two other Peruvian teams have reached a final in an international competition. Universitario de Deportes and Sporting Cristal, both from Lima, were Copa Libertadores runners-up in 1972 and 1997 respectively. Then, in 2002, Conmebol introduced the Copa Sudamericana, roughly equivalent to Uefa’s Europa League. After their victory in 2003, Cienciano stunned Boca Juniors, one of the most celebrated teams in South America, in the Recopa Sudamericana, a competition pitting the winners of the Copa Sudamericana against the Copa Libertadores champions.During their 2003 Sudamericana campaign, Cienciano’s roster had an average age of 28. The club’s budget and income were small compared to Peru’s biggest teams. Cienciano had never won a national championship, yet they achieved the improbable. They beat Universidad Católica from Chile, Brazil’s Santos and Colombia’s Atlético Nacional on the way to the two-legged final, where they shocked Argentina’s River Plate. The decisive second leg was held in the Peruvian city of Arequipa, more than 310 miles (500km) south of Cusco, for capacity reasons.Last week, as Cienciano and Montevideo City Torque waited for the opening whistle, Estrada seemed lost in time and memory. He stared atLa Furia Rojaas they made a blaring entrance on the north side of the stadium. The energy was electric, infecting everyone. Estrada said he had been part ofLaFuria Rojaand traveled with them to Arequipa to see the biggest night in Cienciano’s history.“I had no money, but we were told that we could get there by train – on top of the train. I studied at Cienciano, and it was my school and my team in the eyes of the world. The winning goal made the whole journey worth it,” Estrada says.“I know some people say football is just a game, but that’s because they don’t understand how a team can define you. If Cienciano reach the final again, I will go wherever, but hopefully I won’t have to sleep at a park again.”Between 2010 and now, Cienciano didn’t attain the success many anticipated. They struggled financially, and were relegated to the second division in 2015 before they returned four years later. Despite the rise of teams such as Cusco FC and Deportivo Garcilaso,Cienciano remainone of Peru’s five most popular teams.In the first leg against Montevideo City Torque, tens of thousands of fans believed history could repeat itself. On the way to the quarter-final, Cienciano had beaten Lanús, the 2025 Copa Sudamericana champions, and Botafogo, one of Brazil’s most famous clubs.In the last five minutes, Cienciano led by two goals. Still, the crowd demanded more and urged the players forward in the hope of increasing their advantage before the away match in Uruguay, which takes place this Thursday. The chants and pressure intensified as the visitors resisted and prevented goals the locals had celebrated too early.In the stands, complaints ranged from Spanish to Quechua, the most widely spoken indigenous language in the Andean region. One chant stood out even when the referee blew the final whistle: “Sí se puede”– “Yes, we can”. For Cienciano fans, that chant captured the club’s past – and their hopes of another improbable run.Explore more on these topicsFootballPeruAmericasfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why are two college football teams playing at Wembley on Saturday? | College sports | The Guardian
description: Kansas are taking on Arizona State in the Union Jack Classic, with 60,000 and noisy fans expected at Wembley
Author: Gavin Willacy
Headline: Kansas are taking on Arizona State in the Union Jack Classic, with 60,000 and noisy fans expected at Wembley
Content: The match begins at 5pm on Saturday.Photograph: Hanover commsView image in fullscreenThe match begins at 5pm on Saturday.Photograph: Hanover commsNo Helmets RequiredCollege sportsWhy are two college football teams playing at Wembley on Saturday?Kansas are taking on Arizona State in the Union Jack Classic, with 60,000 and noisy fans expected at WembleyByNo Helmets RequiredGavin WillacyWed 16 Sep 2026 09.20 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHas London hosted college football before?There have been as many college football games played in Tanzania and Italy (one) as there have in England, and twice as many in China and Australia. It’s nearly 40 years since 6,000 or so intrigued spectators watchedRichmond Spiders beat Boston Universityin Crystal Palace. “The gray, misty ways of Richmond proved far more compatible in the Land of the Overcast Sky,” reported the Boston Globe at the time.The 1980s was a time of international expansionism for American college sports, with games in Japan, Milan and Dublin. They have returned to Ireland time and time again over the years. The College Football Classic has become an annual event at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin, where it has drawn in crowds of around 50,000 for the last five years, prompting the NFL to visit the city for the first time last September. It’s the other way round in London, where 20 years of NFL matches have paved the way for the college game.The match between Arizona State and Kansas at 5pm on Saturday – dubbed the Union Jack Classic – is an inevitable reaction to the NFL’s work in the city over the last two decades. “We move a little bit behind the NFL,” says Brett Yormark, the commissioner of the Big 12 Conference – a league of 16 of the most successful teams in college sports.“It’s important for the NFL to open up these markets before we do and develop a fanbase. The NFL have played 42 games in the UK so it seemed to be a mature enough market to bring college football here, versus breaking into a new market that might not have the appetite for the sport or the game. The timing just felt right.”Why is college football going international?Money and exposure. College sport is becoming increasingly professional and universities want to keep the cash flooding in. The top coaches are paid more than $13m a year and the players are paid substantial sums for their image rights. Arizona and Kansas pay their squads around $20m a year.Most of that money comes from TV revenue. Teams in the Big 12 bank nearly $32m annually from broadcasters, with games shown on ESPN, Fox, TNT, CBS, and NBC. Having an international presence is a very handy carrot to dangle to broadcasters.‘I loved my time in the FBI but nothing can compare to the NFL’: Charles ‘Peanut’ Tillman on his unlikely career pathRead more“Our media partners really like it when we go global, because it creates a big-event feel that they can capture – and they are in the big-event business,” says Yormark. “Fox will host their whole college football show – Big Noon Kickoff – here in London. It will be the first time they have ever taken that show international. They’re going to be here all week, making this game into something really big, not only here, but back in the US.”“I’ve always had global ambitions for the conference - it’s good for business,” adds Yormark. “When I was the CEO of the Brooklyn Nets, we took the team to Mexico City, London and China. Football is a global sport. We were presented with an opportunity to come to the UK and took full advantage of it.”There is another reason the universities want to play abroad: to market themselves to international students and advertise their global campuses (six of the universities in the Big 12 have campuses abroad).
