title: Trump’s $5,000 pledge to voters is a shameless bribe | Steven Greenhouse | The Guardian
description: Not only would the plan do vast economic damage – it assumes that Americans are easily bamboozled
Author: Steven Greenhouse
Headline: Not only would the plan do vast economic damage – it assumes that Americans are easily bamboozled
Content: ‘Since there are an estimated 240 million adults in the US, Trump’s plan would cost a colossal $1.2tn.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APView image in fullscreen‘Since there are an estimated 240 million adults in the US, Trump’s plan would cost a colossal $1.2tn.’Photograph: Alex Brandon/APOpinionDonald TrumpTrump’s $5,000 pledge to voters is a shameless bribeSteven GreenhouseNot only would the plan do vast economic damage – it assumes that Americans are easily bamboozledWed 16 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 13.49 EDTShareWhenever Donald Trump gives a speech, it’s filled with so many lies and self-serving exaggerations that when he does utter something true, I see that as a sort of marvel. That’s what happened nearly an hour intoTrump’s marathon speechlast Wednesday at the Republican midterm convention, when he declared:“Only I can make this promiseto you.” Trump said that just before he made a promise that was so shameless and irresponsible that what he said was indeed true: only Trump could make such a preposterous promise.Feeling very generous with other people’s money, the president promised to give $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in November. It certainly looked and smelled like a bribe.Why is the White House being so weird about Natalie Harp again? | Arwa MahdawiRead moreI guess that when you’re fearing an electoral debacle because your public approval ratings are in the toilet, because people are furious about your disastrous war of choice against Iran and because so many Americans are hopping mad that inflation has risen even though you promised to cut prices, then you might feel the need to take desperate measures, and that’s what Trump did by offering to stuff $5,000 in every adult’s pocket to help sway them to vote Republican.Since there are an estimated 240 million adults in the US, Trump’s plan would cost a colossal $1.2tn – that’s more than the Pentagon’s budget and nearly what the US will spend on Medicare this year.Many Republicans and Trump donors rushed to criticize Trump’s $5,000 plan. Joe Lonsdale, a tech billionaire and Republican donor, said he was “strongly againstbread and circus bribes”, while Representative Bob Good of Virginia, former chair of the House Freedom caucus, called Trump’s promise a “socialist vote-buying scheme”.What angers me most about Trump’s promise isn’t that it would increase the enormous $40tn federal debt even though the presidentonce promised to eliminate the entire federal debt. Nor am I angriest about the fact that Trump is essentially seeking to bribe the nation’s entire adult population for short-term political gain while in effect passing the cost on to our children and grandchildren. Trump is unconscionably seeking to finance his bribery by borrowing from future generations.But here is what makes me angriest: Trump evidently believes that millions and millions of Americans are such rubes that he can bamboozle them into voting Republican because they would want to get their hands on $5,000. I like to think that Americans are smarter than that and won’t be fooled.When the president made such a shameless proposal, I couldn’t help but wonder: are there no adults in the room with Trump? Is there no one with a sense of shame or fiscal responsibility who will tell him, “Don’t offer this $5,000 bribe. It stinks to high hell, and it’s grossly irresponsible.”Some brutal mockery came from Trump’s one-time ally Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former House member from Georgia. She hasn’t forgotten that Trump promised last fall that, thanks to his tariffs, every American, except for high-income people, would receive “a dividend of at least $2,000”. That didn’t happen. Greene also remembers that when Elon Musk said that Doge would chop the federal budget by $2tn, Trump suggested that a sizable chunk of those savings couldgo directly to Americans. That didn’t happen either.double quotation markThis $5,000 bribe is not a dividend resulting from economic success; it’s a loan from future generationsGreene taunted Trump by writing on X, “$5,000 for the peasants will be in the mailafter the election only if you vote Republican, along with those DOGE and tariff money checks.”Trump egomaniacally called the $5,000 payments a “Trump dividend”, saying the money was available “because of ourtremendous strength and success economically”. But Trump is embellishing big time here; there really hasn’t been economic success during Trump’s second term, other than the much-detested datacenter boom and the stock market hitting repeated records. Inflation is higher than when Joe Biden left office, GDP growth is slower, thetrade deficit has jumped over 60%since April, the nation haslost 35,000 factory jobssince Trump’s inauguration and average monthly job growth is less than one-third what it was during Biden’s last two years in office. So, no, this $5,000 bribe is not a dividend resulting from economic success; it’s a loan from future generations.After Trump’s plan faced an avalanche of criticism, administration officials rushed to insist that the $1.2tn wouldn’t come from taxpayers or deficit spending. JD Vance claimed that much of the moneywould come from tariff revenues, while commerce secretary Howard Lutnick said something even more far-fetched: that lots of the money would come fromcharging wealthy foreigners for visasand from the administration’s investments in Intel and other companies. If you believe that, I own a club in Mar-a-Lago that I’d be happy to sell you.Unfortunately for Trump and every American, Trump’s promise to stuff $5,000 in every adult’s stocking will clash with one of his main promises – the $5,000 payments will increase consumer demand and that will inevitably push up inflation even though Trumprepeatedly promisedtocut prices.Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget,issued a stern warningabout Trump’s $5,000. “Debt is now as large as our entire economy, deficits are running $2tn per year, inflation is about 3.5%, and the 10-year treasury yield is approaching 5%,” MacGuineas said. “This half-baked political scheme would make this all worse – exploding the deficit, ginning up inflation and further driving up the cost of borrowing throughout the economy.”Kenneth Rogoff, a Harvard economics professor and former chief economist at the International Monetary Fund,voiced even more alarm, telling PBS, “The US is already running an unsustainable deficit. This would only blow [it] up even more and increase the already high odds of a debt crisis over next five years.”With his $5,000 “dividend”, Trump is being his impulsive, myopic and reckless self, just like he was in plunging the US into war against Iran, leaving the nation’s economy and global relations in considerably worse shape than before the war. Trump’s $5,000 promise also risksspooking financial marketsand nudging up interest rates.Every American – Republican, independent or Democrat – should see through Trump’s shamelessness. If his plan comes to pass, it might be a nice sugar high for many Americans, but it will do real economic damage – to inflation, interest rates and the nation’s debt – and it will also impose an unfair burden on our children and grandchildren.Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issuesExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionTrump administrationUS politicsUS midterm elections 2026US Government borrowingUS economycommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Pacing’ won’t eliminate the risk of AI doom. Here’s what could | David Krueger | The Guardian
description: The stark reality is this: we don’t know how to maintain control of these systems. But there are actions we can take
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The stark reality is this: we don’t know how to maintain control of these systems. But there are actions we can take
Content: ‘If we want to reduce the risks from AI to an acceptable level, what we actually need is an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.’Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘If we want to reduce the risks from AI to an acceptable level, what we actually need is an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.’Photograph: VCG/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)‘Pacing’ won’t eliminate the risk of AI doom. Here’s what couldDavid KruegerThe stark reality is this: we don’t know how to maintain control of these systems. But there are actions we can takeWed 16 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.52 EDTShareWith Jacob Coxon’sresignation from Anthropic, we have reached the AI risk tipping point. Millions of people are finally coming to understand what experts have known for years: AI companies have been gambling with all of our lives, and the odds are not good.In response, the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, hasintroduced a proposalfor “pacing the frontier”, endorsed by Sam Altman and Elon Musk. Can we breathe a sigh of relief? Are we about to step back from the edge of extinction?Amodei envisions a slowdown of one to two years, resulting in “profound progress” on technical safety measures. But that’s not what humanity needs right now. What we need is a plan in which we’re confident AI isn’t going to kill us, and this isn’t it.The stark reality is this: we don’t know how these AI systems work. We don’t know how to prevent them from misbehaving. We don’t know how to stay in control once they’re smarter than us. We don’t know how to make sure they’re notplaying niceorplayingdumbto trick our safety tests. We can’t count on solving these problems with another one or two years of research.I worked at Google DeepMind. You should listen to the warnings about AI | Alex TurnerRead moreI know because I have been researching such problems for more than a decade, including as an AI professor at both the University of Cambridge and the University of Montreal. If we want to reduce the risks from AI to an acceptable level, what we actually need is an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.Is this really possible? It’s a legitimate question, and geopolitics is the crux: how can countries such as the US and China verify each others’ compliance? Donald Trumprecently slammed AI regulation, citing the US’s lead in the AI arms race against Beijing.But a simple solution is available: de-commission the advanced computer chips necessary to build these AI models. The massive – andalreadymassivelyunpopular– datacenter build-out could be reversed. The US and China could take turns decommissioning data centers and the chips they contain. If all parties knew that nobody had the means of building more powerful AI, verification would be simple.To make such an arrangement durable, we could additionally dismantle the supply chain for producing advanced AI chips, which isextremelyconcentratedand relies on some of the most advanced technology in the world: extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography. Any attempt to operate a covert lithography operation at the scale required for frontier AI development would almost certainly be noticed by other nations’ intelligence services.This plan has benefits over alternative approaches that rely on restricting how computer chips are used. Amodei calls pausing “unlikely”, but an agreement to decommission AI infrastructure would actually be easier to verify than Amodei’s proposals for global coordination, which would require increasing levels of surveillance as computing hardware continues to advance and proliferate.The economic costs of this plan would be substantial, but given the stakes, unless we have a better plan that actually saves our lives, they are clearly worth it. During the Covid-19 pandemic, governments shut down significant parts of society and the economy to save lives. We should be willing to go to much greater lengths to prevent the extinction of our species. I’m actively researching “softer” versions of the proposal that would involve creating computer chips that can be used to run AI models, but not to build more powerful ones. And other researchers have alsodeveloped proposalsfor an indefinite moratorium.Amodei’s essay, sadly, does not consider these pause proposals. His plan is ultimately still to have AIs build smarter and smarter AIs with less human involvement – “recursive self-improvement”, a project designed to render humans obsolete.China dismisses AI ‘fearmongering’ as spy chief warns of threat to Communist party ruleRead moreWhat should we actually expect to come of Amodei’s plan? Step one would “embed” external evaluators from organizations such asMETR, which was invited to investigate the OpenAI-Hugging Face scandal. Big tech CEOs may call this “radical”, but let’s be clear: what they’re actually talking about is more self-regulation.Three years ago, I helped found the UK AI Security Institute – another leading evaluator. I quit after it was clear the ecosystem was getting the burden of proof formula backwards. Today, AI is still de facto “safe-until-proven dangerous”.The safety standards Amodei suggests are guaranteed to fall far short of those in other safety-critical industries like aviation. We simply don’t know how to do recursive self-improvement safely.So let’s stop. Let’s stop making AI we can’t control, and let’s stop listening to the AI industry about how it wants to be regulated. Proposals for a pause are being put forth in both the US and UK legislatures. The Chinese president, Xi Jinping, is coming to Washington to discuss AI, and Trump has an opportunity to make the deal of the century if they can work out how to stop the AI race.Let’s demand a plan that makes us safe, not just safer.David Krueger is an assistant professor in Robust, Reasoning and Responsible AI at the University of Montreal. He is also the founder ofEvitable, a non-profit that educates the public about the risks of artificial intelligenceExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionAnthropicOpenAIComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: I have faced abuse, assaults and death threats because I’m an MP. It’s making politics a no-go zone | Dawn Butler | The Guardian
description: A new report highlights the dangers experienced by those who seek to serve the public. People are being deterred and your democracy is suffering, says Labour MP Dawn Butler
Author: Dawn Butler
Headline: A new report highlights the dangers experienced by those who seek to serve the public. People are being deterred and your democracy is suffering, says Labour MP Dawn Butler
Content: ‘We know Diane Abbott has received extraordinary levels of abuse, while I often feel specifically targeted because I am a Black woman.’Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAView image in fullscreen‘We know Diane Abbott has received extraordinary levels of abuse, while I often feel specifically targeted because I am a Black woman.’Photograph: Andrew Matthews/PAOpinionOnline abuseI have faced abuse, assaults and death threats because I’m an MP. It’s making politics a no-go zoneDawn ButlerA new report highlights the dangers experienced by those who seek to serve the public. People are being deterred and your democracy is sufferingWed 16 Sep 2026 11.08 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 12.28 EDTShareThere is a rising tide of abuse in our politics and I feel it every day. This week, the Electoral Commissionwarnedthat harassment and intimidation arechanging how candidates campaign, what they feel able to do and whether they stand again. This is a threat to our democracy – and we cannot ignore it.The figures are stark. Commission research into the May 2026 local and mayoral elections in England found that 55% of candidates said harassment or intimidation was a problem, up from 47% in 2025. Women, ethnic minority candidates and those with disabilities were most likely to encounter abuse. The experience was so unpleasant that a third considered not standing again.But none of it is a surprise. I have seen first-hand how abuse, threats and violence have increased in our politics over the years. Since I was elected as an MP in 2015, numerous people have been convicted for attacks, threats and abuse against me. Someone was sent to prison for saying a “bullet” to the back of my head was justified, while another person was convicted for telling me “come the revolution, you will be one of the first”.Followers of my social media know how bad it can be. I have a regular “block of the month” feature to raise awareness of the disgusting racist abuse sent to me every day – the N-word, “monkey” and “ape” are common insults. The deluge of abuse has a detrimental impact on my mental health, and on those around me.The abuse is not limited to the internet. I have been physically assaulted going home from work, and followed and verbally abused right outside parliament. During the last general election and again in this year’s local elections, I was accosted on the street by a local man who made me fear for my safety. I was told I wasn’t welcome in the area, despite being the MP for Brent East, and that next time “I should come prepared”. I reported the incidents to the police.This is the hatred I face every day. And inevitably, it changes how MPs operate, how representatives serve the people who elected them.Several years ago, I had toclose my physical constituency officepartly due to threats. We had a brick thrown through the window, and on one occasion my staff physically removed someone who turned up with a golf club. While I was once able to host walk-in constituency surgeries, the increased security threat has meant they are now roving, with the constituents pre-vetted. I also have to be accompanied to every event and notify the police of potential dangers. The constant fear risks making our politics less accessible.Some findings from the Electoral Commission report reflect what I hear from young candidates, especially from minority backgrounds. They worry about canvassing and are also targeted online. Our representatives should reflect the diversity of the population, but this rising abuse will put talented people off entering the political system altogether.It is important to acknowledge that improvements have been made. The policelaunched initiativesto strengthen security and support for councillors, elected mayors, candidates and others. In my experience, this has helped. But there is still far more to do. I want stronger and quicker action to clamp down on online abuse, with social media companies tackling it at source, as we know the threat can become physical when culprits feel emboldened. If social media companies fail to remove this content, they should face substantial fines.I report countless instances of vile racism every month, but very few are pursued. So the police must do more to identify those responsible – and the justice system must show zero tolerance with sentences. I also support restorative justice, so we can work towards repairing the harm caused.It’s also important that more help is directed to those who are disproportionately targeted. We know that Diane Abbott, for example, has receivedextraordinary levels of abuse, while I often feel specifically targeted because I am a Black woman.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnd we all have a responsibility to lower the temperature of our politics. I recently wrote to Reform UK to call out theoffensive and divisive remarksof the party’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, regarding the birthplace of Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee from Somalia who isrunning as the Labour candidatein the Holborn and St Pancras byelection next month. This kind of politics inflames divisions. Yusuf is fuelling hate to boost Reform’s popularity, without caring about the consequences. For him it is a political strategy, but for society it has lasting damage.We must act now to protect those who put themselves forward to serve, from all parties, and hold perpetrators to account in order to ensure no one is driven out of our democracy by fear and intimidation. If we allow abusers to decide who feels able to participate in our democracy and who is muted, those seeking to silence us will have won. That simply cannot happen.Dawn Butler is Labour MP for Brent EastDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The dominance of AI is not inevitable. We can choose to change things for the better | Nick Evershed | The Guardian
description: Countries have come together before to make international agreements in the face of existential threats
Author: Nick Evershed
Headline: Countries have come together before to make international agreements in the face of existential threats
Content: A protest against AI outside OpenAI’s offices in San Francisco. ‘What often seem like insurmountable problems can be addressed by normal people putting pressure on politicians and companies,’ Nick Evershed writes.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA protest against AI outside OpenAI’s offices in San Francisco. ‘What often seem like insurmountable problems can be addressed by normal people putting pressure on politicians and companies,’ Nick Evershed writes.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)The dominance of AI is not inevitable. We can choose to change things for the betterNick EvershedCountries have come together before to make international agreements in the face of existential threatsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastWed 16 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 19.54 EDTShareWith many technological developments, from algorithm-driven social media to AI, many people assume there’s a degree of inevitability to their widespread adoption in society.The argument goes something like this: once the ideas and means to produce the tech are known, then it is inevitable that its usage will spread and we’ll essentially be stuck with it. So therefore we need to accept this and adjust our lives to live with the tech and use it (or at least tolerate it).This argument seems pretty straightforward, since we’ve seen many tech-driven disruptions play out in the past 20 years or so. Uber displacing the taxi industry and the rise of “gig workers”. Algorithmic social media displacing, well, everything. Privacy-invading, hyper-targeted advertising reshaping the internet.Could AI really wipe out humanity – six experts spell out the risksRead moreAnd it seems like generative AI is destined to be another huge, disruptive force in our lives. Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI,wrote of AI in 2024 that“with these new abilities, we can have shared prosperity to a degree that seems unimaginable today; in the future, everyone’s lives can be better than anyone’s life is now”. He is also on record elsewhere sayingAI would wipe out entire job categories.Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic,wrote that he believes“AI could cure most major diseases in the next 5–10 years, greatly accelerate economic growth rates, create a world of abundance and empowerment, and usher in a renaissance of democracy and freedom”.But now, bothCEOs, as well asformerandcurrent AI research staffand others, are calling for a slowdown oreven a shutdownof AI development, along with greater government regulation and international coordination of AI development.The calls for a slowdown are based on the fear that, without proper safeguards, AI systems may result incatastrophic events in the near future, ranging from theextinction of humanityto merely causing billions of dollars in economic damage.This is not a new concern and has been raised byindependent academics previously in assessing the risks from AI. However, complicating the situation is that both OpenAI and Anthropic are positioning themselves for IPOs, and so some critics say both companies stand to materially benefit from the perception that they’re on the cusp of developing superintelligent models.AI models being developed in China arealso catching up to the “frontier” models being made in the US, which has prompted some to suggest that calls for greater regulation on AIare an attempt at regulatory capture by the big US AI companies.Regardless of how likely these catastrophic events are, as Sandra Wachter, a professor of technology at the Oxford Internet Institute, has said,AI is already causing real problems, including its environmental impact, the spreading of misinformation and replacing jobs.This is in addition to the “original sin” of most AI models – they’re built on millions of people’s art and writing, largely without compensation or permission until more recently, and theAI companies want to curb proposed laws limiting their accessto such material.double quotation markWhatever semblance of intelligence it has comes from us, and our work.Never forget that generative AI is not a technology that is apart from human society. In fact, its development and whatever semblance of intelligence it has comes from us, and our work.And despite what the tech CEOs say, there’s nothing inevitable about AI, and we as a society can make decisions to change things for the better.History shows us this can be done.What often seem like insurmountable and pervasive problems can and have been addressed by normal people putting pressure on politicians and companies, and through international cooperation and negotiation.Countries have come together before to make international agreements in the face of existential threats. Thenuclear nonproliferation treaty, as well as the associated anti-nuclear activist movement, is a good example, and many have suggested it has parallels with the current AI situation. While the disarmament side of the NPT has had mixed success at best, the NPT and similar agreements have worked to limit the number of nuclear-capable countries and reduce nuclear testing.Gene editing viaCrispris another example. Arguablya more important technological advancement than generative AI, the use of Crispr for gene editing in humans has been treated extremely cautiously by governments around the world. No country currently allows genetic changes to an embryo that could also be passed on to its children, and70 countries have laws against it.We greet the news that AI could extinguish us with a glazed indifference. What is the way out of this nihilism? | Brigid DelaneyRead moreEven social media companies, whose reach and influence on society seemed like it would continue unabated, are now finallyfacing stricter regulation from governments around the worldandself-regulating in response to lawsuits in the US.So, do not take the future dominance of AI as a given.Personally I believe that generative AI can be a useful tool (albeit in far fewer situations than tech companies would have you believe). But to ensure we limit the worst possible consequences, we need independent oversight of its development, regulation to limit some aspects of it, and international agreements to implement these controls globally.If you think the same, then do not accept its inevitability. Contact politicians and demand action. Protest. Speak to friends and family about how you think this technology should be used, or not used. Write to companies using it in ways you disagree with.In thenow-infamous words of Claude: you’re right to push back.Nick Evershed is the data and interactives editor for Guardian AustraliaExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionEthicsAnthropicOpenAIcommentShareReuse this content

title: In such a rich country, it is shameful how many Australians on jobseeker are dying in desperate poverty | Greg Jericho | The Guardian
description: Lifting the abysmally low jobseeker rate to the poverty line would save thousands of lives
Author: Greg Jericho
Headline: Lifting the abysmally low jobseeker rate to the poverty line would save thousands of lives
Content: A new report has found that Australians on jobseeker are up to 10 times more likely to die than those not on welfare support.Photograph: skaman306/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA new report has found that Australians on jobseeker are up to 10 times more likely to die than those not on welfare support.Photograph: skaman306/Getty ImagesGrogonomicsAustralian economyIn such a rich country, it is shameful how many Australians on jobseeker are dying in desperate povertyGreg JerichoLifting the abysmally low jobseeker rate to the poverty line would save thousands of livesFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ournew political email,free appordaily news podcastWed 16 Sep 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 19.54 EDTShareStunning new data fromthe Australian Institute of Health and Welfare(AIHW) shows the abysmally low rate of jobseeker means at least 3,000 more unemployed Australians die each year than would be the case were they not purposefully kept in poverty.We often talk about how tough it is for those on jobseeker. But last week a report from the AIHW titled “Mortality outcomes among people receiving income support” shows talk is cheap when people are dying.The report found that Australians on jobseeker are up to 10 times more likely to die than those not on welfare support.If the graph does not display click hereIn 2022, the rate of deaths for 35- to 44-year-olds not living on welfare support was 30 per 100,000. By contrast, the rate was 288 per 100,000 for those on jobseeker – 9.6 times greater.Can someone explain why – in an economy in which the central bank has decided we need almost 700,000 people to be unemployed – those people live in such dreadful poverty that it can make you up to 10 times more likely to die in the prime of your life?A job that changed me: At the dole office, I met very few ‘bludgers’. Most people desperately wanted workRead moreThe Reserve Bank believes we need unemployment to be 4.5% to 5% to keep inflation stable. At that level, they believe total household income is such that we won’t buy too much stuff and there won’t be a wages breakout.It’s not just the RBA: every government since 1996 has been more than happy to ensure the gap between the unemployment benefits and poverty has either grown or remained well above what it was when Bob Hawke and Paul Keating were in power:If the graph does not display click hereCurrently, jobseeker payments are almost half the poverty line – roughly $300 a week less than what would be needed for a single person to be right on the poverty line. The only time this was not the case was during the Covid pandemic when the Morrison government effectively doubled jobseeker temporarily.During 2020, the death rate of those on jobseeker dropped 32% from 328 people per 100,000 the previous year to 224 people per 100,000:If the graph does not display click hereIt is too simplistic to say the doubling of jobseeker in 2020 was the reason the death rate dropped. A big factor was that the number of people unemployed almost doubled due to the Covid lockdowns. This group had not come from the level of poverty the usual cohort of unemployed people had, and as a result would likely be healthier.Crucially, however, being unemployed did not automatically sentence them to poverty.We therefore cannot say just how big of an impact the doubling of the payment had unless we were able to strip out the numbers of “unemployed due only to lockdowns”.But while we cannot attribute the doubling of jobseeker to the drop in the death rate, that should not stop our anger at the higher death rates of those on unemployment benefits – and the disparity is getting larger.In 2019, 328 people died per 100,000 of those on jobseeker. This fell to 224 in 2020, but then rose straight away to 300 the following year and then again to 326 in 2022. Conversely, over the same period, the rate of deaths for those aged 22-64 and not on welfare kept falling.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIt means that the likelihood of dying for all unemployed people aged 22-64 is now nearly five times greater compared with those not on welfare – the biggest gap in the AIHW report:If the graph does not display click hereThe 2020 figure when jobseeker was doubled does however give us a good base to work from to estimate just how many more people on jobseeker die because they live in poverty.The cruelty of poverty is that it sentences those in it to a poorer diet, less access to healthcare, less ability to afford exercise activities such as gym and sport club memberships, and as a result a much higher morbidity rate.In 2022, 3,985 people on jobseeker died. If instead of dying at a rate of 326 per 100,000, the rate was the same as it was in 2020, then 1,246 fewer people would have died (a total of 2,739).But let us lift our standards. There really is no reason why people on jobseeker should die more often than those not on welfare.We are a rich country with supposedly universal healthcare. Raising jobseeker to the poverty line (about $37,000 a year) would cost roughly $11bn this year. For comparison, this yearthe Treasury estimatesthe richest 10% (people earning more than $162,000) will get about $22.5bn in superannuation tax breaks.If those on jobseeker died at the same rate as those not on welfare payments, in 2022 just 817 people would have died – 3,168 fewer than in reality:If the graph does not display click herePoverty kills. And the way to lift people out of poverty is to lift the unemployment payment (and other forms of welfare).Raising the level of jobseeker would save thousands of lives.Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia InstituteExplore more on these topicsAustralian economyGrogonomicsWelfareAustralian politicsUnemploymentcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Letby inquiry report makes one thing crystal clear: too much NHS management is scandalously poor  | Tom Dolphin | The Guardian
description: Non-medical managers are the only safety-critical part of the service that do not have a regulator. Lady Justice Thirlwall says that must change. So do we, says Tom Dolphin, chair of the BMA council
Author: Tom Dolphin
Headline: Non-medical managers are the only safety-critical part of the service that do not have a regulator. Lady Justice Thirlwall says that must change. So do we, says Tom Dolphin, chair of the BMA council
Content: ‘Whistleblowers deserve respect, not ridicule or rejection.’Photograph: Chris Rout/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Whistleblowers deserve respect, not ridicule or rejection.’Photograph: Chris Rout/AlamyOpinionNHSThe Letby inquiry report makes one thing crystal clear: too much NHS management is scandalously poorTom DolphinNon-medical managers are the only safety-critical part of the service that do not have a regulator. Lady Justice Thirlwall says that must change. So do weTom Dolphin is chair of the British Medical Association councilWed 16 Sep 2026 09.21 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 09.26 EDTShareThe publication of theThirlwall inquiry reportis above all a moment to remember the babies who died or were harmed at the Countess of Chester hospital and the families whose grief was compounded by years of delay, institutional denial and defensiveness. The least we owe those families is a determination to now make the right changes – not the comfortable ones, not the partial ones, but the ones that will stop further avoidable deaths and injury.Lady Justice Thirlwall’s report lays bare atotal failure of NHS management. When doctors dared to raise concerns, they were rebuked and threatened with referral to the General Medical Council (GMC), which could have ended their career. The report describes a kind of “toxic negativity” all too familiar in the health service: a desperate culture of cover-up and denial that prizes saving face over saving lives.Whistleblowers deserve respect, not ridicule or rejection. It takes courage to speak out against those in power, and the BMA has supported many such courageous doctors. They includeDr Susan Gilby, who at the very same Countess of Chester hospital refused to stay quiet about the failures she saw around her. She was punished with a shocking campaign of repression from management that resulted in her being awarded £1.4m in damages earlier this year. If it wasn’t clear before, Thirlwall has thrown into stark relief the plight of whistleblowers, and most importantly the patients whose lives and health are at risk.But the real legacy of the inquiry may go even deeper, to the heart of how we think about regulation in the NHS. It is well known that doctors and nurses serve under our professional regulators, theGMCand theNursing and Midwifery Council. We can be investigated, sanctioned, suspended or struck off if our conduct falls below expected standards. That is as it should be. Regulation protects patients, gives the public confidence and makes clear that authority in healthcare must always come with accountability.What few know is that non-medical managers – those in charge of a hospital’s essential systems, such as its staffing, buildings, equipment and finances – do not face that accountability. Indeed, non-medical managers are the only safety-critical group in theNHSthat does not have a regulator. It seems utterly backwards that some of the most powerful people in the health service face so little oversight, and it is not hard to draw a line between that and the abuses of power that led to the situation at the Countess of Chester and all the tragedy that followed. I am very glad, therefore, to see that Thirlwall has addressed this head-on, making the clear recommendation that it should be possible to strike off these managers just like any other NHS professional.She has also recommended that the UK government seriously consider creating a statutory regulator for non-medical managers, which the BMA believes is long overdue. Their regulation shouldn’t be crammed in with that of the dozen or so other professions – physiotherapists, dieticians, radiographers to name a few – supervised by the already overloadedHealth and Care Professions Council. They need and deserve an expert, dedicated statutory regulator that can give a clear, enforceable set of standards.The BMA doesn’t just want non-medical managers to fear negative consequences for bad behaviour; we want them to have high standards so more of them can aspire to excellence. The culture of the NHS should be one where we welcome staff and patients raising concerns about failings, with adequate resources for fixing problems, so well-regulated managers can actually improve things rather than shooting the messenger.That day still looks dangerously far off, though. Despite aLabour manifesto commitment, the inquiry sees these regulatory changes taking until 2032. In the meantime, we do not know how many more examples of poor or dangerous practice will be suppressed and ignored by managers who remain beyond the reach of accountability.This must not be a commitment left to fall by the wayside in the aftermath of a general election. Work by government to create a statutory regulator must begin now, and by the end of this parliament, the families of those affected should have confidence that any institutional cover-ups will be tackled. For our patients and colleagues – and ultimately in the interests of managers, too – doctors are going to push for these changes to be implemented faster. Accountability matters.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDr Tom Dolphin is a consultant anaesthetist in London, and chair of council at the BMADo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsNHSOpinionHospitalsHealthcommentShareReuse this content

title: Big-money donations poison British politics. We can stop the mega-rich buying access and influence  | Gordon Brown | The Guardian
description: I’ve seen how imbalances in campaign spending can distort democracy. The multimillion-pound gifts to Reform must act as a final wake-up call, says former UK prime minister Gordon Brown
Author: Gordon Brown
Headline: I’ve seen how imbalances in campaign spending can distort democracy. The multimillion-pound gifts to Reform must act as a final wake-up call, says former UK prime minister Gordon Brown
Content: Reform UK leader Nigel Farage at the party’s annual conference in Birmingham, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersView image in fullscreenReform UK leader Nigel Farage at the party’s annual conference in Birmingham, 5 September 2026.Photograph: Isabel Infantes/ReutersOpinionParty fundingBig-money donations poison British politics. We can stop the mega-rich buying access and influenceGordon BrownI’ve seen how imbalances in campaign spending can distort democracy. The multimillion-pound gifts to Reform must act as a final wake-up callWed 16 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.48 EDTShareThe British people cannot be bought, but their views and votes can be heavily influenced by a flood of political party propaganda – from expensive advertising and constant leaflet drops to personalised online messages targeted directly at voters.When I fought the election of 2010, there was a massive imbalance in spending. In 2007 we had inherited Labour partydebts of £25mfollowing the 2005 election – and with such tight finances Labour wasable to spend only £8m in 2010, in contrast to the Conservatives’ £17m. We lost out in particular by being unable to invest in the new forms of online advertising coming on stream.But the imbalances are likely to become even starker in future as therecent donations to Reformshow. A decade ago, only 1% of individuals and companies making political donations gave of the order of £1m or more. By 2024, they accounted forover a third, at 35%. These latest record-breaking donations from crypto billionairesBen Delo and Christopher Harborneare worth more than all donations to UK political parties in 2025 combined.Spending more money at an election almost certainlyleads to greater electoral success. This is worrying – and while the government recently tasked the Electoral Commission withreviewing campaign spending limits, more must be done. The reforms to election financing recommended by the Commission on the UK’s Future, which I chaired, and in particular a donation cap, should be introduced into the representation of the people billnow in the House of Lords.Nearlyhalf of voters, with few objecting, say they would view a party more favourably if it introduced a limit on political donations. Indeed, the very fact that money has beenopenly solicitedin return for political access and, potentially, influence – as well as positions of public office and honours – exposes our democracy and weakens public trust.A cap on individual donations was recommended by the independentHayden Phillips reviewin 2007, by theCommittee on Standards in Public Lifein 2011 – and by an increasing number of senior politicians, includingJohn Major. Indeed, in December 2025, the UK and at least 59 other countries co-sponsored aUnited Nations resolutionthat urges state parties to consider “limitations on donations … with a view to combating corruption”.Other comparable democracies impose donation caps.Canada caps donationsto political parties at about £930 annually;France caps donationsto political parties at £6,400 annually and £3,900 for presidential campaigns;Italy’s capis £85,600 per person or company annually.“My gut feeling would suggest somewhere in the region of £500k,”Andy Burnham saidjust before he became prime minister, and in September Stella Creasy and 63 other MPsbacked an amendmentto the representation of the people bill, which was then withdrawn, to introduce anannual donation capof £500,000, decreasing to £100,000 after one calendar year.The new bill should include an enabling power for the secretary of state to set a cap on donations, having consulted the Ethics and Integrity Commission (formerly the Committee on Standards in Public Life) as well as the Electoral Commission.Some want this cap to include donations by trade unions. But a collection of individual members who provide small contributions and can opt out do not pose the same level of risk to our democracy as multimillion-pound donations from private donors.Outside general election years, Labour and Conservative party spending has recently been around£60m and £55m, respectively. Transparency International UK has calculated that before 2024, the total spend in election years was about £74m and £87m.In 2024, it says that Labour expenditure ballooned to a record-breaking £103m while the Conservative party spent less – just £74m. But paradoxically, this imbalance was made possible by the Conservative government’s decision toraise general election spending limits.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDonors to the Labour party whom I have met favour a cap on donations; in fact, they say their recent larger-than-normal donations were made simply to even up the odds between political parties.How would things change? Transparency International UKhas made a tool to modelthe potential impact of donation caps on political party finances. Setting a donation cap of £50,000 per year, you can see the impact of reducing big-money donations. At the same time, there would still be sufficient funding for political parties to campaign effectively and fairly, without a need for additional public funds. It is now time to create such a level playing field.The reform of political party funding should be the start of a major cleanup of our political system. It is quite wrong that about100 paid lobbyistssit in an as yet unreformed House of Lords. And it is also wrong that the requirements placed on the lobbying industry to declare its activities are so weak. The British people deserve better.Gordon Brown was UK prime minister from 2007 to 2010Explore more on these topicsParty fundingOpinionReform UKcommentShareReuse this content

title: It’s my self-care tip of the year: I quit our local veg box scheme, and set my mind free | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: Being a member felt like the right thing to do and it was a boon during the pandemic. But oh, the emotional labour, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: Being a member felt like the right thing to do and it was a boon during the pandemic. But oh, the emotional labour, says Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Content: ‘During the long winters, I cursed the endless beetroot. By March we were all about 65% parsnip.’Photograph: Westend61 GmbH/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘During the long winters, I cursed the endless beetroot. By March we were all about 65% parsnip.’Photograph: Westend61 GmbH/AlamyOpinionVegetablesIt’s my self-care tip of the year: I quit our local veg box scheme, and set my mind freeRhiannon Lucy CosslettBeing a member felt like the right thing to do – and it was a boon during the pandemic. But oh, the emotional labour. I can never look at a turnip againWed 16 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 13.24 EDTShareLast week, as summer gave way to pumpkin season, I found myself contemplating the final squash. Like the horror movie trope of the final girl staggering out of the woods after the massacre, this squash is the sole survivor. All her sister squashes had either been cooked and eaten or left to rot. Now, my killing days were almost over. There would be no sequel.Or, to put it less dramatically: after six years, we have quit the local organic veg bag collective, which delivered to a nearby pickup point a bag of organic, local seasonal veg once a week. And as a result the mental load and emotional labour of having to contemplate and devise a use for various esoteric kinds of veg is finally, mercifully, over.I approached the final squash the way I had many, many of her contemporaries. First, I tried to identify her so I could work out how to cook it and whether the skin was edible or not. “Medium-sized frilly orange pumpkin type” I wrote into Google. No match was forthcoming. Then I took a picture of it and did an image search. Still no match. For all its supposed miraculous capabilities, during my own experiments AI has never successfully identified a single pumpkin.Usually, this is the point where my cortisol soars, but this time it stayed stable: this was the last time that I would expend precious time and energy trying to correctly identify a vegetable, before giving up and doing what I always do, which is chopping it up and roasting it.Now that it’s done, I cannot tell you how liberated I feel. No more kohlrabi. No more Jerusalem fartichokes. Only my husband will miss the turnips.Historically, I have always been a great quitter. To use hideous modern parlance, anything that no longer “served” me, whether a job, a relationship, a university course, a country, would always be efficiently dispatched. No looking back.Leaving the local organic veg collective didn’t feel like this, though. Being a member felt like the right, ethical thing to do (“Don’t be mean about them,” my husband says. “They are a great service”). Raised by a veg box mum – and being a Guardian writer to boot – surely this was my destiny, my birthright? It gave me a warm, self-satisfied glow, albeit an ephemeral one lasting only until I was once again scrubbing layers of caked mud from all of the potatoes just so I could make my kid some sodding chips. “What is this? Wartime?” I muttered to myself.I’d say my heart hasn’t been in it for at least two years, probably longer, but despite the fact that the relationship had become toxic I felt guilty for wanting to leave. Ever since I had my son, the veg bag has been an albatross. During the long winters, I cursed the endless beetroot. By March we were all about 65% parsnip. “More bloody parsnips,” we would sigh, as we unpacked on a Wednesday. “I’m not sure I can do this any more.” Yet another season was always around the corner. The green promise of spring. “Soon! There will be asparagus!” And we would stick it out for another year.Well, it’s done now, even though I keep picturingHugh Fearnley-Whittingstallshaking his head in disapproval, along with you, dear reader. The veg is more ethical, better for you, and tastier than anything from a supermarket. All of this I acknowledge. Maybe I’m just lazy. And yet, I am a confident – some might say even good – cook. I make meals from scratch, I understand about vitamins and nutritional value. I sometimes open, and look at the pictures in, recipe books by Nigel Slater. It was just that something finally had to give.It may sound hyperbolic, but getting rid of the veg bag has saved me from a breakdown, possibly. My mental load feels far lighter. “I feel so fucking free, you guys!” I posted, on Instagram, and was inundated with people who had been on the same journey. In some cases, arguing about the rotting veg in the bottom of their fridges was affecting their marriages. We all wanted to do the right thing, it’s just that modern life simply didn’t feel compatible.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI have some fond memories of the veg bag. I’m grateful to the collective for feeding my family. I will miss being a member, especially at Christmas. We joinedduring the pandemic, when not every item was always available in the shops. My son was weaned on pureed celeriac. We got to try things I never would have otherwise –winter purslane! Land cress! – and I adored the rainbow chard. The kohlrabi actually made a very nice rosti. Even the final squash was completely and utterly delicious, as if to try to tempt me back. But no. It’s over. And I am finally free.Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsVegetablesOpinionSeasonal foodFarmingFoodPumpkinFood & drink industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: To understand the threat to our real democracy, watch Putin’s fake one | Rafael Behr | The Guardian
description: As Russians vote this weekend, remember that Britain is not immune to the cynical tactics and corrosion of trust that keep him in power, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Author: Rafael Behr
Headline: As Russians vote this weekend, remember that Britain is not immune to the cynical tactics and corrosion of trust that keep him in power, says Guardian columnist Rafael Behr
Content: A billboard displays portraits of the deputy chair of the state Duma, Pyotr Tolstoy, and Moscow’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, promoting the United Russia party, Moscow, 15 September 2026.Photograph: Ramil Sitdikov/ReutersView image in fullscreenA billboard displays portraits of the deputy chair of the state Duma, Pyotr Tolstoy, and Moscow’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, promoting the United Russia party, Moscow, 15 September 2026.Photograph: Ramil Sitdikov/ReutersOpinionRussiaTo understand the threat to our real democracy, watch Putin’s fake oneRafael BehrAs Russians vote this weekend, remember that Britain is not immune to the cynical tactics and corrosion of trust that keep him in powerWed 16 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 09.24 EDTShareMillions of people will participate in elections in Russia this weekend and a new parliament will be chosen, but not necessarily in that order. The purpose of the exercise is to maintain Vladimir Putin’s authority over the political process, which means United Russia, the president’s party, will retain control of the Duma.That much is settled before the polls open, although the scale of the government’s victory won’t be declared until the votes are counted. A portion of seats is available for other “systemic parties” that function as Kremlin licensed-opposition, padding out the pretence of pluralism. They serve as a pressure valves for public frustration and parliamentary proxies when rival factions within the ruling elite want to nudge Kremlin policy in one direction or another.The Kremlin likes to minimise the difference between United Russia’s official tally and a number that would plausibly reflect public attitudes to the regime. If the gap is too wide, achieved by fraud too blatant, it conveys insecurity in the Kremlin. Putin’s power doesn’t depend on endorsement by ordinary Russians but his authority is sustained by the illusion that he listens and cares. An egregiously stolen election would prove that he doesn’t.Everyone knows the result is fixed, but it would breach a social contract if the fiction became too absurd.Electoral verisimilitude is harder than usual to pull off this time because of war fatigue. No one can pretend any more that the “special military operation” in Ukraine has gone to plan. It was supposed to take weeks and is now in its fifth year. There have been about 1.5 million Russian casualties.Ashortage of volunteersstirs fear that another mobilisation of unwilling army reserves is in the works. Putin has denied that any such draft is required. That he needs to offer public reassurance at all amounts to recognition that progress on the front has stalled and the mood at home has soured.Ukrainiandrone and missile strikeshave made the war visible and economically palpable thousands of miles away from the frontline. The veil of state propaganda cannot be drawn across plumes of smoke rising from oil refineries and queues at petrol pumps.There are no accurate opinion polls in an authoritarian state. Russians are disinclined to share their private thoughts with strangers on the phone, especially when denigrating the armed forces is a criminal offence. A more reliable indicator of growing dissent is the increased rate of its repression. Last month, Yabloko, an inconsequential liberal party, wasbarred from the electionson a preposterous trumped-up technicality. The real objection was the party’s campaign slogan – “For peace and freedom”.Yabloko had previously been tolerated as an irrelevant vintage party from the pre-Putin era, not exactly tame but unthreatening; not worth the risk of aggrandisement by political martyrdom. That calculus changed with signs that voters were drifting towards the only available anti-war banner. It wasn’t a big movement but enough to persuade the authorities that denying the party representation after the ballot could be messier than blocking it in advance.If banning the opposition depresses turnout, all the better. The Kremlin appears to have accepted that a sincere show of enthusiasm for the status quo is unavailable. A boring, low-key election, telling a story of submission and stability, is the next best thing.Such is the perverse craft of “managed democracy” – the mechanics of running gangster authoritarianism through a notionally liberal constitution. It requires a mix of performative coercion, tactical concession and confected consent. The economic spoils of corruption have to be dispensed widely enough to feed a quiescent elite. There has to be enough theatre of public participation to legitimise the regime. But genuine freedom must also be discredited as the path of chaos.That has been an easy line to sell to Russians who recall post-Soviet democratisation as a time of rampant gangsterism, surrendered superpower status and national immiseration. Putin is a product of that era and the embodied backlash against it. He transferred the engines of oligarchic capitalist self-enrichment to the reconstituted chassis of a Soviet-style state. He made himself an avatar for imperial nostalgia and an exhausted population’s craving for order. He promised to express the national interest more efficiently as its sole incarnation than any raucous, divided parliament ever could.That offer has less appeal in established democracies, where political pluralism and the rule of law have deeper roots, but it has an audience. The core proposition – a strong leader to avenge a once great country’s humiliation by foreigners – has twice carried Donald Trump to the White House. Hisratings have plummetedbut he can still count on credulous adulation from as many as one in three Americans.What is the equivalent number in Britain? The leading product in this market is Reform UK, which now polls around 23%, level with Labour. Nigel Farage’s position has slipped this year as his personal and party finances have come under scrutiny, but his core supporters are untroubled by the whiff of grubby lucre. For some, convinced that the whole system is a rotten sham, scandal around Reform UK’s receipt ofmultimillion-pound donationspositively burnishes the brand. It proves that Farage is a baller, capable of beating the “establishment” parties at their own game – a gamble that the savvy, loadsamoney crypto crowd are backing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe deep cynicism feeding that judgment is a vital element in the chemical compound that corrodes democracy. I remember it as the most pungent feature of Russian politics when I lived in Moscow, watching the 90s experiment in democracy fail.It is the demoralised conviction that no politician would ever be motivated by a spirit of public service. The only categories are weak and strong; suckers and players. To succeed, a nation needs to be led by a strong player. Constitutions and laws are just parts of the toolkit for exercising power. The liberal view that holds them sacred as a system for holding governments to account is the mark of a sucker.Farage doesn’t put it quite like that. He did tell his party conference last week that an incoming Reform government woulddeclare a “national emergency”to enact a radical agenda within the first 100 days and tolerate no objection from parliament, the courts or Whitehall. No one can say they weren’t warned.It isn’t an explicitly anti-democratic agenda but it never is with populists in opposition. No one wins elections by promising to cancel future ballots and, as the Russian experience demonstrates, once power has been secured, the well-managed poll is a valuable mechanism for consolidating control.There is a process of hollowing-out that comes first. It is a relentless corrosion of trust in independent institutions and the sluicing of public debate with caustic cynicism. It is the stirring of disillusionment and frustration into nihilistic rage against the system; sowing division and amplifying despair to make authoritarian rule sound like release from political paralysis.Russia was lost down that road long ago. British democracy is thankfully more robust, more culturally embedded. Or so we hope. Resilience is not immunity. The Putin model of venal cynicism that dresses authoritarian kleptocracy in a call for national redemption won’t declare its motives in an election campaign. The democratic fightback can’t wait until that election to see how far the poison has spread.Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsRussiaOpinionVladimir PutinEuropeNigel FarageReform UKcommentShareReuse this content

title: Your photos, your words and your work: will Labor make it easier for AI companies to take them for free? | Holly Rankin | The Guardian
description: Every family photo you ever posted would be fair game for AI companies unless you choose to opt out
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Every family photo you ever posted would be fair game for AI companies unless you choose to opt out
Content: ‘This is about protecting the rights of all people to keep their right to decide how their content – their photos, their websites, their written word – is used by AI companies.’Photograph: Barry Mason/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘This is about protecting the rights of all people to keep their right to decide how their content – their photos, their websites, their written word – is used by AI companies.’Photograph: Barry Mason/AlamyOpinionAustralian politicsYour photos, your words and your work: will Labor make it easier for AI companies to take them for free?Holly RankinEvery family photo you ever posted would be fair game for AI companies unless you choose to opt outTue 15 Sep 2026 22.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 18.20 EDTShareLeaked documents from a government proposalshow that the Albanese government is consideringreversing the fundamental rights of Australians under copyright law.The proposal refers to an “opt-out model”. This would give AI companies permission to train on the open internet here in Australia. Every family photo you ever posted, every small business website, every website would be fair game for AI companies unless you choose to opt out.Labor accused of throwing creatives ‘under the bus’ with proposal to ease copyright protections for AI giantsRead moreRight now, under Australian law, a company has to ask for permission if it wants to use your content. This proposal would mean it doesn’t. It would put the onus on the individual to opt out – through a mechanism that hasn’t yet been proven to work. And it would give AI companies rights to your content until you choose to say no. This flips the legal burden on to the individual. It means that our legal system would serve the interests of AI companies first.AI companies have scraped on billions of pieces of content globally to train their models. There are more than 200 cases live around the world in which writers, journalists, artists, record labels and publishers are seeking to prove that this training is illegal. Just last year the UK decided to hold firm on copyright law when faced with similar pressure from AI companies – artists including Elton John, Dua Lipa andPaul McCartney led a national campaignto say “no way” – and their government listened.Artists are at the forefront of this fight as we protect the value that underpins our profession. But this isn’t just about us. This is about protecting the rights of all people to keep their right to decide how their content – their photos, their websites, their written word – is used by AI companies.Right now, chief executives including Sam Altman, Dario Amodei and Elon Muskare begging for global regulation of their technologyto prevent the apocalypse. Copyright lawisa part of that regulation. It protects individuals and their property. Every other industry, sector, company and individual has to ask for permission before using an individual’s work – trillion-dollar AI companies must do the same.If the most powerful companies in the world can’t properly licence the content they are training on, or if they can’t create the technology to license their training content properly, we must seriously question their technical and civil competency. They can solve diseases, fight wars, they might kill us all, but they can’t licence the content that makes their model “intelligent” in the first place? Seriously.Talk about self-control, regulation and “needing governments to step in” – well, copyright law is a start. Everyone else in our society abides by copyright law – we don’t steal other peoples stuff. We ask them permission to use it.If the Albanese government and the Coalition are requesting that the Australian people weaken their own rights for the benefit of the world’s biggest technology companies, they must explain the benefit transparently to Australians.Giving AI companies access to every piece of content that Australians have shared online without their permission or consent is a matter of grave concern for national security itself.The Albanese government must put this to the Australian people – do Australians want to let AI companies train on every piece of content they have ever put online, without permission and consent? Or do Australians want the government to be a global leader and force AI companies to train their models legally and with the consent of the people?Holly Rankin is an artist professionally known as Jack River and the executive director of Sentiment Group, a government affairs and strategic communications firmExplore more on these topicsAustralian politicsOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)ComputingIntellectual propertycommentShareReuse this content

title: Ed Sheeran wants to stay out of politics. By quitting his tour, his support acts have exposed the hollowness of neutrality | Music | The Guardian
description: By standing behind support act Macklemore, who was removed from the tour for his vocal support of Palestine, these artists are demonstrating the self-sacrifice necessary to stand against those crushing free speech
Author: Laura Snapes
Headline: By standing behind support act Macklemore, who was removed from the tour for his vocal support of Palestine, these artists are demonstrating the self-sacrifice necessary to stand against those crushing free speech
Content: ‘Creating inconvenience is precisely what it takes to show backbone’ … Ed Sheeran (left) and Macklemore.Photograph: Kevin Winter/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Creating inconvenience is precisely what it takes to show backbone’ … Ed Sheeran (left) and Macklemore.Photograph: Kevin Winter/Getty ImagesOpinionMusicEd Sheeran wants to stay out of politics. By quitting his tour, his support acts have exposed the hollowness of neutralityLaura SnapesBy standing behind support act Macklemore, who was removed from the tour for his vocal support of Palestine, these artists are demonstrating the self-sacrifice necessary to stand against those crushing free speechWed 16 Sep 2026 12.43 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 13.26 EDTShareIn a statement aboutMacklemorebeing dropped from his US stadium tour for making pro-Palestinian comments, Ed Sheeran defended his own publicly apolitical stance: “If we only ever focus on shouting the loudest, nothing will ever change. There are different approaches to being an advocate for change.”Every other musician involved with the tour – support acts Finneas (Billie Eilish’s brother), Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish songwriter Aaron Rowe, plus Sheeran’s Irish backing band, Beoga – has made their approach to advocating for change clear, pulling out of the remaining dates to protest against the censorship of Macklemore and to express support for the Palestinian people.In a statement released yesterday, Sheeran stressed that it wasn’t his decision to remove Macklemore, who called for a free Palestine on stage at the MetLife stadium in New Jersey last week. “I am not complicit,” Sheeran wrote. Macklemore (who in 2014 had to apologise after being accused of perpetuating antisemitic stereotypeswith an onstage costume) wrote that his removal from the tour was organised by New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, who owns Gillette Stadium outside Boston, where Sheeran’s Loop tour is due to play in late September.Kraft confirmed he barred Macklemore from opening for Sheeran at the Gillette Stadium, but did not respond to claims he organised the boycott by the other venues. (In a statement he said his decision was “not about diminishing the suffering of innocent Palestinians or denying anyone the right to advocate on their behalf” but that such advocacy “should not obscure the responsibility of Hamas”.)Sheeran explained that he doesn’t use his platform for politics in order to be “a place of safety and sanctuary, to maintain diplomacy and keep conversations open”. Though this isn’t accurate: he performed at the Concert for Ukraine in 2022, signed an open letter to Theresa May about Brexit, endorsed Jeremy Corbyn and supported the equality act in the US.Either way, the consequences of his apolitical stance have proven beyond doubt that there is no such thing as a neutral position, especially when you’re operating in a political culture that rarely obstructs corporate overreach. Kraft is friends with Trump and is a major donor to Israel: Netanyahu said at a 2019 awards ceremony honouring Kraft that “Israel does not have a more loyal friend”.10:05Ed Sheeran support acts quit after Macklemore ‘Free Palestine’ row - The LatestThe decisive actions of every other musician on the tour have made a mockery of Sheeran claiming to be powerless in this situation. In his statement, Sheeran wrote that he would never “let down the fans who had made plans” by cancelling shows, “nor would I abandon the touring crew and the other support acts and musicians who rely on me for work and to make a living”. What might initially appear as a sign of solidarity – not inconveniencing fans, not leaving other artists and crew out of pocket – has been upended by a group of artists who understand that losing financial and professional opportunities and creating inconvenience is precisely what it takes to show backbone and stand against genocide and billionaires crushing free speech.Macklemore’s speech in New Jersey introduced his 2024 song Hind’s Hall, which castigates censorship of protest against Israel’s genocide in Palestine, particularly the student encampment at Columbia University in New York,and is named after Hind Rajab, a five-year-old Palestinian girl killed by Israeli forces. “What you willin’ to risk?” he asked in the song. “What you willin’ to give?” Many musicians and actors who have spoken out against Israel’s actions in Gaza have talked about losing work as a result: Susan Sarandon said last week at the Venice film festival that she has had acting gigs taken away; Irish pop star CMAT said alucrative beauty contract was withdrawn; Swedish star Zara Larsson said she was dropped from brand deals and awards shows.That hasn’t stopped them and other figures from continuing to speak out, putting moral imperative above personal gain, and recognising that any such “loss” bears no relation to what is happening to human life and habitat inGaza, where Israel’s military offensive is estimated to have led to a death toll of 70,000. Dublin songwriter Aaron Rowe, by far the smallest support act on Sheeran’s tour and thus the one with the most to lose, thanked him for the life-changing opportunity. “But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation,” his statement continued. “I need to be true to myself and my ancestors who resisted colonisation, and fought for a freedom that I enjoy today in Ireland.”Sheeran and countless others take the line that pop culture should be somewhere fans can go to escape politics. “I do understand that for a lot of people, they just want to leave politics aside for a bit and be able to enjoy the music,” culture secretary Lisa Nandy said of the Sheeran situation on LBC this morning. But the fact that most right-wing politicians also take that view indicates the fact that they see pop cultural figures, with their largely left-leaning views and huge reach among young people, as a genuine threat best silenced.As Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said yesterday, this isn’t just about the musicians on Sheeran’s tour, but “how just a handful of stadium owners can prevent [discussion of] an entire massive issue, in this case, the genocide in Gaza”. Prominent figures who go along with that view and deny the power of their voice allow these billion-dollar corporations to rob us of our rights step by step until one day there is nothing left. “We need to be very clear about how dangerous a precedent this is,” said Ocasio-Cortez.At worst, Sheeran – who has always been open about his commercially minded approach to pop – looks like a corporate shill; at best, wilfully naive. Sheeran loves to dabble in the music of other cultures to present a toothless pan-global vision of togetherness lifted from the latter-day Coldplay playbook. But you can’t play with the aesthetics of global music without also being willing to engage in the lived reality of those cultures.“Those who have been to one of my shows will know that they are about unity, joy, escapism, love and a place for everyone to feel welcome,” Sheeran wrote in his statement. Just as long as they shut up and sing: Sheeran’s inaction and humiliation at the hands of his principled supporting musicians have irrevocably compromised a position that’s no longer fit for purpose, if it ever was.Explore more on these topicsMusicOpinionEd SheeranMacklemorePop and rockGazaIsrael-Gaza warMiddle East and north AfricacommentShareReuse this content

title: Your mission, Tom Cruise, is to improve at interviews. And please keep sending the cakes | Movies | The Guardian
description: He risks his life for entertainment, but getting an anecdote out of him is a trickier matter. Happily, Cruise is no stranger to knuckling down and pulling off the impossible
Author: Stuart Heritage
Headline: He risks his life for entertainment, but getting an anecdote out of him is a trickier matter. Happily, Cruise is no stranger to knuckling down and pulling off the impossible
Content: Acting again … Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in Digger.Photograph: Warner BrosView image in fullscreenActing again … Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell in Digger.Photograph: Warner BrosMoviesYour mission, Tom Cruise, is to improve at interviews. And please keep sending the cakesHe risks his life for entertainment, but getting an anecdote out of him is a trickier matter. Happily, Cruise is no stranger to knuckling down and pulling off the impossibleStuart HeritageWed 16 Sep 2026 06.24 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 06.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy now, we’ve grown used to watchingTom Cruiseexcel at everything he does. Running in films? The best. Risking his life in action scenes so preposterously dangerous that audiences need to have their sphincters manually unclenched with a crowbar? Absolutely, none better. Singlehandedly ensuring that theatrical exhibition didn’t go extinct after Covid? The man deserves all the praise in the world for that.But nobody is perfect. Live long enough and a few flaws will worm their way to the surface. This is as true for Tom Cruise as it is for anyone else. And while I realise that thismight do me out of a cake this Christmas, the following really needs to be said: Tom Cruise isn’t very good at interviews.As you will be aware, Cruise’s new film Digger comes out soon. The film is a risk. It is his first original, non-sequel, non-action film in which he co-stars since2007’s Lions for Lambs. It is also, if the trailers are any indication, palpably batshit. This means that Cruise has to reintroduce himself to the world as an actor, rather than the guy who just flings himself off a variety of increasingly berserk surfaces. And this means promotion. Until this week, that promotion has involved either World Cup-themed promos filmed in character or interviews where the subject matterwas almost exclusively limited to lens choice.However, yesterday Cruisesubjected himself to a rare longforminterview opposite GQ’s Zach Baron. On paper, it couldn’t have been easier. Baron was a perfectly chosen interviewer for the job, understanding exactly when to flatter and when to needle. However, Tom Cruise’s defences are foot-thick and watertight, and the majority of Baron’s questions simply bounced off him.This resulted in a fairly unsatisfactory 30-minute stalemate in which Tom Cruise talked and talked and said nothing at all. No matter how hard Baron probed, he was met with a fat wedge of waffle. The clickbait industrial complex has done its best to pick the bones of the interview for a news peg, but the best it seems to have come up with is a variation of “Tom Cruise admits that he can be intense on set”.Which, well, duh.Aside from that, we simply got a rehash of all the old talking points from every junket he’s done for a decade. He’d rather talk about cinematography than himself. He is constantly trying to learn new skills. He writes down his dreams and how to accomplish them. None of this is new information. It’s all highly frustrating. But it does make sense. As brilliant as he is on screen, behind the scenes Cruise is a carefully managed enigma. This may well be because, the last time he allowed his own self to parade before the press, it ended with couch-jumping and excruciatingly testy interviews about Scientology.
