It seems unthinkable now, but that press run went so badly that Sumner Redstone ended upeffectively firing Cruise from Paramount over it.It took Cruise years to build himself back up from that, and the results have been spectacular. The Mission: Impossible films have been some of the greatest of his career. Top Gun: Maverick saved Hollywood. He is now in a position of enormous power and authority. So going back out in front of an interviewer is bound to be a risk for him. But one thing is certain. The Digger promotional cycle cannot just be variations of the GQ interview, because too many opaque soundbites will simply end up boring potential audiences rigid. There will be more interviews – he’s thought to be hitting the podcast circuit soon – so he needs to adapt his strategy.The good news is that one thing Cruise did say in his GQ interview is that, when he sets a goal, he writes down all the steps necessary to accomplish it. This is exactly what he should do here. If his dream is doing press that will make people want to watch Digger, then he knows he will need to work up some new anecdotes – long enough to filibuster, but twisty enough to entertain – while developing a persona that appears to welcome scrutiny while wriggling out from underneath it.It can be done. Robert Downey Jr is an actor with many areas of his past he would rather not touch in print, and he has built up an incredibly charming suit of armour that allows him to breezily bat questions away when they get too personal. This is exactly what Tom Cruise should be learning to do. Or perhaps not; after all, he has made hundreds of millions of dollars by revealing scarcely anything about himself for a decade. Maybe that’s an option, too.But, hey, this is Tom Cruise. When he sets his mind on something, he achieves it. With that in mind, expect a dramatic upward turn in the quality of his interviews from this moment onwards. Thanks for reading. Please still send cakes.Explore more on these topicsFilmTom CruiseDrama filmsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A naked performance artist in the garden with her mum: Rona Bar and Ofek Avshalom’s best photograph | Art and design | The Guardian
description: ‘Lois and her mother Carey are artists and their house is full of art, which seems to spill out of them. The way they express their Judaism was something we hadn’t encountered before’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘Lois and her mother Carey are artists and their house is full of art, which seems to spill out of them. The way they express their Judaism was something we hadn’t encountered before’
Content: ‘They welcomed us with open arms’ … Lois and Carey by Rona Bar and Ofek Avshalom, who work under the name Fotómetro.Photograph: Rona Bar and Ofek AvshalomView image in fullscreen‘They welcomed us with open arms’ … Lois and Carey by Rona Bar and Ofek Avshalom, who work under the name Fotómetro.Photograph: Rona Bar and Ofek AvshalomMy best shotArt and designA naked performance artist in the garden with her mum: Rona Bar and Ofek Avshalom’s best photograph‘Lois and her mother Carey are artists and their house is full of art, which seems to spill out of them. The way they express their Judaism was something we hadn’t encountered before’Interview byChris BroughtonWed 16 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 10.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis photograph is of Lois and Carey, who we found while looking for subjects for our projectProof of Existence. That series involved transforming models into surreal or exaggerated characters based on aspects of themselves, then photographing them in everyday settings. We got in contact with Lois after seeing her work on Instagram. When we went to her house and met her mother, Carey, we became very intrigued by the two of them, by their relationship and by the house itself.The intention of thatinitial photowas to show how they express their Jewish identity in a non-traditional way. Lois and Carey are artists and their house is full of art. It was amazing to see how the things they’re interested in seem almost to spill out of their bodies and on to the walls, in the form of artwork, motifs and symbols. Their story is everywhere; it feels like the house itself is alive.The way they express their Judaism was something we hadn’t encountered before. Lois is involved in performance art, and the fetish community, and her art deals with sexuality and queerness. In that first photo, she’s standing in the kitchen wearing a latex mask and bodysuit featuring the Star of David, while Carey sits drawing at the table behind her. It’s a striking example of one of the themes of the series – how heritage is passed on from one generation to another, being reinvented every time.double quotation markCarey is watering her plants and Lois almost looks as if she is one of themThat photograph became the starting point for a new project, focusing entirely on Lois and Carey and their home. They welcomed us with open arms and it was very easy to work with them, so we just kept going. They gave us completely free rein, and two years after meeting them, we would still be finding new rooms, new walls, new knick-knacks. One of our favourite photographs is of Lois’s abandoned childhood bedroom, with its bright pink fireplace contrasting with the peeling walls.The garden is as impressive as the house’s interior. Carey is obsessed with it and takes care of it daily. Another thing we like to explore in our work is contrast – ordinary acts with an aspect of absurdity or weirdness that provokes or intrigues the viewer and makes them wonder. The pose they are in here is obviously staged, but represents an emotional truth – the unique connection and coexistence of the two. The garden is an extension and symbol of the relationship, in a way. Carey is watering her plants, and Lois is just there in between them, almost as if she is one of them.In some of the photographs, we also see Carey naked. The pair of them are very comfortable being nude around one another, completely relaxed and unguarded, but their closeness is mostly unspoken. They won’t say “I love you” or be very touchy, but they do demonstrate their closeness in other ways. For example, one of our photographs shows Lois tattooing her mother, which is a very intimate act. She does that all the time: it’s as if Carey acts as a canvas for her daughter’s art.Certain themes, such as relationships, individualities and the home as an extension of identity, run through much of our work, which we do under the name Fotómetro. Our first joint long-term project,Us, was started in Tel Aviv and completed in London after we moved there in 2022. After collaborating a few years before, we’d realised we liked the work we did together more than our individual projects, and later we became a couple. Partly inspired by our own relationship, Us involved taking portraits of couples in their homes. People’s homes say so much about them.Our association with Lois and Carey quickly became a friendship – sometimes, we would visit them without even taking the camera. Even since the series became a book, they continue to inspire us. We’re currently working on two films – one about Lois and one about Carey.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: FotómetroFotómetro’s CVBorn:Israel, 1995High points:Exhibiting at the National Portrait Gallery in London as part of the 2023 Taylor WessingPhotographyprize (we will exhibit there again in November – Lois and Carey in the Garden has been chosen for this year’s Winston Taylor Photo Portrait prize). Presenting our solo exhibition, Proof of Existence, at Cicek Gallery, London, in 2025. Winning the Eve Arnold Photography prize in 2025 with our series Lois and Carey. Publishing two photobooks: Us with Snap Collective in 2022, and Lois & Carey with 89Books in 2026. Exhibiting at Photo London 2026 with Bright GalleryTop tips:The most important work is the never-ending process of personal exploration and developing your own artistic voice. The photographs you choose to make and the stories you choose to tell should feel like a calling – something you genuinely need to explore and communicate. An artist should constantly ask themselves: what do I want to say? How do I want to say it? And, most importantly, why do I need to say it? This process of questioning, experimenting and discovering your own perspective is far more important than technique, equipment or following trends. Those things can be learned and acquired, but developing a voice that is truly your own takes time, curiosity and continuous exploration.Fotómetro’s Lois and Carey series will be exhibited at the Head On Photo festival in Sydney, Australia, in November. To see work by Lois Ward-Marvin and Carey Marvin, visit@lois.spookeddand@c.s.marvinExplore more on these topicsArt and designMy best shotPhotographyArtPerformance artfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The secret of Mozart’s genius unlocked – has a teenager succeeded where generations of musicologists have failed? | Classical music | The Guardian
description: US student Linus Chen-Plotkin has analysed music by four canonical composers looking for patterns. Turns out Mozart’s music moves in the least predictable way
Author: Tom Service
Headline: US student Linus Chen-Plotkin has analysed music by four canonical composers looking for patterns. Turns out Mozart’s music moves in the least predictable way
Content: Sensual and surprising … the Sacconi Quartet perform Mozart at the Wigmore Hall in London.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverView image in fullscreenSensual and surprising … the Sacconi Quartet perform Mozart at the Wigmore Hall in London.Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverTom Service on musicClassical musicThe secret of Mozart’s genius unlocked – has a teenager succeeded where generations of musicologists have failed?Tom ServiceUS student Linus Chen-Plotkin has analysed music by four canonical composers looking for patterns. Turns out Mozart’s music moves in the least predictable wayWed 16 Sep 2026 11.06 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 19.48 EDTShareIt’s a question that has taxed musical thinkers for centuries: just what is it about one composer’s music that makes it more distinctive than anyone else’s? Entire disciplines of academic thought, of music analysis and historical musicology, as well as the formation of classical music’s canon of “great” composers, have been given over to this single idea: can it be proved that Mozart, say, was measurably “better” than other composers?Our instinctive feeling about the sensual magic of Mozart’s music is part of the equation, but accounting for preciselyhowhis pieces can sustain a lifetime of listening,whytheir pleasures never seem to pall and are still capable of seeming to surprise us even when we know them inside out: that’s the million-dollar musicological question.double quotation markMozart sets up patterns of expectation in his melodies that he confounds rather than confirmsWhat generations of music analysts have tried and largely failed to do through imperfect means of variously subjective techniques, an 18-year-old US student has managed to prove through a combination of data and interpretative ingenuity.A recent study by Philadelphia studentLinus Chen-Plotkindemonstrates that Mozart’s melodies are more surprising in the way they unfold, moment-by-moment and note-by-note, than those of his contemporaries and successors, Haydn, Beethoven and Schubert.View image in fullscreen‘Better’ than other composers: Will Sharpe as Mozart in Sky TV’s Amadeus.Photograph: Adrienn Szabo/Sky UKChen-Plotkin put 600 movements of these four composers’ piano sonatas and string quartets through his bespoke software to analyse their tunes, based onMarkov chainsand other statistical and mathematical tools (he explains his work here). The data revealed that Mozart’s tunes have a shorter “memory” than other composers. That means the way they move is less predictable: that Mozart sets up patterns of expectation in his melodies and ideas that he confounds rather than confirms.You can instinctively hear that at work in so many moments of his string quartets:the opening idea of the E flat major quartet, K428, which is already slipping out of the realms of the expected as early as its third note; or the opening ofthe Dissonance Quartet, K465, whose entire introduction is a chain of ever-more surprising moves of melody and harmony.View image in fullscreenAnalysis … Linus Chen-PlotkinPhotograph: Chris Ayers/Society for ScienceChen-Plotkin is circumspectabout the consequences of his work, recognising its limits as well as its possibilities. In fact, his statistical analyses shore up the conclusions that musicologists have often made about Mozart’s music: that it’s dizzyingly rich and strange in how it moves from note to note and phrase to phrase, but that Mozart was less interested in finding new or unpredictable structures across entire movements. In fact, if Chen-Plotkin were looking at unpredictability across whole pieces and not at the smaller scale of individual tunes and melodies, he would probably have come up with very different results: my hunch at least would be that Beethoven and Haydn would win those contests.Mind you, Chen-Plotkin isn’t suggesting that maths replaces musicology. As well as being against the use of generative AI in art-making, his ambition is simply to show how statistical analysis can help reveal the underlying patterns behind human creativity. And his work has just begun: he enrols at university this autumn, and has already embarked on a computational analysis of the works and words of Chaucer.Anyway: I’m back to put more Mozart through the random note generator of my fingers as I try – and fail, yet again – to play even one movement of his piano sonatas without making a mistake that not even Chen-Plotkin’s software or Markov’s chains could predict.The Royal Philharmonic Orchestra is 80 this week, and, as you can see on their anniversarytimeline, there’s a lot to celebrate. Which other orchestra can claim a legacy that encompasses some of the most exciting performances of Sibelius ever recorded in the 1950s and 60s? Listen to their founder Thomas Beecham’sperformance of Tapiolato hear the edge of orchestral possibility, just as Sibelius pushes his music to new limits of wildness and experimentalism. Then, in the orchestra’s years with Rudolf Kempe in the 60s and early 70s, it transformed London’s musical life, and made pioneering recordings such asJanáček’s Glagolitic Mass.But this is also the orchestra that Beecham insisted was men-only for as long as he conducted them (until his death in 1961), and which only had its first female musician over a decade later –clarinettist Prudence Whittaker.View image in fullscreenHappy 80th RPO: Vasily Petrenko conducts the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra at the Royal Festival Hall in April 2025’s Multitudes festival.Photograph: Mark AllanIt’s also the same ensemble who would find new dimensions of orchestral kitsch with Hooked on Classics in the 1980s, who recorded the Champions League theme in the 90s, and played at King Charles’s coronation in the 2020s; and it’s the orchestra that played this summer withMandle Cheung, who paid an undisclosed amount to conduct Mahler’s Resurrection Symphony.The RPO have soundtracked the decades from the sublime to the ridiculous; and they’ve surfed financial crisis after crisis over the years. Under Vasily Petrenko’s music directorship since 2021, here’s hoping the sublime continues to win out.This week, Tom has been listening to:Riccardo Minasi’s recording ofMozart’s last three symphonies with Ensemble Resonanz. I’ve been blown away by their ferocious imagination. The rhetorical volatility of these performances, their mix of styles, genres and ideas, isn’t an outlier in how this music should be performed – it’s in the fabric of how these symphonies are composed, and what they mean. Mozart reallyisunpredictable! Listen onSpotify| Apple ClassicalExplore more on these topicsClassical musicTom Service on musicWolfgang Amadeus MozartcommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Very authoritarian, very brutal’: three decades after the UK’s anti-rave crackdown, why is France doing the same? | Dance music | The Guardian
description: With tear gas, grenades and a new law, French authorities are targeting unlicensed music gatherings. Those in the rave scene explore the parallels with the UK in the 90s
Author: Whitney Wei
Headline: With tear gas, grenades and a new law, French authorities are targeting unlicensed music gatherings. Those in the rave scene explore the parallels with the UK in the 90s
Content: ‘Franch ravers completely understood the concept’ … Spiral Tribe rave in Paris, 1993.Photograph: Spiral Tribe Exhibition ArchiveView image in fullscreen‘Franch ravers completely understood the concept’ … Spiral Tribe rave in Paris, 1993.Photograph: Spiral Tribe Exhibition ArchiveDance music‘Very authoritarian, very brutal’: three decades after the UK’s anti-rave crackdown, why is France doing the same?With tear gas, grenades and a new law, French authorities are targeting unlicensed music gatherings. Those in the rave scene explore the parallels with the UK in the 90sWhitney WeiWed 16 Sep 2026 10.29 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Spiral Tribe fled England in 1992, they left behind an indelible mark on rave history. The itinerant sound system collective are best known for their involvement with Castlemorton Common festival, an unlicensed free party drawing more than 30,000 people and lasting nearly a week. After a drawn-out and notoriously expensive trial for public order offences, Spiral Tribe were acquitted of all charges. They decided to drive their repurposed military caravans out of the UK and never look back.Their documented history often stops there. But little known is the fact that they then kicked off “the biggest illegal underground movement thatEuropehad ever seen”, says Spiral Tribe associate Sebastian Vaughan, AKA electronic musician 69db.Many Spiral members, including Vaughan, settled throughoutFranceafter a warm response to the Spiral sound – a 160bpm sped-up version of hip-house with delayed kick drums, known as hardtek or tribe – and to the collective’s punk-rave aesthetic. Over the last three decades, their underground Teknival parties in France grew from about 1,000 attendees in 1993 to tens of thousands in 1995 and up to 100,000 people by the early 2000s, far exceeding the turnout at Castlemorton. French ravers, Vaughan says, “completely understood what the concept was, and they weren’t just following it, they were creating it themselves”. He attributes Spiral’s underground appeal to the country’s likeminded appetite for resistance.But equally, “the French have always been very authoritarian and very brutal in their response to free parties”, says Mark Harrison, another Spiral Tribe founding member. He says he has witnessed the French riot police, known as Compagnies Républicaines de Sécurité (CRS), descend on dancefloors armed with stun grenades and rubber bullets in events from the mid-90s onwards.In 2019, a police raid caused revellers at a Fête de la Musique concert in Nantes to fall into the Loire river, and 24-year-oldSteve Maia Caniçowas found drowned. Two years later, the CRS raideda Teknival rave in Rendonheld in Caniço’s memory armed with tear gas and sting ball GM2L grenades. There were no attempts beforehand at dialogue or de-escalation. The violence resulted in a 22-year-old partygoer losing his hand. Another woman had her cheek pierced and teeth broken by a grenade fragment. Amnesty International France reported on the unnecessary use of force at the Rendon event asa human rights violation.Now, the French parliament has formally enacted theRipostpublic disorder law, targeting unlicensed music gatherings of more than 250 people. Free party organisers could face two years’ imprisonment, confiscation of their vehicles and sound equipment, and a fine of up to €30,000. Even attendees could face up to six months in jail and a €7,500 fine.View image in fullscreenA Teknival event in Italy, 1993.Photograph: Spiral Tribe Exhibition ArchiveIt feels similar to the crackdown Spiral Tribe faced in the wake of Castlemorton: two years later, theUK’s Criminal Justice and Public Order Actcriminalised gatherings of more than 20 people where “the emission of a succession of repetitive beats” was deemed to “cause serious distress to the inhabitants of the locality”.The newly enacted French law aims to protect rural communities whose land has been misused by ravers, such as a May 2024 party thrown in heritage vineyards in the Loire Regional National Park or one inSeptember 2025 in Audeshortly after the region was devastated by wildfires. In May, interior minister Laurent Nuñez, who publicly championed the bill, visited a protest against the policy in his home town of Bourges. The demonstration,he told the press, only served to “strengthen the government’s determination to crack down more harshly on this kind of wild event, which our fellow citizens do not understand”.But critics argue that the law disproportionately affects young, working-class citizens, and free party proponents claim that the gatherings that have gone awry are only a few out of the thousands held every year.Mouillette, a volunteer with the Fonds de Soutien Juridique des Sons, a group of French lawyers supporting free party sound systems, distributes literature on how to properly prepare a party, choose a location and secure and manage the event within legal grounds while also making sure that the rave is a good experience for everyone involved. “Many organisers are very young and need to learn,” she says, “but with the government against us, we cannot educate them.”She says that the prison sentence for partygoers is an illogical move for legislators. The French prison system is already facing adangerous overcrowding crisis– considered the second worst in Europe in a 2025annual penal statistics report– with records earlier this year revealing 86,229 inmates in spaces only suitedfor 62,000.“We will be locked up alongside murderers,” Mouillette claims.When Spiral Tribe and other free party sound systems were created more than 30 years ago, they were a reaction against capitalism and state powers enforcing “a path of normativity that [was] very obedient and subservient”, says Harrison. He thinks that the underground rave movement remains an important laboratory for alternative forms of society. However, “the narrowing of imagination, the narrowing of opportunities created by this authoritarian direction that we’re all being pushed [into] is very disturbing”, he says, calling it “anti-culture”.“For us, Ripost is part of the ongoing trend towards the gradual erosion of individual freedoms and the right’s state surveillance of the population that we are facing since the Covid pandemic,” says Kamille, a pseudonymous spokesperson ofTekno Anti-repression. This collective of French free party advocates assembled in 2022 to change the mainstream narrative around the underground movement after 30 years of virtually no organising power. “There is more and more repression of social movements and protests,” Kamille says. “We consider [this] a global shift towards the right and their desire for mass control of people who are against the system.”‘I fell in a deep puddle running from police’: photographing London’s underground ravesRead moreHow strictly the French government will enforce the Ripost law remains to be seen. But Spiral Tribe members believe that more and more young people are waking up to the hypocrisy and corruption around them.“You would have to be living under a rock to not see the double standards imposed on the population by the establishment,” says Vaughan, citing the abuses exposed in the Epstein files. “The world we live in is a nightmare.” He urges ravers to vote for the far-left La France Insoumise, the only party supportive of the free movement.“We have to remain optimistic,” Harrison adds. “I think this is one of the reasons why power attacks free parties. They want to kill that spirit because they know that one of the most powerful things about a good party is that you feel connected. You feel that unity.”Unmasked presents: Spiral Tribe Exhibition is atReinstate, London, 16-19 September. An accompanying rave, SP23, is at Distillery, London, on 19 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsDance musicFranceEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We weren’t shy. We were queers in leather!’ Sunil Gupta on his momentous photographs of gay life | Art and design | The Guardian
description: From Delhi to New York, from the street to the bath house, he has captured clandestine moments, risked his freedom – and even referenced Romantic painters. Ahead of a major show, the photographer relives his landmark shots
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: From Delhi to New York, from the street to the bath house, he has captured clandestine moments, risked his freedom – and even referenced Romantic painters. Ahead of a major show, the photographer relives his landmark shots
Content: ‘Based on a scene from La Jettée’ … Sunil Gupta, from Sun City (2010).Photograph: Sunil Gupta/© Sunil Gupta. All Rights Reserved, DACS 2025.View image in fullscreen‘Based on a scene from La Jettée’ … Sunil Gupta, from Sun City (2010).Photograph: Sunil Gupta/© Sunil Gupta. All Rights Reserved, DACS 2025.Art and design‘We weren’t shy. We were queers in leather!’ Sunil Gupta on his momentous photographs of gay lifeFrom Delhi to New York, from the street to the bath house, he has captured clandestine moments, risked his freedom – and even referenced Romantic painters. Ahead of a major show, the photographer relives his landmark shotsCharlotte JansenWed 16 Sep 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 05.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘I’ve been very promiscuous,” Sunil Gupta says, reflecting on his experiments with photography since the 1970s. Gupta, who was born in India, brought up in Canada and moved to the UK in 1978 after two years studying in New York, has documented and described queer lives for five decades. In his work, he’s quietly tried to find new ways of seeing, exploring the potential of photography to blur fiction and reality, public space and intimate, clandestine moments. His work explores the ways we love and relate to one another, set against the ever-shifting tides of politics and society.He photographs with love – but it hasn’t been without risk. An exhibition in India was once shut down by the government, and in his early days in the UK, when he was working with fellow photographer Tessa Boffin, he recalls curators “physically shrinking away when we walked in the room – two queers in leather were too much for them! But we were quite aggressively upfront with our sexualities, we weren’t shy about it.”Ahead of his retrospective exhibition at Kettle’s Yard in Cambridge, Gupta talks through 10 landmark images from across his career.1. No 43 from Christopher StreetView image in fullscreenPhotograph: © Sunil Gupta. All Rights Reserved, DACS 2025.This is almost the only photograph in this series that prominently features a person of colour; it was unusual to see Asian people on Christopher Street in New York at the time, and I saw myself a little bit in the person on the right. These two in the foreground are very much what I remember from that time: you get the hair and clothes because you want to look the part, and you find someone to hang out with. Behind them is the counterfoil: the regular gay guys who parade up and down Christopher Street – but here, they’re in the background. I also like the lone figure further down the street – there’s something about the loneliness of cruising on the street.2. From Towards an Indian Gay ImageView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sunil Gupta/© Sunil Gupta. All Rights Reserved, DACS 2026This picture is defining because I’d gone back to Delhi for the first time. I had grown up next to this tomb, which is why it keeps reappearing in the work. I was trying to find a way of photographing gay men in Delhi, but this was circa 1982 – nobody would be in a picture. There was complete silence around the subject of homosexuality. Even people who went out to have sex in public places – there was no chitchat, no language around it. So I began to take headless pictures but it wasn’t really going anywhere. But I liked this, and it made my degree show at the RCA. When I graduated, my livelihood was freelancing. I went to The Guardian, and they said, is there a story? I said yes, then I ran home and wrote a story and they published it in the paper – so it is also my first published picture.3. From Trespass Series 1View image in fullscreenPhotograph: © Sunil Gupta. All Rights Reserved, DACS 2026.I made these montages on the first Apple computers that had lo-res scanners, I had a lot of fun with it. I printed them very big in a coffee shop in Soho. The discussion at that time, in 1992, was the opposite of Brexit – should we go into the single European currency? The left then was quite anti the euro, and it raised a lot of questions for migrants from the Commonwealth – we thought we would lose our right to be here. In this series I imagined Germany as the centre of a united Europe – geographically and economically.4. From ‘Pretended’ Family RelationshipsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: © Sunil Gupta. All Rights Reserved, DACS 2025This began as a project about Clause 28, [later Section 28, a law introduced by Thatcher’s government in 1988 that banned local authorities and schools from “promoting homosexuality”]. In the late 1980s, I was living in a bubble in Brixton, with a white partner, and all the couples we knew were multiracial, and we thought that was cool and how it should be. I began to shoot but it was hard to get Black and Asian models to be in queer stuff in pictures, no one could be out. So they were fake couples, people I knew.5. From Love and LightView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sunil Gupta/© Sunil Gupta. All Rights Reserved, DACS 2026This marked my return to India in 2005. I had met this person in Leh, who was in film and theatre. He was a guru as well. We got together, it was very intense. I turned up in India with my suitcase, by which time he had lost interest. But I thought I would stay. The plan had been to make a series of pictures of us together in various interesting locations – instead it turned into just me in various interesting locations. And then at the end,I met my husband, Charan Singh, at an Aids conference in Delhi. He was a social worker and I was on stage as a person with HIV.6. From Country: Portrait of an Indian Village(taken in 2007)View image in fullscreenPhotograph: © Sunil Gupta. All Rights Reserved, DACS 2025.In London, you walk out and no one knows you. Then you go to this village in India and everyone knows who you are, who your grandfather was, how you arrived. After a few weeks it’s quite claustrophobic. I thought I’d make a project about a village in Rajasthan and I got very involved with it but it was as an outsider. But in this place, I wander around with a camera, I stop and chat. An uncle gave me a 300-year oral history. My cousin has built me a horrible concrete bunker on my father’s small piece of land which he thinks I might like to live in, which is very sweet of him. I guess if everything went belly up I could be there in the bunker.7. From Sun City (main image)This is based on a scene fromChris Marker’s La Jettée. It’s a coming together of a gay photo history I was never taught but I gathered for myself. Each person’s pose references a different historic image – fromRobert MapplethorpetoGeorge Platt Lynesback toWilhelm Von Gloedenand French Romantic painting.8. From the Black ExperienceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sunil Gupta/© Sunil Gupta. All Rights Reserved, DACS 2025.This was part of a show at [London gallery] Autograph in 1986, commissioned by the Greater London Council. The idea of Black then was anybody with heritage that came from a form of British empire – the GLC’s early definitions even included the Irish. I found myself with two struggles – Asians who didn’t think they were Black, and Black colleagues who weren’t looking at Asian culture at all. I thought if I didn’t make the pictures about South Asians there would be no images of us in the show – I made 10 pictures. That exhibition was the start of Autograph. It’s incredible it’s still there.9. From HomelandsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sunil Gupta/© Sunil Gupta. All Rights Reserved, DACS 2026.I was at a very low point. I was approaching 50. I’d been diagnosed with HIV, my work had gone down and my social life had gone. I got a three-year fellowship in Southampton, which was quite extraordinary. I made this project about me as a person with HIV looking at the landscape and where I had come from. These pictures were both made in London; one is in St Thomas’ hospital where I have my treatments, and the unpleasant experience of having a reverse drip coming out of my heart. The other image is on Drummond Street, where I would go to an Indian food place.10. From ExilesView image in fullscreenPhotograph: © Sunil Gupta. All Rights Reserved, DACS 2025.In 1986-7 I got a commission from the Photographers’ Gallery in London. I thought I’d use it to go back to Delhi and do a project about Indian gay men. My informants took me to the places they went cruising and agreed to be in the pictures, up to a point. I would chat to many more people just with a tape recorder. The extracts are from the recordings but they don’t always match the person in the picture. I felt just pictures wouldn’t convey the complexity of what was going on.I think part of my journey has been to put Indian gay men into cultural history. When I was a student you couldn’t find them anywhere. I’m so excited this work has now been acquired by MoMA in New York, so I feel they’re in the history books now. My job is done.Sunil Gupta: Life with a Camera, 1970 – Now is atKettles Yard, Cambridge,19 September to 31 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designPhotographyArtSexualityAids and HIVfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘We thought death could do with a bit of dancing’: welcome to Sondering, the arts festival with its own funeral march | Festivals | The Guardian
description: A brush with mortality inspired sisters Sophia and Camilla Minden to create a unique event featuring a funeral procession, wild swimming … and an ‘emoshpit’
Author: Claire Potter
Headline: A brush with mortality inspired sisters Sophia and Camilla Minden to create a unique event featuring a funeral procession, wild swimming … and an ‘emoshpit’
Content: ‘Fun is allowed’ … Sophia, left, and Camilla Minden, organisers of The Sondering festival in the Lake District.Photograph: Sheenah AlcockView image in fullscreen‘Fun is allowed’ … Sophia, left, and Camilla Minden, organisers of The Sondering festival in the Lake District.Photograph: Sheenah AlcockFestivals‘We thought death could do with a bit of dancing’: welcome to Sondering, the arts festival with its own funeral marchA brush with mortality inspired sisters Sophia and Camilla Minden to create a death-themed event featuring live bands, wild swimming … and an ‘emoshpit’Claire PotterWed 16 Sep 2026 08.59 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 09.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRaised in theLake Districton “music, moss and macaroni cheese,” Sophia and Camilla Minden were mindful of death from a very early age. The sisters shared a bed and played in the woods behind their house, frequently bringing home injured and dying birds, frogs and a rat they named Adrian and fed pate and pork pie. “Everything we’d learned about their diet, we learned from Wind in the Willows,” admits Sophia. The creatures rarely survived, but the death of each one was respectfully honoured with a burial in the garden, words spoken, singing and a stone or flower placed on the grave.What they didn’t expect was that little more than a decade later, they’d be planning Camilla’s own funeral. Diagnosed with late-stage Hodgkin’s lymphoma just after her 20th birthday, she was given an 80% chance of survival, but the other 20% made her investigate her local undertakers (“dated, impersonal and expensive”) and work out what she wanted at her funeral (“spag bol and quite a lot of Michael Jackson”). Navigating “shit wigs” and people’s awkwardness around the subject of dying, she says that she spent a lot of time “bargaining with God”, promising that if she made it through, she’d live life to the full and appreciate every single day.Now 37 and 40, the sisters have retained that mindset, and after initially exploring setting up their own progressive funeral directors, landed on the idea of creating a death-themed festival that would be as much a celebration of life as an exploration of mortality. So unlike other more conference-style or town-based death events, the Sondering, which debuts this weekend, is unashamedly an arts festival where “fun is allowed”. With live music, theatrical performances and a variety of creative workshops from clowning to shroud-making – plus a splash of guided wild swimming in Rydal Water – the programme has been designed to give people the opportunity to participate and express themselves in ways that might be sorrowful or joyful. “It’s OK to cry and ask for a cup of tea, it’s OK to laugh and dance,” says Sophia.View image in fullscreen‘The Lake District is magical, healing’ … Coffin route sign.Photograph: Sophia MindenLocated on a working farm with a capacity of just 300 to create an intimate feel, the festival site was chosen for its proximity to particular geographical features. “The Lake District is stunning, magical, healing,” says Sophia. “And we want to share it in a way that brings the landscape and local history alive,” adds Camilla. At sunset on Saturday evening, a cappella groupMouthfulwill be performing and leading a singing session inside Rydal Cave, making the most of its natural acoustics. And on Sunday, festival-goers will be invited to walk in a slow communal procession with a willow coffin along the old Coffin Route from Rydal to Grasmere. Up until the mid-1800s, this scenic two-and-a-half-mile footpath was how people carried their dead to church to be buried. The coffin – which will be collectively woven on site over the weekend and filled with personal notes of remembrance – will be taken right inside St Oswald’s Church, where there will be a musical performance from kora player John Haycock with Dan Bridgwood-Hill, featuring clarinet, guitar, violin and fiddle. “This is as close to a funeral as we get at the festival,” says Camilla. “We’re not afraid of ritual.”Aimed equally at those who are simply death-curious and those who are grieving the loss of a loved one, most of the music at the festival has been chosen for its “emotion and energy” and includes folk, reggae, opera, electro-punk and an uplifting DJ set on the Saturday night with an “emoshpit” where emotions good, bad and messy can be released.Other acts have an direct connection to death. The improvised singing ofLaurel Morganis inspired by the Celtic tradition of keening, where wails and wordless sounds are used to lament the dead. And sound artistJack McNeillwill be doing a performance with disassembled clarinets and words from poems written by his wife in response to losing three close family members in the same year. “It’s so easy to feel isolated in grief because it’s so rarely explored other than through a lens of sympathy,” he says. “I’d love people to feel less alone, more connected, and I think music does that better than most things.”Sophia and Camilla say some have questioned whether a music and arts festival isn’t romanticising or trivialising death. But they say they’re acutely aware the topic is “too big and too hard” for that. “We’re not saying death isn’t scary or painful or tragic,” says Sophia. “We’re asking if facing up to death together in this way can bring us closer to life and each other?” The ultimate aim of the festival is to encourage people to live as richly and compassionately as they possibly can: “Live like they’re going to die.” Even as children with a garden full of wild animal graves, they tell me their house was always full of dancing, laughter, warmth, generosity and love. “We thought death could do with a bit of that,” says Camilla.The Sondering is atRydal, Lake District, from 18-21SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFestivalsTheatreCraftDeath and dyingLake DistrictfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Girls creator Lena Dunham welcomes baby girl delivered via surrogate | Lena Dunham | The Guardian
description: Writer and actor, 40, had long struggled with endometriosis before undergoing total hysterectomy at age 31
Author: Maya Yang
Headline: Writer and actor, 40, had long struggled with endometriosis before undergoing total hysterectomy at age 31
Content: Lena Dunham and her husband, Luis Felber, on 20 September 2022 in London, England.Photograph: Lia Toby/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLena Dunham and her husband, Luis Felber, on 20 September 2022 in London, England.Photograph: Lia Toby/Getty ImagesLena DunhamGirls creator Lena Dunham welcomes baby girl delivered via surrogateWriter and actor, 40, had long struggled with endometriosis before undergoing total hysterectomy at age 31Maya YangWed 16 Sep 2026 12.45 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLena Dunham has welcomed her first child with her husband, Luis Felber, via surrogate.The 40-year-old writer and actor, known for her creation of and role in the HBO television series Girls, revealed her daughter’s birth in aVogue op-edpublished on Wednesday.Dunham’s daughter arrived 13 days later than expected, with Dunham writing: “I sat on a hospital bed, between the legs of a woman I hadn’t known a year ago, waiting for a glimpse of this person who I had been waiting for with something related to patience, but also none at all. I was so focused on our surrogate – in awe at her concentration, her period of quiet followed by what sounded like a roar – I forgot to look down until I heard our baby’s cry.Lena Dunham’s romcom Too Much convinced me to propose on the spotRead more“I saw her face, gasping just as she did. Her eyes, wide and unfocused, taking in the light and shadow, blinking rapidly,” Dunham wrote, adding: “‘Hello,’ I said. ‘I’m your mama. You … you look nothing like I thought you would, but exactly right. We’ve been waiting for you, do you know that? It was so nice of you to come.’”She went on to describe herself as feeling “bashful and dizzy with joy”.Dunham has faced a series of fertility issues that she has publicly spoken about, including nearly two decades of advanced endometriosis as well as undergoing a total hysterectomy at 31 years old.In a2020 essayin Harper’s Magazine, Dunham explained her decision to walk away from what she described as the “fertility-industrial complex” after an unsuccessful IVF cycle.“The moment I lost my fertility I started searching for a baby. At age 31, after almost two decades of chronic pain caused by endometriosis and its little-studied ravages, I had my uterus, my cervix, and one of my ovaries removed,” Dunham wrote at the time.“Before then, motherhood had seemed likely but not urgent, as inevitable as growing out of jean shorts, but in the days after my surgery I became keenly obsessed with it,” she added.Explore more on these topicsLena DunhamSurrogacyGirlsParents and parentingTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bonnie Greer, writer and cultural commentator, dies aged 77 | Books | The Guardian
description: The British-American novelist and playwright who regularly appeared on current affairs shows will be remembered for her ‘warmth, humour and generosity’, says her husband
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: The British-American novelist and playwright who regularly appeared on current affairs shows will be remembered for her ‘warmth, humour and generosity’, says her husband
Content: Bonnie Greer pictured in 2016.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBonnie Greer pictured in 2016.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianBooksBonnie Greer, writer and cultural commentator, dies aged 77The British-American novelist and playwright who regularly appeared on current affairs shows will be remembered for her ‘warmth, humour and generosity’, says her husbandElla CreamerWed 16 Sep 2026 08.47 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British-American novelist, playwright and commentatorBonnie Greerhas died aged 77.In a statement, her husband David Hutchins said that she died on Tuesday evening following a brief illness.Greer’s “intelligence, courage and distinctive voice made an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life”, said Hutchins. “To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her.”“RIP Bonnie Greer,” wrote novelist Bernardine Evaristo in a social media post. “Very sad news. There was a period in the 90s/00s when Bonnie was probably the most important and high profile black cultural commentator in the UK. Other than her writing, she also sat on many important boards – representing.”In an Instagram post, former deputy prime minister David Lammy wrote that Greer was “a powerful wordsmith and artist, she was eloquent and exacting. A true life force.”Greer was born on 16 November 1948, the eldest of seven children, and grew up on Chicago’s South Side. She studied playwriting under David Mamet in the city before moving to New York to work in theatre. In 1985, she brought a play to the Edinburgh fringe, and ultimately moved to the UK the following year, becoming a citizen in 1997.Greer’s work – which often focused on the lives of minorities, and of women – spanned novels, nonfiction, plays and broadcasting.Her first book, Hanging By Her Teeth, published in 1994, was a novel about a Black American woman travelling through the US and Europe in search of her father. Her later books included Obama Music (2009), about her and the former US president’s connections to Chicago’s South Side, Langston Hughes: The Value of Contradiction (2011), a biography of the Harlem Renaissance figure, and A Parallel Life (2014), her memoir. In 2019, she contributed to New Daughters of Africa, a landmark anthology edited by Margaret Busby. In 2022, she was made a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature.Greer’s stage plays included Dancing on Blackwater, which explored mother-daughter relationships, Jitterbug, composed of seven short plays about cultural divisions, and Munda Negra, for which she won the Soho Theatre Company Verity Bargate award for best play.In 2005, the BBC broadcastMarilyn and Ella Backstage at the Mocambo, Greer’s radio play about Marilyn Monroe and Ella Fitzgerald – in the 50s, Monroe persuaded a nightclub to book Fitzgerald amid racist reluctance, promising to sit in the front row every night. Greer eventually adapted the story into a musical drama for stage,titled Marilyn and Ella. The drama ran at the Edinburgh Fringe, the Theatre Royal Stratford East, and the Apollo Theatre, London.Greer wrote many radio dramas for the BBC, including Rosa Parks, about the civil rights icon, and Ferguson, inspired by August Strindberg’s play The Father and set in the US in 2016, against the backdrop of protests following the police killing of Michael Brown. She also translated and dramatised The Little Prince for a full-cast BBC radio adaptation.She often wrote opinion pieces for publications including the Guardian, the Independent and the New Statesman.In aninterview with the Guardianin 2016, she said that “Black Lives Matter is a rerun. It’s a replay of what we did as student activists in the 60s, the Black Panthers. I understand it because I’ve been through it and seen it.”Greer regularly appeared as a panellist on current affairs shows, including Newsnight Review and Question Time. Appearing in a controversial episode of the latter alongside far-right British National Party leader Nick Griffin in 2009, she heard “something in the audience: a kind of singing”, she later wrotein the Guardian, and turned the experience into an opera, Yes,which opened two years later.She served on the boards of the Royal Opera House, the British Museum and the London Film School, and was chancellor of Kingston University, London. In the 2010 birthday honours, she was appointed OBE for contribution to the arts.In 2009, shewrote thather hero was James Baldwin, describing him as “the person who first moved me and still does”. She was 12 when she read his first book, Go Tell It on the Mountain. “He nailed the emotions I felt right on the head and I read all his subsequent books.”Greer married Hutchins, whom she had first met in the aisle of a supermarket, in 1993. In his statement after her death, Hutchins said that “those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together”.Many writers and politicians shared tributes to Greer on social media on Wednesday. “Bonnie’s voice brought courage, humour and humanity to Britain’s cultural conversation”,wrote London mayorSadiq Khan. “She inspired and opened doors for so many others. And she was great fun too.”Explore more on these topicsBooksBonnie GreernewsShareReuse this content

title: Previously unseen drawings by Moomins author Tove Jansson to go on show in London | Tove Jansson | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Exhibition focusing on Finnish writer and artist’s illustrations will include original art from her first Moomins book
Author: Dalya Alberge
Headline: Exclusive: Exhibition focusing on Finnish writer and artist’s illustrations will include original art from her first Moomins book
Content: A sketch for Princessan Glittergull (1922), to be shown at the Quentin Blake Centre for Illustration.Photograph: Tove Jansson EstateView image in fullscreenA sketch for Princessan Glittergull (1922), to be shown at the Quentin Blake Centre for Illustration.Photograph: Tove Jansson EstateTove JanssonPreviously unseen drawings by Moomins author Tove Jansson to go on show in LondonExclusive: Exhibition focusing on Finnish writer and artist’s illustrations will include original art from her first Moomins bookDalya AlbergeWed 16 Sep 2026 10.08 EDTFirst published on Wed 16 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Moomin books about lovable trolls with hippopotamus snouts who live in harmony with nature are a global publishing phenomenon, having sold up to 30m copies since the Finnish artist and writerTove Janssonwrote and illustrated them between 1945 and 1977.Now previously unseen drawings of her eccentric characters will be among more than 100 exhibits in a major exhibition that is being staged inLondon25 years after her death.Tove Jansson and her Families will open at the Quentin Blake Centre forIllustrationin November, it will be announced on Thursday.Billed as the UK’s first exhibition to focus on Jansson’s illustrations, it will feature sketches, photographs and films, as well as her correspondence with those closest to her and fans of all ages.View image in fullscreenTove Jansson ‘had this very special skill to harness themes that touch the reader’, said her niece, Sophia Jansson.Photograph: Eva KonikoffThe displays will include original art from her first published book,The Moominsand the Great Flood, in which she presented a world “where everything was natural and benign – and possible”, in a story about Moomintroll’s search, with Moominmamma, for their missing Moominpappa and how they found their way to the magical Moominvalley.Jansson’s books celebrate nature, friendship, tolerance and the freedom to be oneself. Enchanting children and adults alike, they have been translated into more than 60 languages, inspiring animated films, television series and theme parks.View image in fullscreenA sketch of Moominpappa with a giant shell has not been shown before.Photograph: Moomin CharactersSophia Jansson, Tove’s niece, told the Guardian: “She had this very special skill to harness themes that touch the reader … on a universal and a personal level – and then disguise them in these stories, so that we think we’re reading about Moomins in Moominvalley and, when you finish the book, you realise that you’re actually reading about ‘us’, about humans and how we interact and all our peculiarities.”Previously unseen material will include a sketch of Moominpappa, a sea-loving adventurer, with a giant shell. It was an early draft for the cover of Moominpappa at Sea, in which the Moomin family moves to a remote island at the mercy of the sea and storms.It is among images that even Sophia, the chair of the Moomins Characters brand, has not seen before, but which have recently come to light: “This is the amazing thing about Tove. She was extremely prolific.”Asked whether this is the first-ever UK exhibition to focus on Jansson’s illustrations, Sophia said: “Definitely, because the one in Dulwich [Picture Gallery in 2017] was mainly to show her paintings.”Paul Gravett, a Jansson expert and guest curator at the Quentin Blake Centre, told the Guardian: “The prose novels are still extremely topical because of the sheer variety of characters that are brought together. They are filled with a lot of love and tolerance, that ‘isn’t it wonderful how very different we all are?’“Moomin celebrates that, enjoying eccentricity and going with the flow of life. This is one of the reasons that they’re not just for children. They have a lot of depth to them.”Gravett said the draft book cover was different from the one eventually published, but “every bit as good”.At the age of seven, Jansson was already writing and illustrating homemade booklets, which she sold to her classmates. Exhibits will include these drawings. “You can see a lot of the same fascination with fantasy and dreams, which came out of her childhood reading,” Gravett said.Her passion for fantasy literature stayed with her. She illustrated Swedish editions of Lewis Carroll’s The Hunting of the Snark and Alice in Wonderland in a horror style. With JRR Tolkien’s The Hobbit, she reinterpreted his characters, making Gollum monstrously large.View image in fullscreenJansson’s books have been translated into more than 60 languages.Photograph: Moomin CharactersTolkien himself was surprised. Realising he had never clarified Gollum’s size, he amended the second edition to describe him as “a small, slimy creature”. The first English edition with Jansson’s illustrations will be published this month by HarperCollins.Jansson was an outspoken political cartoonist, criticising fascism during the second world war, once saying: “Most of all I liked the fact that I got to be beastly to Hitler and Stalin.” In one cartoon, she depicted a woman and little girl in a toy shop with the caption: “Don’t you have a doll that says ‘Momma’?/ ‘No, little friend, our new stock says ‘Heil Hitler!’”She had a special connection with London: at a time when it was rare for female cartoonists to have their own daily strip, her first Moomin series went into print from 1954 in London’s Evening News. Her comic strips were circulated worldwide.Exhibits will include a sketch for one of the earliest examples. Gravett said: “It’s a miracle it survived because it’s covered in coffee stains and it was headed for the waste paper bin. A fellow cartoonist spotted it and rescued it.”Gravett is working on a Jansson book, followinghis 2022 studyof her illustration work.Tove Jansson and her Familiesruns from 21 November to 9 Mayat theQuentin Blake Centre for Illustration, Clerkenwell, LondonExplore more on these topicsTove JanssonIllustrationThe MoominsArtLondonChildren and teenagersPicture booksnewsShareReuse this content

title: Battle of Chile director Patricio Guzmán dies aged 85 | Movies | The Guardian
description: Passionate documentary maker won international acclaim for unsparing but poetic films exploring the impact of the Pinochet regime in Chile
Author: Andrew Pulver
Headline: Passionate documentary maker won international acclaim for unsparing but poetic films exploring the impact of the Pinochet regime in Chile
Content: Patricio Guzmán (right) filming Nostalgia for the Light.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPatricio Guzmán (right) filming Nostalgia for the Light.Photograph: Everett/ShutterstockMoviesBattle of Chile director Patricio Guzmán dies aged 85Passionate documentary maker  won international acclaim for unsparing but poetic films exploring the impact of the Pinochet regime in ChileAndrew PulverWed 16 Sep 2026 09.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatricio Guzmán, the film-maker who chronicled Chile’s bloody 1970s political strife and its subsequent social and political turmoil in films such as The Battle of Chile and Nostalgia for the Light, has died aged 85.According to Chilean news outlet Emol, Guzmán died on Tuesday in Paris after a cardiorespiratory arrest.Guzmán’s chief preoccupation throughout his career was the carnage unleashed by Augusto Pinochet’s coup in 1973 against Salvador Allende, Chile’s elected president.He later told the Guardian: “I’m a film-maker who was very marked by the ways of the dictator. It has remained with me for ever. I cannot leave it behind.” However, he resisted the idea that he was an activist, political film-maker, adding: “I’m not a sociologist. Neither am I a politician. I make films that are metaphorical and poetic; I interpret reality through my own personal way of looking.”Andy Beckett salutes The Battle of ChileRead moreBorn inChilein 1941, Guzmán initially worked in advertising before studying film, first in Chile and then in Madrid. On his return to Chile, Guzmán responded to the febrile political atmosphere after Allende’s election in 1970, eventually completing the mammoth Battle of Chile documentary that chronicled Pinochet’s ultimately successful attempt to overthrow Allende, resulting in the latter’s suicide. Guzmán did not shrink from the brutality of the period, even including footage shot by camera operator Leonardo Henrichsen as he is shot dead by the soldier he is filming.View image in fullscreenA still from The Battle of Chile.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyGuzmán was helped in the endeavour by French film-maker Chris Marker, who supplied film stock and connections that proved vital to make the film. Guzmán himself was arrested but eventually released, but the film’s cinematographer Jorge Müller was not so lucky – along with his girlfriend Carmen Bueno, he wasarrested, tortured and “disappeared” in 1974.Guzmán completed The Battle of Chile outside the country, releasing each of its three parts – The Insurrection of the Bourgeoisie (1975), The Coup d’État (1976) and Popular Power (1979) – through the rest of the 70s. Described by the Guardian as “an outstandingly photographed example of a newsreel film that captures the drama and volatility of the period”, it has continued to attract acclaim since then. Guzmán revisited the film in the mid-90s with Chile, Obstinate Memory, in which he returned to the country after a quarter-century of exile. In 2001 he completedThe Pinochet Case, after the Chilean former dictator wasarrested in Londonin 1998.Patricio Guzmán, Chile's master of documentary, focuses on the starsRead moreThe director moved on to more metaphysical subjects with a trilogy of films starting in 2010:Nostalgia for the Light,The Pearl ButtonandThe Cordillera of Dreams. They sought to explore Chile’s traumatic past by absorbing the country’s magnificent natural landscapes. His final film,My Imaginary Country, was premiered in 2022 and coveredChile’s dramatic 2019 street protests.Explore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsChileAugusto PinochetAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alice Springs heavy metal music venue raises $1m in donations in fight to stay open | Australian music | The Guardian
description: Supporters from around Australia back the Black Wreath, a volunteer-run centre far off the beaten touring track
Author: Katie Cunningham
Headline: Supporters from around Australia back the Black Wreath, a volunteer-run centre far off the beaten touring track
Content: Metal band Snakes perform at the Black Wreath, a heavy metal venue in Alice Springs.Photograph: Shane MulcahyView image in fullscreenMetal band Snakes perform at the Black Wreath, a heavy metal venue in Alice Springs.Photograph: Shane MulcahyAustralian musicAlice Springs heavy metal music venue raises $1m in donations in fight to stay openSupporters from around Australia back the Black Wreath, a volunteer-run centre far off the beaten touring trackKatie CunninghamTue 15 Sep 2026 22.31 EDTLast modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 22.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlice Springs has a population of 34,000 and exactly one dedicated live music space: a heavy metal venue called the Black Wreath. It has hosted hundreds of bands from around the country over the past decade – despite being 1,500km from the nearest city.For musicians in central Australia, the Black Wreath is a one-of-a-kind resource. So when its operators were informed last year of the owners’ plans to sell, they negotiated a stay of execution and began devising a fundraiser that could save the desert venue. A month-long crowdfunding campaign, which called for donations that would let the team behind the Black Wreath buy the venue and place it in a trust,hit its $1m targeton Friday.‘I want to go further’: Justin Broadrick on retiring Godflesh, playing with Phoebe Bridgers – and his new bandRead moreThe Black Wreath’s founder and creative director, a lip-pierced and leather-clad man known mononymously as Pirate, says it feels surreal to have raised so much money for what is a DIY, volunteer-run venue far off the beaten touring track.“I haven’t quite processed it,” he says. “We’re feeling very overwhelmed and a lot of gratitude.”Pirate says the $1m arrived in donations from $20 up to $10,000 and came from supporters around Australia. The grand vision is to use the money to keep the Black Wreath alive to give musicians from central Australia a space to perform, “and for Alice to be a touring destination for other artists year-round”.But the work is not done yet. Pirate says the successful Pozible campaign is just “step one” towards securing the Black Wreath’s future and that “there’s multiple ways that could unfold”. He still has to negotiate with owners, who havean asking price of $1.23m on the venue– a sum higher than the amount the fundraiser collected. Pirate wants to secure additional funding through philanthropy and by “reaching out to some of the biggest bands in the world”. The Black Wreath is still gratefully accepting donations, and has set a new fundraising target of $1,111,111 – a nod to the date of the Black Wreath’s inception: 11 November 2011.View image in fullscreen‘No one nationally recognised this place as a heavy music town’ … Pirate, the Black Wreath’s founder, pictured at Blacken Open Air festival.Photograph: Oliver EclipseThe fundraising campaign comes two years after the Tote, some 2,300km away in Melbourne,crowd-sourced $3m to keep itself open.The Black Wreath was born out of the desire “to put Alice Springs on the map” and “create something that is available as a resource for the entire town”, Pirate says.“I grew up playing in bands with my friends here, and we were extremely limited with pathways and opportunities – no one nationally recognised this place as a heavy music town,” he says. “There was not much we could do with it. There weren’t any studios, venues or rehearsal rooms.”A collective of three bands founded The Black Wreath as a record label and a series of backyard studios, before later leasing what was then a run-down industrial building and turning it into a creative hub complete with a recording studio, rehearsal spaces and stage. The collective expanded and now operates a national heavy music festival, Blacken Open Air, which takes place in April and May one hour outside Alice Springs.Pirate believes the reason the town has such an affinity for heavy metal stems from “the isolation of the place – small-town frustration”.“Growing up with lack of opportunity and a lot of energy, you just identify with metal,” he says. “Metal is a global community. And young people, when you discover that, it makes you feel part of something bigger … [especially if] you already feel like you’re disconnected from the world”.While the Black Wreath was born out of a love for metal, Pirate says the venue serves “every genre of music” and the entire Alice community: “Young people. First Nations communities. The queer community. The headbangers and the rockers and the punks, and also the doofers and the hip-hoppers.”Another beloved live music venue is closing. Is Australia’s precarious rental market killing the vibe?Read moreBut the challenges of running a music venue in one of the most isolated locations on Earth are plentiful, especially given that it only sells alcohol – where most venues make the bulk of their income – “a few times a year”, to cover production costs at select, bigger events.“The expenses of doing it are higher than anywhere else in the country,” Pirate says. “The cost of travel for bringing artists out here is just astronomical … for the last decade or so, it’s been a struggle.”Pirate works as a volunteer and doesn’t draw a wage from the Black Wreath, instead propping it up with income from his various day jobs. The venue is operated “purely for the love”, he says.He hopes the success of the fundraising venture inspires others to fight for live music.“It is a tough time for the music industry,” he says. “And I just hope that people can see the real power of community – the power is in our hands. We can do something about it, and keep fighting to uplift live music.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian musicAlice SpringsMetalNorthern TerritoryRural and regional AustraliaCrowdfundingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Neagley review – this violent Reacher spinoff is a glorious hour off from normal life | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Jack Reacher’s right-hand woman takes the lead in a show which requires you to think about nothing other than baddies being beaten up
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Jack Reacher’s right-hand woman takes the lead in a show which requires you to think about nothing other than baddies being beaten up
Content: New hero in town … Neagley (Maria Sten) on the hunt for evidence.Photograph: Amazon Prime Video/Prime VideoView image in fullscreenNew hero in town … Neagley (Maria Sten) on the hunt for evidence.Photograph: Amazon Prime Video/Prime VideoTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewNeagley review – this violent Reacher spinoff is a glorious hour off from normal lifeJack Reacher’s right-hand woman takes the lead in a show which requires you to think about nothing other than baddies being beaten upLucy ManganWed 16 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNeagley. It’s pronounced “Neely” but after that, honestly, it’s very simple. Neagley is Frances Neagley, Jack Reacher’s friend and former colleague in Reacher (pronounced “Reacher”, though as rarely as possible for our guy is a man of big arms but few words). That’s the hit series starring Alan Ritchson and his arms as the eponymous hero, a monosyllabic meat-mountain around whom a bestselling series of crime novels by Lee Child has revolved for the last few decades.Reacher is a former military police officer who now goes about breaking the heads and faces of those he deems deserving – “a sort of artisanal fascist”, as the novelist and devoted fan Paraic O’Donnell once matchlessly put it. Neagley was his right-hand woman in the days when he put together a special investigations unit to – uh, investigate special things, I guess? Details do not matter much in Reacher. The whole thing is designed to slide seamlessly out of your mind the minute the credits roll, leaving you restored and refreshed by an hour off from thinking about anything other than battered, groaning baddies. Sometimes the action pauses for a one-liner or a shot of Reacher’s bare bottom, but they’re quite restorative, too.Neagley (Maria Sten) has put in several stints over Reacher’s four series and has now earned a spin-off. Hurrah for feminism! Because Reacher-the-programme is not broken, the makers wisely have not fixed it. Except for recognising that Sten is roughly the size of one of Ritchson’s arms and occasionally giving Neagley a baton with which to beat the living crap out of the latest deserving case, business proceeds as usual.We open with her foiling a kidnapper’s attempt to flee with the ransom money she has delivered for a client. Reacher pops up briefly to lend a hand/fist because he’s a good friend and wants her spin-off to be a success, then heads back out on the road. She returns to life as a private investigator but is soon working pro bono to uncover the truth around her childhood friend Tommy’s apparent suicide.View image in fullscreenBest of friends … Reacher (Alan Ritchson) pops up to lend a hand.Photograph: Shane Mahood/Prime VideoTommy (Jhaleil Swaby) was high on drugs when he walked naked into the path of a subway train. But Tommy never did drugs. His mother is sure of it. Neagley is sure of it, too. She thinks it is something to do with Echo Common, the cult-like commune Tommy had become involved with. Neagley, once she has decoded a clue left for her in Tommy’s last letter to his mother, thinks so too. She starts breaking faces to find out more.I long for a life of such simplicity.Meanwhile, the audience is introduced to a sharp-faced and even sharper-suited CEO of a big pharma company intent on creating a market for prescription psychedelic drugs. Could he turn out to be a villain?The beauty of Lady Reacher – sorry, Neagley – is that, as with Original Reacher, you are never left to wonder for long. In fact, you can barely begin mentally questioning the moral virtue of a new character before you are rewarded with very clear proof of your suspicions – often by someone slicing the throat of a fleeting accomplice or bagman awaiting payment.On we go. Neagley has an already established phobia about touching people (this allows her to be Reacher’s friend and never get in the way of that season’s bare-bottom instigator) and a dying dad. It is possible that we will plumb unprecedented psychological depths later in Lady Reacher – I’m sorry, I’ve done it again – by finding out what caused Neagley’s phobia, but if so I am sure her preferred form of therapy will involve breaking faces with a baton rather than putting any of us through a long dark night of the soul.Neagley shares Reacher’s Sherlockian ability to deduce vast amounts of plot from clues that teeter on the edge of absurdity (buckwheat dropped from a wheel arch provides a location, sticky tape residue on a kitchen cabinet denotes an entire family structure and an ex-wife’s address, that kind of thing), so the juggernaut never stops moving.What can I say? If you like Reacher, you’ll like Neagley – especially if, like its progenitor did, it gains more confidence and starts to allow a little levity to creep in. Relax, artisanal fascista – you’ve got this.Neagley is on Prime Video nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewTelevisionreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Bafta-winning documentary makers follow far-right protesters | Television | The Guardian
description: A depressing look at the anti-immigration movement in England ‘Til I Die. Plus: Kevin McCloud is back with Grand Designs. Here’s what to watch today
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: A depressing look at the anti-immigration movement in England ‘Til I Die. Plus: Kevin McCloud is back with Grand Designs. Here’s what to watch today
Content: Shocking … Liam Tomsett in England ‘Til I Die.Photograph: Channel 4View image in fullscreenShocking … Liam Tomsett in England ‘Til I Die.Photograph: Channel 4TV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Bafta-winning documentary makers follow far-right protestersA depressing look at the anti-immigration movement in England ‘Til I Die. Plus: Kevin McCloud is back with Grand Designs. Here’s what to watch todayHollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Ali Catterall,Hannah J DaviesandEllen E JonesWed 16 Sep 2026 01.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland ’Til I Die10pm, Channel 4Here comes the year’s most depressing hour of TV. This film follows Liam Tomsett from Crowborough, East Sussex, who positioned himself as an anti-immigration leader when the government announced that an army camp would be used to house asylum seekers in the town. The cameras follow him and far-right protesters as they wade deeper into the movement. From the Bafta-winning team behind Ukraine: Enemy in the Woods, and the pulled BBC documentary, Gaza: How to Survive a Warzone, it is shocking and scorched with anger.Hollie RichardsonThe Repair Shop: Beyond the Barn8pm, BBC OneThe spin-off that looks more closely at the stories of items after being restored. A vintage steamer trunk owned by the late Paul O’Grady’s husband, André, gets revived, along with a bike once used by gas lamplighters and a wolf statue smashed by the family cat.HRSurviving Earth8pm, Sky OneView image in fullscreenSpine-tingling … Surviving Earth.Photograph: NBCUniversal/2026 Top Alternative Studio LLC and Loud Minds Ltd. All rights reserved.This apocalypse wow series continues and we’re headed to the late Carboniferous period. “Swamp forests” have sprung up, oxygen levels are at their highest: great for dragonflies as big as crows (yikes), not so good for the reptilian Dendromaia battling against a forest fire.Priya ElanKirstie and Phil’s Love It Or List It: Brilliant Builds8pm, Channel 4Kirstie and Phil revisit another pair of success stories. Sarah and Sean’s sprawling Victorian semi in Whitley Bay needed a £70,000 rescue, while Steven and Adeola’s chaotic Stevenage new-build had been pushed to breaking point. With Kirstie fighting awkward layouts and Phil hunting for alternatives, did the couples finally agree to stay put, patch up, or get out?Ali CatterallGrand Designs9pm, Channel 4She chutes, she scores! But is Bryony’s fixation on a hi-tech laundry solution something of a coping mechanism during her challenging self-build project? As series 27 kicks off, the stakes for her and husband Matt’s environmentally minded Cornish home are high, and there’s plenty for Kevin McCloud to raise an eyebrow at.Hannah J DaviesAndrew Davies Remembers … Middlemarch10pm, BBC FourDavies – the writer behind many a classic BBC period drama – looks back at his 1994 adaptation of George Eliot’s Middlemarch. Heated rows with the director is just one thing that made the experience “like carrying three big suitcases across a railway platform”.HRFilm choiceView image in fullscreenSharp, sweet and delicious … Jack Lemmon and Judy Holliday in It Should Happen to You.Photograph: Album/AlamyIt Should Happen to You (George Cukor, 1954),11am, Film4The great Jack Lemmon had his first major film role in this George Cukor-directed story of a young woman, Gladys Glover (Judy Holliday), who yearns to make her mark on the world by any means necessary. Gladys kicks off a curious kind of career by hiring billboards around New York City to display her name, while suitor Pete (Lemmon) attempts to persuade her to find contentment in the crowd. It’s sharp as a romantic comedy, sweet as a prescient satire on the perils of fame, and altogether a delicious treat.Ellen E JonesExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Redwood by Ben Macintyre review – a superbly wrought tale of cold war defection | History books | The Guardian
description: This story of Soviet agent and his MI6 handler in revolutionary Iran is a page-turning masterpiece
Author: Oliver Bullough
Headline: This story of Soviet agent and his MI6 handler in revolutionary Iran is a page-turning masterpiece
Content: Posters of Ayatollah Khomeini during the 1979 Iranian revolution .Photograph: Kaveh KazemiView image in fullscreenPosters of Ayatollah Khomeini during the 1979 Iranian revolution .Photograph: Kaveh KazemiBook of the dayHistory booksReviewRedwood by Ben Macintyre review – a superbly wrought tale of cold war defectionThis story of Soviet agent and his MI6 handler in revolutionary Iran is a page-turning masterpieceOliver BulloughWed 16 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBen Macintyre uses the acronym MICE to describe the reasons people betray their countries: Money, Ideology, Coercion or Ego. In the set-piece that opens his latest work of true-espionage, we discover a new reason: erectile dysfunction.Stressed, drinking too much, under constant surveillance, furious about the corruption of his colleagues and frustrated with his home life, the KGB’s Vladimir Kuzichkin is offering to betray the secrets of his homeland and its Iranian allies, if only a British doctor can help him have sex again.If you have read Macintyre before, you’ll recognise a classic example of his style: the journalist’s eye for salacious detail combined with a historian’s rigour. The rest of Redwood lives up to the attention-grabbing opening scene; I devoured it in a single sitting.If you haven’t read him, he is the author of a hatful of bestselling books about war, politics and secrecy, several of which have been adapted for the screen, and one of which – Operation Mincemeat – has become a West End and Broadway musical. They are sometimes derided as “dadlit”, the kind of nonfiction read by golf club bores and armchair colonels. But Redwood is as far above yet-another-book-about-the-second-world-war as a George Smiley novel is above Jack Reacher.The setting is the immediate aftermath of the 1979 revolution that brought Iran’s ayatollahs to power. The west was on the back foot, having lost a key ally, with the Americans particularly discomfited by Islamists having seized their embassy and taken its staff hostage. The Soviets, meanwhile, thought they had an opportunity to spread their influence south, to a strategic and oil-rich country with warm water ports.Kuzichkin’s job was to further this aim by distributing money, arms and encouragement to the Tudeh party, an orthodox communist movement led by a Stalinist who had spent the previous few decades in exile in East Germany. He ran his operation out of the huge Soviet embassy, where his mostly useless colleagues celebrated even the smallest of successes with vast quantities of vodka, and he really hated it.Literally across the street, in the equally large British embassy, was Ian McCredie, a young MI6 operative who had recently arrived in Tehran with a wife and baby in tow, his task to re-establish a British intelligence presence after the entire team had been forced to leave. He didn’t drink as much as Kuzichkin, but he did discover 50 crates of whisky that a predecessor had imported as a present for the Shah and left in a garage, so was able to ride out the revolutionaries’ ban on alcohol quite well.The relationship between the two men, which becomes one of handler and double agent, is the backbone of the book.
