It is set against the ever-present risk of discovery by the Revolutionary Guard, and given added poignancy by the fact that neither one realises their actions are taking place amid a geopolitical tectonic shift, in which the communists are slipping into irrelevance and the Islamists rising to take their place.This is demonstrated most starkly when, after Kuzichkin has been safely exfiltrated to the UK for debriefing, his controllers send him to Pakistan to share his intelligence about the communists with the Iranian authorities. They hoped this would win them favour in Tehran, but instead it unleashes an orgy of violence and torture against Tudeh supporters which further entrenches the Islamic Republic’s control and does nothing to help the west.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut such weighty matters are leavened throughout by witty turns of phrase: an antiquated coding machine is “not so much user-unfriendly, as overtly hostile”; the head of Britain’s mission in Tehran is “a master of the art of thinking twice before saying nothing”; McCredie’s wife Lucy had nothing to fear from living under an oppressive regime because “she had been educated in an English girls’ boarding school”. So, by all means give Redwood to your father for Christmas, but make sure you read it yourself first: it’s superb.Redwood by Ben Macintyre is published by Viking (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsHistory booksBook of the dayreviewsShareReuse this content

title: In-I in Motion review – Juliette Binoche pulls back the curtain on dance duet with Akram Khan | Movies | The Guardian
description: The actor makes her directing debut with a raw, fascinating film about her 2008 collaboration with the British dancer
Author: Cath Clarke
Headline: The actor makes her directing debut with a raw, fascinating film about her 2008 collaboration with the British dancer
Content: Outside comfort zones … Juliette Binoche and Akram Khan in In-I in Motion.Photograph: Courtesy of Miao ProductionsView image in fullscreenOutside comfort zones … Juliette Binoche and Akram Khan in In-I in Motion.Photograph: Courtesy of Miao ProductionsMoviesReviewIn-I in Motion review – Juliette Binoche pulls back the curtain on dance duet with Akram KhanThe actor makes her directing debut with a raw, fascinating film about her 2008 collaboration with the British dancerCath ClarkeWed 16 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the way that wedding rehearsals can be more emotional than the big day – all the untidy feelings that will be tucked away for the cameras still on show – this documentary from Juliette Binoche feels raw and unguarded. It goes behind the scenes of Binoche’s collaboration with British dancer Akram Khan; their dance-theatre piece, a love story entitled In-I,premiered in London to mixed reviews in 2008. Now, all these years later, Binoche makes her directing debut with a film that is essentially a study of their artistic process. And it’s unexpectedly fascinating, watching two world-famous performers pushing themselves outside their comfort zones, exposed and vulnerable – particularly Binoche, who had never danced professionally before.‘I told him, “Go ahead, do it”’: Juliette Binoche on how a strangling attack as a teen inspired her directorial debutRead moreIn-I in Motion is a film of two halves, ending with a performance on stage in front of an audience, the set designed by artist Anish Kapoor: a vast screen in murderous red. The first half is more interesting, shot fly-on-the-wall style during the months it took to create the piece in a studio. Binoche and Khan work with acting coach Susan Batson, who at one point thunders: “THIS IS FULL OF SHIT!” (never mind La Binoche’s Oscar). For some audiences, it will have a whiff of theatrical cringe; the endless stewing and fretting over how to achieve something truthful is ripe for spoof. But the pure intensity and focus is thrilling to watch.Still, it can feel like an endurance test. There’s no voiceover to explain that 170 hours of footage shot over six months has been edited down. No interviewer to ask questions that might crop up. Like, why did Binoche wait 17 years to compile the documentary? How did she train for the dancing? Were the negative reviews bruising? The person behind the camera during the months of rehearsals is her sister, film-maker Marion Stalens, which might explain how natural and unfiltered Binoche is. Khan remains an enigmatic presence on screen, but Binoche, for all the famous seriousness about her work, is a real hoot.In-I In Motion is at Ciné Lumière, London, from 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsJuliette BinocheAkram KhanDanceTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Whisper of the Heart review – Studio Ghibli deep cut is pep talk on how to live the artistic life | Movies | The Guardian
description: Hayao Miyazaki-scripted 90s teen romance sees an aspiring writer drawn to a potential soulmate thanks to library books and a curmudgeonly cat
Author: Phil Hoad
Headline: Hayao Miyazaki-scripted 90s teen romance sees an aspiring writer drawn to a potential soulmate thanks to library books and a curmudgeonly cat
Content: Tethered to realism … a still from Whisper of the Heart.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyView image in fullscreenTethered to realism … a still from Whisper of the Heart.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyMoviesReviewWhisper of the Heart review – Studio Ghibli deep cut is pep talk on how to live the artistic lifeHayao Miyazaki-scripted 90s teen romance sees an aspiring writer drawn to a potential soulmate thanks to library books and a curmudgeonly catPhil HoadWed 16 Sep 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 06.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile2013’s The Wind Risesand2023’s The Boy and the Heronsaw Hayao Miyazaki break his wizard’s staff, artistically speaking, this lesser-known Studio Ghibli cut from 1995, based on his screenplay, shows he was dwelling on creative responsibilities from early on. Featuring a typical Ghibli protagonist on the brink of adulthood – aspiring schoolkid writer Shizuku (voiced by Yōko Honna) – this teen romance doubles up as an earnest pep talk on how to commit to the artistic life. It’s not quite as sophisticated, though, in its understanding of the interplay between imagination and reality as Miyazaki’s later masterpieces.It also features highly inventive use of that 2010s soundtrack favourite:John Denver’s Take Me Home, Country Roads. Shizuku shows off her fledgling penmanship for a school performance of the song devising hilarious Japanese lyrics that satirise Tokyo’s “concrete roads”. But while her writing shows promise, her love life remains in the fantasy realm. Mainlining library books, she realises that the same name, Seiji Amasawa, keeps appearing on the lists of previous borrowers. It feels like fate is pointing her towards a soulmate – especially when a curmudgeonly cat leads her “like in a story” to an intriguing curio shop near the library.Whisper of the Heart is the sole directorial credit for Ghibli stalwart Yoshifumi Kondō, who died shortly afterwards, and the film remains tethered to realism, flirting with but never quite dispatching Shizuku to some otherworldly Kansas. In fact, it’s actively wary of overinvesting in imagination; even as she pushes her friend Yūko (Maiko Yoshiyama) towards making a choice between two boys, she struggles with her own storybook expectations of romance. Seiji (Issey Takahashi) turns out to be the grandson of the antique shop’s owner, where she is transfixed by a dapper cat figurine. But the reverie crumbles when the lad announces he intends to go to Cremona in Italy to train as a violin-maker.Impressed by his resolve, Shizuku commits to writing a novel, inspired by the figurine. Perhaps limited by the manga source material, Kondō and Miyazaki don’t fully align theshojolove complications with the aspiring artist saga. Instead of detailing how (in her case) creativity is a direct reaction to reality’s shortcomings, they prefer the straight motivational strategy. Talking up discipline, artists as lone-gun nonconformists and, above all, the need to accept imperfections of “rough gems” en route, the film feels like a series of notes to self. With the trademark Ghibli charm and airy optimism in almost every frame, it’s something more than a rough gem but, lacking the symphonic flow of Spirited Away et al, not quite polished to sparkling.Whisper of the Heart is in UK and Irish cinemas from 16 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmStudio GhibliAnimeRomance filmsDrama filmsJapanreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Chewing Gum Dreams review – Michaela Coel’s horny teenage heroine is still a force to reckon with | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Lauryn Ajufo makes Tracey her own in a vibrant revival of Coel’s monologue, capturing the cruelty, confusion and comedy of adolescence
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Lauryn Ajufo makes Tracey her own in a vibrant revival of Coel’s monologue, capturing the cruelty, confusion and comedy of adolescence
Content: Intelligent, inventive … Lauryn Ajufo in Chewing Gum Dreams at Theatre503, London.Photograph: Ikin YumView image in fullscreenIntelligent, inventive … Lauryn Ajufo in Chewing Gum Dreams at Theatre503, London.Photograph: Ikin YumTheatreReviewChewing Gum Dreams review – Michaela Coel’s horny teenage heroine is still a force to reckon withTheatre503, LondonLauryn Ajufo makes Tracey her own in a vibrant revival of Coel’s monologue, capturing the cruelty, confusion and comedy of adolescenceArifa AkbarWed 16 Sep 2026 10.28 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 12.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe self-flagellations of adolescence and its suddenly streaking hormones can make great fodder for comedy. Harry Enfield’s 13-year-old defined its comic pains for one generation. His Kevin is every bit matched by Michaela Coel’s exuberant and offensive Tracey. This revival of Coel’s 2012 debut proves her eternal relevance as a character: Black British and downtrodden, she is upstart, bully, trusty friend and a bewildered girl defined by class and race by her own schoolteacher. She is also horny and desperately infatuated with a white boy, Connor.Beginning as a monologue performed by Coel herself, it is about friendship, sexual discovery and abuse, with Tracey telling us about everything from the girl in class who can lick her own vagina to her beautiful best friend with a controlling boyfriend 10 years her senior. The show went on to be adapted for the Channel 4 TV series Chewing Gum, which turned Coel’s one-woman polyphony into an ensemble of immensely colourful characters and fabulous comedy, but also lost some of its intensity and darkness.Here it is again in its original, distilled form, vibrantly directed by Anthony Simpson-Pike. But like Tracey’s travels through time, thistiata fahodzico-production is also a fascinating exercise in retrospection. You can trace Coel’s talent to this starting point – it spurts out of the script, like the characters’ sexual eruptions.View image in fullscreenVibrantly directed … Lauryn Ajufo in Chewing Gum Dreams at Theatre503, London.Photograph: Ikin YumLauryn Ajufo takes the character out of the shadow of the TV series to make Tracey her own – more pugnacious, earnestly schoolgirlish yet also streetwise, her youthful fears mixed with a child’s dead-eyed cruelty. This is a convincing showcase of Ajufo’s talent as an emerging actor.Tracey’s offensive language often grates. The use of a disability slur and numerous references to fat girls in her class might be dated aspects of the script but more likely reveal the unlikable part of Tracey, a teenage girl learning to use language as a weapon, a cudgel with which to beat a threat.Bits from the first series of the TV show can be sourced back, word for word, such as the brilliant scene in which Tracey tries to extract the morning-after pill from an intransigent pharmacist. As knowing as the show was on screen (like in Fleabag, also based on a one-woman stage show, Tracey confided directly to camera), there is a different kind of theatricality here. Yimei Zhao’s non-realist set has a distorted, dream-like quality and a tube suggesting the temporal portals through which Tracey rolls.It is intelligent, inventive and still arresting. A blast from Coel’s teen past which feels nostalgic and fresh.AtTheatre503, London, until 17 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMichaela CoelreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The play that changed my life: ‘Grime was ostracised but the Royal Court saw it as an art form – and made me a better MC’ | Stage | The Guardian
description: Poet in da Corner by Debris Stevenson revealed that acting in a theatre can have a lot in common with MCing in a club
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Poet in da Corner by Debris Stevenson revealed that acting in a theatre can have a lot in common with MCing in a club
Content: ‘You read it so well you might as well be in it!’ … From left: Jammz, Debris Stevenson and Cassie Clare in Poet in da Corner.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianView image in fullscreen‘You read it so well you might as well be in it!’ … From left: Jammz, Debris Stevenson and Cassie Clare in Poet in da Corner.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianThe play that changed my lifeStageThe play that changed my life: ‘Grime was ostracised but the Royal Court saw it as an art form – and made me a better MC’Poet in da Corner by Debris Stevenson revealed that acting in a theatre can have a lot in common with MCing in a clubJammzWed 16 Sep 2026 06.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBy 2018 I was in my third or fourth year professionally as a grime MC and producer. I was 27 and didn’t have any aspirations in theatre. But Debris Stevenson, a good friend of mine, asked me to help her write one of the first drafts of a song in her playPoet in da Corner. I did that and then she invited me to a table reading session at the Royal Court to read the part of SS Vyper [a pirate radio DJ].The theatre’s artistic director, Vicky Featherstone, said: “You read it so well you may as well be in the play!” I thought she was joking, but the next week I was in rehearsal.I was nervous at first, I’m not gonna lie, but then after the first night I realised it is exactly the same as what I do in music, I’m just doing it with a script.The play is a loose autobiography of Debris trying to navigate her difficult childhood. She had dyslexia and grew up in a strongly religious household. But she discovers Dizzee Rascal’s first album, Boy in da Corner, and it completely changes her understanding of language and what she’s capable of. Her friend Vyper grew up in the same neighbourhood as her, but essentially had different opportunities and a different outcome in life.View image in fullscreenGrime is already quite theatrical … Jammz, Kirubel Belay, Debris Stevenson and Cassie Clare in Poet in da Corner.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/the GuardianI would get up and start screaming and shouting “you’ve stolen my story!” I would meet her on the stage to share my version. So then we begin to tell the story together to get both sides of the picture.Grime is already quite theatrical, especially pre-2004, when the main medium for it was the radio and MCs had to have big characters to stand out from everybody else. I realised theatre is the same thing in a different space. It’s just another form of storytelling.The story really resonated with me. Some people’s stories get co-opted and told from a perspective that might not be so true. And I think that play tackles that very well. Historically, grime had been ostracised to the point of being banned in clubs so to have it in a space like the Royal Court affirmed it is an art form.It definitely made me a better MC, knowing how to make my performances more engaging for an audience and being more confident to bring it into different spaces. It also introduced me to the world of theatre, not just as an actor.I was commissioned by the Royal Court to write my own play and a majority of the projects I work on now are theatre-based, whether that’s as a sound designer, or assisting with the music. I’ve written another play calledBlaze FM, which is about to go on its third tour. So Poet in da Corner changed the trajectory of my life. And it opened my eyes to a lot of other things I can do with the skill set that I picked up from being a grime MC.for colored girls who have considered suicide / when the rainbow is enuf, with music by Jammz, isat the Yard theatre, London, until 17 OctoberAs told to Lindesay IrvineExplore more on these topicsStageThe play that changed my lifeRoyal Court theatreTheatreGrimeHip-hopActingBlack British culturefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater: New Works review – a heavenly night | Dance | The Guardian
description: Skill, craft and beauty infuse pieces including Lar Lubovitch’s Many Angels and Judith Jamison’s A Case of You
Author: Sanjoy Roy
Headline: Skill, craft and beauty infuse pieces including Lar Lubovitch’s Many Angels and Judith Jamison’s A Case of You
Content: Intimations of the sublime … Isaiah Day, Yannick Lebrun, Jacquelin Harris and Jesse Obremski in Many Angels.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIntimations of the sublime … Isaiah Day, Yannick Lebrun, Jacquelin Harris and Jesse Obremski in Many Angels.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianDanceReviewAlvin Ailey American Dance Theater: New Works review – a heavenly nightSadler’s Wells, LondonSkill, craft and beauty infuse pieces including Lar Lubovitch’s Many Angels and Judith Jamison’s A Case of YouSanjoy RoyWed 16 Sep 2026 07.03 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 17.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheAlvin Aileycompany’s New Works programme might be seen in some circles as dated, and it’s true that it is neither cutting edge nor modishly contemporary. Yet it rests on more perennial qualities that underpin the company’s enduring appeal: skill, craft, beauty and humanity, and beneath them an artistic aim that can reach up towards the sublime, out towards the world, or in towards the heart.Medhi Walerski’s Blink of an Eye, new to the company but created in 2011 for Nederlands Dans Theater, tilts towards transcendence, being as spare, composed and unbound as the Bach music for solo violin it inhabits. The eight dancers repeatedly form a kind of visual chord – first a line, later a circle – which dissolves to let solos, duets and trios unspool. The counterpointed lines of movement remind you of the music: limbs stretch like strings, torsos curve and coil like the body of a violin, and the inflections of phrasing are somehow exact yet unfettered. It is a rare, spacious and beautiful composition.View image in fullscreenGlowing with feeling … Caroline T Dartey and Christopher Taylor in A Case of You.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianSo, too, is Many Angels by veteran choreographerLar Lubovitch, made in 2024 when he was 81. Set to the yearning, unsettled sonorities of Mahler’s Symphony No 5, it portrays a kind of heaven where five dancers, against a cloudscape backdrop, form and reform frieze-like tableaux, passing moments of statuesque beauty that melt back into movement. Unhurried, yet quickening towards its end – fleet leaps arcing airwards – this, too, has intimations of the sublime.Two other works speak of more interior worlds. Jamar Roberts’ Song of the Anchorite follows a monkish figure (Yannick Lebrun) on an inner quest. At first he seeks a path, his body reaching and reacting waywardly. A green cloth becomes a key that, once he wears it, lets him find his centre, and a direction. A chilled, jazzy arrangement of a Ravel adagio sets the sensitive mood.‘I was flabbergasted by the sight’: Alvin Ailey dancers on their legendary RevelationsRead moreDiana Krall’s husky cover of a Joni Mitchell song almost overpowers A Case of You, a revival of a 2004 duet by Judith Jamison. The piece is carried by the performances of Caroline T Dartey and Christopher Taylor as the lovers whose intricate entanglements – mirrorings, lifts, slides and switches – seem to glow with feeling.The company’s traditional finale is an old work, Ailey’s Revelations from 1960, which reaches upwards, outwards and inwards – and never seems to go out of fashion.AtSadler’s Wells, London, until 19 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsDanceAlvin AileySadler's WellsJS BachGustav MahlerTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Golden Boy review – Josh O’Connor swings between hope and despair in boxing melodrama | Theatre | The Guardian
description: The Challengers star makes a powerful return to the stage as a New York violinist driven by dire straits to risk everything in the ring
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: The Challengers star makes a powerful return to the stage as a New York violinist driven by dire straits to risk everything in the ring
Content: Hardening resolve … Josh O'Connor in Golden Boy at the Almeida theatre, London.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenHardening resolve … Josh O'Connor in Golden Boy at the Almeida theatre, London.Photograph: Marc BrennerTheatreReviewGolden Boy review – Josh O’Connor swings between hope and despair in boxing melodramaAlmeida theatre, LondonThe Challengers star makes a powerful return to the stage as a New York violinist driven by dire straits to risk everything in the ringChris WiegandWed 16 Sep 2026 05.53 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 17.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleClifford Odets proved himself a contender during the Great Depression but has grown unfamiliar on this side of the Atlantic. Here is a rare outing for his 1937 drama, bolstered by the stage return of Josh O’Connor after a decade on screen. He plays Joe Bonaparte, a New York violinist who, after years of careful endeavour, dismisses a precarious career in music to turn a quick buck as a boxer – risking his precious hands in the process.He is spurred on by a zealous manager, Tom, who even deploys his own lover, Lorna, to keep him satisfied. O’Connor transforms seamlessly as Bonaparte who hardens, bout by bout, with a resolve he deems fitting for the desperate 30s. His professional success and emotional spiral are observed by an anxious father, who irresistibly hymns music over money, and the ruthless gangster who has bought a stake in him.It is a play of opposing forces: cynicism and optimism, instinct and intellect, defence and offence. Staging Golden Boy is principally a question of strings and ropes: how to capture Joe’s gift for the violin and his force in the ring. Sam Yates’s revival adds a prologue of stillness, with O’Connor watching a young boy play the instrument. As the music swells, he draws back the shutters on Rosanna Vize’s half-office, half-home set to reveal musical director Roman Lytwyniw’s elevated string quartet before picking up the violin delicately himself.View image in fullscreenStrings and ropes … Golden Boy at the Almeida theatre.Photograph: Marc BrennerRouben Mamoulian’s 1939 film version added convivial impromptu music recitals to bring Joe’s family together; Yates shows music as a deeply individual, transportive passion preserved from youth, with the quartet often playing Isobel Waller-Bridge’s compositions as if in Joe’s mind (as well as adding suspenseful flourishes). It reinforces the purity of his musical pursuits but O’Connor carries enough boyish innocence – even at 36 rather than the character’s 21 years – to make the addition of a child actor extraneous, although Oscar Prout brings grace to that part on press night.As for the boxing, it almost entirely happens offstage in Odets’ script, which has the beats but not the usual arc of a sporting drama and whose fights are chiefly domestic and internal. A heavy punch bag is intermittently suspended, concealing a video camera that – in Jack Phelan’s video design – gives us a spinning almost newsreel-esque view of the action with each thump. It’s a handsome effect, even if these stylised sequences – and some increasingly expressionist movement direction from Imogen Knight – can jar with what otherwise plays out solidly as a period piece. A sensual episode drawing a violinist into the boxing arena alongside Joe is more awkwardly done.View image in fullscreenHustling … Daniel Mays and Hayley Squires in Golden Boy.Photograph: Marc BrennerBy 1937 Odets was a seasoned Hollywood screenwriter and the play has a hard-boiled poetry and deadpan humour, with the kind of polished lines that fly in a film noir or screwball comedy but are difficult to land on stage. Zubin Varla detonates some as the beady, macabre gunman Fuseli. Playing Tom, Daniel Mays brings a hustle akin to his Nathan Detroitin Guys and Dolls, sometimes literally licking his lips while relishing the dialogue. He captures Odets’ description of an explosive yet vulnerable man while, as Lorna, Hayley Squires perfects her character’s hardness acquired, as the playwright put it, “more from necessity than choice”. She mirrors O’Connor’s tussle between passion and pragmatism. When Joe and Lorna fall for each other, it’s cleverly done partly through music – as she sings Kris Kristofferson’s Help Me Make It Through the Night – but it’s a tall order to build a tragedy around their romance and the production never manages it despite a set of compelling performances and a new epilogue.With Golden Boy, Odets moved from agitprop to melodrama and the play doesn’t fully succeed as a greater social tragedy either, even with the pointed observations of Stanley Townsend as Joe’s father and Richard Fleeshman as Joe’s union man brother. It’s a play heavy with death – even a violin case is called a coffin for a baby – and we hear a bloodlust roar of the crowd for Joe’s fights. But you don’t sense those other lives, across a city and a nation brought to its knees.At theAlmeida theatre, London, until 31 October, and in cinemas worldwide through NT Livefrom 5 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreAlmeida theatreBoxingClassical musicJosh O'ConnorreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I thought I would lose my career’: Orville Peck on addiction and creating his best album yet | Music | The Guardian
description: Though the masked country singer has a No 1 album and duets with superstars under his belt, his demons and mental health caught up to him
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Though the masked country singer has a No 1 album and duets with superstars under his belt, his demons and mental health caught up to him
Content: ‘It’s hard for someone like me because it takes not just admitting to yourself that you have a problem - I also had to reckon with my phobia of conforming.’Photograph: Courtesy of Warner RecordsView image in fullscreen‘It’s hard for someone like me because it takes not just admitting to yourself that you have a problem - I also had to reckon with my phobia of conforming.’Photograph: Courtesy of Warner RecordsMusicInterview‘I thought I would lose my career’: Orville Peck on addiction and creating his best album yetJason LamphierThough the masked country singer has a No 1 album and duets with superstars under his belt, his demons and mental health caught up to himWed 16 Sep 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 09.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOrville Peck was in the middle of a soundcheck when he found out that his idolDolly Partonhad died. It was late August and the masked, pseudonymous country singer was due to perform an intimate set at London’s Rough Trade East in half an hour. The news hit him like a truck. With no chance to process it, he decided to grieve in real time, on stage, before a roomful of fans.“I’m a little bit of a mess right now,” Peck told the audience, perched on a stool with an acoustic guitar. “Dolly was my hero,” he continued, his voice cracking. “As a gay man coming into country music and feeling sort of alone, I think the thing that always felt comforting is, like, just knowing Dolly existed in country. It made me feel like I had a friend there.” He then launched into a rendition of Parton’s iconic hit I Will Always Love You.From Jolene to Islands in the Stream: Dolly Parton’s 10 best recordingsRead more“It felt like an impromptu memorial,” Peck recalls on the sofa of his New York City hotel room three days later, having touched down the night before to promote his new album, Mule. “I had to work through it with 400 strangers. We all got to sort of mourn together. I definitely think everyone there will remember that forever.”Mortality has been on Peck’s mind a lot lately. Mule is a brutally honest chronological account of what he describes as “the most important year of my life”, a period marred by profound heartache and self-destruction during which he split up with his partner of four years, overdosed and nearly died. Its opening track envisions his own memorial – what would have happened if he hadn’t come back from the brink.Prologue (Eulogy of a Man Turned Mule)is an a cappella hymn sung not by Peck, but byEmmylou Harris, Allison Russell and Noah Cyrus, a trio of country muses from different generations whom he compares to the witches of Macbeth or a Greek chorus. “Come walk through the fire, come stand with the few / Who break their own hearts to be saved,” they intone. “But the heart can’t be saved from the wretched and blue / Here lies a man turned mule.”While country has beendominatingthe top spots of the Billboard Hot 100 this summer, Peck emerged from Toronto during 2019’s “yee-haw moment”, as artists likeKacey MusgravesandLil Nas Xwere turning some pop listeners’ ears to the genre, injecting it with disco and hip-hop beats and a modern, queer sensibility. His face obscured, Peck kept his true identity a mystery, but he was open about his sexuality, and undeniably sexy, out of the gate (he recently posed forPlaygirl). That he had a baritone croon that evoked Roy Orbison and Elvis Presley made his arrival all the sweeter. Over the next few years, Peck would duet withElton John,Kylie Minogueand another one of his major inspirations,Willie Nelson, who dueted with him on acoverof the gay country classic Cowboys Are Frequently Secretly Fond of Each Other, score a No 1 album on the UK country charts and scoop up Glaad’s Vito Russo award for elevating LGBTQ acceptance and visibility. In 2025, he made his Broadway theater debut as the Emcee in the vibrant revival of Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club.The 38-year-old musician’s previous records – 2019’s Pony, 2022’s Bronco and 2024’sStampede– were laced with metaphor, at times unspooling like the dusty tales of an omniscient, enigmatic gunslinger. While the bluegrass-inflected Mule is more literal, like an unvarnished memoir, he couldn’t abandon the high drama completely. “I still wanted to add some kind of theatrical element,” says Peck. Today, he wears a white tank, chunky Wrangler x Cherry knit jacket, faded jeans, cowboy boots and a cream-colored Stetson. His penetrating blue eyes peek through a simple suede mask, but his trademark disguise, a black leather upper with a fringed veil, sits behind him on the bed, its golden tassels cascading over the edge of it. His right hand and wrist are wrapped in a thick bandage.“I thought, We’ll start with the most bleak thing possible,” Peck continues. “If I had died in 2023, if that was my legacy, what would these three witches be singing about?”Peck is not afraid to contemplate his own demise, nor is he afraid to be sitting now in the same hotel where he tried to take his own life. “It’s like when people ask me, ‘Oh, do you regret any of your tattoos?’” he says, chuckling at the slight absurdity of the analogy. “And I’m like, Well, I have some that are really shitty, but I would never get rid of them or wish I hadn’t gotten them, because I feel like it’s part of my story.”He would not deny, however, that his overdose may be the darkest chapter of that story. The night it happened, in June 2023, he was preparing to kick off his tour for Bronco with a sold-out concert at the Theater at Madison Square Garden. He went out to celebrate, got hammered, bumped into his ex at a club and spiraled. His management found him the next morning and gave him an ultimatum: he would cancel the tour and get help, or they’d cut ties with him. After rallying to play the packed show that evening, he announced that he was postponing his remaining tour dates to focus on his mental and physical health. Then he flew back home to Los Angeles and checked into a rehabilitation center.View image in fullscreenOrville Peck.Photograph: Aidan KlimenkoWhile he could acknowledge that he was leaning too much on booze, cocaine and prescription pills, he entered the facility begrudgingly. “I was like, I’ll be fine. I’ll play along with the parts that I don’t really think I need, and I’ll just kind of roll my eyes at the stuff I’m entitled to be annoyed about,” Peck says. “I believed that I had it under control.”He details his dismissive outlook and resentment – which he now realizes was just blinding denial – in the first half of Mule. He refers to rehab as “the slammer” and deems it a waste of time in the mockingAlready Gone. In the next track, the clever, ragtime-y Rehab Blues, the reality of his surroundings sets in: watchful eyes, sad sharing circles, stifling seclusion. “So catch me on the evenin’ news: Dumb fag dies from the rehab blues,” he sings sardonically, later confessing, “I hate it here, I don’t care and I wanna die.”‘People think fame is a magic wand’: Jarvis Cocker on old songs, young fans and his granny’s verdict on PulpRead morePeck left the center about a month later, knowing full well that he’d continue to use. He told himself that he wasn’t like the others he’d met there. He wasn’t an addict. “There’s a term for it: We call it terminal uniqueness,” Peck says. “Where a part of you is actually seeing that it’s totally you, but then a massive part of you is going, But I’m different. I can stop.”The root of his resistance, he thinks, was an inveterate aversion to following the herd. Growing up queer and closeted in South Africa and Canada, he had supportive parents – his father was a glam-rock sound engineer and his mother is an artist and a seamstress – but he says he felt alienated from his peers. “That’s where this otherness came from”, he says. “At first, it was put on me … and it was unbearable.” To escape, he turned to ballet and musical theater. He discovered punk and the renegade country of Nelson andJohnny Cash. He found himself drawn to outsize characters like Parton andJohn Waters. His reaction, eventually, was to wear his outsiderness as a badge of honor. That is where Orville Peck, the masked lone ranger, was born.View image in fullscreenOrville Peck performing at music festival Oya in Oslo, 2019.Photograph: Gonzales Photo/Alamy“It’s hard for someone like me because it takes not just admitting to yourself that you have a problem – I also had to reckon with my phobia of conforming,” he says of his struggle to get sober. “In a situation like that, I choose to remove myself in a way that’s like, I don’t need this shit. I’m not the same.” He’d been carving out his own path for most of his life to protect himself. With his successful stage persona, he explains, a defense mechanism to shield his vulnerability had become his superpower. But by 2023, it had become his downfall.After rehab, the partying and blackouts continued. He was still reeling from his breakup at the beginning of that year. Solo and shattered in his house in the Hollywood Hills, he tried filling the void with tricks and flings, including, as he reveals in the song Ring the Bell, an affair with a linebacker for the Las Vegas Raiders. (He remains coy when pressed for specifics, telling me only: “I snogged him and it was hot.”)His recklessness escalated until he woke up one morning that November, after a particularly brutal night, terrified. “I was like, You are gonna lose any chance of getting your relationship back. You’re gonna lose your career. You could lose your life,” Peck recalls. “It scared the absolute shit out of me.”He knew things had to change. “Finally, I was able to drop all of the traumas and the hang-ups and the defenses and the patterns, and all the things that we all walk around with all muddled up, and look at myself in the mirror and say, ‘Get your shit together.’” He pauses. “I have not taken a drink since.”‘I’m trying to figure out where I’m supposed to be’: singer Momo Boyd on making space for herselfRead moreSobriety brought clarity, and a desire to dig deeper. He came to understand that his battle with addiction stemmed, at least partly, from the pressures that accompanied newfound stardom, particularly the tug-of-war between Peck the performer and the man behind closed doors. Mule’s penultimate song, War of the Worlds, tackles this duality. “The dilemma I have on this album is not me versus this character that I’ve created, or whatever people think,” Peck says. “The dilemma is, I am an incredibly sensitive, hurt person who’s carrying around a lot of shit that I have to work on – and then my job requires me to also navigate thousands of people’s opinions of every single breath I take. That creates a dichotomous life, regardless of if Orville Peck is my birth name.”Peck’s attempt to reconcile his two identities – the famous Orville he’d become and the pre-fame dreamer of his youth – gives the album its title, and the name of its closing track. Mules are half horse, half donkey, and they cannot reproduce, he explains. Perhaps they, like him, feel trapped somewhere in between, unsure where they belong, always a little alone. He is quick to clarify that he’s not looking for pity. He just knows he has to figure most of this out on his own.View image in fullscreenOrville Peck’s album art for Mule.Photograph: Warner RecordsWhen he was drinking and on drugs, Peck says, he had “pretty much no ability” to reckon with his past or cope with the bumps in the road. His relationships, friendships and wellbeing suffered because of it. “I had this insane fear of abandonment,” he says. He couldn’t fathom being unlovable or unwanted, so he’d stay in terrible, even abusive situations. He doesn’t do that anymore. “I was just so, so hurt,” he says. “I still hurt sometimes,” he adds, “but now I think I have the courage to face it.”As he approaches three years of sobriety, Peck seems to be riding high. Despite its grim subject matter, Mule is often funny, knowing and buoyant. It’s his best album yet (or at least his catchiest). While he never got to meet or collaborate with Parton, a bucket-list item for him, he did achieve another one of his big career goals, making his Grand Ole Opry debut in July – the first song he performed that evening was, coincidentally, I Will Always Love You. He has become a hero in his own right, showing queer kids that Nashville’s once-conservative country scene may actually have a place for them. And he’s found love again.As our interview wraps, I ask Peck why his hand is bandaged. He laughs, clearly embarrassed, and tells me that he punched his new partner’s mostly finished birthday cake as a joke and fractured his finger on the table beneath it. I look incredulous, but he laughs again and waves it away. “It’s a long story,” he says. His smile suggests it is ultimately a happy one.Mule is out on 18 SeptemberIn the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsMusicPop and rockCountryCabaretMental healthCelebrityinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Alcina review – Handel’s opera of sex and sorcery comes alive in vivid staging  | Opera | The Guardian
description: This revival of Richard Jones and Antony McDonald’s 2022 staging has kept most of its excellent original cast Lisette Oropesa is imperious and gleaming as the enchantress Alcina
Author: Erica Jeal
Headline: This revival of Richard Jones and Antony McDonald’s 2022 staging has kept most of its excellent original cast Lisette Oropesa is imperious and gleaming as the enchantress Alcina
Content: Striking control and presence … Emily D'Angelo as Ruggiero in Alcina at the Royal Opera House, London.Photograph: Ian HippolyteView image in fullscreenStriking control and presence … Emily D'Angelo as Ruggiero in Alcina at the Royal Opera House, London.Photograph: Ian HippolyteOperaReviewAlcina review – Handel’s opera of sex and sorcery comes alive in vivid stagingRoyal Opera House, LondonThis revival of Richard Jones and Antony McDonald’s 2022 staging has kept most of its excellent original cast Lisette Oropesa is imperious and gleaming as the enchantress AlcinaErica JealWed 16 Sep 2026 10.14 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 10.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHandel, but make it fun. Perhaps that was Richard Jones’s brief for his production of Alcina,first seen here in 2022and revived by Sarah Fahie, its original movement director. And of all Handel’s operas perhaps it’s this one, with its desert-island storyline of sorcery and sex – what happens on the island stays on the island – that invites this treatment.Jones makes the “good guys” into members of a kind of puritan cult, so the tension between the moral world and the sensual, instinctive one is less of a gentle pull, more a tug of war. Alcina’s prisoners are transformed by a squirt of her eponymous perfume intobirds and animals– a parrot, a mandrill, a King Charles spaniel, all wearing prosthetic heads so beautifully made that for the past year or two they have been in display cases in the Royal Opera House foyer. The animals are kept busy fawning over Alcina or moving Antony McDonald’s sets around: there’s a huge bed, a greenhouse and an enchanted forest on wheeled platforms, found behind the doors of what might be a hotel corridor. It’s a wide stage, and there’s often at least one singer running across it. Amid all this, the opera’s moments of warmth, insight and introspection risk getting lost or at least overshadowed. It’s brittle, but it is entertaining.The lion, the witch and the warblers: behind the scenes of Handel’s Alcina at the RBO – in picturesRead moreIt’s also very well sung, even if the heft of the Royal Opera House orchestra in the pit, whipped through the score by conductor David Bates, means that the singers don’t always have much room for nuance. For a revival to keep hold of the original cast is usually a good sign, and so it proves again here. The apology made before curtain-up on behalf ofLisette Oropesa– suffering from a heavy cold but singing Alcina anyway – proved redundant; she’s imperious in the role, her soprano gleaming and athletic as she strides across the stage in her Louboutins.Emily D’Angelosings Ruggiero’s flourishes with striking control and presence,Mary Bevan’s softer-edged soprano catches Morgana’s fickle sensuousness andRu Charlesworth’s Oronte has a nice line in singing through gritted teeth. Of the newcomers,Edward Grintis authoritative as the cult elder Melisso and the boy soprano Thomas Mayes sings Oberto with winning assurance, but it’sBeth Taylor’s heartfelt, powerfully sung Bradamante who brings most of the moments where this Alcina is not only fun, but moving too.Until 3 OctoberExplore more on these topicsOperaClassical musicRoyal Opera HousereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mishka Rushdie Momen review – unforced elegance and plenty of fireworks | Classical music | The Guardian
description: A programme based around works by French baroque composers, played on a concert grand, made for an unusual but thoughtful and beautifully played recital
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: A programme based around works by French baroque composers, played on a concert grand, made for an unusual but thoughtful and beautifully played recital
Content: Pristine touch … Momen at Hamburg’s Elbphilharmonie in 2023.Photograph: Daniel DittusView image in fullscreenPristine touch … Momen at Hamburg’s Elbphilharmonie in 2023.Photograph: Daniel DittusClassical musicReviewMishka Rushdie Momen review – unforced elegance and plenty of fireworksWigmore Hall, LondonA programme based around works by French baroque composers, played on a concert grand, made for an unusual but thoughtful and beautifully played recitalClive PagetWed 16 Sep 2026 08.23 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 08.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBach, of course, is commonly heard on piano. The music of the French harpsichordists, on the other hand, isless regularly encountered on a concert grand. Ina wide-ranging programme, Mishka Rushdie Momen bucked the trend, bringing an unforced elegance to the music of François Couperin, Jean-Philippe Rameau and Élisabeth Jacquet de la Guerre.Natural poise and fluid technique ensure lines have room to breathe while remaining within the bounds of baroque keyboard practice. In Momen’s hands, the Allemande from Rameau’s E minor suite flowed like a limpid stream; likewise, the serene Musette en Rondeau, taken at a significantly slower pace than the plucked strings of a harpsichord might allow. Decorations were plentiful yet never self-conscious (the feathered denizens of the Rappel des Oiseaux trilled most politely). Elsewhere, her determined muscularity filled the hall with a richness of tone: in the earthy tread of the Provençal tambourin, for example, or the swagger of a rigaudon that could have passed muster as a sailor’s hornpipe.It was a canny move to include some Ravel, a composer who channelled baroque forms in many of his scores. The Prélude from Le Tombeau de Couperin conjured sunshine and showers, Momen’s laser-focused trills nodding to the music’s 18th-century antecedents. She likewise found poetry in the cooly cerebral Fugue before rounding off the set with a surprisingly weighty Pavane pour une Infante Défunte. The outlier here was John Bull’s Walsingham, a virtuoso late-Renaissance English work. The opening was appropriately spacious, but there were plenty of fireworks later with hands playing hopscotch on the keyboard and fingers a blur.It may lack the innovative spark of Rameau, but there is much to admire in Jacquet de la Guerre’s keyboard music. The pianist brought an improvisatory elasticity to the Prélude from her second suite in G minor and refinement to the subsequent Allemande and Courante. Couperin, however, overflows with imaginative touches. The Forlane from the fourth Concert Royal neatly echoed Ravel, who borrowed the tune wholesale for his famous Tombeau. To finish, Momen’s pristine touch and impeccable balance lent clarity to the metronomic figurations and mechanical hand crossings of Le Tic-Toc-Choc.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicWigmore HallreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Small but mighty! Remembering the GameCube, Nintendo’s purple bundle of joy | Games | The Guardian
description: The first console I ever bought, it was hyped as a threat to the PlayStation, then mocked as a flop. But now, as it marks its 25th anniversary, it’s looked back on with misty-eyed reverence
Author: Keza MacDonald
Headline: The first console I ever bought, it was hyped as a threat to the PlayStation, then mocked as a flop. But now, as it marks its 25th anniversary, it’s looked back on with misty-eyed reverence
Content: A hint of Fisher-Price about it … The new GameCube is displayed at a press preview in Tokyo in August 2001.Photograph: Yoshikazu Tsuno/EPAView image in fullscreenA hint of Fisher-Price about it … The new GameCube is displayed at a press preview in Tokyo in August 2001.Photograph: Yoshikazu Tsuno/EPAPushing Buttons newsletterGamesSmall but mighty! Remembering the GameCube, Nintendo’s purple bundle of joyThe first console I ever bought, it was hyped as a threat to the PlayStation, then mocked as a flop. But now, as it marks its 25th anniversary, it’s looked back on with misty-eyed reverenceKeza MacDonaldWed 16 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 11.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis week marks the 25th anniversary of theNintendoGameCube, the first console I ever bought with my own money. I vividly remember getting on the bus after school with a year’s worth of savings safely zipped into the pocket of my bag and going to a branch of Currys, where I dumped a bunch of notes, coins and vouchers on the counter to collect my pre-order. (It turned out that some of the vouchers from the previous Christmas had expired, but the guy at the checkout clearly felt so sorry for me that he redeemed them anyway. If you’re out there, Currys guy: thank you for taking pity on a desperate 13-year-old.)If it hadn’t been for the ill-fated Wii U console, whose failure to take off in 2012 resulted in the first unprofitable periods in Nintendo’s game-making history, the GameCube would be remembered as the company’s biggest flop aside from the infamous Virtual Boy, from 1995. Released in Japan this week in 2001 (and in May 2002 in Europe), this surprisingly powerful purple cube sold less than the Xbox and the PlayStation 2. With its squat, colourful form and unusual controller, arranged around a big traffic-light-green A button and small analogue sticks designed for small hands, it had a hint of Fisher-Price about it.I didn’t knowanyoneelse who had one. But despite being mocked at the time, the GameCube is now revered, fondly remembered as an uncomplicated box of fun at a time when video games were in their performatively adult stage. The charts in the early 00s were dominated by Grand Theft Auto and Gran Turismo, and yet the GameCube launched with a cartoon haunted-house caper (Luigi’s Mansion) and a game where you rolled monkeys around inside transparent spheres (Sega’s Super Monkey Ball). The idea of a Nintendo console launching with a Sega game was unconscionable to any child of the 90s, but the Cube ended up carrying the torch for that nostalgic flavour of Japanese development into the early 00s, with Sega out of the market and western-made games becoming dominant.View image in fullscreenWhimsical … Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker.Photograph: NintendoLuigi’s Mansion was a strange choice of launch game – really, no Mario? – but it was delightful. The vivacious animation of the ghosts, the diorama-like detail of the haunted mansion and Luigi’s adorable cowardly voice and body language showed how extra power could infuse games with extra personality. Super Smash Bros Melee, with its cast of newly higher-definition Nintendo legends, was inordinately exciting. The GameCube was home to two excellent Zelda games, thewhimsical Wind Wakerand emo-tinged Twilight Princess. Metroid Prime remainsan unimprovable atmospheric classic. It had plenty of more experimental games, too: Eternal Darkness kept track of your character’s sanity and started to show you weird visions or glitch out on you if you let your character spiral into madness. The lavishly animated brawler Viewtiful Joe looked like nothing I’d ever seen. And then there was that Donkey Kong game that you played with a controller shaped like bongo drums.Because I was a teenager in the 00s, I was deeply sensitive to the perception of video games as childish. Shortly after buying a GameCube I started writing game reviews online for money, and got my hands on an Xbox and a PlayStation 2. I became much more interested in the new kinds of games I was playing on those systems: Ico and Metal Gear Solid on PlayStation, Halo and Knights of the Old Republic on Xbox. Super Mario Sunshine and The Legend of Zelda felt like relics of childhood, a mindset that Iwouldn’t get out offor some years. The GameCube felt like the end of something, and it was – just not in the way that anybody expected.Behind the scenes, its designers – and Nintendo’s late president, Satoru Iwata – had come to realise that competing on graphics and tech specs was futile and uninteresting. “Games have come to a dead end,” Iwata told the Japanese outlet Mainichi in 2004. “Creating complicated games with advanced graphics used to be the golden principle that led to success, but it is no longer working … even if the developers work a hundred times harder, they can forget about selling a hundred times more units, since it’s difficult for them to even reach the status quo. It’s obvious that there’s no future to gaming if we continue to run on this principle that wastes time and energy.” Nintendo’s next consoles would be the touchscreen DS and motion-controlled Wii – consoles that would not only separate Nintendo from its competitors but change the market for video games and redefine who games were for.Nintendo has walked a different path ever since: the GameCube was arguably the last console that it designed with “core gamers” foremost in mind (although I think the Switch 2 has veered back in this direction). When I bought it all those years ago, I expected it to be the beginning of a new era for Nintendo, but it turned out to be the end of an old one.What to playView image in fullscreenLike a living sci-fi anime series from the 1990s … Orbitals.Photograph: Kepler InteractivePlaying games with your children can be somewhat fraught. There can be wild variation in tastes and skill levels: plus, kids are often monomaniacs, and there is only so much Minecraft that an adult can play without starting to get a headache. But I am having an amazing time playing games with my seven-year-old, who has become impressively competent all of a sudden.We are working our way throughOrbitals, a cooperative game that looks like a living sci-fi anime series from the 90s. As two space-faring teenagers, we are cutting about in a little ship, docking to salvage tech from ruined ships and solving quite complicated puzzles with tools that shoot lasers, tethers and jets of water.It is fiddly and demanding, and I think if I were playing this with an adult I might want to cry with frustration, but instead I’m amazed and impressed every time my son and I conquer a tricky puzzle involving floating platforms or mirror-reflected lasers. The animation is fantastic, too, bursting with nostalgic personality.Available on:Switch 2Estimated playtime:six hoursWhat to readView image in fullscreenDIY … Kallax Storageborn, Ikea’s mod for The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim.Photograph: IKEAIkea has released a modfor the 15-year-old fantasy RPGThe Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, in which you are followed around by a talking Kallax shelving unit voiced by Matt Berry. Truly, this game will never die.The case brought by the IWGB game workers’ union againstRockstar Gamerskicked off at Glasgow’s tribunals court this week. More than 30 former Rockstar employees arefighting to be reinstatedafter being dismissed last year. In opening arguments, the company has outlined its case that the workers’ participation in a union-organising Discord represented a major threat of leaks and reputational damage. The tribunal runs until 14 October.Hideo Kojima’s forthcoming gamePhysinthas beendropped by Sony, reportedly over budget concerns. Unexpectedly, Xbox swooped in to save the game and pick up the bill, resulting in some rare positive press for Microsoft’s console division in a year of cancellations, layoffs and studio shutdowns.Blizzardhas announced new Diablo and Starcraft games, alongside a(nother) revamp of classic World of Warcraft calledWorld of Warcraft: Forever.For its 20th anniversary in 2021, Video Games Chronicle publisheddeep-dive into the GameCube, speaking to several marketers and developers who were involved with its launch and life. Five years on, it’s stillwell worth a read.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhat to click‘We were bored of traditional fantasy cliches’: inside Playground Games’ 10-year effort to revive FableRaiding the past: Lara Croft relives her first adventure in Legacy of AtlantisMarvel’s Wolverine – a gloriously conflicted lead is let down by crude, boring battling | ★★★☆☆Question BlockView image in fullscreenA current-day folk fable … the Scotland-set adventure game A Highland Song.Photograph: inkleThis week’s question comes from readerDuncan:“Off the recent spotlight on Silent Hill: Townfall, are there more gamesthat take place in current-day Scotland? Dear Esther comes to mind. I remember a Kickstarter for a horror game set among tower blocks ofNeilston Road, Paisley. Then Beeswing by Jack King-Spooner goes in the opposite direction.”Unfortunately, you have unlocked an unskippable cutscene by asking me about one of my obsessions, Duncan.A Highland Songis set in the timeless Scottish Highlands but has the feel of a folk fable;Still Wakes the Deepis a 1970s period piece set on a Scottish oil rig; the forthcoming Gaelic-language horror gameGrease Trap ’99is set in a chippy on the coast. All of those are sort ofmodern.Forza Horizon 4lets you drive around a gorgeous modern Scotland, including a very cute mini Edinburgh.But, yes, most games that feature Scotland go with a historical-fantasy vibe based on all of our castles and romantic scenery. I’m still waiting on someone to make the equivalent of Grand Theft Auto: Glasgow, or a coming-of-age narrative game set in Edinburgh.If you have a question for Question Block – or anything else to say about the newsletter – hit reply or email us atpushingbuttons@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsGamesPushing Buttons newsletterGames consolesRetro gamesNintendofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The other side of Croatia: ‘a landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany’ | Croatia holidays | The Guardian
description: Weekenders from Zagreb head to the rolling green Samobor Hills for nature, vineyards, delicious local food and Habsburg-era architecture
Author: Mary Novakovich
Headline: Weekenders from Zagreb head to the rolling green Samobor Hills for nature, vineyards, delicious local food and Habsburg-era architecture
Content: Vineyards in Croatia’s Plešivica wine region.Photograph: Ilija Ascic/AlamyView image in fullscreenVineyards in Croatia’s Plešivica wine region.Photograph: Ilija Ascic/AlamyCroatia holidaysThe other side of Croatia: ‘a landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany’Weekenders from Zagreb head to the rolling green Samobor Hills for nature, vineyards, delicious local food and Habsburg-era architectureMary NovakovichWed 16 Sep 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘You’re going to Samobor? You must trykremšnita,” my Dubrovnik friends told me before I set off on my trip north. “But I’ve already hadkremšnitain Zagreb,” I told them. They do it better inSamobor, they insisted. I wasn’t about to get embroiled in a battle of the cream cakes in a region where Croatians, Slovenes and Austrians all like to celebrate their own versions of this decadently thick, fat custard slice topped with puff pastry and icing sugar. But I was more than willing – happy, even – to follow everyone’s suggestions to trykremšnitain Hotel Livadić’sKavana Livadić, in Samobor’s main King Tomislav Square, a mere half-hour drive west of Zagreb.View image in fullscreenThe excellentkremšnitaat Kavana Livadić, Samobor.Photograph: Mary NovakvoichIt lived up to the hype – delicately rich, creamy and with a light touch. After spending a few weeks in sun-bleached Venetian Dalmatia, amid the scrubby, limestone Dinaric Alps, I had swapped empires and was firmly in Habsburg Croatia. Here, inZagreb County’sprettiest town, handsome baroque houses in pastel shades of buttery yellow, apricot and pistachio, festooned with stucco, line narrow King Tomislav Square, whose umbrella-shaded cafe terraces were filled with Croatians getting their morning fix of coffee and chatter.The lush green Samobor Hills overlook the medieval town, through which the Gradna – part river, part stream – flows and ripples under wooden bridges adorned with flowers. One of these bridges led to the onion-domed church of Saint Anastasia; another, with a fairytale wooden roof, took me to one of Samobor’s many green spaces, dotted with free red deckchairs, which had the slogan “Volim Samobor” (“I love Samobor”) written in white. In front of them, the stately former home (now thetown’s museum) of one of Croatia’s foremost 19th-century composers, Ferdo Livadić, added to the air of gentle refinement, of culture worn lightly. It was easy to visualise Livadić entertaining his artistic friends, including Franz Liszt, in this august setting.double quotation markHandsome baroque houses in pastel shades of buttery yellow, apricot and pistachio line narrow King Tomislav Square in SamoborAs well as the graceful architectural legacy of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy, this rolling green landscape is crisscrossed with forested trails, particularly within theŽumberak nature park, about 16 miles (26km) west of Samobor, where weekenders from Zagreb come to hike and bike in woods of hornbeam, oak and beech with bubbling waterfalls. Not having time for a full-on hike, I could still drive to Potočna dolina Slapnica, near the Vranjak waterfalls, and scramble up the path beside a series of cascades each more impressive than the last.Closer to Samobor, the hilltop ruins of Okić castle rose to nearly 500m above sea level, one of the best-preserved romanesque fortifications in the country. The Mongols couldn’t defeat it, nor could the Ottoman Turks. Sadly, it defeated me when I attempted to hike to the top. Not realising there was a newer, easier path, I ended up on one that was little else but vertical tree roots. With a newly healed ankle and no phone signal, I thought it unwise to continue. But it’s on my list for next time.View image in fullscreenThe mist-shrouded ruins of Okic castle.Photograph: Ivan Smuk/AlamyA much easier path to take was along the Plešivica wine road, where more than three dozen wineries were scattered on a heart-shaped route between the village of Plešivica (10 miles south-west of Samobor) and the town of Jastrebarsko. In a harmonious landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany, vineyards clung to steep slopes between forested hills, many producing the sparkling wine Plešivica is renowned for. I met Martina and Krešimir Ivančić, whose ancestors were given a noble title and coat of arms by the Austrian empress Maria Theresa in 1759. The griffin on the family crest inspired the name of theGriffin Winery, which came about when a Hungarian count gave them a licence to plant a vineyard in 1773.View image in fullscreenRudarska grebalica: a salty, stuffed pastry from Nikl in Rude.Photograph: Pixsell/AlamyMartina took me to the covered patio of a wooden hut above the vineyards, a suitably bucolic place to taste an elegant and lightly fruity sparkling rose made from red portugieser grapes. We carried on in the extremely stylish tasting room, where plates of cured meats and cheeses accompanied glasses of full-bodied chardonnay.I was also offeredcopanjek, a thin savoury pastry pie of cheese and greens. “They’re very portable, so workers would take them to the vineyard,” Martina told me. This looked like the winemaker’s version ofrudarska greblica, which I had tasted that morning in the village of Rude, about a 10-minute drive west of Samobor, and liked so much I had to have two. Filled with cheese and walnuts, carrots or greens, these used to be made by the wives of Rude’s long-gone miners. They’re such an integral part of the region that they have their own festival every July and have been given EU protected status. AtPekarnica Nikl, in Rude, I met Jelena and Andrejas Nikl, the only authorised bakers of this much adored speciality. Jelena acknowledged the responsibility of keeping up this tradition ofrudarska greblica, especially with the paperwork that came with legal protection – but, she said, it was worth it.View image in fullscreenThe sunny terrace at Korak winery and restaurant.Photograph: Mary NovakovichAll around the Samobor Hills, people were holding fast to their heritage and infusing it with life. The Korak family is one of the most illustrious, with its Michelin-starredKorak winery and restaurantin Plešivica. Not a whiff of Michelin stuffiness or pretentiousness here, just the fourth and fifth generations of a family producing superb wine and making beautiful food in a serene setting facing the vineyards. Brother Bernard is chef (and has worked with Massimo Bottura of Italy’s Osteria Francescana and Ana Roš of Slovenia’s Hiša Franko); sister Vera is front of house; and parents Velimir and Mirjana tend the vines – even the siblings’ grandparents are still making cheese andpršut(prosciutto) for the restaurant.Bernard grows as much as he can – the rest comes from local producers, including the farmer whose pigs are fed on scraps from Bernard’s kitchen. And if it’s not in season, it’s not on the plate. My June visit rewarded me with a truffle tagliatelle, and clams and green beans in a caviar sauce, among other delicious dishes in a five-course tasting menu at €118 (a very reasonable price, and in keeping with the region’s overall lower prices).I could only imagine what delights autumn will bring, especially during the annualWine Daysfestival in Jastrebarsko from 25-27 September. The Samobor Hills will be teeming with autumn truffles and mushrooms, and welcoming the change in season the best way they know – on the plate.Explore more on these topicsCroatia holidaysEurope holidaysFood and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to turn excess olive brine into a lipsmacking salad dressing – recipe  | Food | The Guardian
description: The liquid from a jar of olives is naturally chock-full of savoury flavour, so why should it go to waste? It’s perfect for sprucing up a salad
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: The liquid from a jar of olives is naturally chock-full of savoury flavour, so why should it go to waste? It’s perfect for sprucing up a salad
Content: Tom Hunt's olive brine vinaigrette.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTom Hunt's olive brine vinaigrette.Photograph: Tom Hunt/The GuardianWaste notFoodHow to turn excess olive brine into a lipsmacking salad dressing – recipeThe liquid from a jar of olives is naturally chock-full of savoury flavour, so why should it go to waste? It’s perfect for sprucing up a saladTom HuntWed 16 Sep 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Wed 16 Sep 2026 10.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOlive brine is a simple byproduct that has so much flavour, and it elevates a classic salade nicoise dressing while keeping things colourful, elegant and relatively simple.Salade nicoise with olive-brine vinaigretteThough this one-bowl wonder began life as a simple tomato and anchovy salad with olive oil, it has become more elaborate over time, and the addition of cooked green beans, eggs and even tuna all make sense to me. What’s worth preserving, though, is its Mediterranean simplicity, and the olive-brine dressing adds a lot of flavour without needing loads of extra ingredients.In the spirit of simplicity, this vinaigrette keeps to just three wonderfully flavourful ingredients: olive brine for salt and depth of flavour, red-wine vinegar for acidity and olive oil for substance and piquancy. It won’t hold a stable emulsion in the way a mustard dressing does, so give it another good shake just before it goes on the salad. I buy whole olives with the pits in and pit them myself. They, and the brine, taste so much better that way.Serves4For the vinaigrette2 tbsp brine from a jar of olives1 tbsp red-wine vinegar6 tbsp extra-virgin olive oilBlack pepper, to tasteFor the salad6eggs200g green beans, topped200g cocktail tomatoes, or cherry tomatoes1 red pepper, stalk, seeds and pith removed, flesh sliced into rings½ medium cucumber, skin on and seeds in, cut into large chunks4 spring onions, cut into 1cm lengths (white and green parts)1 small jarblack olivesAnchovy fillets, (optional) to taste; I used a whole standard 50g tin1 small handful basil leaves, to finishPut the olive brine, vinegar and extra-virgin olive oil in a jar, and add a grind of black pepper to taste. Screw on the lid and shake until the mixture emulsifies. It won’t stay emulsified for long, so shake again just before you’re ready to eat. The dressing will now keep in the fridge for up to a week.Put the eggs in a pan of cold water and bring to a boil. Once boiling, add the green beans, bring back to a boil and cook for four minutes. Drain, then put the eggs and beans in a bowl of iced or cold water. Once cooled, drain again and put the beans to one side (they can be left whole or cut into pieces). Peel and halve the eggs.Cut the tomatoes in half, then arrange all the vegetables on a platter. Scatter over the stoned olives and drained anchovy fillets to taste, then finish with the halved eggs, some torn basil leaves and the freshly shaken dressing. Eat straight away.Explore more on these topicsFoodWaste notFood wasteSauces and graviesSaladFrench food and drinkMain courseStarterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Squid ink tomato pasta and honey and fig semifreddo: Chris Leach’s Italian recipes for the end of summer | Food | The Guardian
description: Cooking at this time of year is all about low-effort, maximum-impact options. This savoury dish comes together quickly but looks striking, while the dessert showcases figs at their most flavoursome
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cooking at this time of year is all about low-effort, maximum-impact options. This savoury dish comes together quickly but looks striking, while the dessert showcases figs at their most flavoursome
Content: Chris Leach’s squid ink spaghetti with anchovies, cherry tomato and pangrattato.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.View image in fullscreenChris Leach’s squid ink spaghetti with anchovies, cherry tomato and pangrattato.Photograph: Issy Croker/The Guardian. Food and prop styling: Kitty Coles. Food styling assistant: Grace Jenkins.FoodSquid ink tomato pasta and honey and fig semifreddo: Chris Leach’s Italian recipes for the end of summerCooking at this time of year is all about low-effort, maximum-impact options. This savoury dish comes together quickly but looks striking, while the dessert showcases figs at their most flavoursomeChris LeachWed 16 Sep 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe secret to late-summer/early autumn cooking is to keep things relatively low-effort, not least to assuage those back-to-work/school blues. And that rule applies across the board, whether you’re making a midweek meal, entertaining or serving up a long, slow Sunday lunch. The sauce for this pasta dish, for example, comes together while the pasta is cooking, while the semifreddo pudding makes the most of ripe figs when they are at their absolute best.Squid ink spaghetti with anchovies, cherry tomatoes and pangrattatoThe contrast between the black pasta, the red tomatoes and the golden crumbs is really something else, as are the flavours.Prep15 minCook30 minServes4For the pangrattato150g day-old sourdough or country bread3 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil2 garlic cloves, peeled and finely sliced3 sprigs thyme, leaves pickedFine sea salt and black pepperFor the pastaSea salt400g squid ink spaghetti4 tbsp extra-virgin olive oil, plus extra to finish3 garlic cloves, peeled and thinly sliced300g ripe cherry tomatoes6 anchovy fillets in oil75ml dry white wineFinely grated zest and juice of ½ unwaxed lemon1 small handful picked flat-leaf parsley, finely choppedBlack pepperFirst make the pangrattato. Tear the stale bread into rough pieces, then pulse in a food processor to make coarse, uneven breadcrumbs. Put the oil in a large frying pan on a medium heat, add the sliced garlic and cook gently, stirring, for a minute or two, until fragrant but not coloured. Add the thyme leaves, cook for a further 30 seconds, then stir in the breadcrumbs and cook, stirring regularly, for eight to 10 minutes, until evenly golden and crisp all over. Season with a pinch of sea salt and a little black pepper, then transfer to a plate to cool completely.Bring a large pan of well-salted water to a boil, then cook the squid ink spaghetti according to the packet instructions, until al dente.While the pasta is cooking, put the oil in a large frying pan on a medium heat, then add the sliced garlic and cook gently, stirring, for two minutes, until fragrant and just beginning to colour. Add the whole cherry tomatoes and cook, stirring, for three to four minutes, until they begin to soften and burst, then stir in the anchovy fillets and press them into the pan with the back of a spoon so they dissolve into the oil. Pour in the white wine, turn up the heat and leave to bubble and reduce by about half.Use tongs or a spider sieve to lift the cooked pasta directly into the tomato pan (alternatively, drain the pasta, saving some of its water), then add a splash of the cooking water, and toss and stir until the sauce lightly coats the pasta. Finish with the lemon zest, a squeeze of lemon juice and the chopped parsley, then taste and adjust the seasoning, adding black pepper and more lemon as needed.Divide the pasta between bowls and finish each serving generously with about 50g of the pangrattato (store any excess in an air-tight container and savefor another use: it’s especially good on salads and in other pasta dishes) and a final drizzle of extra-virgin olive oil.Honey, thyme and fig semifreddoView image in fullscreenChris Leach’s honey, thyme and fig semifreddo.Take this out of the freezer about 10 minutes before slicing and serving. Serve with warm honey, fresh figs and toasted seeds for a simple but very special finish.Prep20 minCook45 min, plus coolingFreeze8 hr+Serves6For the thyme cream300ml double cream3 sprigs fresh thymeFinely grated zest of ½ unwaxed lemonFor the honey sabayon3 large egg yolks75g chestnut honey, or good-quality floral honey1 pinch fine sea salt20g brown butter– that is, melted and browned, then left to cool (optional, but recommended)For the fig ripple200g fig jam1 tbsp aged balsamic vinegarTo finish4 fresh figs, quartered2 tbsp warm honey1 pinch toasted poppy seeds1 pinchfennel seeds, toasted and lightly crushedA few picked thyme leaves1 pinch flaky sea saltFirst, infuse the cream. Put the cream and thyme in a small pan and heat until just below boiling. Take off the heat, stir in the lemon zest and leave to infuse and cool for 20-30 minutes. Once cool, strain, then chill thoroughly before whipping to soft peaks.For the honey sabayon, put the egg yolks, honey and salt in a heatproof bowl set over a pan of barely simmering water, making sure the base of the bowl doesn’t touch the water. Whisk for six to eight minutes, until the mixture is pale, thick and has tripled in volume. Take off the heat, keep whisking for two to three minutes more, until the mix is just warm, then fold in the cooled brown butter, if using.Now for the fig ripple. Warm the fig jam, balsamic vinegar and a tablespoon of water until the mix is smooth enough to ripple through the semifreddo, then take off the heat and leave to cool completely.Fold a third of the thyme-infused whipped cream into the sabayon to loosen it, then, taking care not to knock out the air, gently fold in the remaining cream until well incorporated.Now to assemble the semifreddo. Line a small loaf tin with baking paper, leaving plenty of overhang on all sides. Spoon in a third of the semifreddo mixture, drizzle over some of the fig ripple, then use a knife gently to swirl into the mix and make a marbled effect. Repeat twice more with the remaining semifreddo mix and fig ripple, finish with a final swirl of the knife, then cover with the overhanging paperand freeze for at least eight hours, and ideally overnight.Take the semifreddo tin out of the freezer 10-15 minutes before you want to serve it. Once it’s softened a little, lift it out of the tin, using the paper overhang to help you, then place on a board and cut into six slices. Arrange the fresh fig halves around it, top with the warm honey, and finish with a sprinkling of toasted poppy seeds, toasted crushed fennel seeds, a few thyme leaves and a small pinch of flaky sea salt.Chris Leach is chef and co-founder ofManteca, London EC2Explore more on these topicsFoodItalian food and drinkPastaMain courseStarterDessertTomatoesrecipesShareReuse this content

title: The best ice-cream makers in the UK for gelato, soft serve and sorbets – tested | Ice-cream and sorbet | The Guardian
description: Our writer spent the hottest weeks of the year churning through the top ice-cream makers, from compressor models to the cult favourite Ninja Creami. Here’s the scoop
Author: Danielle Amato
Headline: Our writer spent the hottest weeks of the year churning through the top ice-cream makers, from compressor models to the cult favourite Ninja Creami. Here’s the scoop
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterIce-cream and sorbetReviewThe best ice-cream makers in the UK for gelato, soft serve and sorbets – testedOur writer spent the hottest weeks of the year churning through the top ice-cream makers, from compressor models to the cult favourite Ninja Creami. Here’s the scoopKitchen gadgets top chefs can’t live withoutNinja Creami Scoop and Swirl ice-cream maker reviewDanielle AmatoWed 16 Sep 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIlove a scoop or two of the good stuff, even more so when the mercury hits 30C and ice-cream starts feeling less like an indulgence and more like an essential survival tool. This is why owning an ice-cream maker has always made sense to me. I’ve been using the original Ninja Creami for years now, but before that I was spending a small fortune on gelato, fruity sorbets, frozen yoghurt and other such desserts from the frozen aisle.Some might argue that the best ice-cream makers are a luxury, but if you’re a true dessert devotee, I believe they can earn their keep in no time. A tub of Häagen-Dazs will set you back almost £6 nowadays, which is an expensive habit if you’re getting through a pot a week during the hottest months of the year.With your own ice-cream machine, you get an endless supply whenever you fancy it, and you can get creative with flavours, tweaking as you go. It’s also ideal if you have allergies or follow a dairy-free diet, as good allergy-friendly ice-cream can be harder to find. Better still, making your own means you can skip the emulsifiers, artificial flavours, sweeteners and stabilisers found in many shop-bought tubs, so it’s a great option if you’re trying to move away from ultra-processed foods.But with so many options available, where do you start?
